When it came time to get our air ducts cleaned, I had no idea where to begin. I found Honest Air Duct Cleaning on Yelp and, after reading a few strong reviews, decided to give them a try. From the start, the experience inspired confidence. Brandon answered my email promptly, laid out their pricing without any upsell or fine print, and made scheduling easy. Pricing felt straightforward and reasonable, and it was easy to commit.

We initially booked a Friday afternoon window from 3 to 5. Around 2:00, Brandon emailed to say they were running late due to complications with a prior job and gave me the choice to keep the slot or reschedule. That kind of proactive communication is rare and was hugely appreciated. Instead of waiting around, we moved the appointment to the following week and I got my afternoon back. It was a small gesture that signaled respect for my time and set the tone for the rest of the service.

When the day arrived, the technician showed up on time and worked with care. He protected floors and walls, was mindful with his ladder around furniture, and contained the mess as he went. Duct cleaning is inherently dusty, but he cleaned thoroughly afterward; even as a self-described clean freak, I couldn’t find anything to nitpick once he finished. The whole visit took about two hours, and the difference was noticeable. The service felt professional from start to finish.

One small note: they spray a sanitizer into the vents that leaves a strong, clean, dentist-office scent for a little while. They warn you in advance; in our case, the smell lingered close to an hour. Cracking a few windows cleared it quickly. Not a dealbreaker at all—just something to know.

Pizza Cat learned three very important lessons this weekend: never, ever bet against the LA Kings—evah; keep Neapolitan pizza simple; and burrrrrata is the stuff of dreams. On a sun-splashed day with the Kings in the Finals, self-doubt finally gave way to hunger, and Pizza Cat padded over to 800 Degrees, the cool, trendy spot in front of the Monte Carlo.

Past encounters with Neapolitan had ended in full grump-mode—yucky dough, floppy toppings, disappointment. This time, she tried KISS: Keep It Simple, Stupid. Neapolitan is a different creature than its American cousin, and it punishes overloading. So she ordered a basic marinara, skipped the fresh oregano, and added bufala mozzarella for an extra six bucks. Very minimalist, about thirteen dollars total, and surprisingly satisfying. Don’t expect a New York slice; think warm naan-like dough topped with crushed tomatoes and excellent slabs of milky cheese. It didn’t convert her into a zealot, but she didn’t hate it—and now she can tell her food-epicurean friends she can eat Neapolitan without hissing.

The real star, though, was the burrata. Meowzers. Halfway between mozzarella and fresh cream, burrata is silky, lush, and downright purr-inducing. At 800 Degrees it arrives with prosciutto, melon balls, and peppery arugula, a perfect dance of creamy, salty, meaty, sweet, and bitter. It was her favorite bite of 2014 (for now), the sort of plate that makes you wish Giuseppe were nearby to offer a congratulatory kiss.

A meatball detour brought mixed results: reheated in the namesake 800-degree oven, the sphere’s temperature ranged from cool to hot, though the flavor was solid. No bueno on the uneven warmth, but not a dealbreaker.

All told, 800 Degrees delivers a health-leaning Italian meal that feels fresh and modern. About thirty dollars buys a hearty spread, especially if you focus on the simple pies and that transcendent burrata. For a cat chasing good bites and good vibes, this spot purrs. If you’re an American-pizza diehard, manage expectations: Neapolitan is about tenderness, char, and restraint. Go for the texture, the bright tomatoes, the milkiness of bufala, and skip the pile-on. Pair the pie with that dreamy burrata and a meatball, and you’ll leave not stuffed, but satisfied, sunlit, and purring.

Garth tried to be too much a comedian & not as much a multi-platinum singer. Even the most experienced comics become boring after an hour or so...

I came for the songs, but the show leaned hard into comedy and storytelling, and momentum sagged. The history of his influences was engaging at first, then dragged, with too few Garth hits to balance it. Without a full band, the energy dipped, and the guitar mix was often too loud, overshadowing his vocals. Frequent “people” references and constant pacing were distracting. Bright spot: he still has that voice. If he returns to entertainer-of-the-year form with a music-heavy set, I’ll gladly pay; if it’s a pivot to comedy/pub-style gigs, I’ll stick with local acts.

I ordered online and relied on the delivery time in the confirmation email. When the order was 10 minutes late, I called and was told it would be just a few more minutes. Twenty minutes later, I called again and heard “five more minutes.” With only a 30‑minute lunch break, being 30 minutes late is unacceptable. They offered $5 off, which didn’t fix the fact that my lunch was over. I suggested they proactively call customers when running late; instead, the representative hung up on me. Poor communication and customer service. I won’t be ordering from them again.

Made the mistake of eating here on 10/24. From the moment we arrived, the hostess and maître d’ set an off-putting tone with haughty, unwelcoming attitudes, as if seating us were a favor. The wine list is expansive but outrageously overpriced; when we asked the self-described “wine guy” about a solid 90-point WS bottle, his smug “I could actually drink that” quip sealed the snobby vibe. The food was completely uninspired—pedestrian dishes lacking creativity or finesse. Service was merely fair, with awkward pacing and long gaps between courses that sapped any momentum. The night before, we dined at T. Cook’s, and it outclassed this place in every category. Lon’s seems to coast on its lovely patio setting; the kitchen delivers average fare at best. If you do go, call well in advance to secure a decent patio table. Otherwise, choose T. Cook’s and save yourself the disappointment.

Chick-fil-A has become our default “let’s just grab something” spot, the place my girlfriend suggests every time and I half-groan about—only to remember, once we’re there, why it keeps winning. During the Phoenix Film Festival we popped in on Sunday, and everything hit the mark again: quick, hot, and genuinely tasty.

The food is classic comfort done right. I might commit heresy with the waffle fries, but mayo is my dip of choice; ketchup feels like it bulldozes the potato flavor. They stock mayo for the sandwiches anyway, so why not put it to work? The nuggets are reliably awesome—juicy, well-seasoned, and crisp without greasiness—and a cup of sweet tea rounds the whole tray out in nostalgic fashion.

What keeps surprising me, though, is the hospitality. The team greets you with a warmth you just don’t hear in fast food, and they keep it up through the whole visit. Orders come out fast, tables get wiped the moment someone leaves, and the “my pleasure” energy never feels forced.

One moment stuck with me: a female employee walked a customer’s two bags to his car while he ambled alongside, and the dining room collectively side-eyed him. The help was sincere, but there’s a line between accepting courtesy and leaning on it. That said, the staff’s eagerness to serve is part of what sets this location apart.

So yes, I might get tired of choosing it, but I rarely get tired of eating it. For a dependable, friendly, no-fuss meal, this Chick-fil-A keeps delivering—again and again. Just maybe let someone else carry their own bags.

I've been meaning to update my review after I got a second opinion somewhere else, so here it is.

I scheduled a routine cleaning but never received it. During the pocket measurements, the probing felt unusually sharp, and my gums bled. The hygienist told me I needed scaling and root planing, quoted a price near $400, and suggested I’d likely had gum issues for years that no one had caught. Having seen the same dentist since childhood, that claim didn’t sit right with me.

I sought a second opinion. The dentist personally measured my pockets—no stabbing sensation, no bleeding—and explained that my teeth and gums looked healthy. I got my cleaning done without any upsell or alarm, and left feeling relieved.

To be clear, the hygienist and doctor at the first office were courteous. However, the experience left me unsettled: painful measurements, a significant treatment recommendation, and a suggestion of longstanding disease that another professional did not confirm. I’m grateful I double-checked before committing hundreds of dollars.

Based on my experience, I wouldn’t recommend this office. If you’re advised to pursue extensive periodontal treatment here, consider getting an independent evaluation first. It could save you unnecessary stress—and money.

This place is so overrated. What a disappointment! Despite recommendations, the experience left me wondering what all the fuss is about. The meal started with "garlic" bread that was just a soggy sliced sub roll glossed with butter and almost no garlic flavor. The fried calamari arrived limp and greasy, lacking any crunch, with a pool of oil collecting beneath it. The low point was the chicken parm: two small chicken tenders topped with a smear of sauce and cheese, a meager side of pasta, and a puddle of water on the plate. An Italian restaurant serving pasta swimming in water is inexcusable.

While prices aren’t sky-high, the combination of modest portions and poor execution makes it feel like a rip-off. The ordeal doesn’t end inside: parking is a mess. Whether it’s the crowded dining room, the bar, or fast food, finding a spot is an exercise in futility.

With underwhelming food and logistical headaches, there’s no reason to give this place a second chance.

Late Sunday Lunch at a British Pub on Paradise: Good Food, Room to Improve

After a spin down the Strip, my wife and I spotted a British pub on Paradise and ducked in for a late Sunday lunch. The vibe was relaxed—handful of folks at the bar and tables, beer in hand, football on the HDTVs—exactly the kind of casual scene you hope for at a sports-friendly spot. We were greeted promptly, invited to sit wherever we liked, and given menus. We stuck to water, and our waitress, friendly and a bit quirky, absolutely excelled at refills—among the best we’ve ever had, attentive without hovering.

I initially ordered the chicken curry while my wife went for a blue-cheese burger. A few minutes later, the waitress returned to let me know they were out of the curry, so I pivoted to Chicken Marsala. The food arrived after about 20 minutes, which felt reasonable for a Sunday lunch. During the wait, we noticed the staff seemed somewhat disorganized; multiple servers checked on us while a couple of newly arrived patrons appeared to wait longer than they should for attention.

When the plates hit the table, the kitchen delivered. The burger was flavorful, with the tangy blue cheese complementing a well-cooked patty, and my Chicken Marsala was satisfying—savory sauce, tender chicken, and a generous portion. For a place branded as a British pub, the execution on these dishes was solid and exceeded expectations.

One moment at the bar gave us pause: a bartender invited a patron to taste a mixed drink through a straw, then discarded the straw, replaced it, and served the drink to someone else across the bar. While the straw swap mitigates contact, the sequence felt unprofessional and potentially unsanitary.

Overall, this pub has a lot going for it: ample space, plenty of quality HDTVs for game days, and a cheeky “Firkin’” name that suits a lively sports bar. With tighter front-of-house coordination and a bit more attention to bar service standards, it could be a standout neighborhood spot. Not bad, and with clear room to grow.

K-9 Kountry is more than we could have hoped for. Our two Australian Shepherds were painfully anti-social with other dogs and people, leading to embarrassing and sometimes scary situations. From our first conversation, George’s calm confidence and clear plan for rehabilitation made us feel excited and relieved. The results have been incredible: we now have two socialized, well-behaved dogs who enjoy outings and interactions. Equally valuable, George is retraining my husband and me to lead effectively as pack leaders. We recommend K-9 Kountry without hesitation to anyone.

I never know what I'm going to get. Eating at Kyklos is like taking a gamble, but I guess it's a gamble worth trying.

Kyklos is one of those mall food-court spots I’ve drifted back to over time, usually after a shopping run at the Galleria with my mom. It’s convenient, quick, and, on the right day, surprisingly satisfying. My most consistent bright spot has been the salads: crisp, green, and genuinely fresh, with all the right trimmings you’d expect from a straightforward Greek salad. They’re simple done well—and in a food court, that’s saying something.

A recent Groupon nudged me into a takeout run, and that’s where things started to wobble. The lesson: eat your gyros and fries on the spot. By the time I got home, everything was smooshed and dulled—more a casualty of the commute than the kitchen, but the result was the same. Gyros and fresh fries just don’t travel.

I ordered a gyro supreme for myself and a chicken gyro for my boyfriend, with fries and falafel on the side. The sides were a clear miss. The falafel was painfully bad—dry, dense, and aggressively unappealing. The fries were equally forgettable: pale on seasoning and personality. The gyros landed somewhere in the middle. In a mall food court, this should be the surefire choice, something you can grab and eat on the move. Instead, my gyro supreme was buried under an avalanche of feta that overwhelmed everything else. I found myself tunneling through cheese to find the meat, which defeated the point.

Context matters. This isn’t a full-service Greek restaurant, and expecting that level of polish would be unfair. At its best—especially if you dine in—Kyklos can deliver a respectable, quick Greek bite. My advice: stick to the salads, ask for a lighter hand with the feta if you get a gyro, and skip the falafel and fries. With a deal like a Groupon, the value improves, and on a good day, you’ll feel like you won the bet. On a middling day, well, that’s the gamble.

I first passed this place up while walking around the Melrose Street Festival today, but decided to check it out on the way back...

At the Melrose Street Festival, this stand’s menu jumps out with Asian-fusion tacos, teriyaki sliders, and a cold noodle salad. Already full, I tried a coconut curry chicken taco and got my wife a $2 order of fresh tortilla chips with Tika Onion dip. The chips were crisp, and the dip was pretty good—savory with a kick. The taco had nice coconut curry flavor, but the chicken was a tad dry; I prefer thigh, and this seemed like breast. Service was quick and pleasant. I wouldn’t go out of my way to find it, but if I’m back at the food court or stumble on it at another festival, I’d grab another taco and maybe try those sliders.

Title: I am reviewing the pharmacy portion only, not the main store.

I’m writing this review solely about the pharmacy, not the main store. My visiting father needed a routine refill while staying with me in Arizona. Because his prescriptions are normally filled in New York, all Walgreens needed to do was call his NY pharmacy to transfer the prescription—a simple process we’ve done before that usually takes a minute.

Instead, it became a three-day ordeal. Across multiple shifts, the pharmacy staff took down his information three separate times, as if nothing was passed along internally. By day three (Friday), they still had not called. After yet another follow-up from me, they promised to make the call. Ten minutes later, our phone rang—but the caller was asking for the New York pharmacist, which made no sense and only added to the confusion.

Thankfully, this wasn’t a life-threatening situation, but it involved essential medication and deserved far more urgency and competence. Professionalism was also lacking. I was uncomfortable being served by someone with visible facial piercings in a healthcare setting; while personal style is one thing, pharmacies should project a level of professionalism that inspires confidence. Additionally, when I called, I was not placed on hold and could hear employees discussing other customers’ medications and insurance details. That felt like a serious breach of privacy and raises potential HIPAA concerns.

When I finally got confirmation that the transfer call had gone through, I asked why it took three days and repeated follow-ups. The pharmacist replied, “I don’t know, I just work Thursdays and Fridays.” I tried to explain that she was on during part of this, but the conversation went nowhere. She said she’d pass my information to the head pharmacist, who would call when she arrived.

Bottom line: If your prescription requires anything beyond a straightforward fill, be prepared to micromanage and follow up repeatedly. Or consider going to CVS or Walmart, where I’ve consistently experienced better customer service and communication.

NEVER AGAIN: A cautionary tale of a Jiffy Lube radiator flush gone wrong

Preparing for a summer road trip to California, I made a decision I now deeply regret: I skipped my trusted mechanic and went to Jiffy Lube, lured by convenience and a coupon. I’m usually immune to the upsell routine—I’ll happily swap my own air filter—but this time I agreed to a radiator flush. Driving through desert heat, I figured preventative maintenance made sense. It didn’t.

The very next morning, my car overheated immediately—something it had never done before. I turned right around and went back to Jiffy Lube. I was met with a perfunctory explanation about the coolant not being “topped off,” followed by a dismissive send-off. No real inspection, no diagnostic effort—just a pat on the head and a wave out the door.

A block away, the temperature needle climbed again. Hoping it was just that location, I tried another Jiffy Lube. Same story: denial, deflection, and condescension. As a woman, I felt talked down to at every turn, as if my concerns were trivial or my understanding suspect. One employee, clearly uncomfortable with the situation, quietly gave me the regional franchise owner’s number—an act of conscience, but not a solution.

With the car still overheating, I called my regular mechanic, who sent a tow truck. The verdict was swift and maddening: the radiator had been cracked during the flush. I was out $300 for a new radiator, plus the time, stress, and risk of a breakdown that could have stranded me far from home.

My advice is simple: avoid Jiffy Lube, especially for anything beyond the most basic service. Stick with a trusted mechanic who will diagnose, explain, and take responsibility. If you value your time, money, and safety, don’t let a coupon steer you into costly trouble.

B1 can best be described as quirky, eccentric, and totally awesome—a bar with personality to spare. It’s the only spot I’ve ever encountered that tucks a barber shop into its floor plan, and the novelty comes with a surprisingly reasonable perk: a $30 haircut that includes a cocktail. If you’re after an offbeat night out, that alone makes for a memorable story. The vibe leans playful, with an N64 set up so you can sip and game, and even the occasional Jenga match breaking out at tables.

Cocktails are the main attraction here, and you’re in capable hands. Prices hover around $10, in line with other Montreal bars. While my Brooklyn Sour skewed a touch too sweet for my taste, the presentation more than impressed—think tiki mugs, thoughtful glassware, and lavish garnishes that turn each drink into a show.

Food isn’t the focus; beyond a grilled cheese or two, options are sparse. Plan to dine elsewhere, then come for the drinks and atmosphere. For a fun, distinctive night, B1 is worth a visit.

As a lifelong ABBA fan, I walked into this jukebox musical expecting a gleaming cavalcade of hits—maybe a popera where the lyrics carry the plot, or at least a concert-style celebration. Instead, what’s on offer is unmistakably a Broadway musical, complete with a full-fledged libretto grafted onto songs that largely stand on their own. The result is a dialogue-heavy experience that sometimes feels overworked, as if the book is straining to justify the next number rather than letting the music breathe.

That said, the cast is an undeniable hoot. The three leading women, in glittering “futuristic disco” getups, radiate charm and comic snap. Their chemistry, timing, and wink-to-the-audience self-awareness keep the evening buoyant whenever the storytelling bogs down. And the band? Tighter than a gnat’s ass—precision, punch, and sheen that do right by Benny and Björn’s immaculate pop architecture.

The show’s best stretch is the big finale, when pretense falls away and the production simply delivers the songs. Suddenly, the room lifts: you can feel the collective joy of a crowd that came to bask in the hits, full stop.

Who is this for? Primarily women of a certain age, and anyone seeking a nostalgia-soaked night out. If you revere ABBA’s records as stand-alone pop genius, you might be happier dropping the needle at home. But if “Waterloo” soundtracked your prom in ’77—or you wish it did—this show will give you exactly the glitter-drenched singalong you’re craving.

As a New Yorker and unapologetic pizza snob, I came in hoping for Charlotte’s best. This spot is very good, but it misses the hallmark I crave: a truly crispy, crunchy crust. Tony’s in Ballantyne nails that texture, and it’s the difference between great and greatest. That said, the flavor here shines; the balance of cheese and sauce is spot-on, and the garlic knots are downright delicious. Value is excellent, especially given the generous size. I’ll definitely return when I’m nearby. Top five in the city? Absolutely. Blue-ribbon best? Not quite—but close. Still worth a visit for sure.

Total disappointment. I expected better from a place that landed on Food Network; instead, it leaned entirely on shock-value gimmicks. The branding revels in being “bad”—boasting hyper-strong daiquiris, candy cigarettes, and animal-fat fries—but when you indulge, the food must deliver. Mine didn’t. The burger arrived overcooked and astonishingly bland; I asked for pickles to salvage it, only to learn the owner refuses to offer them. That stubborn quirk felt less like personality and more like disregard for diners. If your foundation is excess, you’d better nail flavor, texture, and service. None did. The experience came off touristy, tacky, and performative, built for social media photos rather than a satisfying meal. Novelty can be fun, but it shouldn’t be a substitute for culinary quality. I left with a lighter wallet, a heavier disappointment, and zero desire to return. If you’re chasing a spectacle, you’ll find one; if you’re chasing good food, look elsewhere. Even the hype of a TV feature couldn’t mask the mediocrity.

I used a Groupon for grooming and daycare. Daycare was fine; my dog came home happy. Grooming, however, was disappointing. I asked for my dog's nails to be trimmed as short as possible, yet a week later I had to finish the job myself. The nail trim was sloppy and ineffective. Because of poor service, I don’t plan on returning.

Get Dorian as your guy; he's the one to elevate your night. He's skilled, engaging, and turns dinner into pure fun. Ask for the "Big D" and enjoy. And hey to Kimberly; she'll get you set and keep things lively. They made our evening truly memorable and delightful tonight.

Mad Greek has been a couple of things, including what my wife once dubbed the Best Waffle in the Queen City. Whether waffles are still on the menu is unclear, but what is certain is a solid lineup of short-order plates with a distinct Greek focus. I went straight for the gyro platter, and the experience was reassuring from the start: service was quietly excellent, with an attentive waitress who took my order promptly and kept my glass filled without hovering.

The gyro dinner arrived as a generous mound of sliced lamb, presumably shaved from the spit and kissed again on the grill for extra char. A warm, sliced pita sat to the side, and a substantial tossed salad—Italian dressing, briny feta, and olives—leaned Greek without pretense. Crunchy fries came on their own plate, golden and satisfying. I left comfortably stuffed for $12, a standout value for an out-of-the-box dinner. Mad Greek may have evolved, but it still knows how to feed you well.

Read some of the other reviews and can't understand how people give this place more than 3 stars, especially when they had a complaint about the food!

When we arrived at The White Chocolate Grill, the packed dining room promised a treat. Unfortunately, the meal never rose above average. We opened with spinach-artichoke dip and AZ egg rolls; both tasted like generic chain-restaurant fare, lacking freshness or spark. The entrees were no better. I ordered crab cakes, my husband had trout, and each was bland, forgettable, and, frankly, meh.

With desserts featured prominently and a name that spotlights chocolate, we expected a standout finish. Instead, the Silky Chocolate Soufflé Cake was dry and one-dimensional, missing the lush texture and depth a soufflé-style dessert should have. The White Chocolate Banana Cream Pie disappointed even more: its crust was so thick and hard we could barely cut through it, and it dominated the flavors, burying the banana and cream.

Maybe we’re spoiled by Chicago’s dining scene, but this visit didn’t approach four stars, let alone five. The room buzzed, the service was pleasant, yet nothing on the table felt special. For the price and hype, the experience was underwhelming and not one we’re eager to repeat.
Absolutely the best donut shop around. Freshly made daily with a large selection, every bite shines. Nothing else compares. Consistent quality - I'll be back again and again.

I love this place for its wonderfully fresh food, especially the protein bowls. While the presentation could be more consistent—some days there's plenty of meat, other days barely any—the flavors keep me coming back. Prices run a bit high for the Chandler crowd, but this spot is a welcome, much-needed addition to the area. Don’t miss their seasonal iced teas and lemonade; refreshing and reliably delicious.

Despite booking for baby footprints and handprints pottery, staff seemed unhappy we brought a baby. One team member appeared annoyed and wouldn’t help us prepare, so another had to step in. The visit felt unwelcome and stressful, not the keepsake moment we hoped for. Disappointing; unlikely to return without better hospitality.

Excellent food anchors this favorite spot. Service is usually good, though oddly less consistent than Soba and Casbah. The chef’s tasting menu with wine pairings is a standout experience, and the cocktails are excellent, inventive, and worth the visit here alone.

I'm not sure how good their burgers or pulled pork sandwiches are, but what I ordered was not good at all.

I visited hoping for lunch and chose the chicken Caesar salad wrap. It should be simple, but the kitchen missed the mark. The wrap was stuffed with carrots and zucchini, and the dressing tasted nothing like Caesar, more like an odd tangy sauce that clashed with everything. The place wasn’t busy, yet service was slow; we felt ignored. The only redeeming item was the french fries, which were crisp, but not worth a trip. I can’t speak to the burgers or pulled pork, but based on this experience, I wouldn’t return unless you’re craving something greasy. Quality control and service need attention.

Racing to make a connection at CLT, I chose Fresh Attractions because it was right by my gate and promised speed—unlike Phillips Seafood across the concourse, which is slower but a million times better. Big mistake. The ham and Swiss panini I ordered arrived lukewarm, barely toasted, and carelessly assembled, more mess than meal. The sandwich maker looked indifferent; the cashier initially overcharged me and only corrected it when I pointed it out. That shrugging attitude seems baked into the place, a churn-and-burn spot that assumes travelers won’t return anyway. If you’re a one-off passerby, a mediocre bite might be tolerable. But for frequent flyers who survive on airport fare, this kind of craptastic, half‑hearted food and service is a hard no. Unless you’re starving, skip Fresh Attractions; walk to Phillips—or anywhere—and find something edible and worth your money.

They opened around spring and I've been here maybe three times?

My visits to this new location have been mixed. Seated near the bar once, our server only took the order, dropped off food, and handed the check—no refills, no check-ins, and we had to flag him down just to pay. On other visits, servers were attentive and welcoming, showing the team can shine. The food has been inconsistent; I’ve had better at other Red Lobster locations. There’s clear potential here, thanks to the setting and brand, but consistency in service and kitchen execution needs improvement. Until then, I’d steer diners to the Pineville location and hope this spot tightens up, because it could be great.

I like Dim Sum Chinese.

Dim Sum Chinese won me over despite a few rough edges. The space could use a makeover—think dated décor and a cleanliness level that feels just okay. We visited right after opening and were the only diners, so the vibe was understandably low-key. Service in that quiet window was very attentive, though I’ve heard weekends bring a lively crowd and a completely different atmosphere.

The real draw is the food. We sampled several dishes and were consistently pleased, especially with the dumplings. The pork and shrimp versions were standouts: juicy, well-seasoned, and wrapped in delicate skins that held together without getting gummy. Portions felt fair, and prices were very reasonable, making it easy to try a variety without breaking the bank.

If you’re after solid dim sum at a good value and don’t mind modest surroundings, give this place a shot.

This place is an all around winner in my book.
The food is fresh and really delicious. I’ve tried the tacos, Beach House burger, and the pulled cabbage sandwich; surprisingly, the cabbage is my new favorite, even as a committed carnivore. They offer multiple bread options, including hearty 9-grain for a healthier bite. Quality and flavor keep me coming back; weekly might be the plan. Service is friendly and the vibe is laid-back.

On my first visit to this cozy spot in quaint downtown Dormont, I tried the Tom Yum soup and Pad Thai. The dining room is small and simply outfitted, cooled by a portable A/C in summer, but the warm hospitality and attentive service shine. The Tom Yum was vibrantly spiced and aromatic, with generous, perfectly tender mushrooms, though I wished for a bit more chicken. The Pad Thai delivered a satisfying balance of sweet and spicy flavors, cooked just right. Wonderful food, welcoming staff; I can’t wait to return.

After living nearby for eight months, I finally discovered this unassuming spot—I honestly thought it was a tile store. Inside is a straightforward, old-school bowling alley with prices that are really hard to beat: $2.50 per game before 6 p.m. and $3.50 after. There’s no bar, which might disappoint anyone who likes sipping a pitcher while they bowl, but a connected diner/grill helps fill the gap with casual bites. Don’t expect fancy scoring systems or slick ball returns; the charm here lies in its authentic, retro feel indeed. An arcade and pool tables add to the throwback atmosphere, evoking a community-center vibe. It’s a humble, local joint that’s perfect for low-key fun—and a reminder that bowling can be delightfully frustrating, even when the lanes are friendly and the price is right.

Beautiful Bar and Lounge Under a Three-Story Crystal Chandelier

This striking, multi-level lounge wraps around a towering crystal chandelier that spills light through all three floors. A glass elevator glides beside it, while stairs link each level to the hotel, making it as photogenic as it is convenient. The ground floor sits in the heart of the casino, and it feels like it—loud and noticeably smoky. The second level is the sweet spot: quieter, more intimate, and perfectly positioned for people-watching without the chaos. The third level, by the East Tower, hosts a main bar plus a smaller side bar.

On a recent fight weekend the place was jammed—standing room only, lots of tipsy revelers, and virtually no seats. During the day there were no cocktail servers; drinks are ordered at the bar. Pricing runs about $12–$14, which is a relative bargain for the property. The cocktails were excellent, and a bartender’s off-menu mix was right on point. Because of the crush, we grabbed our drinks and retreated to our suite.

Visit on a weekday night for the best experience: aim for the second level, snag a seat, and linger over a couple of well-made cocktails. With lighter crowds and more staff, it’s a stellar spot to sip and snap chandelier photos.

Initially, this spot ranked among the best Asian food options in Vegas, with a menu that extends well beyond its famous noodles. While adventurous diners might eye the stinky tofu, I’d skip it—it’s overwhelmingly pungent. Far better choices include the refreshing lychee slushee and a satisfying steak and eggs. However, a recent return visit dimmed the glow: service was notably poor. Servers seemed disengaged; we had to repeatedly request water, napkins, and refills, and the check lagged far too long. After two solid experiences, the third was a letdown, prompting me to drop my rating from four to three stars. Great flavors remain, but consistency—especially in service—needs more attention to justify the hype and keep regulars coming back soon.

I had some girlfriends in town for the weekend and by Sunday afternoon we had no food left in my house and we were starving. I tossed out Nana’s as an option—been once, loved it—and the moment my friends heard “soul food,” they practically sprinted to the car.

When we arrived, the place was packed, and that delicious, buttery aroma hit us the second the door opened. We had time to browse the menu, which reads like a hug from grandma, and I settled on smothered pork chops with cabbage and pinto beans and rice.

Every bite felt like home. The chop was fork-tender under a velvety, deeply seasoned gravy. The cabbage kept its crisp-tender snap, with just enough seasoning to make it sing. The beans and rice were simple, soulful, and perfectly comforting.

Despite the crowd, service stayed warm and attentive, portions were generous, and prices fair. The vibe is lively, family-friendly, and full of Sunday joy.

Craving finger-licking, nap-inducing comfort? Nana’s is the move. Pro tip: arrive early or embrace the wait—it’s absolutely worth it. Bring friends and big appetites.

Hate to do it but the service here is an absolute nightmare.

Buying a vehicle should be exciting, not a prolonged battle with basic service. Immediately after purchase, we noticed the rear driver’s-side DVD monitor was inoperable. No problem, we thought—get it fixed and move on. That simple expectation spiraled into a three-week saga of missed commitments, poor communication, and baffling logistics.

On drop-off, we clearly documented three issues: the dead monitor, a DVD drive that wouldn’t read discs, and a remote that didn’t match the one in the manual. A week later came the cheery call: “All is well.” At pickup, the monitor powered on, but the drive still refused to read discs. Back went the loaner; back went our car, with instructions to please make it right before calling again.

Another week passed. Each time we contacted service, we emphasized the same non-negotiable: verify the remote operates all functions. Again, the call arrived—everything perfect, remote included. Two minutes into testing at the dealership, it was clear that while the monitor worked and the drive finally read discs, the remote still did not. The very item we flagged repeatedly remained unresolved.

A new remote was ordered with a promise of next-day delivery. Then: “It didn’t make the truck.” Frustration turned to disbelief. We scheduled a Thursday window, granting 48 hours to get the part in hand. When Thursday came, the plan devolved into a melee; the parts runner was dispatched without a phone, eliminating any real-time coordination. How were we supposed to know they’d arrived—or respond if something went wrong?

As of this writing, we still don’t have a functioning remote. A dealership is only as strong as its weakest link, and our experience suggests those links—communication, quality control, and logistics—are fragile here. If you value timely, thorough service, approach with caution. I hope management reads this, owns the failures, and invests in processes that meet the basic standard customers deserve. Until that happens, I can't recommend trusting them with post-sale support on anything beyond the simplest, single-visit maintenance.

To start, the surly crab apple of a hostess seemed annoyed to have to seat us and was generally unfriendly. Then she seated another table and was slightly nicer to them. At least she told them the specials, a courtesy we were not extended.

We came in hoping for a good beer and a snack, and met a chillier welcome than the draft list. Our hostess seemed annoyed and skipped the specials entirely—odd, since the next table got them. The menu is large, but if English pub fare isn’t your thing, little appeals. I chose a hefeweizen on draft that was just okay. The “junk chips” were a messy, overly vinegary heap that turned soggy fast. Credit where due: our two servers were friendly and attentive, and the complimentary bucket of popcorn softened the blow. Still, uneven hospitality and lackluster food make this a tough sell. Two stars.

Was not impressed. Management seemed to lack an understanding of basic customer service.

I left this shop feeling more frustrated than fresh, largely because basic customer service fell short. I bought a $12 Yelp deal that had expired but retained its $12 face value. Knowing prices had changed, I offered to pay the difference toward the current $17 cut—a straightforward $5. Before the cut, I showed the certificate and was told it would be honored. Afterward, that changed. I was informed they couldn’t apply it because “then I’d have to pay that $12,” as if honoring a previously stated commitment were a personal penalty. Losing a customer shouldn’t be worth $12, and shifting terms after the service is simply poor practice and short-sighted. It felt misleading.

The haircut itself didn’t redeem the experience. I’m used to barbers who communicate—confirming the look, checking preferences, and engaging along the way. My barber stayed silent, which I initially interpreted as focus. The result told a different story: I requested a slicked-back style and left with more of an undercut. Stray strands were left unmanaged, and the lineup looked rushed despite the time spent in the chair. A simple check-in during the cut could have corrected course and prevented the mismatch. I would have been better off saving my time and doing it myself. I don’t mind paying full price for good service, but inconsistent policies and an unsatisfying cut made this a one-and-done visit. Clarify policies and honor your word.

Absolutely gorgeous and worth your time

I’m not a nature person or a hiker, yet Holyrood Park won me over. The ascent can be strenuous, but every step brings rewarding, stunning views. With no set trail, you can mosey up at your own pace, veering off the heavily trafficked path to find quiet pockets of serenity. I loved sinking into a thick bed of wild grasses, river to the right, rolling hills all around. It feels restorative. Every city deserves a Holyrood Park—go, and give yourself time to take it in.

I was excited to finally make it to a Thomas Keller property, having read much about The French Laundry and Per Se.

I’ve long admired Thomas Keller’s storied kitchens, so a Sunday brunch reservation at Bouchon in Las Vegas felt special. The restaurant is lovely. We snagged a quiet patio table framed by greenery and sun, a calm oasis that promised an indulgent morning. Yet as the meal unfolded, a series of service and cooking missteps chipped away at the spell, raising the question of whether celebrity-chef outposts in Vegas risk diluting the excellence they aim to showcase.

Service initially felt a bit loose, the kind of small slips—long pauses, uncertain pacing—that make you wonder if the team was recovering from the previous night’s revelry. It’s Vegas, after all, and the energy of the city can bleed into Sunday brunch. That said, Bouchon’s brand promises discipline: crisp choreography between the floor and the kitchen, and the sort of polished hospitality that anticipates rather than reacts. When those fundamentals falter, even a lovely setting can’t fully cover for the lost rhythm. What remained was a sense of unevenness: competence present, but not consistently aligned.

We ordered oysters, then a Croque Madame and a quiche. About thirty minutes later, our mains arrived before the oysters. The runner recognized the sequencing error, removed the plates, and sent over the manager. He handled it with professional grace—apologetic and clear that this was not their standard. He comped the oysters, which, when they arrived, were briny, fresh, and beautifully presented. A solid recovery, even if the kitchen timing was out of sync.

Unfortunately, the stumbles continued. The Croque Madame was superb—satisfying and crowned by brioche toast so luxurious it felt like a triumph. The quiche, however, was lukewarm. We were hungry enough to proceed, and its custard and seasoning were quite good, but the lack of heat undercut what could have been a standout plate. Hoping to end on a high note, we ordered beignets. They arrived not warm but cold, without the buoyant lift or aromatic allure that makes beignets irresistible.

Given that many reviews rave about Bouchon’s service, I’m inclined to believe our experience was an anomaly—a morning when the team wasn’t firing in concert. The manager’s diligence and sincerity stood out, and the kitchen’s bright spots—the oysters and that magnificent Croque—hint at the capability within. I’ll give Bouchon another try on my next Vegas visit. With a few corrections in pacing and temperature, this brunch could match the property’s aspirations and reputation.

Best Mexican food ever! The enchiladas are out of this world—fast, fresh, and bursting with flavor. Guacamole and salsa with chips were excellent. The bartender was courteous, knowledgeable, and super helpful with local tips. Loved the lively ambiance. An unforgettable experience; I’ll definitely be back soon for more!

Stopped in for the gyro combo—gyro, fries, and a drink. The gyro was tasty, with fresh meat and toppings, though a touch more sauce would have elevated it. Fries were enjoyable overall, but a few were slightly undercooked. Service stood out: everyone was friendly, and a manager or owner even offered complimentary soup while I waited. The dining area was nearly empty, suggesting a slow period or limited foot traffic, but it made for a quiet meal. Despite small hiccups, the value and hospitality impressed me. I’d recommend giving them a try, and I plan to return for another visit.

Absolutly amazing. 7 stars.

After twelve nights at the Jockey Club in February, I can confidently say this property is one of the Strip’s best-kept secrets—and a true oasis amid the frenzy of Las Vegas. Any negative buzz you might see seems to stem from timeshare pitch encounters, not the hotel itself. My stay was seamless, serene, and far beyond expectations.

I booked a standard suite without the Bellagio view directly through the Jockey Club website, assuming I wouldn’t spend much time in my room. At check-in, the wonderful Latrice surprised me with an unsolicited upgrade to a Penthouse suite overlooking the Bellagio fountains. I was genuinely stunned. Walking into the suite was a jaw-dropping moment: expansive, spotless, and fresh-smelling, framed by floor-to-ceiling, wall-to-wall windows looking out to the iconic fountain show. It was the kind of space that makes you rethink your entire itinerary because you won’t want to leave.

The suite felt like a polished home-away-from-home. A king bed with blackout drapes ensured deep sleep. A huge walk-in closet with a safe, ironing board, and iron added convenience. The bathroom included both bath and shower with a hairdryer provided. Two large flat-screen TVs and DVD players—paired with free DVD rentals from hospitality—covered entertainment. A full kitchen, dining area, and separate lounge created a comfortable, tasteful environment ideal for extended stays or anyone wanting more than a basic hotel room.

Amenities are thoughtful and accessible. Down the corridor, coin-operated laundry makes longer trips easy. On the second floor, a heated pool offers just-right relaxation, and the gym, hot tub, and showers are open 24/7. The same area features a sauna, ice machine, several gas BBQ grills, ping pong tables, and a fresh towel station. There’s easy access to parking and the Cosmopolitan from level 1 or 2, placing you steps from the heart of the action while keeping the property’s calm vibe intact.

Cleanliness and maintenance are outstanding. Every space—from outdoor smoking lounges to entrances, lobby, corridors, and elevators—was tidy and well-kept. Housekeeping was prompt and unobtrusive, delivering fresh towels, coffee, and sundries daily on request, and performing a full room clean with bedding change weekly in my suite.

One standout perk: the free shuttle bus offered five days a week (check your welcome pack). It covers the places you’d otherwise need a pricey taxi for, including Smith’s supermarket, the Premium Outlets North and South, and Downtown/Fremont Street.

Staff truly elevate the experience. Everyone I encountered—front desk, housekeeping, shuttle drivers, and security—was friendly, professional, and efficient with a laid-back approach that made me feel taken care of. When I forgot the safe code, security had the issue resolved in under three minutes.

I wasn’t approached once by timeshare reps despite passing them daily. If you’re seeking a quiet, clean, non-gambling, non-smoking retreat right off the Strip, the Jockey Club is a standout. I’m already planning my return to Las Vegas, and I’ll absolutely be staying here again.

I moved to Phoenix from Oahu and this spot delivers island vibes. Hinano on tap instantly reminded me of home. Coconut shrimp rolls were straight-up ono, and the poke was fresh; the sashimi tasted good but was unevenly cut and the presentation needs polish. Bali Hai mango ribs were outstanding—tender, saucy, and memorable. Coleslaw fell flat, but the sweet potato fries were “broke da mouth” good: crispy, sweet, perfectly seasoned. Friendly, attentive service rounded out the visit. Despite minor misses, I’ll definitely be coming back for another round.

Sometimes a single word captures an entire dining experience: no. On a recent Vegas trip, I finally checked this buffet off the list, bundled with a Buffet of Buffets pass. After many visits and seeing middling online chatter, I figured it couldn’t be that bad. Unfortunately, my timing set the tone. I arrived right after the brunch transition, when the comforting, hard-to-mess-up breakfast staples had been cleared, and what remained made me wish I’d come an hour earlier.

The salad bar was the lone bright spot—fresh enough and reasonably varied. Beyond that, things deteriorated fast. The meat selections ranged from forgettable to off-putting. Every chicken preparation I sampled was a study in how to do breast meat wrong: pallid, stringy, and somehow both soggy and dry, with the unsettling texture of wet paper. Even dishes billed with Middle Eastern or Indian spices arrived bizarrely mute, as if the seasoning had been waved over the trays but never actually applied. Flavorless food at a buffet is one thing; flavorless food pretending to be bold is worse.

Service cemented the disappointment. Our server dropped a drink for my friend, then vanished—no check-ins, no refills, not even a cursory glance. By the time we flagged down another staffer, I was nearly finished and desperate for anything to wash down the letdown. In the end, I’d only consider returning if I knew the breakfast spread was still out; those simple, satisfying items might make the value equation work. Otherwise, with so many better options in Vegas, I can only repeat my opening verdict: no.

This brewery feels decidedly average. The decor is attractive and the menu reads well, but the atmosphere is lackluster, especially for a place brewing beer. It aims for upscale and misses. Decent lunch specials redeem it somewhat, yet overall it lands squarely in middling territory.

The dim sum here is delicious!!

I wasn’t impressed on my first visit with friends, but a tip to try the dim sum brought me back—and wow, I’m a convert. Fresh, flavorful baskets and quick service made the difference. I now wholeheartedly recommend their dim sum, served every day from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. It’s a daily treat worth the return.

Banana Republic Caesars Palace Men's Dept: Shockingly Poor Service Upstairs

I visited the upstairs men’s department hoping for competent, professional assistance and left baffled. When I asked for a business card or a product catalogue—basic retail tools—the three associates stared as if I’d spoken a foreign language. “What kind of card?” one said; another asked, “What for?” After I explained, the answer was a dismissive, “We don’t have anything like that here.” Only as I turned to leave did someone ask if I was looking for something specific. Yes, I was—but I couldn’t find it there, and their confusion didn’t inspire confidence. Training on customer communication and product resources is urgently needed. Intelligent, proactive service would make all the difference.

Not the typical place you'd expect to find lots of veggie options. Walk in expecting a token veggie burger, and instead you get an entire vegetarian and vegan menu at Double Wide. The vibe is a quirky mash-up—part sports bar, part biker bar, part hipster veggie haven—drawing an equally eclectic crowd. There’s abundant outdoor seating with picnic tables, perfect for lingering over their delicious plant-based dishes and the huge, well-curated beer list. It’s the kind of spot that would feel right at home in Austin, yet it anchors Carson Street with unexpected flair. Friendly service, fun atmosphere, and standout food. Five stars, without hesitation.

After a 10–15 minute taxi ride from the Strip, my hopes were high, but I left disappointed. I ordered the crispy duck over drunken noodles for $19, and nearly everything missed the mark. The noodles arrived clumped together, bland, and slick with oil from the duck. The duck itself wasn’t crispy—just hard, oily batter with scant meat. Even the sauce, usually the saving grace, was flat and unappealing. For the price and trek, the meal felt like poor value. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.

Food was decent but unremarkable. Sprawling menu seems unfocused, making it hard to excel at any one dish. Bar program disappoints—limited selections and no vermouth, so a Manhattan wasn’t possible. Streamlining offerings could elevate consistency.

With Phoenix’s dim sum scene down to a single stalwart, Great Wall has become the de facto destination. I’ve been coming here since I was little, and while I once favored another spot that’s now closed, Great Wall remains reliable if not remarkable. The classics—har gow, siu mai, BBQ pork buns, turnip cake, sesame balls—are all present, but flavors can feel muted, especially if you’re used to the punchier dim sum in places like Las Vegas. Dining in means waiting for carts to circle, and timing can be frustrating when the item you’re craving never seems to arrive. My tip: order takeout. On our latest visit, we placed a to-go order to eat at my grandma’s, and everything was ready on time, warm, and stress-free. Consistency and convenience make a strong case for skipping the cart chase. Overall, the food is decent—more comfort than culinary fireworks—but given that it’s the only dim sum option in Phoenix now, Great Wall earns its place as a solid, go-to choice.

At $29 including tax and tip, last Sunday’s brunch buffet delivered a solid, if not spectacular, value. I wouldn’t say every bite screamed $29-worth, but with a fun group and a full plate, it felt worth it for the day. The crab legs were the standout: firm rather than mushy, briny, and seasoned to a perfectly salty finish. Comfort picks shined, too—the macaroni rocked, and the potato croquettes were crispy outside, creamy inside. The omelet station turned out a great-looking egg-white omelet for my friend. Overall, the spread offered a decent selection, and most dishes landed in the “pretty decent” camp, with enough highs to keep refills coming.

Service is where this place separates itself. Even as we lingered for over three hours—brunch time between 11 and 2:30—servers checked in constantly, refilled drinks, and stayed friendly. On food alone, I’d call it 3.5 stars; with that hospitality, I’m comfortable bumping it to four.

Do you want to be treated like you are not worthy by rude, dismissive staff? Head straight to Bouchon—you’ll get your fill. We didn’t have reservations and expected a long wait, but basics were mishandled. It took 10 minutes just to place a coffee order at the bar, and after 15 more minutes, no drip coffee arrived. Guests who arrived after us were served first. When my husband asked about our order, the bartender’s response was shockingly rude. The hostess offered no help, staring blankly like a deer in headlights. Overall, service felt indifferent and untrained. We left disappointed and won’t be returning.

Finally, a food establishment where eating with your fingers feels celebrated. Oysters, shrimp, crab, and Cajun fries arrive drenched in a craveable garlic butter dipping sauce, and even the chicken tenders impress. On our February 21, 2012 visit, alcohol wasn’t available, so our group grabbed beers from across the parking lot and enjoyed them inside. The casual vibe includes the fun option to scrawl messages on the wood-paneled walls. Spice heads take note: their “mild” packs surprising heat—eye-watering and mouth-gaping. Come hungry, come messy, and expect bold flavors in a convivial, hands-on setting.

I frequent Fridays for their late happy hour, so I know what to expect from the menu. This location inside Sam’s Town casino delivered prompt service, and the food arrived quickly. However, the pretzel sticks missed the mark—overcooked to a dark brown, edging toward a bitter flavor. Aside from that misstep, the rest of the meal was solid and consistent with the brand. Overall, a decent visit; improve the appetizers.

After a long day of moving furniture, my friends and I dropped into this spot and were pleasantly surprised by its overall quality and cleanliness. The layout offers plenty of rooms for a lively night, plus a gated outdoor area where you can smoke and sip drinks comfortably. Staff were welcoming, and the person who took my order spoke formal English that stood out in a good way. I went for the Caramba Nachos with beef. They were fine but not memorable; the chief issue was the cheese—thin and watery—undercutting the otherwise decent toppings and crisp chips. On the bright side, the complimentary bowl of chips and the self-serve salsa bar are great touches, with enough variety to customize heat and flavor. With better cheese, those nachos could shine. As it is, this place is solid for drinks, hanging out, and service.

Food: This buffet used to be a standout, but each visit lately feels like another step down in quality while the price keeps inching up. The strongest value left is the unlimited beer and wine; there’s usually at least one decent beer on tap, which helps soften the blow. The seafood section has changed over time—crab shelling tools are gone, and the legs now come pre-opened for easier eating. Tip: choose the steamed crab legs; they’re noticeably better than the cold ones. The cocktail shrimp pile is consistently messy and unappealing. On the bright side, the carving station remains a reliable anchor with sausages, turkey, and prime rib. If you come for brunch, expect a crowd at the omelette station—it’s a favorite for a reason.

Service: Front-end staff make a good first impression; the cashiers are friendly and welcoming. The bussers may wear their fatigue on their faces, but they’re efficient and attentive, clearing plates frequently and keeping tables tidy. Communication can be hit-or-miss at the carving station—asking for a rare slice of prime rib has led to some confusion.

Location: Set inside the M Resort, this buffet benefits from being off the Strip. It’s a calmer atmosphere with ample, easy parking and none of the usual chaos. Overall, it’s now an average buffet propped up by convenient perks and free-flowing drinks—fine for a casual outing, but no longer the must-visit it once was.

I have never stayed here. The pool however is quite nice and they even do swim in movies in the summer. my parents use this as their mini-vacation place for the pools and great room rates.

While I haven’t booked a room myself, I’ve spent plenty of time on the property, and the pool is the star. The summer swim-in movies give it a fun, family-friendly vibe, and my parents swear by the combination of multiple pools and consistently good rates. The hotel itself shows its age—there’s a bit of wear and tear—but it remains a decent, comfortable spot. What really elevates it is the staff: every interaction I’ve had has been friendly and accommodating.

Living in the neighboring apartments that share the parking lot, I recently dropped into the bar for a martini. The bartender, an older gentleman, broke the ice with a cheeky “How dirty do you like it?”—and I appreciated the question more than expected. I replied “Very dirty,” and he delivered. He was a great conversationalist and would earn five stars on service alone.

The gin martini rang up at $7.50, slightly steep for a low-key, no-frills atmosphere, but fair for an occasional after-work drink. The bar is small and was quiet during my visit, making it easy to relax without a crowd. I’ll return, though it won’t be my go-to unless I’m planning to hit the pool—guest access rules to the pool notwithstanding. Overall: modest property, standout pool, genuinely friendly staff.

St. Francis promises a tempting weekend brunch—think tasty plates paired with a delicious Bloody Mary—and the kitchen mostly delivers. The food is good, and the service has noticeably improved recently. But the ambiance derails the experience: a Jazz trio performing inside the dining room makes conversation nearly impossible. On a loud weekend, we were shouting across the table. The restaurant needs to decide what it wants to be; turning brunch into a Jazz Club won’t win over guests seeking a relaxed, social meal. Until the volume comes down or the music moves elsewhere, I’ll head down the street for a calmer brunch.

New meaning to Strip Steak: despite the gentleman’s club setting, this spot hides a surprisingly solid restaurant. The kitchen claims prime, but the steak eats more like a well-executed choice cut—still satisfying. Drinks are poured strong and stiff. A fresh Caesar salad impresses, while tender lamb chops could use more salt and pepper. Mashed potatoes and other sides range from fair to good. Convenience is king here: having a decent meal attached to a strip club makes it an unexpectedly practical, fun detour.

Real authentic Mexican dishes, right in the middle of C/U. I’ve been here a few times now, and everything I’ve tried has been spectacular. Having been spoiled in California by taco trucks serving scrumptious goodness everywhere, I’m amazed to find a spot in Illinois where, outside Chicago, nothing compares. Don’t be put off by the looks or worry about the floors and tables—the grocery store and food counter are unassuming and homey. Prices are super cheap for the quality and generous portions. It’s a non-corporate family venture, with the same friendly folks always working. If it looks good and smells tasty, just eat. Alejandro is welcoming—and yes, easy on the eyes—and great at helping you choose.

Hidden in plain sight, this cocktail bar is a pleasant surprise. The menu is extensive and inventive, with bartenders who listen and tailor spot-on recommendations to your preferences. The venue’s design adds to the experience—stylish without feeling pretentious. Prices run higher than typical Southside spots, but the quality justifies the cost and the vibe benefits from fewer rowdy college crowds. You’re paying for craftsmanship and a more refined atmosphere. I also celebrated New Year’s here and had a fantastic time: great energy, seamless service, and well-balanced drinks that kept the night festive without missing a beat.

Rude staff, cramped seats, and aging aircraft make this airline one of the worst in the U.S. Service felt indifferent, comfort nonexistent, and value lacking. Comparable to United or American at their worst. If possible, choose Virgin.

Ate here last week and forgot to write a review.

I stopped in on a Wednesday during prime lunch hour, and while the dining room was buzzing, there was no wait. Our party of three was seated quickly, and the service set a great tone right away. Our waiter was friendly, attentive, and generous with recommendations, which made ordering easy. We went with two pizzas and a burger.

The “Pepperoni” pizza was a standout: two types of meat, jalapeños for a lively kick, and a crust with a satisfying crisp. My own pie arrived looking more like a salad—an avalanche of arugula—though once I cleared off the greens, the pizza underneath was excellent: flavorful, balanced, and nicely blistered. The burger looked fantastic from across the table, and while I didn’t try a bite, my coworker praised the bun as soft, fresh, and likely baked in-house. He ranked it among his top burgers, which says something.

On pure taste and execution, the kitchen delivers. Where this place stumbles, for me, is value. The pizzas are roughly the size of what you’d get at Pizzeria Bianco and run about $14 each. That’s not outrageous, but it is on the high side for what feels like comparable quality. I can find similar pies at NYPD or Mama Mia for roughly half the price, or get a larger pizza elsewhere for about the same money. I can’t speak to the burger’s value since I didn’t try it, though my coworker said he’d order it again.

Bottom line: very good food, polished service, and a pleasant lunch experience—but be prepared to pay for it. I’d call it a solid 3 stars on value, 4 on taste. If price isn’t a concern, you’ll likely leave happy; if it is, you might feel it in your wallet.

Super trendy spot with a standout bakery—decadent, delicious, and unapologetically calorie-laden; I'd return just for the pastries. Lunch was solid and fairly priced, making it an easy pick for a casual meal. Unfortunately, the latte missed the mark—overly bitter and out of sync with the otherwise enjoyable experience. The lively atmosphere and stylish crowd add to the appeal, with plenty of people-watching for everyone. Overall, come for the bakery, stay for the vibe, and skip the coffee.

I'm giving them one star as a 1/2 star is not an option. The owners have obviously given up and focused all their cash on the Plaza across the street, which is just lipstick on a pig. This place is miserable and deserted. You know you've got trouble when you make more money making part of the casino floor a large gift shop. So sad, they used to have a great coffee shop. Huge areas at the back of the building have been walled off, including the elevators to the now closed hotel. If the owners are reading this, I hope they sell and find a buyer and soon. This is a shame.

This property feels abandoned, with ownership seemingly funneling attention and cash to the Plaza across the street—cosmetic fixes that amount to lipstick on a pig. The casino floor is bleak and thinly populated, and when a sprawling gift shop becomes the busiest “gaming” area, you know the operation is in trouble. The once-excellent coffee shop is gone, and vast sections in the rear are walled off, including the elevators to the now-shuttered hotel. The atmosphere is miserable and deserted, stripped of energy and amenities that once made it worth visiting. If the owners still care, they should sell to someone who does—fast. This decline is disheartening, and the community deserves better.

Dr. Moss is the most amazing physician I’ve seen. She’s friendly, caring, and truly listens, never rushing you out the door. I’ve never felt more welcomed or comfortable in a doctor’s office. Her team is equally outstanding—professional, warm, and quick to follow up to ensure everything is on track. Their customer service sets a high bar. Tragically, my insurance no longer covers her, and I’m heartbroken. I don’t know how I’ll find comparable care elsewhere after such an exceptional experience.

Amazing place to read or just relax, lots of loose leaf teas to choose from.

This tea lounge is a haven for reading, chats, and anyone who appreciates a thoughtful cup. The menu spans a wide range of loose leaf teas, with some standout blends, especially among the specialty options. While a few of the more budget-friendly teas—particularly the greens—can be underwhelming, the pricing reflects the quality, and there are plenty of gems to discover.

The best value is ordering a pot: it arrives on a tidy tray with a steeping timer, a drinking cup, and a cup to hold spent leaves. For solo sippers or pairs, it’s perfect. For groups of three or more, the setup becomes awkward, pushing everyone toward mismatched mugs. A party-style tray with multiple cups would solve this and make small meetings effortless.

Service is excellent, the ambiance inviting, and the soundtrack eclectic—from classical one day to indie the next. Hours run late, which helps offset a wish for earlier openings. Add free Wi‑Fi, and it’s easy to give five stars.

Cheap, tasty, fun, and super cute inside, this spot checks every box—and they have happy hour, too. We kicked things off with the Combo Caribe: golden yuca fries with jalapeño ranch, giant squished green plantain chips, and sweet plantains with crema. The yuca fries could have been cut smaller and fried a touch crisper, and I wished the jalapeño ranch packed more heat, but the platter was still good. The sweet plantains were the runaway winner—caramelized, tender, and addictive. For mains, we shared chicken and veggie empanadas and the pulled pork (pernil) with a simple cabbage salad. The empanadas were light, crisp, and satisfying, and the pernil was hearty comfort. Drinks delivered refreshment: an aromatic Earl Grey iced tea and a juicy watermelon agua fresca. I can’t wait to come back and explore the exotic empanadas.

Wow. I’m not sure if Alicia A is an owner or just has a very different experience, but mine aligns far more with Larry’s: really slow service, subpar food, and outrageous prices.

We arrived on a Saturday morning as a party of three and were quoted a 20-minute wait. Thanks to a larger party disappearing, we were seated in about 10 minutes—but the placement was odd: a lonely table in a cavernous, bright orange room that quickly turned into a holding area for the growing crowd. After five minutes, a server appeared to take our order, then vanished again. Drinks eventually showed up, but the portioning felt stingy and the pacing off from the start.

Every beverage came in a tiny 6-ounce glass—the kind you’d expect for fresh-squeezed orange juice. Predictably, those glasses sat empty more often than not, and refills were scarce. It set the tone for an experience defined by waiting: waiting for attention, waiting for refills, and waiting for the food.

We sat for about 25 minutes before our $8 waffles arrived. Eight dollars—for a single chocolate chip waffle. Not a premium chip in sight, just standard semi-sweets, and not a large, indulgent portion either. The waffle was roughly eight inches in diameter and, worse, it arrived completely alone: no fruit, no whipped cream, no side of bacon or hash browns, nothing to justify the price. Texture-wise, it missed the mark entirely—hard, ultra-crispy, and devoid of the malted tenderness that makes a waffle comforting. It felt like it challenged my teeth more than it pleased my palate.

Service didn’t improve after the food landed; long stretches passed without a check-in. The room filled with waiting patrons, adding to an uncomfortable vibe. Most concerning, a pool of yellow liquid under our table remained unaddressed even after we alerted staff.

When a breakfast spot struggles this much with value, execution, and basic hospitality, it’s hard to recommend. If you’re nearby, you might be better off heading across the street to The Good Egg. This visit was all cost and no comfort.

Should this actually be a two-star review rather than three? Probably. I’ve eaten here several times over the years and always appreciated the laid-back vibe and once-reliable comfort food. Unfortunately, my recent visits suggest a restaurant on a slow downhill slide, with service quality eroding each time.

On this visit, the service was plainly subpar. Our server seemed attentive and energetic—just not at our table. A young woman seated nearby received prompt, enthusiastic attention and extras, while my family struggled to get basics taken care of. When a taco entrée we ordered arrived with two tacos after he’d told us it came with three, we asked for clarification. Instead of fixing the issue, he launched into a speech about how some chefs allow three and others insist on two, and how the kitchen and waitstaff “need to get on the same page.” That may be true, but it’s not the guest’s problem.

Inconsistency and inattentiveness usually point to weak management. Too bad. Until the house tightens up, I won’t be back anytime soon.

I’m a subscriber to Blockbuster Online, and the five free in‑store swaps per month are a lifesaver. On a Saturday, after burning through my deliveries, I stopped by this location to trade a couple discs, and the experience was seamless. The associate who helped me was friendly, efficient, and knew the system. The store itself was clean, well‑organized, and stocked far better than I expected. I even snagged two titles that had just been released the day before, which was a pleasant surprise for a weekend—extra star for availability. Between the easy swaps, the tidy shelves, and the convenient location, this branch makes the Online membership feel genuinely valuable. I’ll definitely be returning whenever I need a quick refresh without waiting on the mail. If you’re using the program, this store is exactly what you want for hassle‑free swaps.

My mom and I went here together after work yesterday.

Tucked into a small storefront that’s easy to miss if you’re not looking for it, this intimate spot offers a cozy, no-frills setting with a handful of tables and a compact ordering counter. Dine-in guests are looked after at their tables, which adds a personal touch in a space that otherwise feels utilitarian. On our visit, only one front-of-house staffer was working, and while she was attentive and kind, the pace inevitably suffered—ordering, receiving the bill, and general service all took longer than expected.

We came excited to try the goat curry, but they were out, so I went with the jerk chicken and my mom chose the brown stewed chicken. Both plates arrived with “rice and peas” (rice and beans) and mixed vegetables. Here’s where the first hiccup appeared: the menu lists side dishes in two lines, and while entrees include two sides, the second line apparently carries a $2.50 upcharge per side. The menu doesn’t clearly distinguish this, and we were surprised to see an extra $5 for our two orders of mixed vegetables. It’s a small cost, but the lack of clarity makes it feel misleading.

Once the food hit the table, almost every frustration melted away. The jerk chicken delivered bold island heat without tipping into punishing territory—still very spicy, so consider yourself warned, but deeply flavorful and balanced. Both chicken dishes were incredibly tender and juicy, bathed in those signature runny, savory juices that speak to authentic Caribbean homestyle cooking. My mom appreciated that her brown stewed chicken wasn’t overly salty, a common pitfall that this kitchen avoids. The rice and peas were fragrant, well-spiced, and mercifully not greasy. The mixed vegetables—zucchini, cauliflower, onions, and carrots—were tasty, though less traditionally Caribbean, and they were out of greens that night, which we’d have preferred.

If I could break down the experience: Food earns a full 5 stars, Service a fair 3 stars, and Speed a modest 2 stars. With more staff, the latter two would likely rise, because the effort and hospitality are clearly there.

Despite the menu confusion and the slower pace, I would absolutely return. I’m eager to try the goat curry when it’s available and have my eye on the Jamaican rum cake for dessert. For adventurous eaters in Pittsburgh seeking authentic flavors, Royal Caribbean is a small but rewarding destination worth finding.

Belch oh wait Belch excuse me pleaae. Just got back from this place and we are feeling quite bloated.

We left dinner feeling uncomfortably bloated. The house margarita disappointed; I was glad I’d had a cocktail before my husband drove us over. Chips and salsa were just okay. We both ordered the taco–enchilada combo. The taco was fine—I liked the crisp shell and shredded beef. The enchilada, however, was bland, with weak sauce and what seemed like a half cup of melted cheap cheese; I left it on the plate. Guacamole was decent, service was good, but nothing made us want to return.

Ahhh Vegas...

Our group opted for the Westin this trip, trading an on‑strip address for a calm haven just a short walk away. Pro tip: that walk shrinks fast when you’re in heels—taxis became our best friends. From the moment we stepped inside, the hotel made an impression: a light, lovely scent, abundant floral arrangements, and chic, modern decor setting an elegant tone. Check-in was seamless and genuinely welcoming.

Our room was spotless and contemporary, with a killer view stretching across the Strip’s neon glow. What truly elevated the stay was the staff. From the doorman who greeted us by name to the housekeeper who anticipated little needs, every interaction felt warm, attentive, and sincere. We felt comfortable—cared for—throughout.

The complimentary happy hour and snack reception were a delightful surprise, perfect for regrouping before the night. The casino, while petite compared with the Strip’s behemoths, delivered its own happy-hour fun without the chaos. And that’s the Westin’s magic: tranquility in the heart of spectacle. It’s peaceful, polished, and refreshingly calm—a counterpoint to Vegas at full throttle.

If you crave the energy of the city with a sanctuary to retreat to, the Westin hits the sweet spot. Five stars from us. Viva… well, you know the rest. We’ll be back next time, absolutely.

This hotel changed my whole perspective on fancy living in Vegas.

Palms Place isn’t the first condo-hotel in Las Vegas, but it was my first taste of that style of stay—and it completely reset my expectations. The suite felt more like a chic apartment than a hotel room: two balconies for skyline views, a cozy fireplace, a proper living room, a separate bedroom, and a sleek, modern bathroom. The real game-changer, though, was the dining room and fully equipped kitchen. An empty fridge and freezer (no overpriced mini-bar traps), microwave, stovetops, and a complete set of dishes and silverware made the place feel instantly livable. We could have moved in for the weekend—honestly, we practically did.

That kitchen proved invaluable when my friends returned triumphantly with more than 100 leftover hot wings from a $0.25 special. Reheating late-night bounty without hunting for plastic cutlery or paying room service prices felt like luxury of the practical kind.

While Palms Place sits off the Strip, that never felt like a drawback. In Vegas, you’re cabbing or ridesharing regardless—whether you’re at Mandalay Bay heading to XS, or hopping between mid-Strip spots like Bellagio. The little extra distance actually works in your favor: prices are consistently lower than comparable on-Strip properties, yet the quality competes with (and often exceeds) many mid-tier, three-star hotels there.

That stay spoiled me in the best way. Since then, a microwave and an empty fridge have become must-haves when I book a room. I’ll make an exception for Wynn or Encore, but Palms Place set a new bar for what “luxury” should feel like—thoughtful, spacious, and livable. For anyone open to a slightly off-Strip address with on-point amenities and value, Palms Place delivers a refined Vegas experience without sacrificing comfort or convenience.

Sun Asian Kitchen has a name that promises flavor, and for South Phoenix locals, the location is convenient. The standout is its happy hour: budget-friendly bites and booze, like six generously filled crab puffs for just $3. Still, the kitchen’s output lands only a notch above fast food, and the ambiance suffers. Cheesy decor and three blaring TVs on different channels can make dining feel chaotic—especially if Animal Planet’s gross-out clips are playing while you eat. On the plus side, the staff is attentive and lightning-quick, though their rapid-fire chatter might catch you off guard. If you’re nearby and craving something easy without a long drive, it’s a decent, value-forward stop; just don’t expect a serene, high-end experience.

Bask Balances Community Spirit, Cozy Ambience, and Craft Cocktails

We visited Bask with a LivingSocial deal and unexpectedly found the restaurant hosting an Autism Awareness fundraiser. The house offered a complimentary drink, and profits were donated to Autism Services of Mecklenburg County—a thoughtful touch that set a welcoming tone. This event recurs the last Wednesday of each month from 5 to 8 p.m., and while most guests seemed to be there for it, the room never felt crowded. Only one server appeared to be on duty, yet she was attentive and kept our glasses filled without missing a beat.

The space itself is beautiful: polished but not pretentious, equally suited to dressy attire or a casual night out. The menu is concise rather than expansive, but it covers a range of tastes and budgets, with salads and sandwiches under $10 and entrées peaking near $28. You can preview the offerings on their website.

We started with the crab dip, a rich, creamy spread partnered with house-made potato chips. The chips were thick and sturdy enough to scoop generously, and while the dip looked modest in size, it was hearty and generously studded with crab.
