Unfortunately, the kitchen didn’t match that front-of-house excellence.

We ordered the beef bourguignon ($29) and a lamb shank special ($28). The beef was tender but dominated by an assertive salt pork note that smothered the wine-rich depth the dish should showcase. The lamb arrived with a hardened exterior so tough that a fork struggled to pierce it, edging into jerky territory and making the contrast between crust and interior more jarring than satisfying.

At these prices, execution matters. When a bistro charges near-premium rates, seasoning, texture, and balance must be dialed in; otherwise, it’s hard to justify choosing it over consistently better, less expensive options like Meat & Potatoes, Piccolo Forno, Salt, or Eleven.

There is a bright spot: dessert. The sweets merit a dedicated stop for pastry and coffee after dinner elsewhere. With service this stellar, I hope the kitchen finds its footing—Paris 66 could shine if the cooking catches up.

We celebrated Christmas eve this year at Habitat. I had been wanting to dine here since they opened and this was our first opportunity. Just as we suspected, the restaurant was not at all busy. We both liked the ultra modern interior design, the dark woods and the bright punches of color. We were led to a table by one of the windows with a view of PNC Park in the distance and cold and lonely streets in the foreground. I luckily brought along my coat so I would not freeze. From our table, we also had a view of the open kitchen.

We were greeted by Raja, our warm and friendly server. BJ ordered his typical beer and I got my usual adult beverage, but the moment was marred by a glaring lipstick imprint on the rim—a disappointing start.

The menu is limited. We shared a salad and the roasted butternut squash soup with autumn-spiced crème fraîche. Presented with a flourish, the bowl arrived empty and the soup was poured tableside from a small tureen. Unfortunately, the portion was scant, barely covering the bottom, though the flavor was good.

For his entrée, BJ chose the locally raised grass-fed beef. Prior warnings about toughness proved accurate; even a firm grip and the not-so-sharp knife struggled to cut through. He added a baked potato and a side of white cheddar crab mac, which we both felt needed more flavor.

I ordered the shrimp pad thai. It came in an interesting bowl and was an average-size portion. I enjoyed it in the moment, but later had a bout of hives, which I suspect may have been linked to the dish.

We also shared a dessert. It was intriguing in concept, but ultimately forgettable—much like the experience as a whole.

Habitat nails the look and some theatrical touches, and Raja’s warmth helped. But execution faltered: a cleanliness oversight on a cocktail glass, underwhelming soup portions, a tough steak, and sides that didn’t sing. With a quiet dining room on a holiday evening, the kitchen had room to impress, yet the meal never rose beyond average. Attractive setting aside, it’s not an experience I feel compelled to repeat.

Title: Happy Hour Hopes Dashed by Slow Service, So-So Food, and No Football

We visited this bar on a Thursday night with friends, aiming to catch Happy Hour and unwind. Arriving at 5:45, we found a table toward the back of the bar and settled in, expecting quick menus and timely drinks. Instead, we watched our server pass by repeatedly without stopping. When she finally approached, we ordered cocktails and asked for the Happy Hour food menu, only to wait again. She returned with the drinks, dropped them off, and hurried away before we could place our food order.

After more flagging and waiting, we were told Happy Hour had ended five minutes earlier. Given that we’d been seated and ready before the cutoff, we tried to reason with our server, but she said there was nothing she could do. We asked to speak with the manager, and to his credit, he listened, was gracious, and immediately honored Happy Hour pricing. Unfortunately, the service did not improve. Though polite, our server remained absent-minded, missing empty glasses and letting long stretches go by without checking in.

The food didn’t redeem the experience. The smothered fries were the standout, crispy and indulgent, but most other items were greasy in an unappealing way and lacked seasoning. It was disheartening, as the menu had sounded promising and we had come eager to sample several dishes.

Adding to the disappointment, it was peak football season and the big screen was not showing the NFL game. Instead, the television looped house ads for the bar. Between the service missteps, the underwhelming food, and the missed game, we paid our tab and headed elsewhere to watch. Two stars, saved only by a commendable manager.

We hope this was an off night; better attention, clearer Happy Hour cutoffs, and the game on the main screen could earn another chance from us in the future.

Frank’s offers a refreshingly honest service experience—no pressure sales or upselling like you get at Jiffy Lube. The shop is clean, staff are friendly, and complimentary beverages make the wait pleasant. They detailed my car inside and out and left a bottle of water in the cup holder for the road. Thoughtful, efficient, trustworthy.

We went there this weekend to celebrate my daughter’s 21st birthday.

We arrived around 8:30 p.m. with a party of 14 and found the room far from packed, with multiple open tables. Even so, we waited about 40 minutes to be seated, puzzlingly watching a large empty table sit unused near the front while the host team figured out logistics. Once we finally settled in, our server was warm, attentive, and courteous, and a live band kicked off shortly after, lending the night an upbeat, dance-friendly energy. The crowd clearly enjoyed themselves, and for a moment the delay faded into the background.

What ultimately anchors this as a three‑star experience is the value proposition and mismatched expectations. Attempting to reserve in advance required paying $45 per person upfront, excluding gratuity—a steep $630 commitment for our group. Given that our actual bill, including tip, totaled $334, the prepayment policy felt wildly out of sync with reality and not customer‑friendly.

The vibe also leaned more touristy than country. While the space is undeniably lively, anyone seeking a genuinely country bar may be disappointed; this felt like a polished Vegas take on the theme rather than the real deal.

Drinks added to the letdown. Before we were seated, we grabbed mason‑jar beers, with the only options being Coors Light or Miller Lite. At $18 for the pair, the price stung, especially with such limited and basic selections. A broader tap list or a few craft choices would have justified the spend.

Food was in line with expectations: straightforward, indulgent, and not aiming for healthy. It wasn’t great, but it matched the bar‑food archetype and filled the gap.

Overall, we had fun—good music, a lively dance floor, and solid service. But between the prepay policy, the not‑so‑country ambience, and the overpriced, minimal beer selection, it’s not a place we plan to revisit. Between delayed seating despite open tables and policies that favor prepayment over flexibility, the experience felt engineered for tourists more than celebrants seeking genuine country charm.

We dropped in on a Friday night, eager to try somewhere new, and ended up at this spot I’d noticed earlier in the week. First impressions: the dining room was calm—verging on too quiet for dinner—which makes me think they rely on a brisk lunchtime crowd. The ordering and queueing setup took a minute to decode, but once sorted, my turkey and roast beef sub hit the mark: fresh, satisfying, and generously portioned.

The menu’s range is eclectic—sandwiches alongside coffee and milkshakes—which felt a bit unusual for a dinner visit. I considered a malt but my companions steered us to Culver’s for dessert instead. Service was a bright spot; everyone we interacted with was friendly, and the space was notably clean.

Overall, I’d call it a 3.5-star experience, rounded down given the slow vibe and slightly confusing system. I’m undecided about returning for dinner, but I could see stopping by at lunchtime when the energy is higher.

Overpriced. Mediocre dim sum.

Since the ownership change, Vegas locals have largely moved on—and now I understand why. I gave it one try and that was plenty. Service was curt and indifferent, the dim sum itself was ordinary at best, and prices ran higher than comparable spots around town. With nothing distinctive to offset the premium, there’s simply no compelling reason to return.

Customer service should extend from the headquarters, while in transit and directly to the customers door when you are a courier service.

At approximately 12:20 p.m. in the Ocotillo area, I found myself behind an ON TRAC van marked with logo magnets on both doors. Over the next half mile, the driver’s behavior made a troubling impression. I had my right blinker engaged for a planned turn when the courier abruptly cut right ahead of me without signaling. Moments later, at the first stop sign, I signaled left and came to a full stop; the van neither signaled nor stopped, coasting straight through the stop and turning left as if traffic rules were optional.

Continuing down the curved road where I live, the driver noticed my car approaching and immediately hit the brakes, coming to a complete stop in the middle of the street. I stopped too. He peered into his right-side mirror and shot me an unmistakably annoyed look. My home was two houses up on the left—I simply wanted to get home. After a brief exchange of gestures, he motioned for me to pass. I pulled into my garage, and, curious whether he was still blocking the street, I checked my mailbox. He was. He exited the van to inspect the tires in the lane—without hazard lights—then got back in and drove away.

What stood out was not a single minor lapse but a series of choices that disregarded basic safety, courtesy, and professionalism. Failing to signal, rolling through a stop sign, stopping mid-lane without hazards, and displaying irritation toward a nearby driver reflect a mindset misaligned with the responsibilities of operating a logoed vehicle. Couriers aren’t just package handlers; they’re ambassadors of the brand, and their conduct on the road shapes customer trust long before a package reaches the doorstep.

If this individual had been en route to my home, I would have felt uneasy inviting him onto my property. The experience suggests a need for stronger training and accountability: consistent signaling, complete stops, hazard light usage when stationary in traffic, situational awareness, and professional demeanor under stress. When customer service truly extends from HQ to the curb, it shows in how drivers share the road.

I don’t know who will be delivering my next parcel, but I know who it won’t be.

The Chart House in Scottsdale wears its national legacy like a well-loved blazer: familiar, comfortable, a touch worn at the seams. Its lakeside setting is undeniably picturesque, the kind of desert-sunset view that can paper over a multitude of culinary shrugs, and the service is steady and pleasant. But in a city with a sharp competitive edge, this stalwart feels more nostalgic than noteworthy.

That nostalgia shows in the clientele—multi-generational families who have been coming for years and now bring their kids and grandkids. There’s nothing wrong with that ritual; it’s just not fueling much ambition on the plate.

We started with coconut shrimp and blue-cheese, panko-crusted asparagus. The shrimp was a deliberate indulgence—our guilty-pleasure benchmark from another chain—and here it landed as a forgettable throwaway. The asparagus, by contrast, was the evening’s surprise: hardly pretty, but the tangy, crunchy crust made it the most talked-about bite of the night.

The macadamia-crusted mahi that followed never quite took off. The fish lacked that delicate flake you hope for, and a peanut-leaning sauce sat heavy, muting rather than complementing the mahi’s mild sweetness. A Caesar salad arrived with precisely three croutons and the pre-prepped feel that saps a classic of its snap.

Cocktails, priced around ten dollars, were the bigger letdown. The pours were timid and the flavors even more so; a pineapple caipirinha tasted more idea than execution, and we couldn’t justify a second round with the entrees.

Years ago, a visit to the San Diego Chart House left us optimistic. Here, those hopes went largely unmet. We wouldn’t refuse an invitation—especially with that view—but we won’t be seeking one out. In the end, it’s an overpriced, so-so evening buoyed by scenery. For comfort and nostalgia, it suffices; for culinary spark, look elsewhere.

As someone who roots for mom-and-pop cafés, it might seem odd that I keep circling back to a big-name coffee chain. The reasons are refreshingly simple: location, friendly staff, and a consistent menu. When I need to meet a friend or coworker without hopping in a car, this spot is the only comfortable walk from my neighborhood—and its proximity to the greenway makes it easy to grab a cup and take a leisurely stroll. Convenience here isn’t just a perk; it’s the main draw.

Credit where it’s due: the newer manager appears to be moving the team in a positive direction, giving employees more to be proud of. That said, there’s still room to grow. I’d love to see more proactive customer engagement and less chatter behind the counter. On busy days, listening to extended internal banter or petty griping can be frustrating. A little more focus on guests would elevate the experience from good to great.

Reliability is the chain’s strongest suit. You can count on the same standards and offerings, and the lineup of limited-time items keeps things interesting. I appreciate the sampling of new products—many are tempting without feeling gimmicky—alongside dependable staples.

One standout in customer care is the thought put into free water. Over the years, the setup evolved from a self-serve cooler and mini cups for thirsty greenway walkers, to staff-dispensed cups at the counter, and now to a slender bottle and small cups tucked in a secondary station. This latest iteration strikes the right balance: accessible to everyone, yet tidier and a touch more refined. It’s a quietly fantastic improvement.

The outdoor seating area remains a favorite—I’ve spent many hours there, lingering with a book or catching up with colleagues. And while the pastry case can be tempting, the organic packaged snacks by the register are a welcome alternative for days when a giant muffin feels like too much.

It may not be the scrappy local café of my heart, but for walkable convenience, consistent quality, and thoughtful touches, this chain keeps earning my repeat visits. A bit more customer focus, and it would truly shine.

The food was good but not worth the premium.

We visited hoping to support a local spot and left with mixed feelings. Our waitress was attentive, professional, and made us feel welcome. Unfortunately, the manager or owner’s behavior overshadowed the experience. He repeatedly spoke down to her, yelling, which created an uncomfortable atmosphere. Worse, we watched him drop a handful of napkins in a foot-traffic area near the food pickup station, then pick them up and return them to the clean pile instead of discarding them. That decision raised serious concerns about hygiene and standards. While the dishes were decent, the price point doesn’t match the value when leadership treats staff poorly and ignores basic sanitation practices. We might have returned based on the initial service, but after witnessing this, we won’t be back. It’s disappointing, because we want locally owned businesses to thrive. Respect for employees and cleanliness should come first.

Yes this IS as good as it gets. I’ve shopped several Sprouts, and I was thrilled when one opened nearby. The produce is consistently top-notch, with prices that beat competitors. I also love the bulk section and the well-run meat department. Finding grain-fed and organic options at reasonable prices is rare, yet Sprouts delivers. Friendly service seals the deal. Truly Thx!

this is an expensive hotel.

From the moment we arrived, the experience fell short of expectations. The property touts valet parking, but after driving a pristine rental straight from the airport and double-checking it with three people, we received it back the next day with a conspicuous scratch. The hotel is “investigating,” but the process was opaque and slow, and we waited far too long in the lobby while an unhelpful, unfriendly staff member handled our case. That first impression set the tone.

Housekeeping was equally disappointing. On the second day, after a long outing in the desert, we returned to find our room unmade—no fresh towels, no tidying, nothing. Even worse, the carpet was riddled with stains that belied the hotel’s relatively young age; we were surprised to learn it’s only four years old. The view from our room overlooked an abandoned parking lot, hardly the premium outlook an expensive property should offer. The one undeniable highlight was the sunrise, which was gorgeous—and, amusingly, the only thing that felt truly free.

Comfort wasn’t better inside. The bed and pillows were poor quality; the mattress was overly soft with prominent springs, and we woke up multiple times each night with significant back pain. Later in our trip, sleeping on a simple air mattress felt like a relief compared to that bed. The lobby’s overpowering perfume scent was another misstep—so strong it bordered on painful.

For a hotel that projects a classy image, the reality was inconsistent service, questionable upkeep, and subpar comfort. We won’t be returning.

After an unfortunate staff snafu on check in, we settled into our suite.

We experienced a hiccup at check-in, but once we reached our suite, the stay was delightful. The room was lovely, well-appointed, and the bed comfortable. The remodeled areas deliver a clean, contemporary vibe—refreshingly restrained compared with Vegas’s usual excess. Breakfast at Café Nikki was a highlight: a generous spread of fresh fruits and berries, excellent coffee, and fresh-squeezed juices, all enjoyed on the patio overlooking the pool. Server assistant Amanda deserves special mention for her sweet, friendly service. We also dined at Bacio, where both the cuisine and hospitality impressed. Despite the front-desk misstep, we’d likely return, provided those arrival issues are resolved.

As parks go, this one is ok. It checks the basic boxes: swings and slides for kids, broad grass fields for pickup games and tag, and a lake where people fish, feed ducks, and linger at the water’s edge. You’ll notice plenty of seniors, likely because there’s a senior center on site, which gives the place a relaxed, community feel.

I mainly visit parks to run my dogs, and this spot works fine for that—most days. What keeps things interesting are the geese, who have no intention of yielding the right of way. My large German Shepherd once ambled over to sniff one, purely curious, and the goose exploded into pecks and flapping wings. I won’t lie: we both spooked, and I may have jogged straight back to the car.

Lately the park feels a bit shadier, probably a reflection of the surrounding neighborhood, which isn’t the best. Still, the mix of amenities, open space, and lakeside moments keep drawing me back. It’s not perfect, but it’s familiar, practical, and occasionally unforgettable—thanks, in part, to those fearless geese that roam here.

I found the service here OK and the facilities good, but I had hoped for a much more personal approach.

I visited this clinic with expectations shaped by its website, which suggested a warm, personalized experience. In practice, the atmosphere felt more businesslike—typical of many medical establishments today—though the staff remained polite and respectful throughout. Facilities were clean and well maintained; check-in at reception was straightforward. Despite a light crowd, I waited a little over an hour to be called. Longer than hoped, but better than I’ve seen at urgent care centers. A triage system was in place; people arriving after me were seen first.

Once escorted to the exam room, routine vitals—temperature and blood pressure—were taken promptly, after which I waited another half hour for the physician. The consultation itself was the highlight: unhurried, attentive, and collaborative. The doctor listened carefully, asked thoughtful questions, and took time to discuss my concerns and options.

Overall, the clinic delivers competent, respectful care, but it may not meet expectations for a more personalized touch. If you value thorough, unrushed consultations and can tolerate moderate wait times, this practice is a very reasonable choice.

Came here the other night for a birthday.

The evening started on a promising note. Service was attentive at first, and the fried bhinda (okra) arrived hot and crisp—well seasoned and satisfying. Unfortunately, as we dug deeper, the batch tasted more burnt than fried toward the bottom of the bowl. My paper dosa with cheese had great texture—crispy—but the filling was sparse; they barely added any cheese. The chili naan missed the mark; it was packed with chilies, so each bite tasted like a whole chile, and no one at our table could handle it. When we were ready for the check, and possibly dessert, service evaporated. It took roughly 30 minutes and several awkward waves to flag someone down. The neighborhood is fine overall, though construction and tight parking add minor hassles. Despite the missteps, there were bright spots, and I’d give it another try, hoping for more consistency.

My parents stayed here whenever they visited me at ASU, and for good reason. Less than a 10-minute drive from campus, Arizona Grand is the best full-service resort within easy range of Tempe. As a student, I slipped in for afternoons by the pools to read and unwind, and I loved warming up at the fire pits after dark. It isn’t the cheapest option, but when I return to town, I’ll try to book it if my budget allows. Tip: skip Rustler’s Rooste, but definitely stay here.

Red Carpet VIP is a MUST if you plan on partying in Vegas. They are a professional operation, not some shady promoter you meet on the street.

Here’s how it works: you connect with one of their sales staff, share your budget and the kind of music and vibe you want, and they build your nights (and days) out with smart, tailored recommendations. The biggest surprise was that they actually prioritize value. They don’t push the priciest tables just to pad a bill; they find the setup that makes sense for your group. In our case, we had 10 girls and they suggested a seven-person table at Tryst because the larger option was exponentially more expensive. The table location they secured was perfect, and they can even tell you your exact placement in advance.

Once you lock in the plan, payment is handled through a streamlined system that assigns an amount to each person. No single card gets hit for the entire night, and you avoid the hassle of splitting charges later. The best part is the simplicity at the door: everything is prepaid, so you don’t need to bring cash or worry about tabs.

On the day of your party, a staff member reaches out by phone to coordinate a meeting spot. We never had trouble linking up with our rep, and from there the VIP experience kicks in. You skip every line. Even as guests at the Wynn, we used Red Carpet VIP because the club lines are relentless. Who wants to stand around forever and then negotiate bottle service?

Buying the table in advance also guarantees your spot. More than once we saw same-night buyers turned away because inventory was gone. With Red Carpet VIP, your table is waiting.

Yes, bottle service can seem like a splurge, but with a bigger group it often nets out as the smarter spend compared to individual covers and rounds at the bar. Factor in the time saved and the certainty of entry, and this service becomes close to priceless.

If this existed in New York, I’d use it constantly. In Vegas, it’s less a luxury than an essential. For anyone heading there to celebrate, Red Carpet VIP delivers convenience, value, and true VIP treatment. I’ll be booking with them again and recommending them to anyone planning a night out on the Strip. Skip the stress, lock in a great table, and let a seasoned team handle the details while you focus on making the most of Vegas.

On my wife’s recommendation, I tried this spot and it’s awesome. The snow cones are seriously good—refreshing, flavorful, and perfect for the season. With tons of flavors and a genuinely friendly owner, it’s an easy favorite. If you haven’t been yet, go now, seriously.

My daughter and I had rushed pedicures. The service felt hurried and incomplete; my heels hardly improved. While my toenails were repainted, the entire appointment lasted barely 20 minutes. Overall, disappointing quality and poor attention to detail. I won’t be returning. Not worth it.

A themed fine Italian restaurant at Bellagio delivers a whimsical, sophisticated take on Tuscan dining inside what feels like an elegant European carnival tent. The big-top-inspired decor is playful yet refined, with billowing fabrics, bold colors, and theatrical flourishes that set a celebratory tone. From our booth, the views of the Bellagio fountains were spectacular—mesmerizing and romantic. It was a bit of a long walk from Vdara, but absolutely worth it for the atmosphere and overall experience.

We had a 7:30 reservation and were seated within two minutes despite the room being nearly packed. Service was exceptionally organized, with one server dedicated to drinks and another to our food, keeping the pace smooth and attentive without feeling rushed. My specialty cocktail was delicious and balanced, a great prelude as we browsed a menu that leans into Tuscan classics with creative polish. The tasting menu tempted, but it included lamb, which I don’t eat, so we curated our own feast.

We started with a full dozen seasonal oysters with cocktail and mignonette—briny, pristine, and among the best we’ve had. The insalata mista, featuring organic field greens, marinated Campari tomatoes, pecorino, and balsamic, was bright and impeccably fresh. A Tuscan vegetable and bean soup (frantoiana) with fettunta delivered layered comfort; earthy, herbal, and deeply satisfying.

Prosciutto-wrapped Maine diver scallops arrived with grilled red onions, celery root purée, baby zucchini, pomegranate, and salmoriglio—perfectly executed and flavorful without tipping into saltiness. The grilled beef tenderloin (filetto di manzo), paired with porcini in pâte brick, truffle potato dauphinoise, and a Barolo reduction, was a standout; my husband devoured the 14-ounce steak with sheer delight.

Portions were generous, and we left full and happy. The total bill for two, including one specialty cocktail and no dessert, was $175—fair value for an upscale Bellagio dining room with postcard views. Service earns a 5, decor and ambience a 5, and food a strong 4. For a romantic date, request a booth facing the fountains. Between the theatrical setting, polished hospitality, and consistently delicious plates, this is a memorable, classy night out.

Massive Scottsdale scene with a flashy, gaudy vibe. Came for a business meeting; both steaks arrived extremely rare and had to be sent back. The waiter forgot items, and overall the food was mediocre for the price point. The place is run oddly: bouncer-style staff with earpieces circulate every 15 minutes to “check in,” but it feels intrusive rather than hospitable. If you love big club atmospheres and a status‑driven crowd, maybe it’s your spot. If you prefer relaxed dining, attentive service, and well-executed steaks, look elsewhere. For us, the ambiance overwhelmed the meal, and the service missed the mark. Wouldn’t return.

What can I say it's an airport, it has airplanes.....and so much more!

This airport delivers more than expected. Dining options abound—from a pretzel place to Ruby’s Diner and Nathan’s Hot Dogs—so grabbing a bite is easy. The facility is impressively clean, restrooms included, and clear signage makes navigation straightforward. Slot machines dot the concourses, adding a quintessential local touch if you still want to try your luck. The lone drawback is at Terminal 3: after baggage claim, the shuttle requires a long walk from the ticket kiosk to the actual pickup area. Convenient overall, but that trek feels unnecessary.

From looking at all the pictures on Yelp, MAGR looked like a pretty casual bistro feel eatery, but I guess at night it’s oooh la la time!

Arriving with a group of seven, we were pleasantly surprised by how smoothly the evening began. With reservations, our wait was a brief 15 minutes before being led to a round table tucked into a cozy corner—an ideal setup for conversation and shared plates. The space itself feels airy and romantic: soaring ceilings, rustic hanging lamps, and a warm glow that softens the bustle. It’s the kind of ambiance that elevates a casual expectation into something more polished. And that round table? A thoughtful touch. Too often large parties get stretched across rectangles where chatter turns into shouting; here, everyone stays in the conversation.

Service kept pace with the crowd, friendly and efficient, with a dash of humor. We asked for more bread—again and again—and overheard a playful, “They want MORE bread?” Yes, we do. The crusty French loaf became a recurring cast member, essential for sopping up sauces and spreading appetizers. A small caveat: the paper-covered tables can be a hazard. One of us earned a surprisingly sharp paper cut, so take care.

We opened with the Country pâté, choosing it over the Mousse on the assumption the latter might be too airy. Flavor-wise, it was spot on: savory and well-seasoned. Texture-wise, it skewed coarse, making it challenging to spread gracefully over bread. If you’re a fan of rustic, chunky pâtés, you’ll be pleased; if you prefer silky, you may wish for something smoother. The escargots were a crowd favorite, tender and drenched in a garlicky pesto that begged for extra bread to mop the plate clean.

The soup du jour—cream of garlic—felt tailor-made for the garlic-obsessed. Luxuriously creamy, boldly aromatic, and served in a generous bowl, it sparked communal dipping from neighbors who couldn’t resist. Sharing is easy when the portions invite it.

For a lighter entrée, the scallops gratin (listed as an appetizer) arrived rich and deeply flavorful. Caramelized onions, Gruyère, Parmesan, and garlic layered into an indulgent bake where the scallops played second fiddle to the robust toppings. Delicious, yes—but intense. After four, we were reaching for water. This is best shared, and even one can satisfy a craving for cheesy, garlicky comfort.

Other tastes varied: the seared scallops leaned fishy and unapologetically scallopy—less balanced than the gratin. The steak with herbed butter, while pleasantly seasoned, landed on the thinner, slightly tough side. Both were serviceable but not standouts.

Overall, MAGR delivers a charming night out with solid value. Sit outside if you can and let the Bellagio fountains add a touch of spectacle. Whether you’re planning a romantic date or wrangling a big group, the ambiance, portions, and price point make this a worthwhile Vegas stop. Just mind the table paper—and don’t be shy about asking for more bread.

Good Food, Patchy Service at Encore’s Art-Lined Steakhouse

We dined here a few weeks ago while staying at The Encore and left with mixed impressions. The room is striking, anchored by a massive Botero sculpture and surrounded by bold paintings, with a serene view of the pool from the interior. On a warmer night, the patio would elevate the experience further.

At our server’s suggestion, we opened with ravioli—whether a special or a menu staple, they were a delight: tender, well-seasoned, and executed. For mains, we each ordered the filet; mine came chimichurri-style, a preparation that surprised by being balanced rather than overpowering. Both steaks were cooked precisely to request. Among the sides, the asparagus didn’t impress, lacking the snap and seasoning we’d hoped for, while the scalloped potatoes were a standout—creamy, richly flavored, and baked to perfection.

Dessert was the kitchen’s shining moment. We shared mini cupcakes and a chocolate soufflé; both were excellent, though the soufflé arrived extremely hot without warning, so approach with care. The wine list offered intriguing options, yet we settled into familiar territory with a bottle of Cakebread, which paired comfortably with the meal.

Service was the evening’s weak link. Despite the restaurant being only about half full, our server vanished after delivering the mains and didn’t return for roughly thirty minutes, dampening the otherwise pleasant pacing. Though the restaurant aims for upscale, there’s no required dress code, so expect a mix of attire—you might be dining next to guests in muumuus. Overall, a pleasant meal with room for service improvements.

Ok so I finally got to check out the High Roller, thanks to a friend at Caesars Entertainment—a free walk-on like a boss. I went on a weeknight, and the place was a ghost town; our pod (“bubble”) had only three others. Honestly, I wished we’d had it to ourselves—I had some harmless shenanigans queued up, lol.

The ride itself is interesting, and the views are great for photos, which I definitely snagged. Our cabin didn’t have a bar, but that was fine since we planned to hit a real bar afterward for proper libations. As an experience, it’s cool to do once, especially if you can skip the line and the price. But for me, it’s firmly a one-and-done: been there, done that, and I won’t be rushing back for seconds.

Long wait and rather rude wait staff set the tone. Overall service wasn’t great. The food was okay, nothing special. The menu aims for upscale, organic with a grungy twist. I had the french toast: good custard, but the bread was burned—black without charred flavor, still off-putting. The chorizo sausage is the star, rich and spicy, though you’ll be burping it all day. The best part is eating outside under umbrellas on a nice day, dog at your side. Unfortunately, the long wait, curt attitudes, and uneven execution diminish the appeal. At similar prices, I’d rather go to Vivace, which consistently delivers better hospitality and more polished plates. Zada Jane’s has potential, but on this visit it fell short. Not recommended.

On a recent visit, we paid for parking, a cover, and then got hustled with feeble drinks. My $8 pre-tip Long Island iced tea tasted like pure sweet-and-sour with an eyedropper of tequila. The vodka cranberry was even worse. My bartender friend laughed; his professional verdict matched my own. A friend’s tequila shot arrived with ice crystals — a telltale sign of dilution — and the buzz never arrived, which I guess is their hangover prevention plan.

If you’re paying a cover, you expect something beyond the privilege of entry. Here, the value proposition is thin: full-priced weak cocktails, $4 beers, and the kind of bait-and-switch that leaves you reaching for Five Guys a few doors down or Rite Aid for supplies for the after-party. The late-night scene delivers the typical drunken circus on the sidewalk, and the shot girl’s attire skews closer to strip-club than bar uniform — if that’s your thing.

Bottom line: between watered-down liquor and extra fees, this spot feels more hustle than hospitality. I won’t be back, and I wouldn’t recommend it.

Been with Capstone for many years with Sue. Once I divorced and had to get coverage on my own, Sue retired and had to deal with some dude name Eric. That is when my troubles began. Rarely ever had a question answered even when I needed answers about payments that wouldnt process on my Insurance companies website. Everytime I called their 800 # and tried to speak to a representative I was routed back to Capstone to Erics poor Secretary who seemed to not know what was going. She would forward me to Erics voicemail and I wouldn't even get a courtesy call back. BAD BUSINESS!!! What do you expect in Las Vegas! What if I was in an accident and needed to file a claim? Who would I call? Jumped online and got insurance quotes from different major companies online. Covered by Progressive. Decent rate and if I call, there is a representative available 24 hrs a day.

After years of reliable service at Capstone with Sue, my experience took a sharp downturn when I needed coverage post-divorce and Sue retired. Assigned to Eric, I struggled to get even basic questions answered, including why payments wouldn’t process on my carrier’s website. Calls to the 800 number repeatedly bounced me back to Capstone, where Eric’s secretary seemed uninformed and could only route me to his voicemail. I never received a courtesy call back. The lack of responsiveness felt risky—if I had an accident and needed to file a claim, who would help? Frustrated, I stopped relying on the agency and shopped online, comparing quotes from insurers. I ultimately chose Progressive for a decent rate and, more importantly, dependable access to a representative 24/7. Capstone’s service was once solid, but the transition exposed serious communication gaps. Insurance is about trust and availability; when those vanish, it’s time to move on. Bad business, especially in a market like Las Vegas.

Bad service, reeeally slow chefs. We were the first guests in the restaurant, and after an hour of waiting for sushi/sashimi, the waitress told us they hadn’t even started our order. When did sushi-making start taking so long? We canceled and bounced. I can’t speak to the food quality, because we never got any, but an hour is unacceptable for basics. If you’re staying in the hotel, save yourself frustration and drive to Henderson—there are better Japanese spots worth the trip.

Great place with awesome food, friendly service, clean bathrooms, and a calm Sun City vibe. Southern Asian flavors shine—Thai, Vietnamese, Muong, with a touch of Indian—the Thai is especially excellent. A top lunch spot I keep returning to. Only drawback: the kitchen closes from 2:30 to 5 p.m., so plan your meal times accordingly.

I recently dined at The Carlton inside the BNY Mellon complex for a friend’s birthday, part of a group of twelve. Credit where it’s due: service was the evening’s strong suit. Our waiter was attentive, thorough, and proactive with suggestions. I took his advice on the gnocchi appetizer; it was decent—pillowy enough, sauced competently—solid B, nothing memorable but not a misstep.

For the entrée, I was torn between the lamb chops and the prime rib. The server nudged me toward the prime rib, cooked to the chef’s recommendation. It arrived at about medium-rare, but disappointingly not hot—lukewarm at best. Temperature issues aside, the bigger letdown was flavor. The beef tasted flat, lacking the depth and seasoning that should define a prime rib at this price point. The mashed potatoes shared the same temperature problem, which compounded the impression that the kitchen’s execution was off.

What stung most was the mismatch between reputation and reality. Friends had enthusiastically recommended the prime rib, and they were genuinely surprised when I relayed my experience. For the cost, the food simply didn’t deliver. I wouldn’t return on my own, though I’d attend if another group celebration landed there.

Ironically, the highlight was the $8 coffee at the end—well-made and actually hot. A practical plus: if you park in the BNY Mellon garage, the hostess stand validates. Polished service and conveniences can’t compensate, however, for inconsistent temperature and underwhelming flavors.

pretty terrible.

Ordered delivery through Grubhub: a chicken kabab meal with two sides and penne bolognese with garlic bread. The pasta was decent, but the ranch side salad was missing; they had to return to deliver it. The garlic bread was dry with singed, burned corners. The chicken kabab meal disappointed: the chicken was passable after microwaving, but the pita arrived soggy from being packed against the hot chicken. The “tabouli” resembled anything but; odd orange pieces, flavor like slightly pickled cucumbers and tomatoes, and none of the bright, parsley-forward freshness you expect. The Greek salad arrived undressed, inexplicably topped with melted cheese—a baffling twist that muddied the basics. Overall execution felt careless, from packaging to components, making the meal feel like a bad comedy sketch. If you’re in Tempe and tempted to roll the dice on delivery, consider skipping this spot—especially the salads and tabouli—and save yourself the frustration. With so few reliable options, it’s frustrating to cross another off the list, but this experience was a clear miss. You’ve been warned. Delivery hiccups only compounded the letdown, from start to finish.

Love this place.
The bartenders are super friendly, quick to recommend inventive cocktails, and even swap them out if you’re not into the first pick—no hassle. I love sinking into the lounge seating by the fireplaces; it’s cozy, chill, and perfect for conversation. Happy hour brings a small snacky buffet that pairs nicely with another round. Don’t expect $8 drinks; most hover around $12, but the quality and creativity make the price feel fair. Service is attentive, the vibe is polished yet welcoming, and they even validate valet parking for Scottsdale Quarter. A reliable go-to for relaxed evenings and memorable drinks.

My love affair with the British classic: Fish and Chips can be a fickle relationship.

Too often the chips are soggy, the batter limp, the fish rubbery, or a hollow shell hides a missing fillet. The Globetrotter consistently fixes those failings. Their batter shatters with a golden crunch, the fish is moist and flaky, and the chips are properly fried—hot, fluffy inside, with a satisfying bite. Contrary to a previous review, they seem to have cleaned their act up, and then some. Around 5pm you’ll spot a patient crowd beneath the gleaming neon sign, waiting for generous portions piled into a card box. Expect to pay about £6. It’s not the cheapest, but you’re paying for quality—and finally getting fish and chips done right.

While I can’t vouch for the drinks, they looked like works of art parading past the bar. The food, however, lands squarely in the so-so category - edible but unmemorable. What truly stands out is the decor: an immersive, one-of-a-kind interior that feels transportive and unlike anything else in Vegas. It's worth a special stop to take it all in.

Where the experience faltered was service. The staff seemed disengaged, and the host at the door appeared eager to be elsewhere - an unenthusiastic greeting, a perfunctory seat assignment, then eyes back to a book. Everyone has off days, but the first impression set the tone.

Bottom line: go to marvel at the space and the spectacle of the cocktails; temper expectations for food and warmth. Uniqueness alone makes it a curiosity worth checking out.

I've been a 24 Hour Fitness member for the last 10 years

After a decade with 24 Hour Fitness, I can say this location outperforms the chain's average. Parking is easy most of the time, with predictable crunch between 5-7 p.m. The location is convenient for my routine and daily commute. The equipment mix is solid: a decent range of weight machines and free weights — not the most expansive floor, but far from minimal. Group classes are solid, though they could be more frequent.

The sauna, steam room, and pool are generally in good shape. The steam room does go offline occasionally when someone throws water on the thermostat and blows a fuse, but maintenance turns it around. The salt-water pool is a noticeable upgrade.

Recent locker room renovations brought larger lockers, which I appreciate. The showers, however, are due for an update. Better showerheads would help, and the cleaning products could smell fresher.

Staff here are consistently friendly and helpful, and the sales team has grown less pushy over the years. The Kid's Club is spacious and comfortable for children seven and under.

Bottom line: If you want a dependable place to work out, lose weight, and the flexibility of using other 24 Hour Fitness locations, this gym fits the bill.
Enticing aroma, but flavors disappoint. Sauce is decent, not great. Cole slaw bland. Beans divide us; husband likes them, I don't. Not bad. Would I return? Maybe, expectations still.

Scheduling here was impossible. I called during regular business hours, let it ring about 20 times, finally reached someone who promised a callback to schedule—nothing. When I tried again, I got a busy signal. Another attempt rang endlessly. Securing an appointment shouldn’t be this hard. I’m taking business elsewhere.

I don't know where to start with this place.

When we arrived, the dining area looked chaotic and unclean, with crumbs on the seats. Our server seemed disengaged and rude, setting a tone. The salad arrived limp, with watery ranch dressing that suggested poor preparation. We then endured a long wait for our entrees, only to be served dishes that were cold and bland. The combination of sloppy service and tired ingredients made the experience frustrating from start to finish. I won’t be returning, and I wouldn’t recommend spending your time or money here. Choose someplace that respects customers with cleanliness, courtesy, and food served at the proper temperature.

Pretty sweet.

During a recent business trip, I was bumped from the main resort to a villa due to overbooking, and it turned into a pleasant surprise. I stayed in Building 4, Room 101—a true one‑bedroom apartment. The compact kitchen came stocked with dishes and essentials, making it easy to prepare meals for a small group. A stacked washer and dryer was a welcome, complimentary perk, especially for a longer stay. The whirlpool tub was wonderful, and Westin’s signature Heavenly Bed lived up to its name, delivering restful sleep. I loved having a private patio to soak in the weather and a quieter, separate pool area for both kids and adults away from the bustle of the main resort. Service throughout was friendly and efficient. All told, this villa stay felt comfortable, convenient, and well cared for—I’d happily return.

Not the most life-changing meal I've ever had.

I’d long wanted to try Benihana, and Las Vegas felt like the place to do it. With 115-degree heat outside and a hibachi blazing inches away, the evening was literally and figuratively hot. The chef’s onion volcano—briefly set aflame—was a fun crowd-pleaser, but the mango shrimp I ordered was surprisingly bland, lacking the punch I expected. Service helped salvage the night: our waitress closed with a charming magic trick, somehow tugging a scarf from my sleeve, and left us smiling. Still, for the price, the experience didn’t match the hype. It wasn’t awful, just unremarkable. I’m glad I tried it once, but I don’t see myself returning—to this location or to Benihana in general, ever again.

Really, no stars! I ordered a chimichanga for pick up close to closing. I mentioned I would like sour cream and guacamole as well. I expected a possible charge for sc and guacamole, then again I've other places that already provides it part of the meal. Anywho, I arrive to only having to wait 3-5 min. I lived 5 min. Away, not bad! When I received my meal to go, of course I checked for the guacamole and sour cream to no avail. I politely inquired of absence of side condiments. This is where it gets interesting. I had already checked the receipt and it was charges for .99 twice (guacamole and sc) the cashier stated it was inside of the chimi.

That explanation might pass if the inside portion matched the expectation of a paid add-on. It didn’t. I cut into the chimichanga right there, found a whisper of guacamole and sour cream, then asked for a bit more on the side and offered to pay the difference for what should have been included. For context, their posted prices for 4 oz containers are $1.99 for guacamole and $1.15 for sour cream. I wasn’t asking for freebies—just a reasonable adjustment: about $1 more for guac and $0.15 for sour cream given the minuscule amount already present.

Instead of meeting me halfway, the cashier and waitress held firm: no extra unless I paid full price for both condiments, essentially double-charging after already adding a barely-there portion inside. They even went to the back to confirm and returned with the same stance. Five more minutes passed while the cashier consulted someone on the phone. The answer didn’t change, and my food sat cooling while we debated basic customer service and common sense.

At that point, I asked for a refund and suggested two simple solutions: either pack what they’d already given me and I’d go, or remake the chimichanga fresh with the condiments on the side, properly measured. They refused to remake it, and the refund—just over eight dollars—came with visible reluctance. I left, rode across the parking lot to El Pollo Loco, and salvaged dinner elsewhere. I was really craving a chimi, but not at the cost of time, frustration, and a sense that fairness is negotiable.

The takeaway is bigger than a side of guacamole. When a customer is willing to pay a reasonable difference, rigid policy and penny-wise decisions can turn a small request into a lost loyal patron. Transparency about condiment portions, consistent to-go packaging, and empowering staff to use judgment—especially near closing—are basics that prevent this exact scenario. Give customers the option to have add-ons on the side, honor posted prices logically, and don’t make a refund feel like a favor. A little flexibility would have saved the sale—and the goodwill.

Holy Ravioli! This has got to be one of the premier hotels on the planet. Get lost along its Venice-inspired canals, pause for anchovy-scented bites, and revel in the chorus of street performers at every turn. Add the high-octane Blue Man Group and sun-drenched Tao Beach, and you’ve got a Vegas getaway the Griswolds would celebrate. Luxe rooms, lively casino vibes, and nonstop entertainment abound—casino wins, however, are sold separately.

This place was pretty good, with a trendy yet casual vibe and the fun perk of watching chefs prepare pizzas right in front of you. Our server was a cutie and kept things friendly and efficient. Food-wise, everyone at our table enjoyed their meals, though the prices felt a bit on the high side for what you get. I did have one hiccup: I bit into something hard as a rock in my pizza, which briefly made me worry I’d chipped a tooth. Thankfully, I was fine. Overall, enjoyable spot with room for improvement.

Once a solid 4–5-star spot, this restaurant has slipped in recent months. The removal of Saturday brunch marked the downturn, followed by inconsistent reservation policies and noticeably smaller portions on our last three visits. While the food remains tasty, the value no longer offsets the frustration. Service has suffered too, with undertrained staff creating avoidable headaches. To reclaim its former standing, management should restore generous serving sizes, standardize reservations, and keep new hires off the floor until properly trained, plus attentive managerial oversight.

#500

For our fourth wedding anniversary, my wife and I chose a destination that matches the magnitude of the occasion: the Mansion at MGM, home to Joël Robuchon’s temple of haute cuisine. The evening began with a flourish—a complimentary gold MGM limo pulling up to our door and sweeping us into a world that feels reserved for high rollers and movie scenes. At the Mansion, a stunning hostess with Bond-girl poise welcomed us into a space that radiates hushed luxury. This is what indulgence looks like.

We arrived intending to brave the famed 16-course journey, but realism prevailed; my petite wife would have met her match long before the finish line. We pivoted gracefully to a four-course experience, polished with a steady sparkle of champagne. Service is immaculate, choreography-tight, and ever-so-formal—borderline stuffy for some tastes, though undeniably refined. It’s the sort of place where the napery is ironed to a whisper and every gesture is rehearsed.

Then, a moment of culinary legend: a cheerful “Bon soir!” announced the man himself. Joël Robuchon appeared tableside, shook our hands, and wished us a memorable evening. Staff mentioned he visits about four times a year; we were fortunate. I briefly considered asking him to sign a roll from the astonishing bread cart—a whimsical idea, quickly replaced by the more sensible option of savoring every bite.

The cooking was precise yet generous in spirit. A lobster salad with fruit arrived like a jewel box and tasted even better—bright, sweet, and bracingly fresh. Foie gras was silken, masterfully balanced, and a reminder of why this indulgence endures in culinary lore. The veal cheek, tender to its core, married the comforting depth of a slow-braised cut with the plushness of fine steak—luxurious and utterly satisfying.

Dessert brought its own celebration. The team surprised us with an additional course for our anniversary: a white-and-yellow meringue fruit confection that was as elegant as it was delicious. We ordered two more desserts because, why not, and then the dessert cart rolled in like a finale—lavish, irresistible, and emblematic of the house’s generosity.

Three hours later, blissfully full and thoroughly pampered, we stepped back into the limo and into the night. This is an experience built for milestones: opulent, meticulously executed, and unforgettable. Go for the complimentary limo, stay for the parade of craftsmanship, and raise a glass to dining as theater. Highly recommended.

I vacillated between giving this boutique a 3 or a 4, and ultimately rounded up, hopeful that future visits will be even more successful. After meaning to check out Poor Little Rich Girl (PLRG) for what feels like forever, I finally popped in after following them on Facebook—a smart move, as their posts make it easy to spot new arrivals and even call to have items held until day’s end.

First impressions were a bit mixed: we walked in without a greeting, which felt off at first, but it quickly became clear one associate was on break and the other engaged with a customer. As soon as the break ended, the returning associate welcomed us warmly and offered to take my selections to the fitting room—simple, attentive service that set the tone for the rest of the visit. The store itself is compact, well laid out, and impressively organized, with everything in excellent condition.

Sizing is where PLRG shines for some and falls short for others. If you wear a medium, you’ll be thrilled; the selection of medium tops is huge, and skirts in the size 4–10 range are plentiful. However, shoppers who lean toward very small or larger sizes may find the racks a bit sparse. The workout section is still small but growing, and the brands are compelling—think lucy and other quality labels—with a better spread of sizes in that corner, making it worth a browse.

The merchandise leans heavily into polished, name-brand pieces—Banana Republic, Ann Taylor, and similar labels—ideal for building a versatile wardrobe with elevated basics. I left with two blouses I felt great about. Prices, while fair for the quality, made me selective; not a knock on PLRG, just a personal threshold for pieces I wasn’t absolutely thrilled by.

If you’re planning a visit, make a mini outing of it. Grab tea or coffee at Luci’s around the corner, shop and/or consign at PLRG, and reward yourself with a cupcake next door once you’ve finished trying things on. The 16th St. and Bethany area makes it easy to turn a quick stop into a pleasant afternoon. I’ll be back—and I’m optimistic I’ll find more pieces that truly delight me next time.

Grade: D-

An absolute waste of money. Outrageous prices, poor service, and okay food served in thimble-sized portions. It seems geared toward being seen by the “cool, hip art crowd” at the lame Overture Center. A Food Fight Inc. operation—what a shock. Save your money and stay away.

Went for a staff lunch and started with buffalo wings—crispy, saucy, and awesome. Service felt a bit overwhelmed, and my 16oz ribeye ordered medium arrived well-done. I sent it back, and the replacement was cooked closer to the mark. Management comped the wings, which I appreciated. Mixed experience overall, but solid recovery and excellent wings make me consider giving them another try.

Another great option for people looking for good, clean fun. It was a little hard for us to find, I wish I could help you on how to get there but truth is, I don't remember!

This automotive attraction offers a polished, family-friendly outing with plenty to admire, though a few caveats keep it from must-repeat status. Admission felt a bit steep, but there are discounts for hotel guests, AAA members, and military. The collection includes seriously cool pieces: a Marine Corps tribute, JFK’s car, the Chinese presidential limousine, the suburban from The Sopranos, and muscle like the Judge.

The space is smaller than expected, and the predominance of Rolls-Royce—about 85–90% of the lineup—dampens the novelty after a while. Rolls are impressive, yet seeing so many of the same marque can make the experience feel repetitive. For enthusiasts who crave variety, that imbalance may be a sticking point.

Overall, I’m glad we went. It’s a solid pick if you have a discount and appreciate pristine presentation. Without a deal, I’d probably skip a return visit, but it’s still a fun one-time stop.

I have bought three laptops within the the last 3 months and each time I have gone into Best Buy in hopes of getting service like they used to give way back when.

After three separate trips to buy laptops in as many months, I kept hoping Best Buy would deliver the service I remembered. Instead, the computer department felt understaffed and inaccessible. Finding a sales associate took far too long; when someone finally appeared, they were rushed, short, and unable to discuss basic specs or real-world differences between models. Years ago, Best Buy’s team educated you, helped you compare options, and sent you home confident in your choice. Today, it feels like a transactional push, not a consultative experience, and that points to thinner training and fewer people on the floor. I was ready to spend real money, but I needed informed guidance. I ultimately took all three purchases to FRY’s, where my questions were answered clearly. It’s disappointing to watch a once-reliable resource slip. If Best Buy wants loyal customers back, it needs to reinvest in knowledgeable staff and the patient, informative service that built its reputation.

WinCo, a northern chain opened in Arizona, felt like a Walmart clone—minus the bagging service. After a full walk-through, I found similar prices but noticeably less selection. The kicker: you bag your own groceries, which is fine for a small haul but inconvenient otherwise. Worse, the meat department had a fishy odor that put me off. With comparable costs, fewer choices, and self-bagging, I won’t be returning.

I’d been to Komol a couple of times for lunch, but never for dinner and never with my husband. A $25 restaurant.com gift certificate felt like the perfect excuse for a date night, and the quiet, intimate dining room set exactly the right tone when we arrived. Komol is small, often with only a handful of tables occupied, but the atmosphere is warm and inviting rather than empty.

We started with the stuffed chicken wings. They were more intriguing than craveable—cleverly prepared, generously stuffed, and well fried—but ultimately a one-and-done order for me. I’m glad I tried them, happy to move on.

For mains we shared the hot and spicy pork hock curry and the beef chili mint. Neither dish matched our expectations, and that turned out to be a very good thing. I don’t usually gravitate to curry, yet this version was deeply flavorful, richly spiced, and wonderfully balanced. The beef chili mint was equally compelling: tender slices, bright herbal notes, and a chili kick that lingered without overwhelming.

Komol lets you choose your heat level from one to ten. We both went with a six. We’re the type who find most “hot” dishes elsewhere to be more mild than menacing, and even we found this heat level almost too much—almost. The slow burn heightened the aromatics and kept us reaching for another bite.

Dessert was a simple pleasure: fried bananas with coconut ice cream, hot and cold playing nicely together to finish the meal.

Service throughout dinner was attentive and friendly—until the check arrived. When we presented our restaurant.com certificate, our server placed it back on the table with a flat “we don’t take these anymore.” It was surprising, since we’d purchased it specifically for Komol and it carries no expiration. We asked a few questions, but hit a wall, and what stung wasn’t the policy so much as the lack of recovery. No “we’re sorry, let us take care of the two beers” ($8). No “dessert is on us” ($4). A small gesture would have preserved an otherwise excellent experience.

Delicious food, intimate vibe, stronger in my book than Lotus of Siam—but that awkward finish costs a star. Still, I’d return for the pork hock curry, adjust the spice to a five, and hope for policy communication next time.
Fantastic juice bar—try the Kaleaid. Bottled cold-pressed options now available; pricey, yet delicious, fresh, and totally worth it, truly.

As much as I want to like Bean

I recently tried to dine at Bean, hoping for a welcoming vegan experience, but was turned away for bringing a personal coffee mug. Staff asked me to leave it in my car, implying I should buy their coffee instead. This felt unnecessarily rigid and dismissive of customers who simply want to enjoy a meal. I wasn’t carrying outside food—just a mug. The contrast with Fern was stark: they were courteous and accommodating, and I happily spent my money there. Policies should balance safety with hospitality. Until Bean revisits its stance on outside beverages and shows greater respect for patrons, I won’t be returning. I want to like Bean, but customer experience matters. When they start valuing diners over strict rules, I’ll gladly give them another chance. For now, I’ll pass.

The best thing about Double Wide is the outdoor seating and the cute servers. They also offer a decent selection of beers, making it a pleasant spot to hang out with friends. Prices are fair and it’s good for groups, but the food fell short for us. My burger with onion rings lacked flavor, and my dining companions weren’t impressed either. The onion rings were bland, and T9’s fries arrived soggy. On the plus side, the menu features plenty of vegetarian and vegan choices, which is great for non-meat eaters seeking meatless meals.
Delicious food with great prices. Variety of chicken bowls and plates; fresh, flavorful, must-try. Highly recommended.

I know this show is supposed to be amazing and I'm pretty sure it is the most popular Cirque show on the Strip, but I was a little underwhelmed.

From fourth-row seats, every splash and expression felt immediate. Production values are undeniable—sumptuous costumes, striking makeup, committed performers, and aquatic stagecraft. Up close, the chaos impresses, but cohesion is scarce.

The absent storyline left me adrift. At one point a man on fire strode by while sea monsters rose, French aristocratic servants marched, and a Riff Raff–like butler danced—simultaneously. I turned to my husband: “What the eff is this shhh?” The sensory overload blurs impact rather than building it.

As a water show, I prefer La Reve, which balances spectacle with clarity. For acrobatics, Zumanity and Absinthe deliver more focused thrills and a raw intimacy. This production excels at sheer scale and technical feats but often plays like a collage of disconnected tableaux.

It’s clear why it’s the Strip’s most popular: grand and visually lavish. But if you prize narrative cohesion, pacing, or cleaner choreography, stronger options exist. Go for the visuals, not the plot. Consider your preferences before booking tickets.

Worst Thai EVER!!!! ZERO STARS.

I rarely write harsh reviews, but this experience was shockingly bad from start to finish. The jasmine tea tasted like tap water, utterly devoid of aroma. My friend’s Pepsi should have been foolproof, yet it was flat and off, as if the machine was broken. The soup of the day had a bizarre flavor like egg mixed with barbecue sauce. Egg rolls arrived tasting of freezer burn, which made us want to leave, but we stayed hoping the mains would redeem things. They didn’t. My curry was thin and watery, and my friend’s entrée had an acrid, ammonia-like taste. When we politely flagged the issues after a single bite, we heard laughter from the kitchen about our complaint, and received no apology or effort to make it right. The dining room was empty, and the kitchen seemed staffed by unsupervised kids. Overall, this was a disgusting experience, and I wouldn’t return even if you paid me. Spend your money elsewhere.

Aruba Hotel & Spa delivers a very specific kind of Vegas experience: gritty, retro, and tailor-made for quirky, hip events that celebrate mid-century cool. If you’re coming for a festival, rally, or themed weekender with a crew, this spot can be a blast. If you’re expecting polished luxury, look elsewhere.

The property’s biggest strength is its event scene. During Atomic Frolic and a Vespa scooter rally, the hotel handled crowds smoothly with spacious rooms, plenty of seating, and an easygoing, welcoming vibe. Bartenders were friendly, drinks were cheap, and the staff kept things moving without dimming the fun. For retro lovers, the atmosphere hits that “old Vegas” note—a bit scruffy, very personable, and unmistakably nostalgic.

Rooms, however, are basic and show their age. Expect thin walls that carry every sound, dated finishes like bargain tile, older mattresses, and plumbing that can be temperamental. As a crash pad after a late night, they’re passable; as a place to unwind in quiet comfort, they fall short. Managing expectations is key: bring earplugs, embrace the throwback feel, and think of the room as a place to sleep between parties rather than a destination in itself.

Policies can be stricter than you might assume. At the scooter rally, security enforced a no-smoking rule indoors. It’s unusual for Vegas and may disappoint smokers, but it keeps the venue air clearer for events. Plan to step outside for a smoke.

Logistics require a bit of planning. The hotel sits off the main tourist corridors, and cab drivers may not always know the address. Save the location in your phone, use rideshare, or be ready to give directions. As for the “Spa,” it’s not front-and-center—ask the desk for details if you’re hoping to use it.

Bottom line: Aruba earns four stars for its hospitality toward niche, retro events and its lively, old-school charm. The rooms are a compromise, but for groups chasing memorable nights, cheap drinks, and a scene that feels authentically vintage Vegas, it’s hard not to have a good time.

I brought my Honda in for brake repair and initially the older service advisor seemed courteous. Weeks later, after I completed the dealership’s online survey with honest feedback, he called me, berated my answers, and demanded to know why I hadn’t rated them “excellent.” He raised his voice, insisted they’d given perfect service, and made me feel intimidated for simply sharing my opinion. That phone call erased any goodwill from the visit. If this is how they treat customers who respond truthfully, I won’t return. Surveys are supposed to gather candid experiences, not punish them ever.

Despite its name, this deli falls short of New York standards. My Chicken Caesar wrap was undersized, and the potato salad “side” arrived in a tiny to-go ketchup cup—barely a spoonful. The food tasted just OK, nothing memorable, though the shop is convenient, clean, and pleasant. Portion sizes and quality need serious improvement to justify the NY branding. As it stands, it feels more like a local spot than a true New York deli; perhaps a rebrand to Chandler Fresh Deli would set expectations more appropriately. Service was polite but unremarkable.

If there were an option to give zero stars, I would. My husband and I booked a private ride and left deeply disappointed; it bore little resemblance to the advertisement. I’ve already sent a detailed letter outlining the many issues, but in short, the experience felt misleading and subpar. We won’t be returning. Save your money and time—there are far better alternatives nearby. Try other providers first.
Service was slow and overpriced. Quoted 20 minutes for a watch battery, but it took an hour and cost $100. Frustrating experience, poor value, and I wouldn’t return or recommend them.

5th & Wine is my go-to whether I’m craving salad, pasta, or a perfectly cooked steak. The bartender nails wine pairings every time, elevating each dish. There’s even a cozy private room—ideal for intimate celebrations; a friend’s birthday there felt truly special. And don’t miss the spicy fries: crisp, bold, and addictive. I find myself craving them long after I’ve left, again and again.

Service was very good.

We started with the oysters casino appetizer, which missed the mark for us and we wouldn’t order again. We split the cioppino—there’s a $10 split fee, but it includes an extra soup or salad—and the kitchen thoughtfully plated it in two bowls. The cioppino was delicious, rich, and satisfying. Though we were full, we shared a crème brûlée; good, but not memorable. We left stuffed and happy. We’ll definitely return, but we’ll steer clear of the oysters next time.

Located at the new M Hotel, this cafe made a perfect stop for a late-night bite en route to Vegas. The experience started strong with warm, soft dinner rolls and lightly whipped butter—memorable. We all opted for the Prime Rib special at $14.95, an undeniable value. The meat was cooked well, yet the deeply savory au jus stole the show, elevating each bite. Curious, I added the Hawaiian French toast; it arrived delicately sweet, dusted with macadamia nuts and pineapple, a tropical twist that worked. To drink, the fruit lemonade was a standout: a shareable pitcher brimming with strawberries, blueberries, blackberries, raspberries, mango, peach, orange, and lime—refreshing, bright, and fun.

Service stumbled at the outset with a delayed greeting, but once seated, attentiveness and pacing were on point. Between the warm bread, solid prime rib, and vibrant lemonade, this cafe shines as a late-night option for travelers and after-hours diners alike. For value, flavor, and a welcoming finish, it earns a confident five stars.

I have five - and counting - Jamie books on my kitchen shelf. I love the simplicity of his recipes but also the attention to detail and love for his craft. I also love the magnificent drool-worthy pictures. Okay, okay, I confess; I have a severe foodie crush on Jamie and I compulsively pour through his recipes on a very regular basis.

How was my first visit to Jamie’s Italian? The setting alone is worth the trip. Nestled in the oh-so-regal Assembly Rooms, the restaurant is a stunner: ruby-red furnishings, elegant chandeliers, a cocktail bar, and hanging meats. Jamie-personalised napkins add a wink of whimsy. The overall effect is modern, playful grandeur with a faint Grand Budapest vibe.

We were greeted warmly and seated straight away, a polished start. The menu reads like a love letter to Italian comfort: familiar pastas and seasonal salads alongside antipasti boards and clever sides. It’s the kind of card that tempts you into ordering more than you planned. Service kept pace without hovering, and the buzz from the open kitchen lent a convivial hum that suited the space. Prices felt fair for the quality and setting.

Fresh from the Fit Festival upstairs, I tried to be virtuous with the Market Superfood Salad: avocado, shaved fennel, candied beets, Italian sprouting broccoli, creamy cottage cheese, pomegranate, and smashed nuts and seeds, all brightened by a fennel-blossom Sicilian harissa. You can add grilled chicken or smoked salmon. We shared warm bread and dips, too.

Here’s the rub: there’s a time and place for salad, and this wasn’t it. Though flavorful—and the nibbles were lovely—I kept wishing I’d gone for a silky carbonara or the signature Jamie’s Italian burger. This is a room that calls for going all out, not restraint.

Next time, I’m arriving hungry and unapologetic: cocktail in hand, pasta twirled, and zero regrets.

The only reason Capital Grille gets more than 1 star is because of atmosphere. I've heard mixed reviews from others, so there is a chance you'll have a fine meal. My birthday dinner here was totally unacceptable.... and fortunately they credited almost the whole meal for 5 people. The steaks were.... no exaggeration.... Sizzler quality. Gritty, overcooked, blah--- ick! To give them the benefit of the doubt, there was probably an inconsistency issue here. Maybe they got a bad cow! Whatever the case, for these prices and for them to maintain their chain reputation, this should have never happened.

The Capital Grille’s atmosphere impresses, but my birthday dinner was a disappointment. Despite hearing mixed reviews, our table of five received steaks that were gritty, overcooked, and oddly bland—closer to Sizzler than a premium steakhouse. To their credit, management comped nearly the entire meal, acknowledging the misfire. I’ll allow that inconsistency may have played a role—maybe an off night or a bad cut—but at these prices and with a polished chain reputation, such lapses shouldn’t happen. If you go, savor the ambiance and service, but temper expectations for the kitchen. There’s a chance you’ll fare better; I didn’t.

Very lame. Pot sticker appetizers arrived lukewarm and undercooked, smothered in a viscous orange goo with virtually no flavor. The kung pao chicken tasted La Choy-ish—missing heat and sweetness—while the peanuts seemed stale, like they’d been recycled from a zoo cage. Overall, a complete disappointment. Serviceable at best, but not worth a return visit. We will not be back.

AZ celeb DJ Came Highly Recommended — But Our Wedding Experience Was Far From Professional

We chose AZ celeb DJ after Seville Golf and Country Club recommended them as their preferred DJ. With that endorsement, we felt confident we’d have a smooth, memorable reception. Unfortunately, the experience did not match the expectation.

The first red flag came during planning. We drove over an hour for a scheduled appointment only to discover there was no appointment on their end. To their credit, they rescheduled and added a lighting package to make amends, which initially reassured us. At the meeting, we selected most of our music and the DJ suggested a special anniversary dance. We spent the following weeks carefully curating songs for our first dance, parent dances, cake cutting, and other key moments.

On the big day, the earliest feedback from guests was that the DJ was rude and seemed to have a chip on his shoulder from the moment he arrived. The music felt repetitive, cycling through the same few songs rather than reading the room. More troubling, he never implemented the anniversary dance he had recommended, nor several of the other dances we had requested. He also failed to announce our cake cutting, leaving guests unaware it had even happened. Without clear emceeing, the evening lacked structure; guests and vendors were unsure of the timeline, and we found ourselves trying to provide direction during what should have been a carefree celebration.

Midway through the night, the DJ informed us he was about to play the last song. We hadn’t realized the contracted end time was earlier than we expected. When we asked to extend, he required cash on the spot to stay an extra hour and acted visibly put out, as though our request—and payment—were an inconvenience. Several guests later shared that he raised his voice at them near the end of the evening, which is the last memory we wanted our loved ones to take home.

It felt as though our Sunday wedding received second-tier treatment. Regardless of the day, couples deserve professionalism, respect, and the experience they paid for. While the lighting add-on for the initial scheduling mishap was appreciated, the execution on the night matters most. We hoped for a DJ who would guide the flow, honor our selections, and celebrate with us; instead, we encountered missed moments and unnecessary friction.

Based on our experience, we cannot recommend AZ celeb DJ. Do yourself a favor: choose a company that confirms details in writing, communicates clearly, respects your timeline, and treats your occasion with genuine care.

I wanted to like this spot. On my first visit, it had just opened and something was clearly amiss—my pizza took 30 minutes. Chalk it up to growing pains, I thought, and returned later. The second time was promising: quick turnaround, a decent pie, and at $4.99, the price felt very reasonable for downtown.

Consistency, however, fell apart on subsequent visits. On the third trip, both of us ordered the veggie, yet our pizzas looked like they came from different kitchens. My friend’s toppings were barely visible; mine had more, and when I politely asked for a few extra mushrooms, my pizza maker obliged. It felt like a small win, but the discrepancy was hard to ignore.

Visit four sealed it. We both received extremely sparse toppings—think maybe 10 very thin mushroom slices—and asked to add more so the pie at least felt like a veggie pizza. Her pizza maker responded abruptly, saying no and pointing us to the $7.99 “unlimited toppings” price. Mine was kinder but echoed the policy. The message: pay more or accept a nearly bare pizza.

While the cheap-and-quick concept is appealing, stinginess with toppings, uneven execution, and curt service undermine the value. A budget price only works if the product is satisfying. When the difference between decent and disappointing hinges on luck and upsells, I’d rather spend the extra $3 elsewhere for better food and a more consistent experience.

My wife and I have been shopping from the time they opened several years ago. I don't remember when that was but quite a few years ago.

For seasoned travelers, few local shops capture the joy of discovering global treats like this Phoenix staple. Over the years, my wife and I have relied on it to reconnect with flavors we loved abroad—especially in the chocolate aisle. Their selection spans countries and brands, with special editions rotating seasonally, so you may not always find the same bar twice, but that’s part of the fun. While I’m not a big wine or beer drinker, the shelves appear robust, and friends praise the breadth and value. What truly sets this place apart is the staff. Team members are consistently knowledgeable, attentive, and proactive. On multiple visits, I’ve asked about a hard-to-find item only to have an associate stop what they’re doing, walk the aisles with me, and either track it down or suggest reliable alternatives.
