If they don’t carry something, they’ll point you to where you can find it elsewhere. With several locations around Phoenix, convenience is a bonus—but service is the reason we keep coming back. Friendly faces, curated tastes, and genuine help make every visit worth it.

I usually love this place for its tasty breakfast burritos and tacos, but today's visit was deeply disappointing. I discovered a short, curly black hair in my machaca burrito and had to throw it away immediately, which left me feeling ill. It's heartbreaking, because this spot was my go-to and the closest option. I also noticed someone in the kitchen without a hairnet. Please improve your health and hygiene standards; until then, I won't be returning.

My first impression was rough: a 30-minute check-in despite a short line, and staff didn’t offer the same water, coupons, or maps others received. Our first room reeked of burnt cooking oil, so we requested a move. No free Wi‑Fi—even while attending a timeshare presentation—hardly says “best foot forward.” On the plus side, the new room was spacious with solid amenities, though the décor screamed 80s porn-star chic—if that’s your vibe. The pool is pleasant but spends much of the day in shade from nearby buildings. There’s no on-site restaurant, but the attached mall provides convenient shopping and quick eats.

Dear Chef Ramsay, are we not worthy?

Ramsay’s name promises a proper British pub, but what arrives is a polished, crowd-pleasing facsimile. The cooking is careful, ingredients good, and plates pretty, yet the soul—those robust, unapologetic flavors—gets dialed down to suit the Strip.

Fish and chips lands halfway. The cod is perfect—moist beneath a crisp shell. The chips, oversized like fried baked potatoes, are fluffy, almost delicate. Sweet, vegetal mushy peas round it out.

Shepherd’s pie gets Americanized with beef alongside or instead of lamb. The rustic, earthy punch softens; the stew’s unapologetic fat yields to a buttery potato crust. Tasty, yes, but it leaves you longing.

The pork belly roll is pork heaven, though noticeably leaner than its British cousin. Served in its own jus with roasted carrots and pea purée, it’s restrained and satisfying.

Order the beef short rib and cheek sandwich. Juicy short rib meets sweet braised cheeks on sourdough; horseradish aioli, roasted pepper jam, and onion marmalade add heat and jammy depth. A clear win.

The beer list is passable, with British ales sharing taps with ubiquitous macro lagers. Expect resort-level Vegas pricing.

The room is contemporary with a theme-park gloss: a pub by décor, not by spirit. It lacks the boisterous camaraderie of a true local. Tourists will feel right at home—“I love Las Vegas” tees welcome.

If you crave the roar and heft of a London local, you’ll taste the compromise. Still, there are pleasures to be had—especially in that sandwich—and the kitchen’s technique rarely falters. Come for polished comfort and celebrity sheen; look elsewhere for the messy, lovable heart of a pub.

Fantastic dining experience for our family of four, including two kids. The food was delicious and arrived within 15 minutes of ordering. Service was attentive and friendly; the manager checked on us multiple times. Efficient, welcoming, and kid-friendly, highly recommend, and we’ll definitely be back.

Took my teenagers to the early show and it was a hit. They loved it, I loved it. Food was fine—classic bar fare. Lots of younger kids around, but this really shines for teens. Dinner out is usually chaotic for us, yet this was peaceful, fun, and fuss-free. A genuinely great night for mom. Indeed perfect.

As a loyal Eggingtons patron for more than two decades, I’ve consistently praised the kitchen’s creativity and consistency. The food is, without fail, wonderful—comforting yet polished, and worth returning for time and again. That long history is exactly why a recent experience, planned as a Bridal Shower Bruncheon for my sister-in-law, was so disappointing on the service side. It didn’t diminish the food, but it did reveal gaps in communication and event handling that felt at odds with the hospitality I’ve come to expect.

I booked a large-party reservation two months in advance for the Saturday before Mother’s Day, knowing it’s a high-demand time. The request was simple: have the table ready shortly before 11:30 so I could set up cupcakes, games, and favors. I arrived at 10:55 to drop off the cupcakes and confirm the setup. The hostess accepted the items and my name, and said the table wasn’t ready yet—understandable, at that moment. I returned at 11:20 expecting to stage the celebration, only to find the table still occupied and the lobby filling. After waiting another 10 minutes with balloons and gifts in hand, I asked for an update. The reply was essentially that it “wasn’t quite 11:30,” and that bills were being collected, but a glance revealed the seated party still actively eating. We didn’t get seated until close to noon, which derailed the plan to greet guests with everything in place.

Once seated, the meal itself was seamless. Plates were excellent, and the staff working the floor handled the rush well. What was missing was acknowledgment and recovery. There was no proactive apology, no effort to relocate us temporarily, no offer of coffee, muffins, or a small gesture for the bride-to-be. For a long-time patron hosting a milestone event, that lack of communication and care was disheartening.

Busy weekends are challenging, and turn times can slip. But if there’s a possibility a large party cannot be accommodated at the promised time—especially when setup is required—the reservation should not be accepted as-is, or a transparent buffer should be communicated. A few fixes would go a long way: pre-block event tables with extra time, assign a manager to greet and update the host upon arrival, provide a staging area for decorations, and offer a modest amenity—perhaps the bride’s favorite raspberry mocha—when delays occur. These are small gestures, but they ease the stress of hosting and transform a misstep into a memory of thoughtful service.

Eggingtons remains one of my favorite places to eat, and I will continue to return for the food. I hope management revisits reservation policies and host-stand training to match their culinary excellence with equally polished hospitality. Loyal patrons—and special occasions—deserve that level of care.

While the Smith Center itself is wonderful—a beautiful venue—the will call experience was disappointing. The attendants were rude and impolite, leaving a poor first impression. Customer service needs improvement to match the venue’s standards.

Recovering from minor surgery, I’m on a limited diet, so my friend and I sought a spot with simple, unfussy seafood—no heavy pasta or cream sauces. Bluewater Grill turned out to be just right. The dining room was calm and nearly empty, though it was early on a Thursday, which likely explains the quiet. Our waitress was warm and attentive, even if she did mix up my order; in the end, the replacement was an even better choice. The standout was the Grilled Artichoke appetizer: smoky, tender, and downright addictive. I’m inspired to try recreating it at home. Overall, the menu skews fresh and straightforward, ideal when you want seafood without distractions. Service was caring and relaxed. I’d happily return, and when bread and pasta are back on my menu, the Salmon Crostino is first on my list.

This kitschy, 50s diner–inspired spot nails the look with a cool, throwback interior, neon glow, and cozy booths that make you want to linger. I’ll admit I haven’t tried the food—my all-time favorite restaurant happens to sit two doors down—so I come here strictly for the bar, and that alone keeps me returning. The beer selection genuinely rocks: thoughtful, rotating taps that include quirky finds like Rock Bottom’s Uppity Jag-Off IPA from craft beer week. The bartender-owner is a gem—welcoming, knowledgeable, and eager to guide you through what’s new. He’ll happily pour tastes so you can discover something you actually like, and he somehow remembers us every visit, giving the place that warm “Norm!” vibe. The music usually hits the right notes, and conversations at the bar tend to be easy and fun, which only adds to the charm. We’ll keep dropping in for a couple of pints whenever we’re in the neighborhood, because it’s unfailingly fun and there’s always something interesting on tap. Service is quick, friendly, too.

noms.noms.noms.

Strolling out of the Golden Nugget, I stumbled upon a gleaming little patisserie tucked just past one of the check-in counters, all marble, glass, and temptations. In Vegas, “super cute” usually means “super pricey,” so I braced for sticker shock. Instead, I found indulgence at an unexpectedly friendly price: ginormous cupcakes for just $3, and coconut macaroons—available plain or generously chocolate-dipped—at similarly affordable rates.

Those macaroons deserve a special shout-out. The chocolate wasn’t merely a whispery drizzle; it was a substantial, truffle-like cap that turned each bite into a small celebration. Texture-wise, the macaroon itself walked the line perfectly: soft without being mushy, coconutty without veering into sunscreen territory. I’ll admit I kept these all to myself while friends rang in a big 3-0; some treats are meant to be savored solo.

The cupcakes are the headliners, though. They’re huge, showy, and—most importantly—good. The red velvet I snagged for a friend was moist and flavorful, crowned with a cream cheese frosting that hit that sweet-tangy balance just right. Later, after carting around two more cupcakes like precious cargo, I finally sampled the chocolate-on-chocolate. Rich, satisfying, and exactly the kind of classic you hope it will be.

In short: if you find yourself downtown, this spot is worth a detour. Would I trek from the Strip solely for a cupcake or macaroon? Probably not; the logistics of getting downtown can be a buzzkill on a short trip. But pair it with a wander through Fremont Street, and you’ve got a sweet, affordable win that feels like Vegas without the markup. The gleaming space and those oversized treats seal the deal, an easy yes whenever you’re nearby and in the mood to indulge.

I am here at least once a week - rain or shine. I don't know if this is a good or a bad thing - probably good for my belly, bad for my heart.

As a Buffalo alum, I’m picky about wings, and Buffalo Wild Wings comes closest to the Western NY benchmark. This location nails it: upbeat atmosphere, attentive staff, and craveable food—good for the belly, maybe not the cardiologist. Service is quick and friendly.

On game days, screens are everywhere, pulling sports fans to both bar and dining room. It’s lively but not overwhelming, and I prefer it to the Hualapai & Flamingo spot, despite being smaller; it feels smoother.

If you’re new to B‑dubs, the sauce heat scale helps, steering you from mild comfort to fiery thrill. Not feeling wings? The menu’s broad, with salads, burgers, and plenty of shareable appetizers.

Don’t overlook the dry rub seasonings: salt & vinegar for tang, chipotle BBQ for smoky-sweet, classic buffalo, and desert heat for a bold kick.

Best of all, they’re open 24 hours. When cravings strike, it’s nice knowing a plate of wings is always within reach.

A great place from the hotel side.

At this property, the hotel side shines. The front desk and housekeeping were courteous, friendly, and helpful, and issues—like a loose fridge or misaligned shower door—were fixed immediately. Our suite was well appointed and roomy, though lighting was dim, making it hard to read or work.

Unfortunately, the casino and restaurants didn’t measure up. Restaurant staff seemed disengaged, spoke limited English, and struggled with orders, which made communication frustrating. The buffet was underwhelming compared with nearby casinos, and the slot machines felt tight. I’d recommend staying here but dining and gambling elsewhere.

Be prepared for a trek from parking to the buildings. On the plus side, many guests enjoyed the pool, though we arrived during sweltering heat and were later caught in a severe monsoon storm—an unlucky stretch of weather. Overall: comfortable suites and excellent hotel service, but weak food and gaming options. If you value good service and spacious suites, this makes a solid base.

My husband and I stopped in about an hour ago for donuts and an iced caramel coffee. The coffee arrived with no syrup; mistakes happen, so I politely asked the cashier, Karesa, to add caramel. Her response was shockingly rude: she snatched the cup, rolled her eyes, and shoved it back into my hand with a sarcastic “is this better?” so forcefully the lid nearly popped off. The interaction felt truly hostile and disrespectful, turning a simple fix into an uncomfortable scene. The donuts were fine, but service matters. I don’t expect perfection, but I do expect basic courtesy. I won’t be returning to this location. I’d rather pay a bit more up the street at Starbucks, where staff consistently handle corrections with professionalism, kindness, and respect.

All you can eat Korean food. Hmmmm.... sounds good to me.

An all-you-can-eat Korean spot that delivers solid value. The bulgogi is nicely marinated, and the variety is impressive—dozens of meats to choose from keep the grill busy. For the price, it’s an appealing deal. As others noted, the pre-cooked dishes are underwhelming; the real payoff is at the tabletop barbecue, where freshness and customization shine. Ambiance is fine and service more than decent. Remember, this is AYCE: temper expectations on premium quality. Consider it a fun, satisfying grill experience—not a luxe, Bellagio-style buffet.

This place was lovely! As an out-of-towner, it offered a perfect local experience. Arrive very early to snag a seat; fortunately, there’s a new outdoor waiting area if you don’t. The tableside guacamole was a standout—freshly prepared and delightfully accented with pomegranate seeds. I ordered their specialty pork dish; while flavorful, it was a bit dry for my taste and left me slightly disappointed. Service was friendly, the atmosphere cozy and sweet, and the overall vibe welcoming. Despite the pork miss, the strengths outweigh the shortcomings. For authentic ambiance, great guac, and a charming setting, I’d confidently rate it a solid four stars.

Please keep in mind while reading this review that I am a complete wimp when it comes to spicy food.

I make a hobby of seeking out falafel across Arizona, so I was curious to try this spot. The falafel “meat” isn’t bad compared to some places, but it tastes boxed—confirmed by our waitress—and the seasoning ran hot for my palate. The tzatziki was a surprise, too. I love the cool, cucumbery American-style; the authentic Greek here was saltier and spicier, which overwhelmed me. The hummus packed a sharp zing that burned my tongue; to me it tasted like spicy, chunky ketchup with a hit of ascorbic acid.

That said, the experience wasn’t without charms. The room is handsome, with a deep blue ceiling, white fans, and tasteful Grecian accents that make the space feel airy. Service was friendly and helpful, and prices struck me as reasonable. Portions were fair for the price.

If you love bolder, spicier flavors, you may find the dips and falafel more exciting than I did. If your tastes skew mild, consider asking for samples or sticking to gentler options. Me? I’ll keep searching for that cool, creamy tzatziki I crave—and a falafel that’s clearly made in-house.

At over $30, Aria’s buffet disappoints. I expected a spread comparable to Wynn or Bellagio, but the selection and quality fell short. Flavors were bland, variety limited, and nothing stood out enough to justify the price. It’s a forgettable experience. If you’re spending more than $30, take your appetite and cash to a different, better buffet somewhere else instead.

A Standout Paddling Hub: Two Years Into a Couples Membership at Brittingham

We’re in our second year with a couples membership at Brittingham, and it remains one of the best values in town. The fleet is impressively varied—SUPs, single and double kayaks, canoes, and paddleboats—and the process couldn’t be easier. You check in, grab a paddle or oar, stroll to the landing, and a friendly team member is right there to steady the craft and send you off with confidence.

As avid SUP fans, we originally learned at Rutabega, but after a few frustrating missteps there—like a finless board that staff wouldn’t swap and a puzzling shoes-required rule—we tried Brittingham and haven’t looked back. Rentals here are plentiful, affordable, and backed by staff who are laid back yet attentive, always ready with quick pointers and thoughtful answers.

The experience extends beyond the water. Brittingham’s patio is a gem, with comfortable seating and a snack lineup that goes beyond the basics: gourmet grilled cheese, ice cream, sodas, and French press coffee. It’s the perfect place to decompress after a paddle and soak in the lakeside vibe.

Owner Stephan Reinke is almost always on-site, setting the tone with a calm, accommodating presence that centers guest enjoyment. Perhaps most inspiring, Brittingham has helped transform what used to be a neglected, even intimidating, park into a welcoming community asset. For paddlers and neighbors alike, this place delivers value, hospitality, and a genuinely positive impact every season.

This spot delivers exactly what you’d expect from a straightforward sports bar: plenty of screens, cold drinks, and a menu that mostly plays it safe. Across several dine-in visits and a few takeout orders, the food has been serviceable but rarely memorable. The burger landed with a thud—filling yet forgettable—and the Reuben skewed soggy and underwhelming. The standout, surprisingly, is the chicken tenders: crisp, juicy, and genuinely craveable, they’re the one item I’d go out of my way to order again. If your priority is catching the game and having a few rounds, this venue fits the bill, with pricing that is refreshingly affordable. For food-first diners, though, expectations should stay modest. Solid for sports and value; just temper hopes for culinary thrills beyond those excellent tenders, and friendly enough service.

Dec 19, 2011 the front desk allowed an early check in for a fee.

I arrived on Dec 19, 2011 and paid a fee for early check-in. Expectations were modest, but the first room was a shock. The tub had visible hair and soap scum, the bathroom counter held smears of toothpaste, and half-used shampoo and conditioner bottles lingered on the floor. Oddly, the bed was made perfectly, which made the oversight elsewhere even more perplexing. The worst discovery came as I tossed paper into the trash: a condom that appeared used. I called the front desk immediately. The agent offered to send housekeeping or transfer me, and about twenty minutes later the bellman delivered keys to a new room.

The second room initially seemed clean. After a quick shower, however, I found myself standing in ankle-deep water due to a sluggish drain. While drying off, I noticed short, curly hairs around the base of the toilet—definitely not mine. Not wanting to make a scene, I decided against requesting a third room, though in retrospect I should have asked for a full refund and moved to a different hotel.

The following mornings brought minor comforts and new frustrations. The in-room coffee was actually decent, but housekeeping never cleaned the mug, replaced it, or restocked coffee packets. The same cup sat with about an eighth of an inch of old coffee in the bottom, day after day.

Even with an inexpensive bill, basic cleanliness and maintenance are nonnegotiable. The front desk’s solution—room transfer—was polite but ultimately cosmetic, as housekeeping and plumbing shortcomings persisted. These lapses suggest more than an isolated miss; they point to weak standards and poor supervision. I will not return, even if comped. The old saying applies here: you get what you pay for, but guests should never have to compromise on hygiene. That is unacceptable.

Je fréquente ce restaurant depuis un certain temps et c’est l’une des meilleures tables de la Rive-Sud. Carte des vins vraiment sublime, service hors pair, et la salle arrière est à couper le souffle; tous sont sympathiques. Attention toutefois: les prix sont élevés et certaines portions ont parfois rétréci. Évitez de laisser le serveur choisir votre vin en fixant un budget; sélectionnez pour respecter vos goûts et le portefeuille.

Disappointing Meal, Lovely Music

I left underwhelmed. Most meats were passable at best, and the salad bar was outright awful. I won’t return. Staff were friendly, but seemed to angle for extra tips, which felt off. The only saving grace was the charming live music, which earned my two-star rating. If you want a better experience, Brazz remains the safer, superior bet. I’ll stick with what I know.

I love breakfast, and Cottage Cafe gets it right. Their classic American morning fare hits the spot, with generous portions that guarantee you’ll leave full. The coffee service is excellent, and the staff is friendly, fast, and attentive without being overbearing. Best of all, the prices are reasonable. If you’re craving a hearty, satisfying start to the day, this spot delivers.

I’ve been coming here basically since the place opened and have yet to have a bad experience. Service can occasionally run a bit slower than usual, but unless I’m being completely ignored, I don’t find it off-putting.

I first visited on a friend’s recommendation to try the chicken fried steak. Sitting down with the menu, though, it struck me that ordering chicken fried steak at a BBQ joint is a little like asking for a hamburger at a Mexican restaurant—possible, sure, but not what you came for. So, I still haven’t gone there.

What I do come for are the meats. The pulled pork is moist with a gentle, smoky backbone. The turkey is thinly sliced yet packed with clean, smoked flavor. The smoked sausage doesn’t eclipse versions elsewhere, but it’s solid and satisfying. The ribs are tasty and flavorful—even for someone who isn’t a huge rib person. My absolute must-order is the burnt ends: big, booming smoke, tender brisket ends that never disappoint. Strangely enough, the brisket itself is the one item I don’t love here.

Sauce matters, and Dillon’s original cajun style is my pick—slightly kicky without tipping into sweetness. For those who prefer gentler heat, the sweet and mild sauce was crafted for the Sun City crowd, and the name nails it.

As for sides, everything I’ve tried has been good. I usually keep it classic with a potato option and beans; why mess with what works?

Given the proximity to Sun City, expect early crowds, especially on busy nights. Plan ahead, bring a little patience, and you’ll be rewarded with reliably tasty barbecue. There’s a reason I keep coming back. And who knows—maybe one day I’ll finally order that chicken fried steak.

Make sure you try shoes on in-store; once you exchange, there’s no going back. I asked to speak with the district manager and was promised a call—never happened. Someone else called instead, offering no help. Rigid policies, poor communication. Not a good company at all. Shop at Nordstrom instead. Truly disappointing experience.

We arrived around 3:30 a.m., rolling in late after dinner and hoping for a decent nightcap. There was a predictable line, the kind that seems to favor the tall and flashy, and we were just a normal group. By luck alone, we got in, though the $50 cover stung. Inside, the venue felt small and underwhelming. The music never found a groove—more background than energy—and the drinks matched the vibe: forgettable and overpriced. The crowd was equally meh, offering little of the excitement you expect in Vegas. Overall, this spot is serviceable only if you’ve missed out on better clubs elsewhere.

LOVE Chompie’s!!! A weekend staple for dog-loving hikers and gluten-free foodies

Chompie’s has become my happy place in Scottsdale for casual eats, the kind of spot that anchors your weekend routine and never lets you down. My friend and I hit the trails with our dogs every Saturday morning and beeline straight here for brunch on the patio. We always sit outside with the pups, and in three years of going at least weekly, we’ve never had terrible service. Sure, there’s one server who doesn’t seem thrilled about the patio (maybe it’s the dog crowd), but everyone else is consistently warm, quick, and thoughtful. Within minutes, we’ve got water bowls for the dogs, a hot coffee for me, and a diet coke for my friend—like clockwork.

I first found Chompie’s thanks to Man vs Food and my mom, who insisted we try it when I moved to Phoenix. Now it’s a non-negotiable when she visits, often twice per trip. She’s worked her way through french toast, Reubens, and chicken and waffles, and loved every bite. The sandwiches are legendary—so generously stacked they easily stretch into one or two more meals.

With celiac disease, I stick to the gluten-free menu, and I’m never left wanting. My go-to is the gluten-free bagel with lox platter: fresh, satisfying, and surprisingly hearty. On the rare occasion I stray, the gluten-free Reuben or GF waffles hit the spot. The dogs? They always get their plate of bacon, which they inhale with enormous thanks.

One of my favorite upgrades: Chompie’s now carries a range of gluten-free desserts and pastries. My non-GF friend and I often split the chocolate-peanut butter brownie—rich, gooey, and dangerously addictive. If I didn’t have a dog to wrangle on the way out, I’d probably leave with a box for “later.”

Bottom line: friendly patio vibes, endlessly reliable service, massive portions, and a stellar gluten-free selection. We’ll be back tomorrow with the Danes, just like every weekend, for our post-hike brunch ritual.

This place recalls old-school Goodwill—only with better finds. The "home" section is a bit junky, but the clothing racks are packed with affordable pieces in decent condition, not just uber-faded shirts with bleach spots. Prices are fair, selection is broad, and it's absolutely worth checking out.

I stopped in hoping to find furniture and decor, and left with a pretty vase and a woven basket to corral shoes by the front door—both under $10. Someone clearly puts time into arranging stock: gift baskets, bundled wine books with glasses and decorative stoppers, and tasteful window displays make browsing inviting. Prices felt fair and the merchandise seemed thoughtfully curated. Note that card purchases under $10 incur a $1 transaction fee; it didn’t bother me since proceeds support a charity, but it’s good to know before you check out.

The cashier was warm and helpful, and mentioned rotating 25% discounts each day—one for military, another for teachers and students, etc. The schedule changes weekly, so you can’t count on a fixed day, which is puzzling.

Overall, this is a tidy, well-run shop with creative displays and budget-friendly finds. I’ll be back to see what new treasures and themed bundles they put together next.

Service was abysmal: I waited 45 minutes for my meal. As a solo diner, I was hit with an automatic 18% gratuity without consultation. The dingy atmosphere hardly inspires confidence, especially when ordering raw fish. Their “salmon” tasted off—rubbery and nothing like the real thing—making the experience worse. Between the sluggish service, sneaky charges, and unappetizing seafood, this place isn’t worth your time or money. I won’t be returning.

I’ve been a longtime CBW patron, but recent visits feel mixed. Prices have crept up while overall quality slipped. The pizza remains delicious, and salads are good, yet most other dishes seem average for Pittsburgh. Beer is okay—drinkable, not memorable. Service often runs slow, muting a cool vibe. Portion sizes are fair, but the value isn’t what it used to be. Still, CBW works for a casual visit: stop in for a pint and a pizza, and set expectations for service and consistency. Go for the staples, not a full dining experience.

Another great vacation in 2014. Can't say enough nice things about our experience. Great staff. Great Pool. Terrific lazy river. New deli in the lobby for the early risers in our group.

We returned for another family getaway. The staff is warm and attentive, and the pool complex is a highlight. Whether you’re sinking toes into the sandy-beach entry, swimming laps, or playing water volleyball, there’s something for everyone. The Lazy River steals the show: we never tire of pushing each other under the waterfall or into the flow from the giant water jugs. Add an immaculate BBQ area and a handy lobby deli for early risers, and the days practically plan themselves.

This isn’t the Ritz, and it’s not the Hard Rock—and that’s the appeal. Furnishings are simple but clean, with the focus on comfort and convenience. Our unit had a real kitchen, a comfortable bed, and the pullout was better than expected. The steam shower was a treat, and the lanai offered views, even looking west toward the parking lot. Families should note: the uptown shuttles fill up fast and won’t wait, so be early.

We’ll stay here again and again. Across ages, everyone found something to love, and we wish we could share photos to prove it.

Heard a lot about this place, so we had to try it last weekend. The lounge is the star—super kick-ass and a must-go. The Grill is fun to watch, though the food is just okay, better suited for a casual lunch than a destination dinner. Plan to dine elsewhere, then swing by late night for drinks and apps. Expect a dark, atmospheric space with good music, tons of TVs, sexy U-shaped couches, greenery dividing cozy sections, and a striking water feature framing a central fire pit. A very cool, must-see lounge.

Hip Mexican spot at the Hard Rock with a legit Happy Hour. Don’t miss the Appetizer Sampler and the off-the-chain fried ice cream. Service is friendly and fast, making this a go-to for flavorful bites.

I'm grateful for the help from this hospital, but unfortunately, I'm regretting coming to this hospital.

Living just six minutes away, I hoped this hospital would be a convenient choice. I arrived around 7 a.m. and was first seen at 7:45, then sent back to the waiting room, where I sat for two hours without updates. When I approached the front desk to check whether anything else was needed, the staff seemed confused; I was asked about tests I’d never been sent to complete. One nurse called me in and, minutes later, another called me again, unaware I was already being seen. The lack of communication among staff was striking and prolonged my visit. By nearly 11 a.m., I was still waiting on test results. The facility looks tired and in disrepair, which doesn’t inspire confidence. To their credit, most people I interacted with were kind and tried to help, but kindness couldn’t offset the disorganization. In hindsight, I wish I had taken the longer drive to St. Rose for a smoother, more coordinated experience.

I've now visited all of the Souper Salads in the Valley, & like this one a little less than some of the others only because of the seating arrangement. I like a booth along a wall or high divider, preferably in a corner. Here they have booths, but they are out in the middle of the room, & then there are small tables along the walls. Same excellent food & very low prices as the other locations, though. :-))

After visiting every Souper Salads in the Valley, I rank this branch slightly lower solely because of its seating layout. I prefer wall-side booth seating with high dividers, ideally tucked into a corner. Here, booths sit in the center, while smaller tables line the walls, which makes the dining room feel less cozy. That said, the food remains consistently excellent, fresh, and plentiful, and the prices are low, just like the other locations. Value shines; ambience could use tweaking.

Meh.

This Old Navy feels stuck in basics. You’ll find jeans, tees, and staple items, but the more trendy, interesting pieces seem to skip this location entirely. If you’re hunting for the newer styles they’ve rolled out in recent years, you’re better off heading to Arizona Mills or the Mesa store near the 101 and Country Club. The sale section here is often picked over, too, with slim sizes and limited variety. For value and selection, just go to the Mills—you’ll have better luck.
We sit in the bar and enjoy good food and people-watching. Plenty of TVs with sports. A bit pricey, but quick when it’s not busy. Friendly wait staff. Covered outdoor patio with misters.

Das Stövchen ist die Konkurrenz zu Kippe / Cafe Emaille /Cafe Bleu etc.

Das Stövchen tritt als günstige Alternative zu Kippe, Café Emaille und Café Bleu auf. Preis-Leistung scheint zu stimmen, doch ich zahle für bessere Qualität lieber etwas mehr. Positiv hervorzuheben sind die Flammkuchen: knusprig, frisch und wirklich empfehlenswert. Viele andere Speisen wirken dagegen nach Fritteuse und Convenience – gut, wenn es schnell und billig sein soll, weniger, wenn man Wert auf Qualität legt. Das Frühstück ist reichlich und solide, allerdings ohne Besonderheiten. Der Biergarten ist nett, der Service flott und meist freundlich, wenn auch gelegentlich etwas übercool. Die Atmosphäre erinnert stark an eine Studentenkneipe; entsprechend wird viel geraucht, was den Essgenuss schmälert. Im Winter steht ein beheiztes Zelt im Biergarten – ökologisch fragwürdig, daher für mich Punktabzug. Insgesamt: günstig und okay, aber kein persönlicher Favorit; für einen schnellen Snack geeignet, für Genussmomente würde ich andere Adressen vorziehen.

WONDERFUL EXPERIENCE!

I dined at the Eiffel Tower Restaurant for brunch for the first time, and it was a standout—one of the weekend’s best memories. While I’m not typically a devotee of French cuisine, the menu felt welcoming and wonderfully executed. The ingredients tasted fresh, the flavors were balanced, and the preparations were elegant without being intimidating. It’s the kind of French dining that invites newcomers in, offering quality and comfort in equal measure, and making classic techniques feel accessible.

Service was, in a word, fantastic. Our server struck the ideal tone: respectful, professional, and genuinely warm. The server assistant was impressively attentive while still honoring our space, even anticipating needs with near-telepathic timing—she arrived with a refill of coffee just as I was turning to ask, cheerfully announcing, “I’m here!” From the host stand greetings to the check-out farewell, the hospitality was seamless and consistent. It was, frankly, the best customer service I experienced anywhere in Vegas.

The ambiance blends comfort and class, with generous windows and tasteful decor that make the room feel bright, sophisticated, and relaxed. And then there’s the view: a breathtaking panorama of the Bellagio fountains paired with an unobstructed look down the Strip. Watching the water show unfold while you dine creates a memorable rhythm to the meal, and the skyline frames the experience beautifully.

With its inviting food, exceptional service, and unforgettable views, this restaurant is now a must-do on every future Vegas trip. I’ll be returning for dinner next time—and I’m even open to staying at the hotel. Consider me a raving fan.

More like 3.5. Please don't stab me with your CenPho torches.

Sushi in Phoenix remains a puzzle for me. I know I live in the desert, and expectations should adjust accordingly, but after bouncing around several cities big and small, I’m finding the Valley’s sushi scene the hardest to love. That said, Hana shines where Phoenix consistently excels: service. The staff here is warm, attentive, and genuinely welcoming—good enough on its own to earn a return visit.

I’ve only tried the rolls so far, so consider this a snapshot rather than a final verdict. With so many raves floating around, I walked in expecting fireworks. Anticipation is a double-edged sword, and mine may have dulled the sparkle a bit. The roll lineup is broad, but like much of Phoenix’s sushi, it leans heavily into shrimp, panko, and crunchy, deep-fried comforts. It’s a crowd-pleasing formula, just not the adventurous, fish-forward experience I crave. I want offerings that push beyond California rolls, spicy tuna, and breaded somethings—more pristine nigiri, seasonal specialties, and inventive, lighter combinations that let the fish do the talking.

All that said, the rolls I had were well-made, generously portioned, and satisfying. Flavor was good, rice was balanced, and the value felt fair. If you’re in the mood for hearty, approachable rolls delivered with stellar hospitality, Hana fits the bill. If you’re seeking a more daring, purist-leaning sushi experience, temper expectations—or try the nigiri and specials next time. For now, a solid 3.5, with room to rise.

I like Panda Express and the new layout—it’s clean, efficient, and inviting. However, service attitude matters when I’m choosing where to eat. I’m purchasing their food with my money, and I can go elsewhere. Please improve staff professionalism: smiling, attentive service, and respectful communication should be standard, regardless of age or experience. A visible, engaged shift manager could help keep the restaurant running smoothly and ensure guests are treated well. Also, save the gossip for after hours—focus on customers while on the clock. With these fixes, I’d happily return.

My husband went to the riders course at this location and was so disappointed and disgusted by how he was treated he didn't even go back for the last day of class.

Overbooked class meant crowded practice and confusion. A second instructor was brought in; his yelling and contradictions undermined the resident instructor, breeding hostility. Mixed messages and an abrasive tone crushed confidence instead of building it. After spending $600 on tuition and required gear, we expected supportive coaching, not intimidation. The experience was so discouraging my husband skipped the final day. Until this location fixes class sizes and instructor conduct, we cannot recommend it to new riders.

Steak lovers, take note: this place serves some of the most tender, flavorful beef I’ve ever tasted. The kitchen’s 21-day aging pays off in melt-in-your-mouth bites that are beautifully seasoned and cooked to perfection. While my rice arrived undercooked, the staff handled it flawlessly, swapping in creamy mashed potatoes within moments—comforting, buttery, and delicious. Service was attentive and responsive, turning a minor hiccup into a satisfying solution. Between the superb steak and thoughtful hospitality, this spot earns high marks. If you crave a wow-worthy cut that’s tender enough to spoil you for others, make this your next dinner destination.

Dined here with the family during our last Vegas trip, and this spot lived up to the hype. The waitstaff was exceptionally attentive and genuinely knowledgeable, guiding us through the menu with confidence. As a longtime Bobby Flay fan, I appreciated our server’s on-point recommendations—especially the Partida blanco margarita, bright with fresh lime and balanced with agave. It was so good I hunted down the tequila back home in Jersey. Our steaks had minor temperature issues, but the team corrected them immediately and, impressively, removed them from the bill without us asking. That level of service speaks volumes. The atmosphere is lively yet comfortable, perfect for a celebratory family meal or a night out. With bold flavors, polished hospitality, and a can’t-miss cocktail program, this is a must-visit in Las Vegas. I’m already planning my return—and thinking about that margarita again.

This is a pretty cool place, with sand...and water.... and, well that’s it really. The pool is tiny, and the sand’s condition raises cleanliness questions—do they ever replace it to prevent germs? Sand coats the walkways, making footing slick; I slipped a few times and my mom nearly fell. The lazy river is minuscule, more creek than river, fitting maybe a dozen people, which kills the relaxing vibe. For a venue built on sand and water, maintenance and safety need attention: refresh the sand, keep paths clear, and expand the water features. With those fixes, it could be genuinely enjoyable instead of mildly frustrating. Staff were pleasant, but the layout hampers enjoyment overall.

I wanted to love this AYCE sushi spot. It’s close to home, the early reviews looked promising, and I went in ready to make it a regular. Unfortunately, after a visit with a party of six, I don’t see myself returning.

There were two standouts: the ahi poke and the baked green mussels. The poke was attractively presented, and the crunch from the chips added a satisfying contrast that made the dish feel thoughtful and balanced. The mussels were tasty too, though it’s hard to tell whether that owed more to the generous layer of yum yum sauce than to the mussels themselves. In hindsight, I wish I’d ordered more of those two and skipped the majority of the rolls.

The rolls were where things faltered. Once they hit the table, it was nearly impossible to tell them apart—most looked the same and seemed to share a similar set of ingredients. The crunchy, fried options were especially underwhelming. The heavy fry masked any fish flavors, making it difficult to identify what we were eating, let alone judge freshness. The non-fried rolls were just okay—nothing offensive, but nothing memorable. A small but important detail: the menu didn’t indicate how many pieces each roll included, and we assumed the standard eight. By the end, we were struggling to finish what we’d ordered, which dampened the experience and contributed to overall fatigue with the sameness of the rolls.

Nigiri was a mixed bag. I tried the salmon and tuna; they were fine, not unpleasant, but lacking the freshness and clean flavor that can elevate even a simple bite.

Service landed somewhere between adequate and frustrating. There was only one server working the room, and while I personally didn’t find her rude, others in my group felt she was pushy about front-loading the order. In most AYCE settings, we prefer to order in waves to avoid waste and gauge what’s worth repeating. Here, we were encouraged to order a lot upfront, and the server only returned later to take dessert selections. One of my half-order choices never arrived, which I noticed only because everything else was full-sized—and, frankly, I didn’t mind skipping it by that point.

There’s potential here—tighten up roll variety, be transparent about portion sizes, encourage staggered ordering, and focus on freshness—and this neighborhood spot could win people over. As it stands, it wasn’t enough to bring me back.

When I walked into the Cornish Pasty Co., I immediately felt like I was home.

There’s an instant coziness to this place that’s hard to fake. The setup is unlike any restaurant I’ve visited: pew-style bench seating flanking long communal tables, bottle candles flickering at each spot, and a lived-in, laid-back vibe that invites you to settle in. My friends and I were seated right away, and our server, Mike, had our drink orders taken and filled without delay. The heavy, oversized glasses added to the rustic charm, and even the metal plates seemed to transport us to another time.

Once we made our choices, the wait for food was reasonable—about 10 to 20 minutes before our order was up and another five before it was on the table. I went for the Philly Pasty, a hearty pocket packed with meat, Swiss cheese, peppers, and onions. The crust was the standout: golden, crunchy, and beautifully executed—exactly what a pasty crust should be. The filling, however, arrived lukewarm. It still tasted good, with a balanced mix of savory flavors and just the right hit of peppers and onions, but the temperature dulled the experience. A hotter center would have elevated an already promising dish.

Service throughout the meal was attentive; Mike checked in regularly and kept things moving. That said, the sight of him listening to an iPod and snacking while on duty didn’t inspire confidence. He also ducked into the dish station now and then. It wasn’t disruptive, just a bit odd for someone actively waiting tables.

Even with those quirks, the overall experience was positive. The atmosphere is memorable, the food is satisfying, and I’d return to this location without hesitation—next time with a simple request: make sure that beautiful pasty arrives piping hot.

First visit to Xinh Xinh today for lunch.

I ordered rice vermicelli with chicken and peanut plus a spring roll. Flavors were fresh, balanced, and delicious; the spring roll was crisp and satisfying. Service, however, lagged: we waited a long time to place our order, no one checked on us, and our drinks weren’t refilled. The vermicelli portion wasn’t quite filling; I wish I’d added an appetizer or side. Despite the service hiccups, the food quality shines. I’ll return when craving Vietnamese, hoping for more attentive, timely service next time. Prices seemed fair for the portions.

The Weary’s Reuben is uniquely crave-worthy—if I go too long without one, I start pining for it. It comes with an incredible potato salad, too. While most folks rave about Bob’s Bad Breath Burger, I say make the Reuben your first stop. Service can be slow or inattentive, but hey, it’s Willy Street—that laid-back, hippie vibe is part of the charm and memorable.

Went to Raul and Theresa’s last night on our quest for the best Mexican in Phoenix, and we left impressed. We started with a $15 pitcher of strawberry margaritas—bright, not overly sweet, and generously portioned at six servings; mom and I each had three and loved the value. Food hit the table fast, and both the waitress and hostess were genuinely friendly, setting a warm tone right away. Portions are downright huge, the kind that spill over a big plate, so come hungry. If there’s a blemish, it’s the pre-dinner chips, which didn’t taste particularly fresh. Thankfully, the salsa more than redeemed them—zesty, balanced, and addictive. For price, portion sizes, speed, and hospitality, Raul and Theresa’s delivers. We’ll gladly return and won’t hesitate to bring out-of-town company for a satisfying, crowd-pleasing meal.

A fascinating stop for vintage Vegas lovers, this free (donation-supported) venue showcases uncommon historic photos and concise narratives you won’t see elsewhere. Exhibits feel fresh and evolving, inviting repeat visits to catch new additions. Engaging, educational, and easy to enjoy—highly recommend dropping in to explore again soon.

Was I on a date? A silence and a look had me paying for a meal costing half my intern week’s pay. There was no offer to split, no talk about expectations—just a bar afterward and her leaving with someone else. The restaurant was fine, but the experience felt transactional and deflating. If you value clarity and courtesy, discuss the bill early. Otherwise you may end up footing the whole thing and feeling foolish. Lesson learned. Next time, set expectations.

Rediscovering a Neighborhood Standby at The Parlor

Living within walking distance, it’s easy to overlook a familiar spot in favor of the latest Phoenix restaurant hype. When my sister visited at 5 p.m. on a Friday, we chose convenience over traffic and headed to The Parlor—a decision that reminded me why neighborhood standbys matter. We were seated immediately, a pleasant surprise during happy hour, and with the patio doors open, the room felt airy and connected to the beautiful spring weather.

We started with a couple glasses of wine, each $2 off. The selection is solid and the discount makes for an easy, low-key start to the evening. For a shared bite, the Fritto Misto at $5 was crisp and light, if a touch under-seasoned. Paired with lemon and a simple sauce, it was still a satisfying snack without weighing us down before the main event.

The happy-hour pizzas are the real draw: at $7.99, you get a full-sized pie generous enough for one and easily shareable depending on appetite. We ordered the Pesto, Pepperoni, and a Cheese for my son. All three were genuinely good—blistered, well-tendered crusts; balanced toppings; and fresh, bright flavors. The pesto delivered aromatic basil and nuttiness, the pepperoni had a classic, slightly spicy snap, and the cheese was clean and comforting. Not “good for happy hour”—just good, period.

Service was excellent throughout. Even as the dining room grew busier, the team stayed engaged and upbeat, refilling waters and checking in without hovering. The family-friendly atmosphere stood out, too: plenty of tables with young children, patient servers, and a relaxed energy that makes dining with kids feel effortless.

Value, quality, and ease converge here. The Parlor proves you don’t have to chase the newest opening across town to enjoy a great meal. With well-made pizzas, breezy indoor-outdoor vibes, and staff who keep pace with the rush, it’s a neighborhood gem worth revisiting. I left kicking myself for overlooking it—and I’ll be back soon to explore more of the menu.

After two visits in two weeks, Wild Tuna has become a favorite for my boyfriend and me. We shared miso soup, a Philadelphia roll, Rainbow roll, the Salmon & Garfunkel, and Surf & Turf; each dish was fresh, flavorful, and well worth the price. Consistent quality and generous portions will keep us coming back again soon.

Pre-Wine Tasting Dinner Disappoints Despite Friendly Service

We visited this ristorante ahead of a wine tasting Groupon and opted for dinner first. Initial impressions were underwhelming: the space feels a bit run-down and could be cleaner. We started with the cheese plate, which arrived as large, unwieldy chunks alongside prosciutto that didn’t taste particularly fresh. Without crackers or bread, it was awkward to eat until our waitress—pleasant throughout—eventually brought warm bread rolls, surprisingly the highlight of the meal.

For mains, my husband ordered “fresh pasta with shrimp and pesto.” The pasta and shrimp were indeed fresh, but the sauce tasted like plain oil rather than pesto, leaving the dish excessively greasy; he managed only the top third. My penne al forno fared better, baked nicely but notably bland until we supplemented it with those cheese chunks.

As self-professed coffee snobs familiar with true Italian espresso, we found both the espresso and cappuccino disappointing, reminiscent of drip coffee run through an espresso machine. Desserts, however, were a bright spot and nicely executed.

Service was genuinely welcoming—we were greeted before we even stepped inside—and other diners seem to praise the pizza and subs. If we lived closer, we might return to try those. Based on our experience, though, this is a friendly spot with some fresh ingredients but uneven execution, a need for basic accompaniments, and room for improvement in coffee and cleanliness.

Las Vegas is lucky to have an option as authentic as Kabuto. I had the omakase set, and the nigiri was outstanding—clean cuts, perfect rice, and seasonal whitefish shining throughout. It’s whitefish season, and their lineup of snapper from Southern Japan was especially memorable. However, the grilled items fell short, lacking the finesse and balance found at the sushi bar. There’s a noticeable disconnect between kitchen and counter quality. Next visit, I’ll skip the cooked courses and double down on the nigiri set exclusively.

I've been a loyal AJ's shopper for years, which makes my recent catering attempt especially disappointing. Planning a party should feel welcoming and seamless. AJ's ads promise catering can be ready with two days' notice; I came in nine days ahead to be safe. After a long wait, I was finally helped by Emily, who had been on her lunch break. I apologized for the interruption, but the interaction never recovered. We waited while she washed her hands, and the tone felt rushed and begrudging rather than collaborative.

I outlined the size of my event and was told to double the order. Fine. I agreed to two hams, a crown pork roast, and the full dinner spread. Then I was lectured about ham sizes and, ultimately, told that the day I needed was already at maximum capacity. Being "squeezed in" didn't inspire confidence. At that point, I decided to take my business elsewhere.

A short drive to Whole Foods solved everything. In one visit, I secured full-course meals for 20 people with clear pickup timing and courteous service. The contrast in tone and clarity was stark and immediately reassuring.

AJ's food quality has always been excellent for my past parties. But hospitality matters. Don't make customers feel like a burden, and don't advertise flexible timelines if staffing or capacity can't support them. Better scheduling for breaks, proactive communication about order limits, and a can-do, solution-focused approach would go a long way.

I skipped buying wine and other essentials at AJ's that day. I hope management addresses these gaps so longtime customers can plan parties there with confidence again.

Came here with some friends for drinks the other night.

From the first sip, cocktails were outstanding. Our group ordered one each from the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd course: the Rum Punch, Apple'onia, and Hot Buttered Rum. Each was balanced, flavorful, and served. Lucas, our waiter, was prompt and full of spot-on recommendations that elevated the experience. If the night had ended at the table, this would have been a five-star visit.

Unfortunately, the front-of-house soured the evening. The gentleman who seated us was openly judgmental, insinuating that one of our diverse group "smelled funny" and nearly denying entry despite our reservation. We were eventually led to the back cigar lounge, which turned out to be a main corridor for staff hauling trash and supplies. Throughout our visit, we felt in the way, repeatedly interrupted by curt "excuse me" from employees squeezing past. For a place we hoped would be a cozy, convivial rum lounge, it felt more like, to borrow a phrase, the Upper Bread Crust Rum Lounge, polished on top but abrasive underneath.

My wife and I frequent Phoenix restaurants weekly and rarely encounter such treatment. Great drinks cannot compensate for rude, judgmental hospitality. We will not be returning.

After reading Bri D.’s account, I have to agree—and add my own frustration. If a cafe can’t deliver breakfast within 40 minutes of ordering, it shouldn’t be in business. Breakfast is supposed to be quick: eggs, toast, coffee—ten minutes, tops. Instead, I sat watching the clock and empty table space, wondering what went wrong. In the time I wasted, I could have waited at The Good Egg, been seated, and eaten. I finally walked out, hungry and annoyed. This place? A hard pass. Save your morning and go elsewhere.

Father’s Day should have begun with a celebratory breakfast, but our visit to Betty’s Nosh quickly became an exercise in frustration. Despite having a 9:00 a.m. reservation, we were seated with standard double-sided menus and left to peruse them for ten minutes. When our pleasant server returned, she revealed that the restaurant was only offering a $25-per-person brunch buffet or two alternative entrées. The disconnect was jarring: no signage at the door, no verbal heads-up with the menus, and the same surprise rippled through other tables as they sat down. On a busy holiday morning, transparency matters.

Reluctantly, our party of six opted for the brunch, hoping for value and variety. The lineup included omelets, carved prime rib, two kinds of potatoes, mac and cheese, salad, veggies, fruit, French toast, and desserts. The omelet station offered promise, but execution ruined it. My made-to-order omelet was undercooked and runny; my son’s arrived with ham despite a clear “no ham” request; and my husband’s plate came ringed with oil or butter. When a teenager at home can better handle an omelet pan, it’s a sign the kitchen needs retraining and quality control.

The prime rib, to its credit, was decent, though not remarkable. Everything else suffered from presentation and taste. As we moved along the two-table buffet, the chafing setups used flimsy grocery-store aluminum pans that screamed pre-prep and corner-cutting. Buffets often rely on advance preparation, but thoughtful presentation elevates perception and encourages appetite; instead, these pans conjured images of a family reunion picnic. The mac and cheese was bland, the potatoes unmemorable, and the French toast sat cold and listless. Even a buffet needs seasoning, heat management, and attention to detail.

Desserts offered the final letdown. The small assortment was dry, forgettable, and felt outsourced from a bakery that prioritizes shelf life over flavor. On a day when guests are paying premium prices, every station should strive to impress; the dessert table did the opposite.

Our servers were warm but clearly overwhelmed and underinformed, repeatedly apologizing and deflecting blame to management and the kitchen. While empathy is appreciated, guests don’t want to hear internal chaos; they want good food and competent service. If the restaurant planned a brunch-only service, it should have been communicated at booking, posted prominently at the entrance, and announced before menus were handed out. With a tight schedule and a holiday crowd, leaving wasn’t practical for us, but the experience felt like a bait-and-switch.

In the end, we paid a premium for a buffet we never intended to order and left feeling shortchanged. Betty’s Nosh needs better communication, improved buffet execution, and a serious tune-up at the omelet station. Until then, it’s hard to recommend this Father’s Day experience.

I'm kind of a snob when it comes to service. I like it. I expect it and I know when its sub par, as it is as the Monte Carlo.

As a traveler who values attentive, well-organized service, I chose the Monte Carlo for a second stay because the rooms were reasonably priced and the location is central—two undeniable perks. Unfortunately, a quieter trip made the shortcomings harder to ignore. Basic in-room information was missing: no spa details, no entertainment guide, and no TV channel listing. When I called the concierge for a spa brochure, I was told to come down and fetch one myself—a small slight, but indicative of an indifferent service culture.

These may seem like minor oversights, yet on a property this size, small lapses accumulate into a less-than-stellar experience. Dining didn’t redeem things. The on-site premium steakhouse, Brand, felt overpriced, and the staff came off as brusque rather than polished. I cut losses and headed to Gallagher’s at New York–New York, where the meal and hospitality were spot-on—a reminder of how good service elevates everything.

To its credit, the Monte Carlo delivers value and a convenient base on the Strip. But travelers who prioritize thoughtful touches and proactive hospitality may find better fits nearby. I won’t write it off entirely, yet next time in Las Vegas I’ll be exploring other options that deliver both price and the caliber of service I expect. For me, that matters a lot.

A promising first taste undone by a distressing customer service episode

I visited Havana Grill for the first time with a semi-large group on the patio, and I truly hoped it would be a new go-to. To start on a positive note, the complimentary bread was warm, fresh, and genuinely tasty—one of those small touches that set a pleasant tone. I also tried the passion mojito, which was vibrant and refreshing, though a bit steep in price.

Unfortunately, the evening took a sharp turn. Unbeknownst to most of our table, there was an incident at the front involving one person in our party and a hat policy. Before we could make sense of it, the General Manager stormed to our table and demanded that the entire group leave immediately. The delivery felt abrupt and hostile, and being shouted at in front of other guests was embarrassing and bewildering, especially as many of us had no idea what had transpired. We were ushered out with full drink cups and unfinished plates, yet still handed checks with an automatic 18% gratuity added.

We had planned to spend the evening enjoying appetizers, entrees, and cocktails, but the handling of the situation overshadowed any positive impressions from the food and drinks. I have since filed a complaint with the owner, and, regrettably, I won’t be returning. If you choose to visit, I sincerely hope your experience reflects the potential I glimpsed in the kitchen rather than the unfortunate customer service I encountered. Such a disappointment.

Can't beat the view

The setting is spectacular, and service is attentive, with beautifully plated, high-end dishes. Unfortunately, the flavor doesn’t match the price tag. While the menu looks impressive, the taste falls short for the cost. It’s fine for a special occasion if someone insists, but not a must-visit. I’ve had better meals elsewhere for less, so I won’t be rushing back anytime.

We chose this spot for our three-year anniversary and left happy, if not swooning. The setting isn’t particularly romantic, with the hum of casino players in the background, but the food more than makes up for it. The bread is out of this world—seriously addictive—and the gumbo is the star. I loved that they let you choose your spice level from 1 to 10. A 5 delivered bold flavor with a pleasant kick; if heat isn’t your thing, a 3 or 4 should feel comfortably moderate. The bowl was loaded with goodies: tender cooked oysters, plump shrimp, okra, and other savory bits, all tied together by a rich, satisfying broth. Stirring in the side of dirty rice takes it over the top.

Weekday hours are on the early side, closing around 9 p.m., so plan accordingly; fingers crossed they stay open later on weekends. I’m already plotting a return trip with friends to explore more of the menu—and to finally try raw oysters for the first time. While the ambiance leans lively rather than intimate, the flavors, portions, and value make this a destination worth the price and the time. So good. Truly so good.

title: I live in Las Vegas and have eaten at this Buffet several times and found it satisfactory, but I recently received a coupon for 1/2 off the buffet. The buffet was advertised as $9.99. I drove across town and presented my coupon only to be told that by using the coupon, the 1/2 off would be deducted from the $14.99, the original cost of the buffet. I was told that if I didn't use the coupon, I would pay, $9.99. With tax and using the coupon, the meal was $8.76 even though they advertised it as 1/2 off. I think this was a trick and deceiving. I complained to the cashier and she agreed but said there was nothing she could do, she had been informed by the manager to charge the higher price. I said I felt this was wrong and a type of false advertising and would not eat at Gold Coast Casino again. If the casino wants to give a discount, it should be what it says it is and not deceive the customer. I did enjoy the crab legs. The prime rib was flavorful. All in all, the buffet was good and I would eat there again.....with or without a coupon.

As a Las Vegas local, I’ve visited Gold Coast Casino’s buffet many times and generally found it satisfactory. Recently, a mailed coupon for “1/2 off” prompted me to drive across town, expecting the advertised $9.99 buffet to be reduced accordingly. At the register, I was informed the half-off applies to the “original” $14.99 price, not the $9.99 promotion. The cashier even acknowledged the confusion but said management required charging the higher base. Using the coupon, my total with tax came to $8.76—clearly not half off $9.99—leaving me feeling tricked by deceptive advertising.

That frustration aside, the food was good. The crab legs were a highlight—sweet, plentiful, and well chilled. The prime rib was flavorful and properly cooked, and the overall spread met expectations for a value-oriented casino buffet. Service at the line was efficient, and the dining area clean.

Still, the coupon policy undermined the experience. If the casino wants to offer a discount, it should honor the plain meaning of its advertising, not bury the deal in a higher “original” price at the register. Transparency matters, especially to locals who come back often. I’d return for the buffet on food merit alone, but I won’t rely on their coupons again in future.

I came for the fish tacos and left disappointed. I prefer a light batter, but these were heavily breaded and fried; my first two bites were mostly crust with barely any fish. They do offer different varieties, so maybe others fare better, but based on this experience, I likely won’t return.

This pizza was a disappointment

I watched young staff mold dough barehanded; when I raised it, they said gloves weren’t needed—gross. I accidentally left my purse at a table and came back to find it still there, unremarked by anyone. Is anyone supervising? Between hygiene and inattentive service, I won’t be back.

Shock value only goes so far. I spent most of the show bored, despite the occasional jump scare. The most memorable moment was when I zoned out, looked left, and a performer in a reptile costume slithered right next to my seat, moving like a lizard. I yelled, "You scared the shit out of me," and everyone laughed. Beyond that, the spectacle felt flat: drag-queen aesthetics without charisma, simulated antics that were neither sexy nor compelling. I’m not a prude—just someone who expected creativity, humor, or narrative. Unfortunately, it delivered noise.

Dude, this place rocks. The cauliflower-potato wrap on a gluten-free tortilla was crazy delicious. Tomato bisque and mixed bean side were Dee-Lish. Friendly vibes, quick service, satisfying flavors around.

The place is in a sketchy neighborhood, the inside was a dump, the charbroiled beef was all fatty, and the Penang was mediocre.

Despite the buzz, this restaurant disappointed. The location felt unsafe and the interior was shabby. The charbroiled beef arrived overly fatty, and the Penang curry lacked depth. My jasmine tea barely resembled jasmine. Dessert fared worse: sticky rice undercooked, fried banana greasy, and coconut ice cream powdery with little flavor. I don’t understand the hype—maybe it’s the wall of celebrity photos from years past. With so many better options in town, I wouldn’t return or recommend. Even the basics missed the mark, leaving a forgettable experience.

I'm giving this place a 3.5! (and that's a good thing)

For wallet-conscious Korean BBQ cravings, this spot delivers exactly what it promises: solid value and plenty of meat. While many all-you-can-eat places creep past $30 after tip for dinner, this one undercuts the competition, making it a go-to when budget matters. The quality of the meats and banchan is pleasantly respectable—definitely not “cheap buffet” fare—and while the spread isn’t flawless, it comfortably lands around a B- overall.

The selection is where it shines. Expect at least four marinated meats alongside three or four “dry” cuts, spanning beef, pork, and chicken. Seafood options like shrimp and squid add some welcome variety. Beyond the grillables, there’s a lineup of cold salads and small plates, plus appetizers such as pot stickers and grilled fish. Sushi rolls are present, but they’re not the star; if sushi is your priority, you’ll be happier at a dedicated AYCE sushi spot.

Desserts are minimal—much like at places such as Sura—but that’s hardly a deal-breaker at Korean BBQ, where most people leave too stuffed for sweets anyway. A surprising highlight: the rose tea. It’s fragrant, refreshing, and easy to drink by the pitcher.

Bottom line: there are certainly more premium Korean BBQ experiences out there, but for the price, this place is hard to beat. It hits the spot when the meat cravings kick in, offers a satisfying variety, and keeps the check reasonable. A very honest 3.5—earned the good way.

Great happy hour spot for casual drinks and bites. The baked goat cheese is outstanding, especially with their warm baguettes. Service stayed friendly and efficient despite our large group. Comfortable vibe, value, and a place I’m happy to add to my HH rotation. Definitely returning.

Our whole family are die hard CSI fans, so we wanted to see this exhibit.

As longtime devotees of the show, we arrived hopeful that the CSI experience would let us flex our investigative muscles. Instead, it felt more like a small corner of a science museum geared toward very young visitors. The premise is compelling: choose one of three crime scenes, survey the evidence, and work through lab stations to crack the case. We picked Case 3, rumored to be the hardest, and dove in with notebooks ready, eager to apply observation and deduction.

That enthusiasm evaporated quickly. After the initial walk-through of the crime scene, the very first station essentially listed every item you were supposed to notice, undercutting any sense of discovery. From there, the labs walk you through pre-digested findings. You don’t analyze materials so much as copy down what the exhibit spoon-feeds you. Rather than feeling like investigators, we felt like stenographers, dutifully recording obvious details already decided for us.

The autopsy room continues this pattern: it clearly explains the cause of death, leaving no room for inference or independent thought. At the end, you input your “findings” to solve the case—findings you didn’t actually generate—and then you’re offered a $5 upsell for a CSI agent certificate. We declined, yet our kids later received emails with certificates attached, which raised eyebrows and had us double-checking our credit card statement just in case.

The biggest disappointment was the length. Even if you take your time, the entire exhibit wraps in about 30 minutes. If visitors were allowed to work through all three cases, it could stretch closer to an hour and feel more substantial. Why access is limited to only one case remains puzzling, especially for fans who would relish more complexity and replay value.

On the positive side, we didn’t pay full price. We used the 3-for-$54 deal at New York-New York (http://www.nynyhotelcasino.com/entertainment/entertainment_3for54.aspx), which brought our per-ticket cost down to $18. Bundling made the day worthwhile because the other attractions were far stronger. The Bodies Exhibit was genuinely amazing and worth full price; the Shark Reef was also very good. In hindsight, we would skip the CSI exhibit and choose the Titanic exhibit or simply ride the roller coaster.

As a concept, a hands-on forensic experience is fantastic. In execution, this one assumes the intelligence of a first grader and overexplains to the point of condescension. For CSI fans hoping to think critically, follow leads, and piece together evidence, this exhibit is too shallow and too brief. Had we paid full price, we would have been genuinely upset.

I first stumbled upon AA Bakery while desperately searching for "lo por baang" for my mom. After a quick cry for help on Facebook, I was directed here. How did I not see this place sooner?

AA Bakery offers a wide array of Asian-style pastries, breads, and cakes, and on first glance it’s an easy spot to like. The onion bread and custard buns are solid, fresh, and satisfying, but beyond that, the selection didn’t win me over. I picked up an assortment of wife cakes for my mom—nicely packaged, with far more flavors than the usual winter melon—but the texture missed the mark. Instead of that hallmark delicate flakiness, these were dense and a bit odd-tasting, which dulled the nostalgia I was hoping to gift. Service was efficient and friendly, and prices are fair. With so many stronger Asian bakeries around the valley, I don’t see myself becoming a regular. Still, if I’m nearby, I’d gladly swing in for their Hong Kong-style egg tarts.
Ate here yesterday; three fish tacos. Today I'm sick, likely food poisoning. Very disappointed—won't return. Beware the fish tacos here.

All other movie theaters have now been ruined for me! And here is why:

After one visit to this luxury cinema, I’m ruined for regular theaters. The plush, solid leather recliners redefine comfort, making two-hour runtimes feel blissfully short. Prices are refreshingly reasonable—about $1.50 more than the usual multiplex—which makes the upgrade an easy yes. Concessions elevate the experience: beer, wine with generous pours, and gourmet sausages that beat standard popcorn fare. Programming is strong, too, with plenty of film choices and a screen perfectly scaled to the room, delivering crisp, immersive viewing.

A few tips: reserve seats ahead; even booking a day in advance nearly left us without options. Arrive early, as concession lines can stretch. And be kind to the staff—hospitality is hard work, and a little grace goes a long way. Verdict: worth the hype every single time.

A Disappointing Encounter at Island Style: Communication and Courtesy Absent

After years of patronage and introducing friends and relatives to Island Style, our most recent experience left us stunned and deeply disappointed. At 5:45 p.m., we called to confirm they would be open; posted hours are 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., but we were told they sometimes close early if business is slow. Russell, who works for the owner, Gina, assured us they were open and asked how many would be dining. We confirmed seven adults and one child for 7:00 p.m., and he said, “Sure, sure.”

We arrived at 7:02 p.m. to a locked door and a CLOSED sign in the window. The interior was dark—lights off, no one inside. We knocked several times and even called twice, but there was no answer. With guests in tow, it was embarrassingly awkward to be left at the door without explanation, especially after confirming our arrival only an hour earlier. After waiting about ten minutes, we left and chose a reliable favorite that consistently delivers good food and respectful service.

The next day, we called to share what happened. Russell’s response was shockingly rude and dismissive. He barked, “No can help… No cook… I no can cook so I had to close.” He added that the cook had to leave because her baby was sick and that he had to drive her because “she no drive.” Emergencies happen; anyone can understand that. But the lack of communication—no sign explaining the situation, no call back, no attempt to let us know after confirming our party—was unacceptable. When we suggested he could have left a note or notified us, he grew hostile: “Sista, you only making me mad.” There was no apology, no accountability, and no courtesy.

We also asked whether Gina could step in; he dismissed that, saying she had her own restaurant to run. The attitude was clear: our plans and our business didn’t matter. That’s not how you run a customer-facing operation.

We’ve supported Island Style and brought them new patrons. After this experience, we won’t be returning, and we’ll be telling others about the inconsiderate treatment and unreliable hours. Businesses thrive on trust and communication. If you promise to be open until 9 p.m. and confirm a 7 p.m. party, you owe your customers a minimum of respect—especially when emergencies arise. Courtesy costs nothing. Until management addresses staffing, communication, and basic customer service, we recommend choosing establishments that value their patrons and uphold their posted hours.

Horrible customer service

I visited this alterations shop for the first time and was met with standoffish staff. When I returned to pick up my pants, I noticed the zipper was broken. I pointed it out, and they refused to repair the zipper or reimburse me for the fix. The pants were brand new, and there’s no way I would have walked out of the fitting room with the zipper down. It seemed clear the damage occurred in their shop.

When I asked to be reimbursed for the tailoring, the owner argued with me for ten minutes. He said he could fix the zipper but, out of principle, would do nothing, and claimed he had many high-end clients and didn’t need my business. The lack of accountability and dismissive attitude were unacceptable. I left disappointed and frustrated. If you value respect and responsibility, consider taking your garments elsewhere. Truly unacceptable experience overall.

I really enjoyed our visit to this unique museum. We scored a better-than two-for-one Groupon deal, which made the outing an easy yes. Plan generously: I strongly recommend allowing at least four hours to take in the full experience—our three-hour visit wasn’t nearly enough to see and savor everything. Throughout, there are clever surprise exhibits that deliver a full-on atomic experience; I won’t spoil them here, because discovery is half the fun. You’ll even receive a special badge for the Area 51 exhibit, a neat little keepsake. Unfortunately, that particular gallery felt amateurish and proved disappointing compared with the rest. The good news: the remainder of the museum is engaging, informative, and exceptionally well done. For value, variety, and memorable moments, this museum is a standout. Go—you won’t be disappointed. Highly recommended.

I'll admit from the get go, I understand Chinese buffets are not where one would go for gourmet chinese but this place wasn't even really GOOD.

Expectations were modest going in, because Chinese buffets rarely promise gourmet fare. Even with that mindset, this buffet missed the mark. The selection looked passable, yet vegetarians will find little beyond green beans, desserts, and fruit. The signage touted sushi, but offerings were cooked mussels and shrimp on ice—no rolls whatsoever.

As for taste, most dishes fell somewhere between bland and disappointing. The orange chicken lacked any hint of citrus or spice, and the meats were mostly fatty with dull seasoning. I tried to make a meal of the green beans—usually my buffet staple—but they were wrinkled, withered, and ate like bark-covered twigs. After a couple bites, regret set in.

Service, however, was a bright spot. We were seated promptly, beverages arrived quickly, and our glasses stayed filled throughout. The dining area seemed clean, though I cannot speak to the restrooms.

In sum, efficient service and a tidy room cannot compensate for a buffet that delivers so little in flavor, freshness, and variety. Vegetarians and anyone seeking authentic taste should look elsewhere. Overall, value felt lacking.

Went there for the first time 3 weeks ago

As a longtime jazz lover, I’d had this spot on my list for ages—my jazz piano teacher, Tim Whalen, used to perform here weekly—so a friend’s birthday finally gave me the perfect excuse. First impression: it’s pricey. Final verdict: worth every dollar.

The room hums with low-lit sophistication and the promise of live music, and the service matches the tone—quick, attentive, and, crucially, well-paced. Courses glide in without that rushed, plate-piling chaos too many upscale places mistake for efficiency.

We started with briny, impeccably shucked oysters and a daily special: an ahi tuna concoction that set the night’s theme. For mains, we split the ahi tuna steak and a porterhouse. The kitchen takes a confident approach to tuna—slightly undercooked to spotlight pristine freshness—and absolutely nails it. It’s the best tuna I’ve had in ages: clean, ocean-sweet, and luxuriously tender. The porterhouse drew nothing but praise from the carnivores at the table, seared with authority and juicy to the bone.
