We then stood outside their doors for thirty minutes, calling repeatedly, with no answer and no update. To date, we’ve received no response from the company at all. I am now contacting Groupon to request a refund. The entire experience felt unprofessional and rude, and it was incredibly embarrassing to be stood up after inviting friends. For a company relying on customer trust, this reflects very poor customer relations. I wouldn’t recommend booking until communication and reliability improve significantly soon.

I would like to give this place zero stars for many reasons but it made me give it at least one.

After moving to the area, we chose this spot for a quick bite and a drink at the end of a long day unpacking. We sat at a table because we planned to order food. The bartender never acknowledged us, let alone came over to take our order, so my boyfriend went to the bar and placed orders for both our meals and drinks. There were three of us; we each ordered a meal and added chips and salsa to start. The chips and salsa never arrived, and my entrée was wrong—I ordered a beef chimichanga but was served chicken enchiladas, which isn’t a close substitute. At no point did the bartender check on us, ask whether we needed anything, or even offer another round. We kept going to the bar ourselves for refills and, eventually, to settle the check. It was frustrating and disappointing enough that I vowed not to return.

Hoping it was a fluke, we gave it a second chance and sat at the bar to make service easier. I stepped away to use the restroom; when I returned, the bartender still hadn’t greeted my boyfriend and was engrossed in a conversation with an employee who seemed to have just clocked out. We waited several minutes without so much as eye contact. As we stood to leave, the bartender finally turned and asked, “Oh, can I get you guys something?” We said no and walked out.

Across two visits, the pattern was the same: indifference, inattentiveness, and basic service failures. Acknowledging guests, taking timely orders, delivering what’s promised, and checking back are Hospitality 101. Mistakes happen, but they require prompt attention and a willingness to make things right—none of which we experienced.

If you value being served, receiving what you ordered, and feeling welcome, I’d suggest choosing another place. Management should reassess training and expectations, clarify whether tables are actually serviced, and adopt simple standards—greet within a minute, monitor tickets, verify orders, and check back. The location is convenient, but convenience doesn’t outweigh chronic neglect. After two tries, the message was clear: one star only because zero isn’t an option.

Typical casino cafe vibes meet standout value at this spot, where drink deals steal the show: $8 bottles of wine and $1 screwdrivers, mimosas, and Bloody Marys. The signature Reuben hits the mark with a solid portion and classic flavor, but the surprise star is the loaded potato salad. Studded with bacon and green onions, it’s creamy, savory, and downright addictive—worthy of a dedicated feature on the menu. Come for the bargains, stay for the sides; I’m already planning a return visit with friends for more potato salad.

I live down the road from Bubba Phatz and stopped in for BBQ. Even starving, we couldn’t enjoy it: brisket was jerky-hard, pulled chicken had a strange chemical taste, and the ribs were burnt to a crisp. The coleslaw was bland, and the mac and cheese barely had any cheese. For $47, I walked away feeling ripped off. This was one of the most disappointing meals I’ve had. Beware before you waste your money.

I didn't come away wowed but it was a good experience.

I didn’t leave dazzled, but this restaurant delivered a good night out. The menu offers plenty of variety, and the live jazz adds a cool, relaxed vibe that sets the tone. We started with oysters that, while fresh, ran on the smaller side. I split a Caesar salad; the dressing leaned bland, though a few anchovies nudged it closer to the classic profile.

For the main, the Lobster Fra Diavolo read like a cioppino with a gentle kick: half a small lobster tail, mussels, clams, a couple of large shrimp, and fettuccine tangled in a spicy tomato sauce. It wasn’t especially hearty, but the flavors were agreeable. The standout of the evening was the wine—a 2000 Elk Cove Pinot Gris—which paired nicely and lifted the meal.

Service hovered around typical: friendly enough, efficient, but not particularly memorable. The nightly specials sounded creative, and other diners rave about the steaks, so I’d be inclined to return to explore the meat options. Overall, an average meal buoyed by ambiance and wine, with room to sharpen execution on the details.

Finally, a DSW in Tempe!

DSW in Tempe delivers a treasure trove of shoes and accessories, with a wide range of brands, styles, and a surprisingly strong purse selection. I always beeline to the clearance section, then happily wander each aisle—like a kid in a candy store—because there’s always something tempting. Service is cheerful and friendly, making the hunt even more fun. Joining the rewards program pays off: points add up quickly toward coupons (I redeemed a $10 coupon this visit), and birthday discounts sweeten the deal. For variety, value, and an enjoyable shopping experience, this location hits the mark.

Oh la la! Hawaiian fusion food at its best. I opted for the $35 prix fixe dinner and couldn’t resist the generous portions. Overall, the food was outstanding. The Vietnamese wraps were fresh, but the fish sauce skewed too salty and sour, lacking dilution and a touch of sugar. The salmon was perfectly cooked and absolutely delicious. The chocolate soufflé was decadent—expect to gain a pound after that rich finale. Service was attentive and friendly throughout. For value, variety, and bold flavors, this spot nails Hawaiian fusion with only minor missteps. Highly recommended.

Hidden in a giant warehouse, this pinball paradise delivers pure nostalgia and thrills. Rows of machines span decades—vintage classics and modern hits—with the Iron Man 2 table stealing the show. Each game includes a placard detailing origin and history, turning every play into a mini museum visit. Staffers occasionally demo games, and it’s genuinely entertaining to watch their skill. It’s an affordable, addicting way to spend (and lose) a little money in Vegas—fun, informative, and endlessly replayable for all ages.

I recently visited Dickeys. The staff was amazing—friendly and upbeat—but value missed the mark. For two people, our total was about $40, yet portions were small. Attempts to compensate with half-melted ice cream and pickles felt underwhelming. While service shined, pricing and portion sizes made the experience disappointing. Lower prices and more generous servings would likely bring more repeat customers. Great people, but food and value need improvement.

I will not be ordering from here again.

The pizza was strictly average, with bland, flavorless toppings, and the sampler plate arrived watery and tasteless. For what they charge, the quality is unacceptable. To make matters worse, the driver ignored my delivery note asking not to ring the doorbell because a baby was sleeping; they rang it twice and woke her. The only highlight was the garlic bites—really great—but not nearly enough to outweigh the price and other disappointments. Oddly, the “medium” pizza was closer to an extra-large at most places, yet still underwhelming. Between bad food, poor service, and inflated costs, this is an easy pass for me. Keep away.

We stayed here over Labor Day weekend. I don't think you can find a better location in Montreal, it is right in the middle of Old Montreal.

We stayed here over Labor Day weekend, and the hotel’s location is hard to beat—right in the heart of Old Montreal, steps from cobblestone streets, galleries, and the river. Our room was very nice, with a great view, and most of the staff we encountered were friendly and professional. Still, service quality varied from person to person, which occasionally dulled the polished impression. The newer section we occupied felt modern and well maintained, and housekeeping kept things tidy throughout our stay.

The biggest disappointment was the restaurant. Breakfast was just okay: one morning they ran out of danishes, and on two mornings getting a coffee refill proved nearly impossible. The food itself was fine but unremarkable, with dishes that felt under-seasoned and bland. Service inconsistency showed up again on Sunday, when we waited thirty minutes for our plates. My wife’s meal arrived hot, while mine was cold—suggesting our order had been delayed or forgotten, especially since the server reconfirmed it at the table.

Noise was another hiccup. Friday and Saturday nights were peaceful, but on Sunday we heard someone in high heels pacing above us, and the room sounded as if it opened onto the terrace bar during a party. It made for a restless night. I’m not sure whether that’s down to thoughtless guests or the layout and soundproofing in the newer section where we stayed.

On the plus side, the mattress was fantastic—plush, supportive, and hard to leave in the morning.

Ultimately, this is a beautiful hotel in an exceptional location, and our stay was enjoyable despite the flaws. Would we return? Possibly, but with Old Montreal offering plenty of alternatives, we’d weigh the options. With tighter restaurant operations, more consistent service, and better noise control, this place could be a top choice.

Loco Patron is a standout Mexican cantina in Scottsdale offering great value and flavor. We come for lunch often, and the Mon–Fri $9 lunch specials are a true steal in Scottsdale. Service has been consistently friendly and efficient, and the patio is perfect for kicking back with a margarita. We’ve never had a bad meal—favorites include the ground smothered burrito platter, carne asada platter, crunchy fish and mahi mahi tacos, Loco Taco Salad, Classic Taco Salad, enchiladas, and the comforting tortilla soup. A fun, reliable spot for good food and drinks.

An impressively eco-friendly, energy-saving library with solar panels in the lot that double as covered parking, and an atrium-like openness reminiscent of San Jose’s MLK Library. However, the design makes sound carry: elevator dings echo across levels, and quiet areas aren’t always enforced—groups chatting and people streaming without headphones can disrupt concentration. The fifth-floor reading room ran hot during my study session, though AC was comfortable elsewhere. On the bright side, the Wi‑Fi is fast and reliable, and the space generally feels welcoming. I appreciate that staff and patrons are, for the most part, respectful of unhoused visitors seeking relief from the heat or access to public computers. Overall, worth a visit.

Amazing! Stop searching and go buy tickets! I grabbed seats last minute and left thrilled. This show outshines Cirque—funnier, edgier, and packed with jaw-dropping acrobatics. Even after joining the line late, we still scored excellent seats, boosting the value. From start to finish, it delivers nonstop laughs, daring stunts, and electric energy. Truly entertainment at its best—don’t miss it. Worth every penny and your time.

Walking into this Sally Beauty felt like stepping into a full-fledged warehouse compared to the closet-sized locations I’ve visited. It’s about twice the size, with aisles lined with an impressive range of products and well-stocked shelves. I popped in after work to grab a nail polish and was greeted at the door—polite, if not overly enthusiastic. I didn’t need assistance, thanks to a quick plan and a $5 Sally Beauty Club coupon, but the cashier was friendly and efficient at checkout. Between the space, selection, and straightforward service, this store made an easy errand even easier. I’ll definitely be back. Parking was convenient and the store was clean throughout.

Pretty good loco moco and I'm not normally a loco moco person.

I came in skeptical, but their loco moco won me over. A juicy beef patty over rice, topped with a perfectly fried egg and smothered in savory gravy—comfort food that hits all the right notes. Maybe I’m craving some Hawaiian flair, but this is the best loco moco I’ve had in Las Vegas so far. For clarity, this review is only about the loco moco; I haven’t tried the burgers or anything else. And a PSA: calling something an “Aloha Burger” or throwing pineapple on it doesn’t make it Hawaiian.

Much better hotels available in same price range

We spent five nights here and left disappointed by value and service. The property has only one restaurant and a bar/pool lounge serving the same limited menu, so dining gets repetitive fast. The “green” housekeeping program promises a $5 credit for each day you skip service, but the coupon is usable only at the hotel restaurant, bar, or pool lounge—not at Starbucks or in the casino—further limiting its usefulness.

We declined housekeeping until Tuesday, when we requested full service. That night, the complimentary robe sent with the laundry was not returned. On Wednesday, though still in the green program, we were not given the $5 coupon. We reported both issues to the preferred customer desk before checkout. Instead, we returned home to find a $35 charge for the robe and no adjustment for the missed green credit.

Finally, the casino is small and very smoky; the cigarette odor permeates and detracts from the experience. With comparable hotels offering better amenities at similar prices, we’d look elsewhere.

I’ve dined here many times and prefer the lively bar. This spacious spot boasts a bar area, sushi bar, dining room, and private rooms. Happy hour shines with abundant drink and food specials. Traditional sushi satisfies, but their inventive specialty rolls are absolute must-try highlights, every visit.

It felt like it took this place forever to open.

After the long wait, the payoff disappointed. The atmosphere is bland, with mismatched paint, outdated dining sets, and a garage-sale vibe. There’s no music, leaving the room awkwardly quiet and uncomfortable. The food isn’t terrible, but it’s nowhere near the high side of good—serviceable at best. For a better experience, Shanghai Buffet just east on Bell offers tastier dishes and a far superior ambiance. I wanted to like Zen, but it misses the mark. Sorry, Zen; I won’t be back.

The steaks were cooked to a medium rare as requested. Good stuff.

At Outback Steakhouse, our steaks arrived perfectly medium-rare, tender and flavorful—exactly as ordered. The lobster tails, however, were overcooked and a bit rubbery. We mentioned it after finishing, and our attentive server handled it graciously, offering a free appetizer for next visit; service throughout was friendly and responsive. We shared the iconic Bloomin’ Onion—call it an Awesome Blossom if you will—crispy, salty, indulgent, and undeniably fun, though it does leave its mark in the breath department. Overall, the meal was decent: not the best steak you’ll ever have, but far from the worst, and reliable for a casual night out. With solid value, chain comfort, and staff who make things right, Outback delivered a satisfactory experience despite the misstep with the seafood.

Very nice concept for a bar.
Clean, pretty atmosphere without pretension. We loved the special s’mores martini—fantastic flavor and presentation. The graham-cracker dust along the rim, held by chocolate sauce, added nostalgic sweetness and texture. A creative cocktail that elevates a bar into a memorable experience.

Disappointing and underwhelming sums this shop up. If you’re hunting for dated Disney character costumes for kids, you’ll find a small, limited selection, plus a few generic tees and assorted, overpriced trinkets. Beyond that, it’s ho-hum territory—not worth the walk from the Outlet Mall across the parking lot. Hoping to snag Disney DVDs? Forget it. You can’t buy them in Disney World Orlando, and you can’t buy them here either. The lone bright spot: an Ariel costume that could make a little mermaid fan’s eyes light up. Otherwise, prepare to leave empty-handed or frustrated. With sparse variety, stale inventory, and high prices, this is a pass for most shoppers. Two stars. Save your time.

Not good

I purchased a Groupon and booked months in advance to secure a spot for me and my girlfriend. When we arrived at our scheduled time, there was only one person available because the other staff member was late due to the 101 freeway closure. As a result, my pedicure began while my friend sat and watched. The second technician didn’t show up until after my pedi and mani were finished and midway through my friend’s pedicure.

Unfortunately, the mani-pedi itself was underwhelming. There were no massage chairs, and the “massage” was minimal—more like a quick polish change with a bit of exfoliation. The technician who helped me was very sweet, but it didn’t seem like mani-pedis were her specialty.

Midway through, we were told we’d have to come back another day for the hair blowout, even though it was part of the Groupon and we were the only clients there. That left me wondering what the point of making an appointment was if the full service couldn’t be delivered.

The facial, handled by the late-arriving technician, was actually quite good, but it was supposed to be an hour and lasted closer to 30 minutes. She did fix my nails afterward and kindly offered to wash my hair, but by then I was too disappointed to continue.

Overall, the experience felt disorganized and rushed, with inadequate staffing and poor time management overshadowing any positives. The staff members themselves were nice and tried to make amends, but the operation didn’t feel like a fully equipped salon. I don’t plan to return, and next time I’ll check Yelp before jumping on a Groupon. Two stars, awarded solely for the workers’ courtesy.

LOVE LOVE LOVE this place!!!

We discovered this gem last year and, back in Vegas, we’re counting down to Wednesday for its opening so we can get our food on. The dishes are authentic, and the servers are attentive, friendly, and welcoming. Delightful: go hungry, leave happy. You won’t be disappointed.

After 23 years of eating sushi, this was the worst. The fish tasted lifeless, the rice was mushy, and the rolls fell apart. Service was indifferent and rushed; our plates arrived alarmingly fast, likely because few were ordering. Dropping $120 felt like a total waste. I won’t return and can’t recommend this place.

Well apparently I'm not the first one to say this, but this place has horrible food and service.

Walking into this bar late Sunday afternoon, the room was empty—a promising sign for a quick, low-key lunch. We were seated promptly, and that’s where the efficiency ended. Despite the lack of crowds, service stalled at every touchpoint: water took ages, food took longer, and the check later still. It wasn’t a one-off lag; it was a pattern of inattention that turned a casual meal into a test of patience. We kept glancing toward the bar and the pass, but no one seemed to notice or care. It set a tone of indifference that never lifted. In an empty dining room, a check-in occasionally shouldn’t be a stretch; here it felt like wishful thinking.

Menu-wise, options skew heavy and meat-centric, with virtually nothing for those seeking lighter fare or meatless dishes. Vegetarians and vegans, take note: you’ll be cobbling together sides at best. I settled on grilled vegetables, and they arrived tasting unmistakably of lighter fluid—a harsh, chemical note that overwhelmed any natural flavor. By the time the plate reached the table, the vegetables had cooled significantly, compounding the disappointment. Presentation didn’t help: a careless scatter that looked more like an afterthought than a bar’s attempt at appetizing.

Originally, I was inclined to give two stars on goodwill alone, but revisiting the experience makes the rating clear. With unresponsive service, limited meatless options, off-putting flavors, and lackluster presentation, this was, unequivocally, a one-star visit.

I love this place.

Tucked in the arts district, this bar feels like stepping into a wonderland of strange, fascinating oddities. Their “elixirs” are inventive and reasonably priced, backed by a stellar cocktail and beer selection. The atmosphere is effortlessly chill, the staff and patrons are genuine and welcoming, and the outdoor space under the night sky is pure magic. A seasonally changing menu keeps things fresh, inviting you to discover new, eccentric creations every visit. I’ll absolutely be back to frolic here again soon.

Great staff

Our group of 20 was accommodated flawlessly—and we returned with 40. Outstanding hospitality for large parties. Spring rolls rival Brodard, shaking beef with red rice is on point, and banh khot is delicious. The team didn’t miss a beat. We’ll be back on our next Vegas trip.

I've experienced way better. I do not recommend this spa for a massage, at least by the person that did mine.

I stayed at the Stratosphere on April 15, 2011 and booked a 75-minute massage for $175. I’m used to paying around $85 for 90 minutes back in Texas, but I understand Las Vegas pricing. Knowing exactly what I needed, I was very clear up front: deep tissue, therapeutic, no fluff. They asked if I preferred a male or female therapist; I said either was fine as long as they could deliver firm, focused pressure.

I was assigned a smaller male therapist who seemed knowledgeable, and at first I felt optimistic. Unfortunately, the session never matched my request. What I received felt like a Swedish-style rubdown—light to moderate pressure—with none of the deep, targeted work I expect in a true therapeutic treatment. I reiterated during the session that I needed significantly deeper work on my shoulders, back, and calves, but the pressure never reached a level that addressed muscle tension. For a premium price and shorter duration than I usually book, it was a clear disappointment.

The next day, I called the spa manager to explain the mismatch between what I asked for and what I received. I requested a partial refund as a reasonable resolution. The manager offered a return visit for another massage as a make-good, but my schedule didn’t allow it. I declined and reiterated that a partial refund would be fair under the circumstances. No adjustment was provided.

I don’t question the therapist’s friendliness or general knowledge, but for travelers seeking a true deep tissue massage—firm, corrective, and results-oriented—my experience fell short. At $175 for 75 minutes, I expected a high-caliber therapeutic treatment and left without meaningful relief. If deep pressure is your priority, confirm your therapist’s specialty in advance or consider other options in Las Vegas. Based on this visit, I cannot recommend this spa.

Talk about bad customer service

This husband-and-wife operation is defined by an unfriendly vibe. The wife greets you with a scowl—if she greets you at all—and the entire experience feels purely transactional, as if your presence is a nuisance. Signs clutter the space, including a notice about a fee for a second drink refill (how many people even get one?), and the condiment station is policed so strictly you wouldn’t dare move the chili peppers. It’s not welcoming or hospitable. The pizza itself is pretty good, especially when you’re hungry, but it would shine more with a proper wood-fired oven. Good food, disappointing service.

From the moment we approached the door, the customer service at this restaurant was over the top. We hosted a graduation dinner for my grandson on 6-12-2014, and the team made it unforgettable: a congratulatory sign with his name greeted us outside, and customized menus rolled like diplomas added a charming touch. Our waitress was wonderfully accommodating, and every course was very good. Throughout the evening, we felt like the only guests in the house, thanks to attentive, thoughtful service. Exceptional hospitality, delicious food, and heartfelt details—great job, and keep up the outstanding work. Highly recommended.

Ordered the Western omelet, and my partner had the Big Bad Wolf—both were phenomenal. Yes, prices feel high once you consider ingredient costs, but the flavor and execution are hard to replicate at home unless you’re an exceptional cook. Portions were satisfying, service friendly, and the breakfast left us craving more. We’re already planning a return visit to tackle their eggs Benedict. Highly recommend for a standout brunch.

Saturday at Lavo skewed older—think 30-plus—but the vibe was lively enough to make losing track of the night easy. I had fun, even if the crowd was dense, the room sweltering, and shoulders constantly brushing past. Less fun: the post-restroom setup. Sinks greet you, yet there were no towels, no soap—just running water. Great energy, but basic amenities need attention too.

Disturbing experience at Signal Butte PetSmart and Banfield: safety and accountability concerns

I recently had to rush one of my dogs to the Banfield inside the Signal Butte PetSmart after he suffered a seizure in the middle of the night. My regular Banfield had no available appointments, so I headed there hoping for immediate care. I brought my other dog along to take care of routine needs. For context, my larger dog was attacked as a puppy by another big dog and has been fearful and reactive toward large dogs ever since. I always try to manage that carefully, especially in public spaces.

While we were waiting in line at the Banfield check-in counter, an older gentleman with a very large dog stood behind us. My big dog became agitated, and as I tried to restrain him, my other dog slipped loose. In the chaos of those few seconds, the large dog behind us grabbed my smaller dog by the neck, lifted him off his feet, and shook him like a rag doll. It was terrifying and traumatic. My dog ultimately needed surgery to repair a torn shoulder, and the bill was well over $600.

Within moments, a store manager approached. While I was still on the ground with my injured dog, he pointed at me and said something along the lines of, “So, you let go of your dog’s leash.” I already knew that, and hearing it in that moment felt unnecessary and dismissive. More troubling, the manager quickly told the other customer he could leave without taking his name or any contact information. In my view, this was a critical lapse in judgment and procedure.

Afterward, I contacted animal control and was told that leash laws may not apply the same way inside buildings; I also asked about recourse for medical expenses and was advised that small claims court could be an option. I then reached out to the district manager to file an official complaint. The response I received boiled down to, “What’s your part in this?” I acknowledged that I lost grip of the leash, but I explained that staff actions—specifically letting the other party walk out unidentified—left me unable to pursue any recovery of costs. My concerns seemed to be dismissed, and I ended the call feeling unheard and frustrated.

Based on my experience, I have serious concerns about safety, incident handling, and accountability at this location. In situations involving injuries—human or animal—basic protocols should include capturing contact information, documenting events, and showing empathy. I no longer feel I can trust that my dogs will be safe there, and I will not be returning to the Signal Butte PetSmart. I hope they review their training and policies so future customers don’t face the same preventable hardship.

My husband and I were very excited to go here...However, we weren't very excited once we ate there.

We arrived buoyed by glowing recommendations from parents, friends, and a radio segment, and the line snaking around the corner seemed to promise greatness. Unfortunately, the experience didn’t live up to the hype. I ordered a small cheeseburger with BBQ sauce, grilled onions, and grilled mushrooms. The toppings were a letdown: the onions and mushrooms tasted more sautéed than truly grilled, the BBQ sauce was barely detectable, and the flavors muddled rather than elevated the patty. Removing the toppings actually improved the sandwich, which says a lot.

My husband’s small cheeseburger with A1, tomato, and lettuce fared slightly better, but he summed it up as just “okay.” The fries were similarly underwhelming. If you prefer thick-cut fries with the skin on, you might enjoy them, but ours were more soggy than crisp. The portion size bordered on absurd—we shared one order and still tossed more than half the bag.

With so many promising signs, it’s disappointing to walk away unsatisfied. Will we return? Probably not. Throughout the meal we kept saying, “It’s just not Smashburger.” A couple of days later, still craving a good burger, we went to Smashburger—and left happy.

Just walked out

We’ve had a string of good meals here lately, which makes this visit especially frustrating. I took my daughter in after soccer for a quick bite on a Tuesday and was told there’d be a 15‑minute wait. Fair enough. The host said the bar was first come, first served, so we grabbed a high‑top. No menus were on the table. After 2–3 minutes, another couple sat nearby. The bartender greeted them first, told us someone would be right over, but offered no water or menus. We waited a few more minutes. When a server finally appeared, they helped the other couple first. So much for first come, first served.

Here’s a clue for non‑parent servers: a kid in a soccer uniform is hungry. After nearly 10 minutes without menus, water, or acknowledgment, we walked out. The host didn’t seem to notice or care.

It’s a shame, because the kitchen has been on a roll. Basic hospitality—greet promptly, offer water and menus, and honor seating order—shouldn’t be optional.

At the Arboretum Chili’s, the chain’s corporate pivot toward Southwest fare is on full display—and not for the better. Once my dependable spot for hosting guests, with reliable burgers and fresh salads, this location now leans so heavily into Tex‑Mex that the rest of the menu feels like an afterthought. Most shocking, the fajitas—a longtime Chili’s staple—were flat-out awful: tough, chewy steak, noticeably smaller portions, and none of the sizzle or satisfaction they used to deliver. The new hot, spicy taco shells show up on seemingly everything, turning dishes into one-note heat bombs rather than balanced plates. You can still find a few of the old standbys, but they seem diminished by comparison. After years of patronage, my wife left vowing never to return. For us, this is a disheartening decline—and a real shame. Indeed disappointing.

Worst. Service. Ever. Worst. Layout. Ever.

My stay was marred by indifferent staff and a cascade of maintenance issues. The room’s AC wouldn’t cool below 72, the ceiling fan was broken, and the shuttle driver’s attitude was downright rude. When problems arose, employees acted like they couldn’t be bothered. The biggest insult was the timeshare presentation: pitched as a 90-minute session, it stretched into nearly three hours of relentless pressure. “No” should be enough, yet the hard sell never let up, turning a vacation into a chore. Between the poor layout, unresponsive service, and aggressive sales tactics, this property failed at every turn. I won’t return—and after this experience, I’ll avoid any Bluegreen properties altogether.

I have given this place four tries two lunch one dinner one brunch on Sunday and all failed in the food department.

My early visits at the outdoor tables were plagued by service missteps: painfully slow pacing, unreachable refills, and plates whisked away before we were finished. Unfortunately, the food didn’t redeem the experience. Pretzels arrived dry, salads were wilted, and a friend’s sandwich came on a parched bun with an overcooked filling. I chalked those stumbles up to growing pains from a newly opened kitchen and returned with optimism.

To avoid the service issues, I sat at the bar on subsequent visits. The bartenders were consistently sweet and attentive, yet the kitchen still missed the mark. A hummus plate lacked flavor, and a simple request to swap vegetables for bread seemed unduly difficult. My friend’s pizza was underdone, with a pale, white crust, and I decided to skip dinner altogether in favor of a glass of wine.

The final straw came at Sunday brunch. The quiche—browned on top—had a raw bottom crust, with eggs that were cold, watery, and undercooked in the center. It was a disappointing cap to multiple chances offered.

This spot is just a minute from my home, and I wanted to become a regular. For now, I’m pressing pause until I see consistent, positive feedback indicating the kitchen has found its footing. I genuinely hope it improves soon.

As a longtime Cirque du Soleil devotee who has seen more than ten productions, I can say Mystère now stands among my absolute favorites. The show brims with astonishing stunts and razor‑precise acrobatics, but the most unforgettable moment was a breathtaking duo act that showcased just how powerful, balanced, and resilient the human body can be. Every performer was remarkably talented, executing complex sequences with fluid grace and apparent effortlessness. If you love acrobatics and want a front‑row look at graceful flexibility fused with raw strength, this is unmissable. Is it pricey? Sometimes. Is it worth the splurge? Absolutely—every minute feels like money well spent. Mystère captures wonder from start to finish beautifully.
Solid basic gym with rare crowds, friendly staff, clean facilities, and upbeat music. Affordable membership makes it a no-frills fitness option.

After a week in Vegas and sampling at least ten burger joints, this spot was the clear standout. Generous portions, perfectly cooked patties, and a friendly, attentive waitress made the meal memorable. Drinks were excellent, the vibe great for people-watching, and, best of all, the prices weren’t inflated—a rare find on the Strip. Tucked away in a corner, it feels like a hidden gem rather than a tourist trap. We left satisfied and impressed, and we’ll absolutely be back on our next trip.

A 3 star despite the love for Earthy?

As someone who eats gluten-free, I arrived at Earthy with high hopes after so many recommendations. The shop itself is terrific—shelves packed with GF staples I’d happily buy—but the café menu doesn’t match the promise. Gluten-free options are sparse, and when you retail the very ingredients, it’s hard not to expect more. My brunch was just okay: a tasty smoothie, but the portion felt small for the price, and nothing else stood out. Solid vibe, quality, but limited choice keeps it off first, second, or third list. I’d return to shop, not eat.

Fifth meetup for The Breakfast Club UYE and I finally lost my UYE "V-card"—ha! It was great finally putting faces to names in the Yelp community. First visit to this location for breakfast; I’ve hit the Tempe spot by Arizona Grand several times for dinner and drinks. Service ran a little slow, but with several large parties I didn’t mind—I was too busy chatting and making new friends. The complimentary chocolate fondue fountain stole the show. Hello, pineapple and strawberries! For my main, I ordered the Huevos Rancheros. It was fine—nothing special, not terrible, just middle-of-the-road. Still, the vibe and company made the morning. Big shout-out to Monica O. for organizing. Looking forward to many more meetups. Count me in for the next one.

I didn’t try the restaurant, but the venue made a strong impression. The decor is stunning, stylish, and thoughtfully curated, though the music runs loud, evoking a fun walk through the 90s on the way to the elevators. The terrace is a decent size, not huge, yet we snagged a table for six quickly, which was a pleasant surprise. Mojitos were a highlight: crisp, refreshing, and remarkably affordable at around $7; I even asked the bartender to repeat the price. Service was friendly and efficient. With a great view and a relaxed, social ambiance, this spot shines as a casual hangout for drinks and conversation. If you’re sensitive to volume, note the soundtrack; otherwise, it’s an easy recommendation for a laid-back evening. Great value overall.

Pros: A spacious, pleasant outdoor seating area is the clear highlight. Cons: Cocktails tasted weak, and both drinks and food suffered from an unacceptably long wait, with service surprisingly inattentive for a weekday night. My dish was passable—more saved by an overload of cheese than by flavor—while my fiancé disliked his entrée. Overall, the experience felt underwhelming and poorly executed. Unless things change dramatically, we don’t plan to return.

Well that certainly was mediocre.

The reviewer stopped in for a beer and pretzel, not a full meal. Service: immediate upsell from the gift shop overshadowed ordering—30 seconds to place order, 5 minutes sales pitch. Beer: Hofbrau Hefeweizen, decent but unremarkable in today’s crowded craft landscape. Pretzel: standard, jarred dipping sauces, nothing special. After finishing, the waitress returned to push gift shop merchandise; when declined, she reacted negatively, making guests feel pressured. Ironically, the reviewer had been eyeing T-shirts beforehand and might have bought one organically, but the hard sell soured the experience. Overall impression: atmosphere felt more like a tourist trap than a welcoming beer hall; the focus seemed on merchandising rather than hospitality. For those seeking authentic gemütlichkeit and standout Bavarian bites, this stop may disappoint. In a city full of options, there are plenty of places to enjoy a solid hefeweizen and a warm pretzel without the sales pressure. Hofbrau, sadly, wins the tourist-trap prize this visit. Not recommended for relaxed sipping.

I had these visions of a gran miniature gold resort with winding paths and waterways. Not sure why; all the reviews say it is nice and small, and quiet... they were right.

Located about 20 minutes west of the Strip, this mini-golf spot is local and non-touristy—exactly the low-key experience I wanted. The young staff were polite. The 18-hole course is tidy and straightforward, favoring simple, satisfying play over gimmicky obstacles and loud theming. Maintenance was mostly good, though five or six greens had sand tracked in from nearby traps, which made putting a chore. I ended up sweeping those areas myself; the attendant apologized and, in a thoughtful gesture, gave us free passes to return.

Overall, it’s a fun, outdoor course that delivers quiet, clean, no-frills mini-golf—ideal for an easy hour with family or friends. I wouldn’t make a special trip solely for it, but if you’re nearby or need a break from the Strip, it’s a pleasant option. With a bit more attention to clearing sand after windy days, this local venue could be a consistently smooth, relaxed experience worth revisiting.

Taking a scenic drive out of Phoenix for Easter brunch, we found this spot pleasant but imperfect. Service hovered on the inattentive side—never rude, just a bit ‘I’m ignoring you.’ What stood out was the décor: striking artwork sourced from the art store two doors down. It elevated the atmosphere and impressed us. A fine experience with memorable ambiance, though service could be more attentive.

One of my favorite spots in Chandler, this Greek café is a gem for fresh flavors. The owners are warm and welcoming, and the checkered tables add an authentic touch that transports you to Greece. My son can’t get enough of the hummus and pita, while my go-to is the gyros sandwich with the salad combo. Vegetarians will love the crisp salads, and the house dressing is to die for. Highly recommended for casual, delicious dining.

Everyone should experience Binkley’s at least once, and not only for the food. This is dining as theater. I chose the four-course tasting with wine pairing, and from the first moment it felt curated and choreographed. Each course was presented with flourish, and the wine steward’s intros added narrative to every pour. Beyond the four mains came a procession of tiny, inventive bites—before and after each course—that turned the evening into a rolling series of surprises.

The setting underscores the spectacle: gleaming china, fine crystal, crisp linen napkins, and personalized menus that make the night feel singular. For devoted food lovers, the menu reads like a playground of ideas. Plates arrive as edible art—compositions you might expect in a culinary museum—and, importantly, they taste as good as they look. The main courses were beautifully executed, and I left genuinely happy to have gone.

So why four stars? Because I probably won’t return. Like a brilliant show, the magic dazzles the first time, but repetition diminishes it. Strip away the performance, and what remains—while very good—doesn’t, for me, justify the roughly $150 per person when considering food and wine alone. Having “seen the show,” I’m less compelled to pay for an encore.

That said, you should go at least once. Binkley’s delivers an immersive, memorable experience that blends craft, creativity, and ceremony in a way few restaurants attempt. If you value novelty and story as much as flavor, it’s a must. If you prioritize repeat value over spectacle, treat it as a special one-time event. Service is polished and pacing deliberate, reinforcing the sense of occasion, from start to finish.

From Five-Star Favorite to Frustrating Letdown at Prime

I’ve long considered Prime at the Bellagio a must-visit in Las Vegas. Even though we don’t stay at the Bellagio, we regularly made the trip for special occasions, bringing different friends to share in what used to be a reliably superb experience. If I’d been writing about our earlier visits, this would have been an easy five-star rave: polished service, beautifully prepared steaks, and a ritual nightcap of dessert and coffee on the terrace with a front-row view of the fountains that felt nothing short of magical.

Two visits ago, celebrating my birthday, we noticed the first cracks. The food had slipped—less precision on temperatures, less vibrancy on the plate—but attentive service and that incomparable terrace finale still carried the night. I hoped it was an off evening.

Our most recent visit in 2011, however, turned that hope into disappointment. When booking two weeks in advance, I requested coffee on the terrace after dinner and was told the entire meal could now be served outside. Great—until I learned terrace tables couldn’t be reserved and were first-come, first-served. Why a prime feature can’t be reserved remains a mystery, but we took our chances and were ultimately seated outdoors.

From there, the evening unraveled. Our server, Luis (if I recall correctly), was curt, and the support staff felt disorganized and slow. The kitchen sent the wrong steak: my daughter ordered a medium-rare Kobe filet mignon, but received a well-done New York strip. When we explained the error—emphasizing we’d planned to compare the Kobe filet with my regular filet—the server insisted we’d ordered the strip and warned the kitchen would be “mad” if we sent it back. We did anyway. The correct steak took another 30 minutes, during which my entrée and our sides cooled, forcing us to pick at my plate to keep the evening moving. For two people, the bill topped $400.

Not wanting to spoil what remained of my daughter’s birthday, I handled the rest privately. I sent a detailed, constructive email to the manager. She replied promptly, apologized, and asked for my phone number to discuss further, adding that she didn’t want to lose us as guests. I sent it—and never heard back.

Prime still boasts a spectacular setting, but lofty prices demand consistency, gracious service, and responsive management. Until those return, the terrace view alone can’t justify the trip. I truly hope it does, because the memories here were once unforgettable for all the right reasons.

Great service. Great food. Great atmosphere. My husband and I stumbled upon this spot for lunch and left impressed. Though I know of the chef’s show, I’ve never watched it; the food alone won us over. The Caprese salad was fresh and flavorful, a bright start. My penne alla vodka was truly to die for—silky, rich, and perfectly seasoned. My husband’s meatball sub hit all the comforting notes he loves. We split the Nutella cake—nice—but the salted caramel ice cream stole the spotlight. Service and a welcoming vibe seal the deal. Highly recommend stopping in.

From Impressed to Appalled: A Hazardous, Disorganized Visit to Ted Wiens

I previously had an excellent experience at another Ted Wiens location, so when my check engine light came on, I returned expecting similar service. Instead, this visit became a case study in safety lapses and customer service failures.

I parked beside a temporary sign placed on the ground and staked into a parking line. Shockingly, nearly half a foot of the metal stake was left exposed. As I backed out, it impaled my tire. Before that, I had already waited about 20 minutes without any acknowledgment, despite staff walking in and out of the office.

When I alerted the manager to the tire damage, his response was, “Well, what do you want me to do about it?” He offered a tire at cost, but I had a spare at home and went to get it. Upon my return, the front desk attendant declared my tire wouldn’t fit—overlooking that my rims are aftermarket and the tire was correct. The manager then instructed staff to install the tire and perform a smog check I never requested.

After mounting the tire, no one informed me they were finished for another 15 minutes. The wait would have been more bearable if the air conditioning in the lobby had been working; on a 106-degree day, that matters.

This location’s glaringly exposed hazard, dismissive tone, miscommunication, and lack of basic courtesy undermine trust. Securing signage, greeting customers promptly, confirming services before performing them, and maintaining a comfortable waiting area are fundamentals—not luxuries. Given this experience, it’s hard to reconcile the brand’s good reputation elsewhere with the negligence and indifference I encountered here. I left disappointed, overheated, and with far less confidence in this location’s commitment to safety, service, and accountability.

Big screens can't redeem the truly disgusting state of this theater. I hesitated to set my purse down; seats and cup holders were filthy, floors littered. We saw people leaving with cleaning supplies. Bring wipes, or better, choose a different cinema.

One word: Eww.

This hotel feels trapped in a greasy 1970s time capsule, and not in a charming, retro way. The moment you step inside, the ceilings press down uncomfortably low, giving the entire space a claustrophobic, dated vibe. Comfort is an afterthought. There’s no in-room air conditioning unit—just an old-school crank window without a screen. On a stormy Vegas night, ours was left open, and rain soaked the clothes and shoes we’d set nearby. It’s a strange, impractical setup for any modern hotel, let alone one on the Strip.

We booked last minute, prioritizing budget over amenities, and the stay proved the old Vegas adage: you get what you pay for. As a one-night crash pad, it was tolerable. Anything longer would be a stretch. The property cries out for a top-to-bottom renovation—higher ceilings, proper HVAC, and basic safeguards like screened windows would be a start.

To be fair, the location is a genuine plus, placing you on a convenient part of the Strip with easy access to nightlife and attractions. But unless price is your only criterion, look elsewhere. Spend a little more for comfort, safety, and sanity—and save this spot for the demolition wish list.

Idiots. (TSA)

At a recent TSA checkpoint, I witnessed one of the most baffling examples of queue mismanagement I’ve ever seen. Only one x-ray machine was operating, yet staff opened three different lines feeding into that single bottleneck. One queue swelled to roughly 60 people, then was split into two after the ID check, creating a predictable choke point at the x-ray belt and a backlog at the podium. To compound the chaos, a third “priority” lane was opened, but agents waved through anyone not already trapped in the backed-up line, effectively allowing late arrivals to leapfrog those who had waited 30 minutes or more.

The result was a slow-motion pileup and an infuriating loss of place; I went from standing directly behind my brother to 20–30 people behind him with no explanation. When I tried calmly pointing out the obvious flaw—one lane feeding five lanes that collapse back into one—several agents dismissed the feedback. The podium attendant seemed unaware of how their ad hoc rerouting had broken the flow.

This wasn’t about speed so much as basic fairness and operational logic. With one x-ray machine, open one well-managed queue, enforce lane rules, and stop redirecting passengers in ways that reward cutting. Better training in crowd flow, clear communication, and opening additional screening capacity when lines spike would prevent this needless frustration.

OK, so Paradise Bakery is a chain restaurant. But, I had lunch there today, so you're going to hear about it. I've had Paradise on several occasions, but this was my first visit to their new Raintree location.

Paradise Bakery may wear the chain label, but the Raintree outpost delivers comfort and quality that feel anything but generic. The headline, unequivocally, is the cookie: chewy, almost underbaked in the best way, and—brilliantly—included with your sandwich so you can skip the guilt and savor the indulgence. Sandwiches are consistently satisfying, anchored by fresh bread and bright ingredients; the Tuscan Chicken is a standout, layered with savory depth that keeps you coming back. Round out lunch with the pasta salad, a cool, herby counterpart that balances richer bites. Service is quick, the dining room clean and casual, making this a dependable stop for a crowd or a solo bite. Come for the sandwich, stay for the cookie—and don’t be surprised if the cookie steals the show.

It was a class field trip

We visited as a class, with our professor ordering for everyone. The barbecued sausage was standout—smoky and flavorful. The steak arrived tender and juicy, cooked right. I tried cooked pineapple for the first time; a bit unusual, yet sweet. The salad bar was average, but the buffet-style staples, vegetables, and fruits offered variety. Overall, a solid spot for meat lovers, with satisfying proteins and decent sides, ideal for group outings and feasts.
This is one of my favorite pizza spots. We go every Friday for lunch. I love the meat pie and the Hawaiian special. Consistently tasty and reliable, a place worth checking out.

Brilliant. Opens around 7:30 and, though a bit tricky to find, this spot is worth it. I had the best strawberry crepe of my life this morning, paired with friendly service. A few outdoor tables make for a quiet, lovely breakfast. I’m definitely coming back tomorrow for bliss.

Searching for a taste of Midwestern pizza? This spot delivers the best in town, especially the thin-crust Meat Lovers—crispy, savory, and irresistibly satisfying. The tiramisu leans custard-heavy, yet remains delicious. While in-house service can be hit-or-miss, delivery is consistently smooth, making it our go-to. We recently moved and already miss having it nearby. Value is another win: coupons like $10 off $30 make it easy to stock up. We typically order two pies—one for now and one for the fridge—because leftovers are just as craveable the next day. Reheats beautifully every single time.

I had heard good things about Canteen, so a group of us decided to try it out before our show at the Improv.

Canteen delivers on flavor but stumbles on function. Visiting in the heat of summer, we opted for indoor seating only to discover there aren’t traditional tables inside. The space is arranged like a lounge, with benches flanking low tables barely a foot off the ground. While that setup suits cocktails and small bites, it’s a logistical challenge for a full dinner—especially with tacos, tortas, and saucy enchiladas that can drip and sprawl. In cooler months, the patio offers plenty of normal-height tables, which makes the inside layout puzzling if you’re planning to eat a proper meal.

The saving grace is the food, which is genuinely good. Our group sampled a range of tacos, a torta, and enchiladas; everything was fresh, well-seasoned, and satisfying. Though we skipped drinks ahead of the Improv’s minimum, the bar menu looked broad and tempting, suggesting Canteen shines as a spot for pre-show sips and snacks.

Service was straightforward, but there’s uncertainty hanging over the place: the hostess mentioned they’re closing next month. Whether that means a temporary remodel—hopefully with regular tables—or a permanent shutter wasn’t clear. Given the ambiguity, and the indoor setup, I’d wait for patio weather before returning.

Bottom line: Canteen’s kitchen is worth applauding, and the vibe works for casual drinks. For a sit-down dinner, the low tables are a hassle. If they rethink the interior seating, this could be a go-to; until then, timing and temperature matter.

What a great experience—twice. On a bustling evening, we chose the chef’s tasting menu with wine pairing, and from the first pour to the final bite, it felt like a perfectly choreographed dining affair. Each dish arrived with artful presentation and, more importantly, flavors that surpassed their looks. The wines were spot-on and generously poured, and the service was as polished as the stemware. While the tasting menu carries a premium over a standard three-course à la carte, it represents real value when you consider the price of the lobster pot pie on its own; factor that in, and the tasting becomes a savvy choice rather than a splurge.

Michael Mina’s signature lobster pot pie finally made sense of the hype. Deconstructed and cooked in its own vessel, it’s plated from the pot directly onto your dish, allowing each element—golden crust, tender vegetables, and impeccably cooked lobster—to shine. Don’t expect the heavy, cream-laden filling of a freezer-section standby. This is pot pie reimagined, refined, evolutionized. I’m not typically a lobster enthusiast, yet I’d happily return for this dish alone, any day. The rest of the menu held its own, too, with courses that struck the balance between innovation and comfort.

By dessert, after a couple of pre-dinner cocktails and the full pairing, I was admittedly a bit looped—and so excited about the Hungarian Tokaji that I promptly knocked over my glass after two sips. Our server, having clocked my anticipation, replaced it without hesitation and poured a fuller measure than before. That moment encapsulated the hospitality here. Pleasant and knowledgeable staff are table stakes; what distinguishes extraordinary service is attentiveness. Timing was pitch-perfect, dishes arrived and were cleared with subtle efficiency, questions never interrupted a mouthful, and water glasses were topped off before we even thought to ask.

If you can, request a booth in the dining room. It’s cozy, comfortable, and ideal for discreet people-watching—an amenity that enhances an already polished room.

On our second night, we stopped in solely for drinks before another reservation—because, frankly, casino bar cocktails can be uninspired. The hostess, bartender, and waiter all remembered us from the night prior. We began with specialties from the menu, then the bartender shifted to creating custom concoctions tailored to our tastes. Two hours slipped by, and we barely made our next booking. Disclosure: when your bar tab hits a few C-notes, the drinks and service should justify it. Here, they did.

I’d recommend Nob Hill to anyone who loves food, regardless of palate preferences. There’s something for everyone—even if your diet is liquid for the night. Consider us eager to return.

Beyond the food and drink, the ambiance contributes to the sense of occasion: softly lit yet lively, with just enough buzz to feel celebratory without straining conversation. The pacing of the tasting allows you to savor, never rush, and the pairings are chosen to complement rather than overpower. It’s dining as experience, and it resonates.

Finally Gave This Hidden Neighborhood Katsu Spot a Try

Tucked into a brand-new strip mall deep on the south side, this small, cozy restaurant is the kind of place you discover by happenstance or word of mouth. It sits beside a smoke shop and a dry cleaner, set back in a residential area, and if not for a flyer and local buzz, it would be easy to miss entirely. That low profile is part of its charm, but it may also be its biggest challenge. For diners outside the neighborhood, it’s a bit of a reach; for locals, it feels like a well-kept secret waiting to be found.

Inside, the space is modest but inviting, with a straightforward setup that keeps the focus where it belongs: on the food. Katsu is the star here, and for the price, the portions are impressively generous. Each order comes with miso soup, and the plates themselves are satisfyingly loaded—comfort food that doesn’t skimp.

Service is warm and personal. Meeting the owner was a highlight; he greeted me like a first-time regular, walked me through the menu, and made sure I understood the options. A standout touch is the DIY katsu sauce station at every table. With a tray of ingredients laid out for mixing, you can tailor the sauce to your exact taste—an interactive flourish that makes the meal feel both custom and homey.

I ordered a combination plate—katsu paired with shrimp tempura—served with rice, shredded cabbage, and miso. It was executed well: the breading on the katsu was light and crisp without overpowering the meat, and the seasoning struck a welcome balance, flavorful without tipping into saltiness. The shrimp tempura held its crunch, and the sides rounded everything out simply and effectively.

One quirk of timing: on a Monday night I was the only diner, which made things feel a little awkward as the staff’s attention—friendly as it was—naturally settled on me. Still, the experience stayed positive, and the food spoke for itself.

This is the kind of place I’d return to, even if not every week. Prices are a notch up from casual takeout, but the value shows on the plate. With a bit more marketing—and perhaps a boost once the sports bar next door opens—this hidden spot has real potential to become a neighborhood favorite. A solid thumbs up.

Good, Not Great: Solid Value Amid the Hype

I arrived with sky-high expectations and left mildly underwhelmed. The meal was good—fresh, plentiful, and fairly priced—especially if you can really put away a plate or three. The selection is impressively broad, covering crowd-pleasers across cuisines, but nothing stood out as memorable or hype-worthy. Long lines and the buzz from friends primed me for something extraordinary; perhaps I hit an off night. In the context of Las Vegas, I’ve had better, and I’d rank the Cosmopolitan’s buffet higher for both quality and flair. Still, this isn’t a bad choice: if the wait is short and you’re craving variety at a reasonable price, it delivers a satisfying, if unspectacular, experience. I’d return—just not after queuing for an hour.

KoMex is 0/2 for me, so far.

I came to KoMex craving quick, handheld comfort with a Korean-Mex twist—and left twice with great flavors but a fork-and-knife ordeal. On my first visit, I gambled on the bulgogi Philly cheesesteak. It looked fantastic and tasted even better: tender, marinated beef, melty cheese, and all the right savory-sweet notes. Unfortunately, the moment I unwrapped it, the sandwich collapsed, spilling its contents across the plate. So much for a grab-and-go pick.

Round two, I opted for a burrito, the ultimate easy-eating staple. Again, the flavors and quality impressed, and service was friendly. But the tortilla split lengthwise as soon as I unwrapped it, and the burrito exploded into a pile. Back to cutting and scooping, not biting and savoring.

KoMex nails taste, ingredients, and hospitality; the execution of “portable” items is where it stumbles. Overstuffing, saucy fillings, or insufficiently sturdy bread and tortillas undermine the convenience these menu choices promise.

If you’re dining in and don’t mind a mess—or you plan to use utensils—the bulgogi and burritos are worth a try. If you want true handheld ease, consider tacos, bowls, or ask for sturdier wrapping. I’ll give KoMex one more chance. After that, I’m calling it.

I stopped by on a weekend for a straightforward oil change and car wash, and left disappointed. Despite driving a new car, I was immediately pushed toward a synthetic oil package “starting at $70.” If I’m paying dealer-level prices, I’d rather get dealer-level service. The setup seemed convenient—fuel before the wash—but the execution wasn’t. Attendants are supposed to pump, yet two employees just stared and did nothing, so I pumped my own gas. After that, I waited roughly ten minutes while the lone active staffer finished with another customer, spending more time talking than moving the line.

Reading other reviews, my experience isn’t unique. The common thread is a lack of leadership and customer-service basics: train staff on courtesy, acknowledge customers promptly, explain options without hard sells, and be transparent about pricing and wait times. This place could be a quick, one-stop convenience, but convenience means nothing without professionalism and efficiency.

Until management establishes clear standards, staffs adequately, and prioritizes the customer over upsell scripts, I can’t recommend this location. If you’re going to charge premium prices, deliver premium service—or expect customers to take their business to a dealer or a shop that respects their time.

I haven't visited America's Taco Shop locations, so I can't compare, but this spot disappointed. I went for lunch with a couple of friends and we left unsatisfied. Portions were skimpy, flavors forgettable, and prices felt steep for what we received. The burrito was oddly flat, lacking heft and fillings, and the rest of the meal didn’t redeem it. For the cost, we expected more substance and taste. Sadly, we walked out nearly as hungry as we walked in. I won’t be returning, and can’t recommend this location.

Eeeeeehhhhh.

I found myself in the Seven Hills/Anthem area at my parents’ house and needed dinner items, so I opted for this Vons over my usual store because it was close—and because I love their in‑store baked bread. The parking lot was packed, so I parked far away to avoid any drama.

Inside, the store felt congested. Aisles were clogged by shoppers pausing to chat and others absorbed in their phones, creating bottlenecks. I tried to be polite—“I’m going to sneak past you,” “I’m right behind you”—but the vibe was more annoyed than accommodating. Navigating with a child added to the challenge, especially when our cart came with someone else’s leftover drink stirrers that I had to fish out before little hands found them.

On the plus side, I did score a decent deal: organic broths on sale with card, two for $5. I grabbed veggies, canned tomatoes, dry lentils, and a loaf of sourdough. Credit where it’s due—Vons’ bakery bread is consistently excellent, and this loaf reminded me why I sometimes make the detour. I love bread, and theirs hits that fresh, tangy spot I crave.

Checkout was where the experience really unraveled. Only four lanes were open and each was stacked deep. The atmosphere turned tense, with customers fretting over item counts for the express lane and grumbling about who “had too many” in their cart. Employees were repeatedly paging for help at the front, yet relief seemed slow. The gentleman ahead of me struggled with the debit card machine, and rather than guiding him, the cashier waited for him to figure it out, which prolonged the line and the collective frustration. I grabbed a Mountain Dew to treat my patience, but the wait still felt punishing.

My total came to just under $30 for broth, a loaf of bread (picked loose, cheaper than packaged), vegetables, lentils, canned tomatoes, and that drink. For what I bought, the bill stung. Vons has a reputation for higher prices, and today it lived up to it. Between the crowded lot, clogged aisles, slow checkout, and premium pricing, I left feeling more irritated than satisfied.

I’ll keep driving next time, even if it’s less convenient. Convenience doesn’t count for much if the shopping trip ratchets up stress and empties the wallet. Here’s hoping I’m the kind of future grandma who’s fun, badass, and kind in the aisles—because a grocery run shouldn’t feel like an obstacle course.

Got dragged in here by John R. because he had a coupon from work for “Medical Workers Appreciation.” It promised 20% off the entire bill and a free craft beer or appetizer, a combo that convinced us to give this place another chance. That optimism faded fast.

As usual, no host in sight, so we seated ourselves. We arrived at 12 a.m. thinking we’d catch happy hour, only to learn HH is Monday–Friday at 12 a.m., and this was technically Saturday. Missing out on $5 specialty cocktails stung. The dining room was uncomfortably cold—bring a light sweater if you go.

Our server took about 15 minutes to acknowledge us. When we mentioned the coupon, we were told we couldn’t use it. No clear explanation, just a flat refusal. Between the promotion being denied and the happy hour timing technicality, it felt like two strikes before we even ordered.

Food took a long time to arrive, echoing our last visit. The beau ordered steak and eggs; surprisingly, the server never asked how he wanted either cooked. Despite that, the steak came out with good flavor and was cooked nicely, while the rest was just okay.

Inconsistent service, confusing policies, and slow pacing overshadowed the few bright spots. With clearer promotion rules, warmer ambiance, and sharper service, this could be redeemed. As it stands, we’ll likely pass next time.

Cheap and delicious. A level above fast food. I had the Thai chicken wrap—the peanut-chili sauce was spot on—for only $6. My husband enjoyed the Italian sandwich loaded with provolone, pepperoni, and assorted meats, also $6. Fast service and bold flavors make this a great spot for a quick, satisfying bite.

Nope. Not Liking This Place

We gave this spot three honest tries, largely because we live around the corner and hoped our first impressions were off. Unfortunately, the food never rose above mediocre. On the Italian side, dishes were bland and one-note, with sauces lacking depth and any real spark. The Mediterranean offerings didn’t fare better; the falafel arrived mushy and nearly tasteless—creative presentation can’t make up for missing flavor. Even our kids pushed aside their kids’ meals, which says a lot. Convenience alone can’t justify another visit. After three attempts on different days with different orders, we’re calling it: this kitchen just doesn’t deliver satisfying taste. We won’t be returning.

I know that others may disagree, but I was not impressed with the pizza. Yes, the $5 price is a great deal, but a bargain isn’t worth much if the food disappoints. The crust tasted like cardboard—dry, tough, and lacking any chew or flavor. There was barely enough sauce, leaving each bite bland and unbalanced. For me, pizza should be satisfying and well-made, not just inexpensive. I’d rather pay a little more for a truly great pie than settle for a cheap one I don’t enjoy. Value without quality isn’t value.

Pho Saigon 8 in Las Vegas lives up to its reputation as a local favorite. Visiting on a friend's recommendation, I found the experience reliably satisfying—proof that it’s hard to mess up good pho. While it may not be the absolute standout bowl I’ve had, the differences among pho spots are subtle to me, and this one delivers on all the essentials. Service is fast, friendly, and efficient. The menu offers plenty of options, portions are fair for the price, and the dining room is clean and tidy. If you’re craving a comforting, hassle-free pho fix in Vegas, Pho Saigon 8 is a solid choice.

Very good authentic Mexican restaurant to eat at.

This cozy, family-owned spot delivers the kind of homestyle Mexican fare that keeps you coming back. The two main guys at the counter are genuinely welcoming—attentive, friendly, and intent on making you feel at home. My bean and cheese burrito was simple perfection: warm, fresh tortillas wrapped around creamy, homemade beans and melty, flavorful cheese. My boyfriend’s carne asada burrito was generously stuffed—piled to the brim with tender, well-seasoned steak.

The dining room is small but spotless, and despite passing this place countless times on the way to Paradise Video, I’m kicking myself for not stopping in sooner. A fun endorsement: even a Taco Bell employee from across the way popped in for a bite while we were there.

Beyond the burritos, the enchilada sauce deserves the spotlight—rich, balanced, and deeply satisfying. Come for the hearty portions and authentic flavors; stay for the warm hospitality. If you’re craving real-deal Mexican comfort food, this little shop more than delivers.

On Christmas eve found this shop open for wire and ended up sitting there and trying new juice and just hanging out and had a great time. Shout out to Joey he was great and answered every question that was asked. My wife got a kick the the shop has a koi fish pond inside. Also the prices are great and a lot to choose from. I will return to this shop even if it's just to hang out and vape with good people.

I popped in on Christmas Eve looking for wire and ended up staying to sample new juices and hang out. Huge shout-out to Joey—friendly, knowledgeable, and patient with every question. My wife loved the unexpected koi fish pond inside, which adds real charm. Prices are excellent, with a wide selection of flavors and gear. The atmosphere is welcoming, with good people and zero pressure. I’ll absolutely be back, even if it’s just to relax, chat, and vape with this great community. Clean, cozy space.

I visited with my husband and two kids on a Sunday afternoon, and while the exterior looked a bit rough, the inside was clean and tidy, if sparsely decorated. A singer doing Spanish karaoke added a fun, lively touch. We came for the pupusas and they delivered: inexpensive, a little oily, and wonderfully cheesy. Three varieties are on offer—plain cheese, cheese and bean, and pork with cheese and bean—and we tried them all without disappointment. Next time I’ll ask for them “well done,” since a couple were a bit doughy in the center. The accompanying slaw was fine but unremarkable. Value is a standout here, especially with the weekday special of 12 pupusas for $12. Overall, this is a no-frills, family-friendly spot where the food is the draw. Despite minor quibbles, we left happy and plan to return.

It feels more like a modest concert than a must-see spectacle. By the end, I felt I could have gotten the same experience by listening to an album. The bar is overpriced, though pours are generous, and outside drinks aren’t allowed, so budget accordingly. Seating greatly impacts enjoyment: unless you pay for premium seats, you’re likely too far from the action to feel involved; if you’re an avid MJ fan, that mismatch makes the cost hard to justify. The performance itself isn’t bad—competent musicianship and a few lively moments—but nothing truly transcendent. Production values are decent, crowd energy fluctuates, and sound is serviceable. I don’t regret going, yet I wouldn’t rush back. Overall, it lands squarely in the middle: fine for a casual night out, but not memorable enough for diehards.

I’ve visited several times, and this place shines at lunch. The beer list is fine, and the flatbread-style pizza topped with lemon and arugula was a standout—bright, crisp, and genuinely delicious. On a trusted recommendation, the portobello sandwich rivals, if not beats, The Bread Company.

Evenings are less my speed. The crowd and the menu lean pretentious, with an atmosphere that feels carefully curated to signal exclusivity. My partner jokes it’s tailor-made for Chico’s devotees swapping notes on braided leather belts—clever, but it captures the vibe. I’ll trade mood lighting for actual heat, and the chile dishes here seem shy on spice; a Chile Relleno that tasted more bell pepper than chile says it all.

Still, there are hits: my youngest brother inhaled a fried bacon appetizer and left grinning. Come for lunch, stay for the pizza, and temper expectations for dinner.

Terrible customer service overshadowed what used to be a favorite spot for shrimp fajitas. We sat at our table for an hour waiting for our order, with no updates from staff. Frustrated, we finally got up to leave. When I informed the manager, he didn’t apologize or show concern. I handed him $5 to cover the soft drinks we’d had, and he took it—missing a clear chance to make things right for an unsatisfied customer. That lack of empathy sealed it: I won’t be back, and I’ll warn friends and family to steer clear from this place.

Can I give less then 1 star?!?!?

If I could give zero stars, I would. This towing company is the epitome of what not to hire: inconsistent quotes, surprise fees, and drivers who seem indifferent to basic customer service. I was quoted a cheap rate over the phone, only to be charged nearly double when it came time to pay. Their slogan, “we take pride in our service,” felt like a bad joke; the only pride on display was in maximizing the bill. If you need a tow, make this your last call. Demand a written estimate and be prepared for a bait-and-switch. Save yourself frustration, money, and time—choose a company that values honesty over profit.

Aria Las Vegas: Sleek Design, Clunky Details

On a recent visit to Las Vegas, we chose to stay at Aria. As expected from a newer property, the casino and restaurant areas look polished and inviting, and we sampled a couple of on-site spots. This review, however, focuses on the room.

The room felt compact, though tastefully decorated with contemporary finishes. The sticking point was climate control: despite setting the thermostat as low as 62, the temperature never budged from 70. Not a dealbreaker, but over time the mismatch became an irritation, especially overnight. After long days on the Strip, coming back to a room that wouldn’t cool further undercut the sense of retreat one expects at this price point, which disappointed.

Aria leans heavily into in-room tech, with two wall-mounted control panels and a bedside touchscreen that manage lights and drapes. On paper it’s impressive; in practice, it’s undermined by lag. Commands took one to two seconds to register, prompting extra taps and making some buttons seem unresponsive. That delay turns a convenience into a minor daily hassle.

The bathroom design adds to the mixed bag. A very heavy sliding door looks sleek but is awkward in use; once it’s moving, it’s hard to stop smoothly. The shower enclosure includes a tub inside the stall—an unusual layout that may perplex guests accustomed to separate fixtures.

Taken together, Aria delivers style in public spaces and a well-appointed, modern room, but functional quirks detract from comfort. With more responsive controls and a thermostat that honors settings, the experience could match the property’s polished image. As it stands, it’s a nice hotel that didn’t quite win us over, and we’ll likely look elsewhere next time.

Delicious food can’t redeem a flawed experience. Despite an OpenTable email confirmation, the hostess claimed she “didn’t take the reservation,” leaving us stranded without notice. No cancellation, no accommodation, and no apology from the manager. Reliability and basic courtesy matter as much as flavor. When a restaurant ignores confirmed bookings and shrugs at the inconvenience, trust evaporates. Regrettably, I’ll take my appetite—and future reservations—elsewhere despite the kitchen’s talent.

I brought two cars for oil service and had the transmission fluid replaced on one. About four weeks later, the transmission warning light came on. My independent mechanic found the transmission sensor broken off and appeared to be glued back with Bondo. Over the past two years, the only shops that touched this truck were this location and the dealer, so I suspect this happened during the recent service, though I can’t be 100% certain. That uncertainty is why I’m giving two stars instead of one. Between the original visit and the subsequent repair, my quick lube ended up effectively costing around $250.

I haven't stayed personally stayed here, but I was here for the Rock and Roll Las Vegas Marathon.

While I didn’t book a room myself, I spent time in a friend’s room before the race and came away impressed. The space felt generous, with two single beds, plenty of room to move around, and a sleek flatscreen that made downtime relaxing. From the 32nd floor, the view stretched over the street below and framed the bold Mandalay Bay logo—an iconic touch that added to the experience. The bathroom stood out, too, with a separated toilet and shower that gave it a more upscale, residential feel. Overall, it felt like a taste of luxury living without being over-the-top.

The broader property matches the grand scale you expect on the Las Vegas Strip. I loved having a Starbucks on-site for an easy pre-race caffeine fix, even if that’s a common amenity across multiple resorts. I skipped the casino to keep the trip budget-friendly, but walking through it, everything looked clean, organized, and calm, punctuated by the occasional celebratory shout from a lucky table. It had an energetic vibe without feeling chaotic.

One of my favorite details is the resort’s distinctive gold exterior, which helps it stand out among its neighbors and gives it a signature Vegas flair. Parking was abundant and straightforward—a big plus for visitors juggling events and logistics.

Even as a non-gambler, I would have happily stayed longer. Mandalay Bay delivers a polished experience that’s easy to enjoy, whether you’re racing, relaxing, or simply soaking in the Strip. I’ll consider it for a future stay, though my travel sights are set on exploring more of Europe in the near term.

These are not real French treats

Despite the name, the patisserie’s “macaroons” reveal a fundamental misunderstanding of French pastry. They are macarons—one “o”—and these versions are among the most amateur I’ve encountered. The shells have oversized feet, while the cookie itself is airy and thin, riddled with pockets that betray improper technique; a proper macaron is light yet uniform, with batter present throughout. The filling compounds the issue: instead of a silky ganache, it’s a sugary buttercream more suitable for cupcakes. The result is cloying and texturally off, far from what you’d find in Paris. To be fair, the chocolate croissant was decent, flaky and pleasant, which earns an extra star—but the macarons need serious refinement.

Horrible service and overpriced food

Last weekend, we came for a movie and were stunned by the service breakdown. We sat in the lounge for 30 minutes while staff clustered and chatted; no one made eye contact, and no one took our order.
