When a server finally did, our order arrived wrong—we’re vegetarians, and we were given chicken. Worse, we discovered a long hair in our popcorn. Despite the fiasco, we were charged in full, hair and all. When we ordered a second beer, the server took the glass we were still drinking from before the replacement arrived.

Today, we returned for an early kids’ movie, and the same problems persisted: slow service, popcorn after asking twice, and a second beer that never came. This theater used to feel classy and well run; now concessions are overpriced, service inattentive, and the experience frustrating from start to finish. Owners and investors should step in before this venue is run into the ground. This is the Biltmore—guests expect better. Management, please respond and explain how you plan to restore standards and prevent repeats of these issues.

Nice place. The staff is nice

Authentic mom-and-pop vibes define this spot. The staff is friendly, and the pizza itself is solid, though prices lean a bit high. Curious about their pide, I found it overly spicy and surprisingly cheese-free—likely not appealing to an American palate or anyone who prefers plain, classic pies. If that’s you, skip the pide and stick to standard pizzas. You’ll recognize the place from their frequent TV ads. For consistently good pizza, Milanos remains a safer bet.

Espionage is a quintessential stop for anyone sampling Edinburgh’s nightlife. Spanning five floors and charging no cover, it caters to both dance enthusiasts and minglers. Expect a varied soundtrack that keeps the energy high, plus plenty of corners to chat over drinks if you’re rhythmically challenged. With so much space, it can get crowded—buzzworthy and perfect for Stag and Hen parties looking for momentum. The location is spot-on, nestled among a cluster of clubs and bars, making it effortless to hop between venues and shape your night as you please. Friendly locals add to the charm; you might even pick up a Scottish accent—whether you nail it is another story. For a free-entry, multi-level adventure with reliable tunes and a built-in bar crawl, Espionage delivers a fun, flexible night out in the heart of the city.

I get it...I really do!

When a long-awaited Vegas bachelor-party weekend turned into a solo getaway, I decided to do it my way and spend Sunday at the range. Finding one open on a Sunday was the first win; actually locating it was another story. Aldebaran is a broken, stop-and-start industrial street that snakes behind the Strip, and as a non-local I spent far too long looping around warehouses and cul-de-sacs.

When I finally arrived, the first clue this wasn’t a traditional range was the lobby: hardwood floors, track lighting, guests scrolling on iPads, and a decidedly lounge-like vibe. The staff, friendly and upbeat, leaned into a cinematic, Tomb Raider aesthetic—hot pants, drop-leg holsters, the whole theme-park sheen. There’s a niche for that: a turnkey “shoot your dream gun” experience tailored to visitors.

Where the disconnect happened was me rolling in with my own gear. I had an AR-15, a tactical shotgun, a modified M44, a 9mm, and a .40-cal Smith & Wesson. The wide eyes said it all. A manager appeared promptly, polite but clear: this venue caters to curated experiences, not walk-in shooters with personal arsenals. He kindly pointed me toward a true shooting range better suited to my plan. I took a photo, bought a t-shirt, and moved on.

Bottom line: if you’re a tourist eager for a guided, Instagram-ready taste of recoil without the hassle, this place delivers with professionalism and polish. If you’re an enthusiast looking to run your own firearms and drills, set your sights elsewhere. Either way, call ahead, confirm policies, and bring a good GPS; Aldebaran will test your patience. Credit where it’s due: hours that include Sundays are a rare plus, the facility is immaculate, and every interaction was safe, courteous, and efficient—even if it wasn’t my scene.

Stopped in for a quick bite on the strip and left underwhelmed. I paid $8 for a slice and a drink, which felt steep for what I got. The pizza tasted bland, with a skimpy, forgettable tomato sauce that failed to bring any richness. Convenience aside, the quality didn’t justify the price. With plenty of nearby options, I’d look elsewhere for better flavor and value instead.

A Longtime Favorite Loses Its Flavor: C.B.’s Liver and Onions Disappoint

For years, C.B. has been our go-to when a craving for liver and onions struck. It wasn’t perfect, but they usually hit that elusive rare-to-medium-rare sweet spot—something most kitchens won’t even attempt. Add a reliably crisp Caesar salad, good coffee, and a rice pudding I’ve genuinely enjoyed (though it’s become noticeably sweeter of late), and the place held steady as an unpretentious, budget-friendly standby.

Lately, though, salt has become the star of the show—and not in a good way. Thick, chewy bacon that tastes like it’s been recooked from breakfast and heavy-handed gravy have pushed recent meals firmly into sodium territory. On our most recent visit, I tried to eliminate the usual culprits: hold the bacon, skip the gravy, and please, no added salt or butter. I even asked them to leave off the herbal butter that so often overwhelms the vegetables with a flavor I can’t stand.

On paper, the special was a great deal—$12.95 for two pieces of liver, salad, dessert, and (sadly) substandard garlic bread. The vegetables arrived simply prepared and were fine, and the baked potato was serviceable if overcooked, with a telltale brownness inside. But the liver—the reason we were there—was beyond disappointing. Despite my explicit request for no seasoning and a rare to medium-rare cook, both the liver and onions arrived literally swimming in oil. Worse, the liver was incinerated: charred black around the edges, dark throughout, and tough, exactly what I’d tried to avoid by specifying the doneness.

The service, to their credit, remained stellar—attentive and friendly, even as the kitchen faltered. We’d arrived late, just after 7:15 p.m., with closing time at 8 p.m., and by the time the food reached our table there was no realistic window to send it back. I did my best to blot away the grease with napkins, but there’s only so much you can salvage when the main event is cooked to oblivion.

Here’s the rub: the value is undeniable only when the food is edible. A bargain plate that ends up as an oily, overdone mess isn’t a deal; it’s a disappointment. We’ve sampled plenty across the menu over the years, and the liver and onions was the lone repeat-worthy item. If even that falters, there’s not much reason to return. Add in an interior that’s more than a little “dated,” and it’s hard not to suspect the positive buzz comes down to price and portion size over quality. Good service and a great Caesar can’t carry a meal this flawed.

After a wild night on the Vegas Strip, all we wanted was a comforting bowl of pho. With none in sight, we settled for a cafe advertising ramen—a small thrill tempered by doubt. 

The bowl that arrived confirmed our fears: topped with sliced chicken breast, green onions, and—bewilderingly—carrots. Yes, carrots. The broth tasted straight from a can, more Campbell’s than countertop simmer, thin and flat. The noodles were limp and forgettable, the kind you’d expect from late-night instant packets, not a kitchen claiming ramen. 

We sampled just the ramen; the SF Club sandwich was shrug-worthy—edible yet unremarkable. Service didn’t help. The staff looked overworked, the pace glacial, and refills required flagging someone down. Coffee sat empty far too long. 

Verdict: 2 stars. If you’re prowling the Strip for a restorative bowl, keep walking or venture off-strip to a dedicated noodle shop. Here, ramen reads like a menu afterthought rather than a dish made with care. Stick to simpler cafe fare and temper expectations. Late-night atmosphere was fine, but with comfort food, execution matters. A steaming bowl should feel soulful; this one felt assembled from pantry odds and ends. Next time, I’ll wait for real ramen or proper pho.

Outstanding service from a team that values punctuality and pride in their work. They arrived on time, paced themselves, and delivered a meticulous, professional clean with exceptional attention to detail. The owner is personable, straightforward, and clearly knowledgeable. Their thoroughness earned my repeat business, and I’m already looking forward to their next visit with confidence again.

Made a reservation here for New Years Eve before heading out to Hogmanay.

I booked a New Year’s Eve table before Hogmanay and found the bar more appealing than the restaurant. It’s a cool spot for a pint, but the menu felt predictable—pork belly, steak pie, fish and chips, soups—and the food was just okay. The wine list was limited, and our waiter offered little guidance. Service was polite, though not especially attentive. For the price, value is fair, yet nothing stood out. I’d return for lunch or drinks, when the casual atmosphere fits, but I’d skip dinner. If you want memorable food and wine, look elsewhere; for a relaxed bar, it works.
Friendly staff and late hours make this spot convenient, with an organized menu and solid roll selection. Close to home. Downside: kitchen closes before last call.

My mother has been in Sante for 14 days now.

After touring several facilities, we chose Sante, and in just 14 days it has proven to be an exceptional choice. Sante is, first and foremost, a care facility focused on rehabilitation. My mother receives daily occupational and physical therapy in a well-equipped gym, complemented by speech therapy for cognitive reinforcement. Group activities fill the long recovery hours, providing social engagement and motivation.

Meals are a highlight: a chef prepares food to order, with a menu that changes day to day and tastes delicious. The environment feels like a warm, lovely hotel—the building, dining room, and client rooms are inviting and comfortable.

What truly sets Sante apart is the staff. From administration and nursing to therapy, assistants, hosts, servers, social services, transportation, and cleaning, every person greets you with a smile and addresses questions or concerns immediately. Our family has been impressed by their attentiveness and genuine care. We could name so many individuals who have gone above and beyond, but truth is excellence here is universal.

We are profoundly grateful for the care given to our precious mother. Sante has delivered competence, compassion, and peace of mind—everything families hope for in a rehabilitation setting.

From the moment we walked in to the moment we left, our family was satisfied. My son and I ordered New York strips, cooked perfectly: juicy, well-seasoned, and downright delicious. My wife's salmon was exceptional, flaky and vibrant, while my daughter declared her chicken sandwich the best she's ever had. Service matched the kitchen's excellence: our waitress was attentive, knowledgeable, and never hovering. We finished with a dessert that was to die for, a memorable finale to a stellar meal. If there was a hiccup, it was the background music, a touch too loud upon arrival, though it balanced out as the room filled. Overall, a great dining experience we're eager to repeat.

Over the past month, I’ve noticed Smith’s bakery case has thinned out, with cake slice variety running scarce. I’d been craving a black forest slice, only to find it mysteriously gone. After my husband asked a baker, we learned a new cake decorator decided to stop making it—heartbreaking for loyal fans. I’ve already filled out multiple comment cards begging for its return.

Despite the dessert letdown, we still frequent Smith’s. Prices remain among the lowest in our area, and the store generally delivers on value and convenience. A recent perk: the nearby Smith’s gas station, where you can save about 15 cents per gallon. If they bring back the black forest cake, it’ll be close to perfect again.

Polished is such a popular nails salon, all the girls with cute nails around town that I had complimented happen to get their nails done at Polished.

There’s no denying Polished’s appeal at first glance. Their selection is expansive, from classic creams to dazzling glitters, and their nail art capabilities are impressive. I’ve gravitated toward the glitters, and one standout set featured a gorgeous ombré on my ring fingers, blending a baby blue into a deep turquoise with seamless finesse. Polished primarily promotes gel over acrylic, touting it as “better” for your nails. In my experience, that claim didn’t hold up—after removal, my nails felt extremely weak. While that may not reflect the salon’s technique alone, the aggressive upsell on gel feels questionable without a balanced conversation about potential downsides.

Where Polished truly falters is service. Across three visits—including one appointment with the owner—the vibe was consistently cold. Staff rarely engaged, offering more mean mugs than smiles, and basic courtesies like a greeting at check-in were missing. Most alarming, the owner openly gossiped and cursed with another manicurist during my service, swapping stories about a drunken customer. It’s unprofessional and uncomfortable, especially when you’re paying for a relaxing, pampering experience.

Bottom line: Polished delivers eye-catching results and an enviable color library, but the atmosphere and professionalism don’t match the polish on your nails. If you prioritize design options and can tune out the attitude, you might still enjoy the outcome. If respectful service and a welcoming environment matter to you, keep searching. I won’t be returning, and I’d only recommend Polished to those unbothered by rudeness and the hard sell on gel.

If you are looking for unique furniture or that perfect accent piece this store is full of options.

This shop is a treasure for distinctive furniture and standout accents. After months searching for the perfect bench—height, length, texture—Rebecca guided me from concept to completion and delivered exactly what I envisioned. She’s a humble, hands-on owner who gladly goes the extra mile, sourcing pieces beyond her wonderfully eclectic display. It’s also ideal for last-minute gifts, from original dry-humor cards to lavish candles. Whether furnishing a room or browsing, expect inspired finds, friendly expertise, and a memorable shopping experience every visit.

A nice location and pleasant atmosphere. Service started very well, but went downhill fast.

This spot makes a strong first impression: inviting, comfortable, and seemingly well run. Early service matched the mood—prompt greetings, clear explanations of specials, and speedy drink orders. Unfortunately, the experience lost momentum as the meal progressed, and by the end, both the kitchen and front-of-house had undermined the goodwill established at the start.

We began with both appetizer specials. The deep-fried meatballs were fine—crisp outside, decently seasoned, but forgettable on their own. Interestingly, they made more sense later alongside the entrees, where they felt like a heartier accent rather than a standalone star. The sampler of popular appetizers was a mixed bag. Fried mozzarella sticks and fried ravioli were the clear winners: hot, crunchy, and comfortingly familiar. The calamari, however, arrived limp and soggy, a textural miss that no amount of fresh lemon could fix. The shared marinara dipping sauce didn’t help; it was thin, timid, and so bland that even a sprinkle of crushed chili couldn’t wake it up.

For the main course, we ordered spaghetti Bolognese with a substitution of fettuccine. The kitchen obliged, but the sauce skewed strangely creamy, turning the color from bright red to muted orange and smoothing out the texture that a good ragù should have. It lacked depth, brightness, and the meaty nuance expected of Bolognese; frankly, a chain version would outperform it. Midway through, our server apologized for forgetting the salad and offered to pack it to go, which we declined.

Service faltered sharply after the plates hit the table. Once we finished, we waited—stacking dishes to tidy our space—while the dining room remained only moderately busy. Two servers stood in the kitchen, and after roughly twenty minutes we had to flag the maitre d’ to summon help.

In the end, the setting and a couple of fried starters couldn’t offset bland sauces and inattentive service. A pizza passing by looked promising, but not enough to gamble on a return. With better seasoning, a sturdier fry on the seafood, and sharper floor management, this could be a contender; for now, it’s a miss.

Would give zero stars if I could. I tanned at the Greenfield and Brown location until the owner abruptly closed without notice. I lost prepaid units and a $115 lotion, and customer support has been painfully unresponsive—getting help feels like pulling teeth. Based on my experience, I strongly recommend avoiding this business. Do not tan here.

Great place for lunch with a cozy indoor-outdoor vibe. The meatball sandwich is my favorite, savory, satisfying, and delicious. I haven’t tried the pizza; it’s dinner-only, but friends rave about it. Deducting one star for scarce parking, otherwise a welcoming spot worth visiting.

Craving something sweet, I ordered the tiramisu. At $6.50, it’s steep for a counter treat but still cheaper than restaurants. The tiramisu itself was absolutely delicious—pure goodness in every bite. However, the chocolate shell didn’t agree with me; it was too rich and left me feeling sick (coming off Paleo probably didn’t help). I’d order it again, but next time I’ll skip the shell.

Le Cafe earns kudos for genuine hospitality and responsiveness. After my initial visit, the manager reached out with a thoughtful note seeking feedback—and they’ve acted on it. The kitchen is refreshing its polenta recipe, rolling out a new sauce for the duck, and adding welcome flair to the chicken dish. That commitment to listening and improving deserves recognition; I’m happily adding a star for effort and care. The message felt sincere, timely, and focused on making the guest experience better. Bonus: the duck I had was downright scrumptious. With this kind of attention and delicious execution, I’ll be back soon. Keep up the great work.

I LOVE MEXICAN. El Burro proves it with tacos that deliver pure joy. As the sister spot to Round Corner Cantina, it keeps the focus tight and delicious. I’ve only sampled the tacos—two kinds, to be exact—but the carne asada stands out: tender, juicy, and perfectly seasoned. I finally branched out to the shrimp tacos and they were so, so, so, so good—bright, fresh, and craveable. Staff are genuinely friendly; visiting three days in a row probably helped, but the vibe feels welcoming regardless. The space is small with limited seating, geared mainly toward take-out, so plan accordingly. My only “complaint” is self-inflicted: I keep ordering the same thing because it’s that good. For reliable, flavor-packed tacos, El Burro is an easy favorite. Any day, anytime.

It's a bit ironic that there are like a million Red Mango's in LA... yet my first taste came in Las Vegas. Expecting a Pinkberry clone, I was pleasantly surprised: Red Mango is, to me, decisively better. The menu keeps it simple—original and green tea yogurt—with a familiar roster of toppings like fresh fruit, mochi, and more. Where it really separates itself is flavor and texture. While Pinkberry leans tangy and distinctly yogurt-like, Red Mango’s base is creamier and slightly sweeter, edging toward soft-serve ice cream without losing freshness. Each spoonful feels lush yet clean, making the toppings complement rather than compensate. After one visit, I’m officially switching teams. Move over, Pinkberry—Red Mango just won my frozen yogurt loyalty for good.

Not good Mexican food. Overpriced and disappointing. Tacos are meaty but bland; tortillas taste old. Burrito overloaded with green peppers. Wack experience, quantity over quality. I won’t return again.
Very nice service and a beautiful setting, but the food was just okay. For the prices, I expected much better. I probably wouldn’t return—unless I won the lottery and felt extravagant.

Returning to an old neighborhood favorite can feel like opening a family scrapbook, and that’s exactly what led us back to the Applebee’s at 24th Street and Baseline in South Phoenix. After dropping my daughter at her in-laws and not wanting to trek back to Chandler, my son and I decided to revisit the spot that had been our go-to for eight years—a place where birthdays, casual dinners, and countless catch-ups had unfolded. It was St. Patrick’s Day around 7 p.m., and despite the holiday crowd, we only waited about 15 minutes for a booth. Settling in, we traded stories about the times we’d been there, including the infamous evening my son ordered only celery while the rest of us were starving—a silly memory that still makes us laugh.

We chose the 2-for-$20 deal, and the meal hit the right notes: hearty, familiar, and nicely prepared. Our server was friendly, attentive, and quick, keeping refills coming and checking in without hovering. It felt like the Applebee’s we remembered—comfortable, affordable, and easy. The food tasted great, the pacing was spot-on, and the vibe was exactly the kind of casual community atmosphere that made this location a family hub for us.

Then, right as we finished and paid, everything changed. My son glanced down and quietly said, “Oh my,” before urging me to move fast: a mouse had just run by our feet. Shock gave way to queasiness; I wanted to be sick. We tipped our server—she genuinely did a good job—and made for the door. I did stop to tell Patrick, the kitchen manager, what happened. He was calm and courteous, explaining that mice can come from across the street and promising to notify their pest control provider.

I understand that urban restaurants contend with pests, but seeing a mouse in the dining area undermines trust in sanitation and safety. For a place loaded with warm memories, it’s heartbreaking to say we won’t be back any time soon. I hope management takes swift, thorough action—because the service and food were solid, and this Applebee’s has the potential to be the reliable neighborhood spot we once loved. For us, though, the surprise scurry was a dealbreaker.

We went back to have dinner again tonight so I could try more pizzas and a salad.

We returned for another dinner to sample more of the menu, starting with the Chicken My Pesto pizza. The crust was nicely done—not burned—and while it arrived a touch cool, the flavors still delivered: bright pesto, tender chicken, and a satisfying chew. I paired it with the Going Green salad, which was fresh, crisp, and well-dressed. My husband chose the Spicy Butcher and enjoyed every bite.

Dining out is about more than food; service, attitude, and the overall experience matter. On that front, Michael once again saved the day. He spotted us, came over with a warm welcome, and set the tone with genuine hospitality. That kind of attention keeps guests coming back, even when minor hiccups happen behind the scenes.

Parking is straightforward, the vibe is friendly, and the pizza lineup continues to tempt. We’ll be back to explore more pies—and, thanks to Michael’s care, we’re happy to overlook the drama.

I've heard good things about Tuesday Mornings so I decided to give it a try.

Stepping inside, it felt like a smaller, more cramped version of Last Chance, with far more housewares than clothing—a drawback for me since I’m not a Last Chance fan. I truly hoped to like it, but nothing thrilled me. Many items appeared shopworn or slightly damaged, and the “clearance” prices weren’t compelling. When a tag makes you exclaim, “That’s a clearance price?!” it’s hard to feel you’ve found a bargain. Maybe I’m frugal or don’t frequent high-end stores, but value matters. I went on a Friday afternoon, so perhaps timing is the issue. Still, based on this visit, I’m unlikely to return anytime soon.

Bought my third Mini with Jordan, Zack, and Scott, and the experience was outstanding. My new Countryman is a joy, and the team made me feel at home, part of something special. Dawn in service has been amazing since 2004 at Mini on Decatur, and I’m excited to continue with Kevin, who kept me informed on my previous Mini’s repairs. Professional, friendly, and transparent—this is why I’m Mini Cooper 4 Life—forever loyal.

Wow. I really hope they reopen or relocate. This was the convenient spot to get boba and good Asian food. What I am to do!?

Heartbroken losing this convenient boba and Asian eats spot. Quality service and reliable flavors made it a neighborhood staple. Please reopen or relocate—we’re craving menu!

Mistakes.... again. :(

I’ve been to most Zipps locations across the Valley and usually love the vibe—especially in Chandler. It’s a lively scene with plenty of TVs and a patio that’s ideal for catching a game in the fresh air. There are TVs everywhere, so you never miss a highlight on the patio or inside. The crowd is friendly, the drinks are cold, and the menu is a cut above typical sports-bar fare. The chicken focaccia is a standout: hearty, flavorful, and exactly what you want with a pint.

The trouble, at this particular location, is service that misses the mark far too often. On multiple visits, my order has arrived incorrect or not at all, and the follow-up feels indifferent. Servers seem stretched thin and short on the kind of personality and attentiveness that elevate a casual meal into a great experience. Coming from a hospitality background, I value a smile, clear communication, and a timely apology when things go wrong.

The fix is straightforward: stronger training, better multitasking, and empowering staff to own mistakes with grace. I want to see servers who are efficient and having fun, because that energy reaches the table. Zipps already nails the atmosphere and the food; if service catches up, this location could be a favorite again. Keep up the great work on the menu, and here’s hoping the next visit brings smoother, more considerate service.

I like this branch.

This small library branch offers a limited on-site selection and activities, but its strengths shine through: friendly, helpful employees and an impressively clean facility. Inter-branch requests for books or media arrive quickly—usually within 1–2 days in my experience—so the size rarely feels like a constraint. The only real drawback is the awkward, undersized parking lot. Because the branch sits on the Hamilton High School campus, plan your visit to avoid peak student traffic, especially at lunch and right after school (around 2:30–3:30).

Just got out of here

As a longtime Olive Garden regular, I didn’t expect my neighborhood location to be the one that finally let me down. I went with my mother during a busy period and was given a choice: wait about 25 minutes for a table or sit immediately in the bar area. Hunger won, so we chose the bar, only to discover an arctic blast from the overhead air conditioner aimed squarely at us.

To the staff’s credit, the hostess acknowledged the issue and said she’d have the vent adjusted. Ten minutes later, the cold air was still whipping across our table. Uncomfortable and frustrated, we asked to switch our dine-in order to takeout. We chose the mixed grill and the chicken Alfredo fettuccine, each paired with the chicken and gnocchi soup, and waited roughly 25 minutes before heading home.

That’s when the real disappointment set in. The chicken and gnocchi soup—normally a creamy, comforting staple—looked thin and tasted even thinner. Instead of the familiar rich, white broth, it appeared almost transparent, as if it had been heavily watered down. The breadsticks were their dependable selves, but they couldn’t rescue the rest.

The chicken Alfredo fettuccine missed the mark entirely. The menu describes blackened chicken, and that’s what I’ve consistently enjoyed in the past. This time, the chicken was breaded, more reminiscent of chicken Parmesan—something I specifically avoid. Between the diluted soup and the off-the-mark entrée, my appetite vanished. Ultimately, the meals went uneaten and were passed to the dog, a disappointing end to what should have been a comforting dinner.

I’m granting two stars solely because of the excellent hostess—tall, brunette, unfailingly friendly—whose warm demeanor stood out amid the chills. Otherwise, this visit left me nauseated and reluctant to return, despite the location being so close to home. I hope management addresses temperature control, recipe consistency, and accuracy between menu descriptions and what arrives to guests.

Ferraro’s is conveniently close to my workplace, and a co-worker chose it for her going-away lunch. I’d never been, but I’m always eager to try something new—especially Italian. As we walked in, former mayor Oscar Goodman was leaving; he paused to chat and praised the food. He was right. I ordered the salmon livornese and a cup of lobster bisque. Both were excellent: fresh, balanced, and beautifully presented. Service was friendly, and the price felt reasonable for the quality. Ferraro’s delivered a delightful experience, and I definitely plan to return soon.

Not impressed. After waiting ten minutes for drinks, twenty minutes to place our order, and an hour for food, we learned they were out of baked potatoes. The long delays and disorganization were frustrating. When we voiced our concerns to the manager, our server gave us glares, which felt unprofessional. We enjoy Applebee’s, but this experience was disappointing enough that we won’t return to this franchise again.

I guess you can't expect too much from a casino cafe, but this place was a bit spendy so yeah, I did expect more.

Despite its price point, the cafe delivers a “meh” experience. The dining room is harshly lit, and the cafeteria-style table layout strips away any sense of comfort or atmosphere. Service was sluggish for a slow night. We told our server we had a show to catch; after dropping the food, he vanished. When the check finally arrived, he disappeared again, leaving us waiting 20 minutes to leave. The food itself matched the two-star consensus: edible but uninspired, not justified by the cost. For a casino venue, convenience might be the draw, but with bland fare, bright lights, and slow service, it’s not enough. I won’t be returning.

Imagine arriving with your family for a simple meal, only to wait five minutes just to be acknowledged and seated. We were finally placed beside a rowdy bachelor party playing with an inflatable doll—while a child sat at our table. Uncomfortable, we asked to be moved. The relief was short-lived. Moments later, a different waitress marched over to say the new table wasn’t clean, contradicting the first server who had just wiped it down. Then came the kicker: she claimed the table was actually reserved and brusquely told us to return to the original spot, delivering the message with attitude rather than apology. Throughout, the noise was relentless—far beyond lively and into unbearable. We’ve come to expect dependable service and a pleasant atmosphere from this chain, but this location fell dramatically short on both counts: disorganized seating, poor communication, and zero consideration for families. We won’t be returning, and recommend others look elsewhere.

Very rude staff and an awful experience. I visited with a group of friends—mostly couples—and simply asked for a table. A suited host, acting ridiculously self-important, demanded we buy a $450 bottle to sit. The policy felt predatory, the attitude dismissive, and the vibe unwelcoming. Easily the worst Vegas venue I’ve visited.

This spot delivers standout flavors worth a visit, but the service needs serious attention. The all-male crew is a mixed bag—some friendly, others visibly disengaged. Our server ignored repeated attempts to get his attention, forcing us to fetch our own water and bread. Despite the lapses, the kitchen shines, making the meal memorable. If you’ve never been, go for the food and temper expectations on hospitality; with improvements, this could be an exceptional experience.

Now then, on with my last restaurant visit of 2013 — Hey, I did say I was a little behind didn’t I? — which brought me to the rapidly changing region of Griffintown

Griffintown has been evolving at a dizzying pace, and Le Bureau Tapas Bar has sat on my to-visit list since summer. A friend who lives nearby finally nudged me there for a midweek drink and bite. On a quiet, snowy evening, the space immediately set the tone: a relaxed lounge vibe with dim, flattering lighting; handsome wood bars and bar tables; leather banquettes anchoring the room; and just enough industrial edge—exposed brick and visible ducts—to feel modern without slipping into cliché. It’s a setting that practically spells happy hour.

Le Bureau’s cocktail list is broad and well considered, exactly what you want in a room like this. Over the evening we cycled through a Manhattan, Negroni, Old Fashioned, and Tom Collins. Each was well executed—balanced, properly chilled, and confidently poured—suggesting a bar team that respects the classics and doesn’t overcomplicate them. Nothing showy, just solid, satisfying drinks.

The food leans tapas, drawing on a mix of influences that encourages ordering a spread. We did just that: Patatas Bravas arrived with a chipotle-lime sauce in place of the traditional spicy tomato, a smoky, bright twist that worked. Cod croquettes were crisp and golden, with a silky interior and a sunny amarillo sauce that lifted each bite. The standout of the night was the pancetta-wrapped figs, that irresistible sweet-salty interplay you hope for, done with care. Beef skewers were decent on their own, but the chimichurri that accompanied them stole the show—herbaceous, garlicky, and vibrant. Grilled chorizo with onions brought pleasant warmth, though the sausage felt gentler than the punchy chorizos I usually crave.

If there’s a caveat, it’s value. Portions trend small for the price, which makes Le Bureau less ideal for building a full dinner without racking up a sizable tab. As a 5 à 7 destination, though, it shines—attractive room, unfussy service, well-made cocktails, and tasty bites that scratch the itch between work and evening plans.

I’ll be back for drinks and a couple of plates, happily settling into that leather banquette while the snow drifts outside. For a complete meal, I’d look elsewhere or arrive with the expectation of grazing. As a lounge bar experience in the heart of a neighborhood on the rise, Le Bureau hits the mark—and sometimes, that’s exactly what you’re after.

Cheers!

My experience here was pretty much sub par.

I visited with my family and ordered several coffees and salads, only to learn they’d run out of coffee. Despite notifying staff, the pots were never refilled throughout our visit. The salads were fine, but the lack of such a basic item and inattentive response overshadowed everything. Disappointing overall, and we left feeling let down on an otherwise busy afternoon.

Consistently Good Results, But a Frustrating, Unacknowledged Delay

I’ve frequented this location several times and have left impressed by the customer service and the way my car looked. On my most recent visit, though, the experience fell short in a way. I came in for a standard wash and vacuum and, after an upsell, agreed to a full detail—fair enough, my car needed the extra attention. When I asked for a timeline, I was told 45 minutes to an hour. I paid at 2:28. By 3:30 I was getting restless; by 4:35, with no car and no updates, I was over it. The vehicle was finally finished at 4:45.

To their credit, the detail was excellent; the team put in the work and the car looked great. The issue was the gap between the quoted time and reality, compounded by the lack of empathy or accountability when I raised the concern. One employee shrugged, “that sucks,” and another admitted the estimate was wrong, but no apology, explanation, or gesture to make it right followed.

If you come here, expect strong results, especially on a full detail—but ask for realistic timing and communication. A simple apology and accurate estimates would restore trust.

Without the Channel 15 Smart Shopper card, this visit would have been a two-star experience. I went in hoping for a “Take Me Back” cheesesteak, but it was only okay: overcooked steak and stingy cheese whiz, mostly smeared on the bun instead of the meat. The pepper bar is a bright spot for pepper lovers, with four or five varieties to choose from. Unfortunately, our sandwiches were dry and lacked flavor, making them barely worth the two-for-one Thursday Smart Card price overall.

Beyond the Concrete Box: Cozy Beer Sanctum with Addictive Wings

From the street, this place looks like a location scout’s dream for a post‑apocalyptic prison planet: a stark concrete cube marooned on asphalt, offering no hint of life within. Step through the door, though, and the mood flips instantly. Inside is all the warmth of a comfortable college beer bar—dim, friendly, and cluttered with breweriana that telegraphs how seriously they treat their taps. Bartenders greet you with easy banter and guidance, and the tap list spans sturdy classics and lively seasonals, with enough handles to tempt every palate. I wandered in during a meetup of fellow hop-heads for a tasting led by a visiting scholar from Odell Brewing. I missed the formal lesson but did my homework by osmosis, starting with an Odell Myrcenary Double IPA that hit every resinous, citrusy note my inner beer nerd craves.

The revelry naturally led to a craving for wings, and this house does them right. The baseline is dry-style, which means extraordinary crunch; that crisp shell is the key to a great wing, and they nail it. The Jamaican Jerk rendition skips sauce in favor of a generous dusting of elusive, aromatic spice—ginger and allspice wink through—delivering layered flavor without sogginess. For heat-seekers, the Smokin’ Jalapeño Firehouse wings bring a slightly wetter rub centered on red jalapeños. They sounded intimidating, but I dove in and found a thrilling, manageable burn that never bulldozes the meat’s savor.

Because the wings lean dry, they invite dunking, and the dips are not an afterthought. The ranch is solid, but the blue cheese is something else entirely—thick, tangy, and mysteriously addictive, the kind of dressing that makes you plot which bites deserve it and which need only a whisper.

Between pints, jokes, and the good-natured ribbing of new friends, the room’s vibe lands somewhere between neighborhood haunt and informal classroom. It’s the ideal antidote to the wage‑week grind: a spot to shrug off metaphorical shackles, ignore both imaginary purple moons, and hunker down with kindred spirits over great beer and exemplary wings.

In short, don’t judge this bar by its bunker-like exterior. Judge it by the crackle of its wing skin, the confidence of its spice blends, the addictiveness of its blue cheese, and the breadth of its taps. Inside the concrete box is a cozy sanctuary for beer lovers—and a wing program worth a pilgrimage.

Dimming Lights, Diminished Quality: Appetizers Shine, Entrees Disappoint

We ordered the RF Mixed Grill; the chicken arrived blood-rare, the ribs tasted parboiled then briefly grilled, and the Elgin sausage was overly fatty. Not worth $24. My wife’s carnitas were tough and clearly needed more time—we smoke ours 12–13 hours at home, so we know the difference. Be sure to check your plates—the kitchen clearly isn’t. At these prices, expectations are higher, and serving underdone poultry is unacceptable. This is what happens when places scale up: quantity over quality.

There were bright spots. The Fried Avocado with crab, spicy remoulade, and chives was excellent, and the Rotisserie Chicken Flatbread with roasted chiles and pepper jack hit the mark. The ambiance leans western and very dark; staff kept fiddling with the lights, to the point it felt distracting. Have a drink and shareables, but skip the mains until the kitchen tightens temperatures and textures. The next day we tried Blue Adobe—ten times better at less than half the price. Until consistency improves, I’d look elsewhere for entrees.

Bombay’s new off‑campus outpost, set in the former Basmati building, signals a confident step into more refined dining—and it’s fantastic. Open only a couple of weeks, the team already operates with impressive polish. Service is attentive without hovering, and the kitchen delivers in spades. The room feels warm and polished, a comfortable upgrade from campus haunts.

Meals begin with a clever Indian riff on chips and salsa, a lively overture that sets the tone. The naan is exemplary—pillowy, lightly blistered, and fragrant—among the best around. The Tandoori lamb shines brightest: so tender that a butter knife glides through, with smoky edges and a juicy, perfectly seasoned interior. Across the menu, temperatures land exactly where they should, flavors are balanced, and portions feel generous yet just right.

Value matches quality. A two-person tab around $40—including appetizers, extra naan, and drinks—feels eminently fair, and there’s enough food to leave you happily stuffed with leftovers for later. Beyond the plate, hospitality stands out. The owner makes the rounds, checking in and sharing a thoughtful philosophy: dishes made to order, rooted in his father’s original recipes. It’s a personal touch that underscores the restaurant’s commitment to craft and care.

Bombay’s new location brings its beloved flavors to a broader, non-student audience without sacrificing soul. If early days are any indication, this place deserves to thrive—and likely will.

Came here for lunch and was greeted right away. The space is pretty large and was bustling between 1 and 2 pm. I asked for a to-go menu and was surprised by the huge selection—Japanese, Thai, Hawaiian, and Chinese dishes all in one place. I wasn’t sure what to expect, but I went with the meat jun: thin slices of steak dipped in egg batter, kind of omelet-ish, served with a savory sauce. It came with rice and salad and cost around $7–$8. Prices overall were reasonable, mostly under $10. The food was really good, the portion satisfying, and the staff friendly and attentive. For fast, tasty, affordable pan-Asian comfort, I’d definitely come back again very soon.

Sent Brandi a few Thomas the Train cake photos for inspiration, and she absolutely nailed it. Smooth, easy communication and transaction. The cake tasted great, too. We’ll definitely use her again for our other son’s birthday.

Living in the Valley, I took advantage of a Travelzoo deal: $69 massages at the Biltmore for my daughter and me. Unfortunately, the experience fell far short of expectations. From the outset, the included beverage—advertised as a glass of champagne or apple juice—was mishandled. My 20‑year‑old daughter was told they were out of juice, and I had to specifically request my champagne as no staff member offered it.

The massage itself was the poorest I’ve received, lacking pressure, flow, and attentiveness. At checkout, the disappointment continued: a mandatory 20% gratuity was added based on the undiscounted full price, and no one asked how our services were. Hoping for resolution, I emailed a complaint to the Biltmore back in August. To date, there’s been no acknowledgment or follow‑up, which speaks volumes about their guest care.

With so many Valley resorts competing and offering summer discounts, customer service and consistency matter. Given this experience, I won’t return to the Biltmore spa. For better value and professionalism, consider Camelback Inn, Hyatt at Gainey Ranch, or Hotel Valley Ho—each has delivered welcoming service and superior treatments in my past visits.

Never again! Terrible hotel. I wonder how they have got 4 stars. We arrived to a dirty bathtub with standing water that wouldn’t drain. Maintenance never showed, and when we asked for another room, the front desk manager shrugged, saying “it happens.” What happens—rooms not cleaned before new guests? There’s no fitness center, and parking is a mess: their garage lacks space, so they told us to park off-site and promised to validate. To top it off, we were charged for services we never used, requiring multiple calls to get the fees removed. The indifference, poor housekeeping, inadequate amenities, and billing issues made this stay unbearable. I would give them zero stars. Save your money and sanity; choose a different hotel.

Wow! This place was awful.

Walking in, I was greeted by a chorus of shouted slogans and a patronizing tutorial on how to read the menu and place an order, which set a grating tone. After a roughly 15‑minute wait, my sub arrived. It wasn’t awful, but it was utterly forgettable—so bland that I can’t even recall what I ordered. The much‑touted lemonade was the biggest disappointment: harshly artificial, cloyingly sweet, and reminiscent of something chemical rather than refreshing. Service felt performative instead of welcoming, and the overall atmosphere was noisy and awkward. For the price and time, I expect food and hospitality that stand out in a positive way; here, neither did. I left unimpressed and have avoided going back. When I pass by now, I keep driving. Overall, I would not recommend this spot to anyone.

Stop #1 for the Light Rail Pub Crawl was Rula Bula.... at least for me - and it was my first time there!

Kicking off the crawl at Rula Bula made for a memorable first visit. I arrived with my mother-in-law-to-be and we slipped onto the lively back patio, where a big, friendly crowd of fellow yelpers set a fun tone. The patio itself is a standout—spacious, relaxed, and perfect for a social afternoon. I ordered a Stella, while my companion opted for an Irish coffee; both hit the spot.

Service was commendable. Kate, our server, handled a challenging situation with grace: staggered arrivals, lots of separate tabs, and a bustling scene. Aside from one minor discrepancy overheard, she kept everything running smoothly.

The biggest drawback was the restroom condition. A filthy setup, an empty TP dispenser in one stall, and a door that wouldn’t latch in another are hard to overlook and detract from the experience.

Location is a win—right off the Light Rail on Mill Ave—and the menu looked robust and appealing, even though we didn’t eat this time. Based on the atmosphere, service, and positive buzz, I’d return to try the food, hoping the restroom maintenance receives attention.

Sometimes I feel like the odd one out on Chuck Box. After five or six visits, sampling both the burgers and the chicken sandwich, I still don’t get the hype. The food is okay—edible and occasionally satisfying—but nothing that rises above average. The one standout? The onion rings, which are legitimately fantastic: crisp, golden, and well-seasoned.

Service, unfortunately, has been consistently underwhelming. I’ve only encountered a pleasant staffer once; most interactions read as brusque or flat-out rude. Another frustration: burgers aren’t cooked to order, which undercuts any claim to freshness. The condiment setup doesn’t help either. Everything sits out in the open, and watching the line shuffle past gives me an uneasy, frankly unappetizing feeling, like the toppings are just collecting ambient… everything.

What knocks this from a tepid three stars to two is the cash-only policy paired with an overpriced in-house ATM. It’s 2013—nearly 2014 already. Whatever principled stand this is meant to be, it mostly inconveniences customers. Get a card machine and meet the moment for everyone.

Each time I visited, the place smelled unpleasant, the bathrooms were dirty, and the décor felt like a dated Aladdin set. Service was consistently poor—servers forgot parts of my order or took forever to bring food. I recommend skipping this spot and heading to The Sushi Factory on Eastern instead. Their staff is friendly and attentive, the atmosphere is upbeat, it’s much cleaner, and the location is convenient. As a sushi lover, I always end up returning to the Eastern location.

If I am going to spend $7.59 on yogurt, it had better be the best yogurt I have ever tasted. Was this the best yogurt I ever tasted? No. Absolutely not. The soft serve frozen yogurt they used to sell at Smitty's blows this out of the water!

Walking into Mojo on a sweltering afternoon, I expected that a $7.59 cup of self-serve frozen yogurt would deliver something exceptional. It didn’t. Smitty’s soft serve delivered creamy balance without the confusion or cost surprises.

Frustration started at the door: the place was packed, only one employee, and no instructions for the DIY setup. I assumed you grab a cup, pull a few swirls, add toppings, and pay a flat rate. Instead, it’s priced by weight—an expensive lesson when you’re figuring it out on the fly. The single staffer seemed overwhelmed, so questions went unanswered and the line inched along.

Without clear pricing or guidance, the sticker shock hit at the register: $7.59 for a cup I assumed was a flat rate. In a time when budgets matter, clarity matters too.

With no option to sample, I tried a small squirt of nearly every flavor (skipping pistachio). Most were overly tart. The standout was the cafe latte, the only flavor I’d consider revisiting.

Toppings are where Mojo shines in breadth, but the cheesecake bites were a letdown; they didn’t taste like cheesecake. If you promise cheesecake, deliver cheesecake. Beware: dense add-ons make the price climb fast.

To be fair, a couple of factors weren’t Mojo’s fault: it was brutally hot, the yogurt melted fast, and I’m lactose intolerant. Still, staffing, clear signage, and sampling aren’t weather-dependent—they’re basic service.

As a franchise, consistency should be a baseline. Maybe this location is off, but the product and process felt generic and confusing, not premium. For $7.59, I expect clearer guidance, better-balanced flavors, and toppings that taste like their names.

Sorry, Mojo. I’m just not that into you.

I'm only a teenager and yet I'm a hardened Vegas veteran because my mother is a slot machine addict

Revisiting my childhood hotel nearly a decade later was a harsh wake-up call. Circus Circus bills itself as a family destination, but the experience felt tired, grimy, and anything but fun. If you’re bringing kids, you’ll find far better value and energy at New York-New York, which is cleaner, livelier, and attracts a less seedy crowd.

The rides—often the selling point for families—were a letdown: dirty, rough, and underwhelming. What should have been a highlight felt more like a relic, with maintenance and presentation clearly lagging. Back in the room, restful sleep was elusive. Housekeeping felt perfunctory at best; surfaces didn’t inspire confidence, and noise bled through at all hours. Between the cluttered common areas and the constant din of large, rowdy crowds, the atmosphere skews chaotic rather than kid-friendly.

Parents, consider the true cost of a “deal.” A budget rate loses its shine when you’re battling headaches, poor sleep, and the stress of navigating worn facilities. Vegas offers plenty of family-friendlier options that don’t sacrifice cleanliness or comfort.

Credit where it’s due: the 1/2 lb, footlong hot dog for $3 is a small triumph and the stay’s sole memorable perk. Otherwise, in a city built on spectacle, don’t settle for less than a good time.

While Root 174's food is beautiful and interesting, their flavors are only decent. The decor could be better and the wood-bench seating is uncomfortable.

Our evening started at the bar. The cocktails were well-made: I recommend the Pickle—built on cava and pickle-forward—and the Root Remainder, which nods to root beer without turning cloying.

Appetizers were a mixed bag. The watermelon, tomato, feta, and mint salad offered lovely texture from crunchy, sweet corn, though the watermelon lacked peak-season sweetness. The bone marrow crème brûlée read mostly buttery, and the Brussels sprouts were carried by a bacon-pepper glaze; anything bathed in that sweet lacquer is hard to dislike.

Entrees, however, fell short. The pork belly bánh mì skewed too fatty, and a duck liver mousse felt like an awkward, off-putting addition. A roasted chicken breast with chickpeas, pistachio, and tomato was overwhelmed by spice, muting nuance. Both the wagyu beef and flat iron steak were cooked well, but their potato, carrot, and onion side came thick and heavy, weighing down the plates. Not one of us finished our mains.

Dessert was the highlight: a flourless chocolate cake paired with beet ice cream, and a comforting bread pudding dusted with white chocolate powder and ground hazelnut—both delightful.

Overall, our first meal at Root 174 was decent but uneven. At this price point, there’s stronger value and a more polished experience to be found at Eleven, still my benchmark for modern American dining in the city.

Fancy décor can’t disguise the shortcomings at TAO. Despite arriving absolutely starving—the kind of hunger that usually makes even average dishes shine—our plates were bland and felt hastily thrown together. The bigger shock came with the check: roughly $300 for three of us, and we hadn’t run up a tab of cocktails to justify it. For what we received, the value simply wasn’t there. The room is undeniably gorgeous, all polished surfaces and moody lighting, but it plays like a distraction from underwhelming food. The lone bright spot was our server: attentive, friendly, and cool, a fellow Angeleno who kept things pleasant. Unfortunately, good service couldn’t rescue the meal. If you’re paying for ambience, maybe; if you’re paying for flavor, look elsewhere.

I wish this place had better service; every visit feels out of sync. The hostess/cashier still struggles with the register months in, and greeting guests seems optional—you can stand at the podium while staff averts their eyes. The owner appears friendly but is often bussing tables, not effectively. Meanwhile, 20 people wait while five tables sit empty, and the team fixates on cleaning one spot instead of seating guests efficiently.

The food started strong on first visit, but quality has steadily declined. I kept hoping they’d iron out the kinks, yet the inconsistencies persist. It’s disappointing, especially since Southern Highlands needs all the reliable restaurants it can get. Judging by the smaller crowd, I’m not alone in feeling this way.

With better training, clearer roles, and sharper front-of-house coordination, this place could thrive. Until then, the service bottlenecks and sliding food quality make it hard to recommend.

Great location, but that's about it

I’ve lived here for a month and a half, and the headaches started immediately. My in-unit washer first sparked and caught fire, then on a separate occasion flooded the entire apartment. Maintenance is glacial unless you walk to the office and push, and every time they insist they “just received” the request. Soundproofing is nonexistent—conversations carry through the walls—and a nearby train blasts its presence every 30 minutes, day and night. For the price, the value isn’t there. Even the balconies are a gamble: some are spacious, others are so tiny you have to squeeze to stand outside. The only positive is the location. I’m counting the days until I can move out.

I visited Dr. Haydee Docasar on 8/20/09 for a routine yearly Pap smear and made it clear I did not want any additional tests because my insurance at the time would not cover them. After the appointment, I received a small $6 bill from Quest Diagnostics for the Pap and paid it. Then, unexpectedly, a second bill arrived for $160 for CPT code 87591—tests for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Unknown to me, a sample from my visit had been sent out for these screenings without my consent.

I tried to resolve the issue with AWP, exchanging messages with an employee named Jimmy, but after repeated missed calls and no response, I assumed it had been corrected since I hadn’t authorized any tests. On 1/30/10, I was shocked to receive a collections notice for the $160. On 2/12, I sent a formal letter contesting the charges. During my visit, no one asked my permission or discussed additional testing; nor was I told that samples would be sent to Quest. I was there for a Pap smear only. I asserted my right of refusal and asked Dr. Docasar to cover the bill.

On 2/18, AWP responded, stating that Dr. Docasar follows American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology recommendations: for sexually active patients aged 19 to 35, a yearly Pap includes screening for gonorrhea and chlamydia. Those standards were not marked anywhere on the paperwork I was given, and no consent form or verbal explanation indicated that STD testing was bundled with the Pap. Dr. Docasar agreed to pay the charges—then promptly dismissed me from her care and AWP. That decision was fine with me.

I’m giving two stars solely because she ultimately paid the bill. This practice should never order tests without explicit patient consent. Being blindsided by lab charges erodes trust and creates unnecessary financial stress, especially when those bills go to collections. If I had been told these screenings were “mandatory” with a Pap, I would have put my pants on and walked out. Communication and consent matter. For anyone considering this office, read the filtered reviews too; my experience suggests policies are applied without adequate discussion, leaving patients to deal with the fallout.

Took the family to Body Worlds today. Arrive early—it's crowded. Exceptionally educational with wonderful displays. Highly recommend the audio tour for deeper insights. A memorable, family-friendly experience worth it.

This is the first time we checked in and checked right out of a hotel!

From the moment we opened the door, a musty, cat-litter-like odor hit us. We requested privacy, yet a bachelorette party was placed next door. We reported the smell and were offered a new room, but the second room had the same odor, looked worn, and faced a dilapidated apartment complex. Cigarette smoke seemed to linger around the property.

Having stayed at the Biltmore and Four Seasons, the contrast in upkeep and service was jarring. The manager’s parting comment—“there will be plenty of other guests happy to have your room”—sealed our decision to leave. Overall, the property felt more like an aging apartment block or college dorm than a hotel worthy of its rates. We will not return and cannot recommend it.

WOM—Waste of Money! Our group of two adults and three kids paid over $50 for a five-minute maze and five tickets to a short laser obstacle course, then waited 45 minutes for a single round. The experience felt rushed, overpriced, and poorly managed. The only one thrilled was the owner behind the curtain, cashing in. If you value your time and money, skip this place entirely.

GO somewhere else to get your windshield replaced where they know what they are doing

I’m on my second windshield from Safelite and will not let them touch my car again. As a USAA customer, I expected a professional installation. Instead, I received low-quality glass that was installed incorrectly twice, followed by explanations that didn’t add up.

From the first replacement, I had persistent wind noise, like a door was ajar, that never existed before. When I pressed the technician about the seal, I was told it would never be a tight fit because of the rubber piece at the base of the windshield, and that my “only option” was to replace that part for about $400. That sounded off, so I had my Toyota dealership inspect the second install.

Their assessment was blunt: the lower rubber piece is cosmetic and doesn’t create the air seal; the glass was set too low in the molding; the top wasn’t sealed properly, which is causing the airflow; and the new windshield itself had jagged, uneven edges. In other words, the root problems were poor installation and questionable glass quality, not an unrelated rubber trim.

Two attempts, the same issues, and a shrug toward an unnecessary, expensive “fix” is unacceptable. Save yourself the hassle and the noise. There are better, more meticulous shops out there that will install the right glass the right way the first time.

Let me start with the standout: the cornbread was genuinely delicious—warm, tender, and perfectly sweet. Unfortunately, the catfish arrived as a heavily battered fillet; while seasoned well, the thick breading overwhelmed the fish, and I’d expected a whole fish. The yams tasted straight from a can, which was a disappointment, and the mac and cheese skewed toward Velveeta-style, with a processed, inexpensive-cheese profile that wasn’t for me. Fried chicken was lightly fried and lacked the crisp bite I look for, though the collard greens were nicely cooked and well seasoned. The vibe feels touristy, but the staff were friendly and the crowd pleasant. I didn’t get to sample the homemade cakes, though they looked tempting. Overall, there are a few bright spots, yet consistency and freshness need attention. I’m glad I tried it, but I’d return for cornbread and greens, and skip the rest.

We ordered Barro’s thin-crust Mega Meat pizza and cheese breadsticks for delivery, and the experience fell short. The pizza arrived only warm, and the thin crust was flat-out awful—whether undercooked or just poorly executed, it tasted limp and unappealing. The breadsticks were definitely undercooked, gummy rather than golden. We’ve ordered from Barro’s many times, typically thick crust for pickup, and have had good pizza in the past. This delivery, however, was disappointing enough that we won’t order it again. We may still go in or pick up, but we’ll avoid delivery. Barro’s should tighten quality control on bake times and delivery temperature. Clear communication about crust styles could also help.

I will leave it to others to give la Brasserie T more than 3 stars. I is a nice place, modern and elegant, and somewhat affordable. But I think it is overhyped and overpriced; for my own taste at least. I can imagine why many people would love it though. This is the place to go for a 100% safe dinner, if you are willing to pay 10-15$ too much for it. You are 100% sure to have a good service, fancy food well presented and a clean ambience. 
La Brasserie T delivers a polished, modern experience with attentive service and beautifully plated dishes in a spotless room. It’s the definition of a safe bet: you’ll eat well, be treated kindly, and feel comfortable. The problem, for me, is the value. Factor in an extra $10–$15. It feels overhyped and slightly overpriced for what’s on the plate. The food is competent rather than thrilling, more about presentation than personality, and the ambiance leans toward curated and sanitized. For a date night or a business dinner, it fits. If you chase surprises, bold flavors, or neighborhood character, Montreal offers numerous spots that out-cook and under-charge this place. La Brasserie T will please many; I just can’t join the chorus beyond three stars.

ahhh... Palazzo, which means "palace"... holds up to its name. This place frickin impressed me. We had six girls in one suite and never felt cramped; with thirteen in our group, having two adjacent suites made our all-girls getaway seamless. The bathroom was a dream—spacious, well-lit, and more than adequate for heavy primping. Decor throughout is simple, chic, and tastefully executed, and the tech touches are fun: two TVs in the living area and a mini screen in the bathroom made downtime surprisingly delightful.

Dining was another highlight. Grand Lux Cafe delivered delicious crabcakes at very reasonable prices, and its 24-hour service is a lifesaver. When a to-go order went missing, Palazzo handled it professionally and offered a $50 voucher redeemable at any of their restaurants—an impressive commitment to guest satisfaction. Being connected to The Venetian adds even more appeal; popping over to Bouchon Bakery for pastries became a daily treat.

In short, Palazzo earns its name. From thoughtful design to responsive service and convenient dining, it turned a simple trip into something special. Worth every penny, especially for groups seeking comfort, style, and that extra touch of Vegas luxury. I’d return and recommend it without hesitation to friends.

Best idea for a bachelorette party EVER! This show is an absolute blast—hilarious, cheeky, and packed with high-energy pelvic thrusts and MJ-style moves. I was surprised by the polished choreography, tight routines, and unexpected singing and lip-syncing. The performers thrive on crowd interaction, making it easy for anyone who wants to jump in and be part of the fun. Whether it’s a bachelorette or a divorce party, you’ll have an entertaining night. Highly recommend for an unforgettable group outing!

Attend a Broadway in Arizona performance at ASU Gammage and you’ll be handed “Gambill,” a local riff on Broadway’s Playbill. Cute title, unfortunate omen: what follows often feels like a gamble on whether you’ll hear anything you paid—upwards of $120—to experience. My husband and I first visited in April 2013 to see David Sedaris. We sat in the second row and still strained to catch a word. Sedaris actually restarted his talk because the audience couldn’t hear; when the volume finally climbed, a harsh, persistent buzz accompanied every sentence.

We chalked it up to an off night and optimistically bought Broadway in Arizona season tickets. Big mistake. Across multiple shows, the sound remained muddy, thin, and inconsistently amplified. Unless you land in a narrow sweet spot in the center orchestra, expect to read lips. At Once, the dialogue and lyrics dissolved into a wash, and the gentleman in front of us abandoned his assistive listening device one song into the second act.

The physical plant doesn’t help. The seats feel tired, and the restrooms are dark and dank, but all of that would be forgivable if the audio weren’t so chronically poor. It’s disheartening to watch performers give their all while their work evaporates in a haze of echoes and buzz. At these prices, patrons deserve clarity and warmth, not distortion and guesswork nightly.

ASU needs to take these audio issues seriously—whether that means tuning the system, addressing the acoustics, or investing in upgrades. Until then, the cute nickname lingers with an edge. We won’t be taking any more chances on “Scammage.”

I wish I had checked Yelp before dining at this Chinese restaurant in Caesars. The space is admittedly charming, with tanks of tiny goldfish—some even drifting upside down—adding whimsy. Unfortunately, the food doesn’t live up to the décor. Despite advertising “authentic” hand-pulled noodles, what arrived was anything but: a so-called best-seller of hand-pulled noodles with shrimp/pork wontons featured soggy, thin strands with zero bite, forgettable wontons, and a bland broth reminiscent of instant Cup Noodles. The portion was modest, the price steep—$17 for a small bowl of blah. Hosts in elegant cheongsam at the entrance set an expectation the kitchen simply doesn’t meet; the experience felt more casino spectacle than culinary craft. If you’re chasing genuine noodle texture and depth of flavor, look elsewhere. Tip: don’t go. If you do, go for the cute fish and keep your expectations low. My one star is solely for the whimsical aquarium; the food earns none.

I enjoyed a tasty frittata and a rich espresso shake—both were delicious. Service was excellent, prices reasonable, and the convenience of drive-thru or dine-in stood out. Outstanding customer service. Highly recommend this spot.

I ordered the chimichurri hash and found it average, while my dad’s sherry mushroom omelette was outstanding. Coffee was meh—Seattle bias, perhaps—but the olive bread landed in the good-not-great zone. Unfortunately, service ranged from poor to average, turning what could have been a 4-star experience into a 3. The kitchen shows promise with some standout dishes, yet inconsistent execution and lackluster hospitality make it hard to recommend without tightening service.

The Paul Mitchell School delivers quality results at a budget-friendly price, but be ready to invest time. I booked a Groupon for a shampoo, cut, style, and full highlights. Despite reading a review that warned of a three-hour appointment, I assumed it was an exaggeration. It wasn’t. My visit stretched to four hours. To their credit, these are students honing their craft, and my stylist was steady, meticulous, and personable. She kept conversation flowing and made the long sit more pleasant. The end result—a clean trim and even highlights—was satisfying, for the value. Still, four hours is a long time to sit anywhere, and that’s the trade-off. I’d return, but only with a Groupon and a cleared schedule. If you’re patient and plan ahead, you can leave pleased with your hair—just prepare for the time commitment that comes with a training environment.

We picked this place because… #1 we love Brazilian, #2 we had a discount from Last Minute Tickets

We visited this Brazilian steakhouse lured by our love of rodízio and a handy Last Minute Tickets deal, and left with mixed impressions. Service was friendly, and gauchos kept skewers coming, but proteins felt conservative. Other Brazilian spots have served alligator and chicken hearts; here, the focus stayed on beef—plentiful but predictable.

The salad bar stole the show. Roasted vegetables were deeply flavorful, and the cheese breads/biscuits were addictive, warm, and airy. Paired with a bright raspberry mojito, that trio shines.

Value matters, and we recommend snagging the discount—about $3 per person via Last Minute Tickets—to soften the bill and set expectations. Without it, the experience might feel basic compared to more daring churrascarias.

Overall, we’d give it three stars: solid drinks, excellent sides, and dependable cuts of beef, but lacking the culinary adventure we crave. Here’s hoping they get bolder with their proteins and bring a few risks back to the rotisserie.

Never again. Hadn't been to this place in 18 years. It seemed pretty decent in 1996, but today...I have no idea why anybody would want to eat here again after tasting the food for the first time.

Returning after an 18-year hiatus was a mistake. What was decent in 1996 has devolved into a forgettable, subpar meal. The salad arrived with limp lettuce and a dressing so diluted it tasted like flavored water. The soup, served piping hot, offered no flavor, just heat. Tacos should be a safe bet, yet these were so uninspiring that a packet of Fry’s taco seasoning at home yields better results. Credit where due: the servers were friendly and my wife enjoyed the pudding. Beyond that, there’s little to recommend. For your time and taste buds, steer clear of the Metro Center location. I won’t be returning.

Store AZP-51 has been nothing but horrible to me and my family since they opened. We’ve given them multiple chances over many years and across several vehicles, but our experiences have only gotten worse.

It started with our Escalade. After routine work, we noticed the lug nut cover was broken—something we had never had an issue with before their service. We contacted the store, and the manager called to apologize, promising to replace the cover because we’d been loyal customers for years. That promise was never honored. No follow-up, no replacement—just silence.

Yesterday was the last straw. I brought my VW Beetle in because of a simple screw in the tire. After removing the tire, the staff told me the tread measured 5/32 and 6/32, and that at 4/32 the tires would need replacing. They immediately launched into tire specials and sales talk. I declined and asked them to just fix the screw. Instead, one of the men took a flathead screwdriver and shoved it into the tread, tearing away rubber to expose the wires underneath. He walked back out with the screwdriver still lodged in my tire. I was stunned. They then said, for “safety reasons,” they wouldn’t put that tire back on the car and tried to push me into a replacement—first new, then a used tire they suddenly offered for free when I refused.

When I mentioned my daughter works at a dealership and could get me new tires for less, he disparaged her workplace, implying any deal would mean bad tires. I left with their used tire, only to realize at home it was a Michelin filled with air, while my set is Pirelli filled with nitrogen. I returned within 20 minutes to get my original tire back. They couldn’t find it. While I waited, I overheard a staff member on the phone with another Discount location bragging about how they had “sold more tires and made more profit.” Given what had just happened, that comment was infuriating.

Eventually they located my tire—but now the “free” used tire had become a “loaner,” and they wanted it back. I didn’t want their tire in the first place. I wanted a simple, safe patch and an honest interaction. Instead, I felt manipulated, pressured, and dismissed.

Between the unfulfilled promise on the Escalade, the screwdriver incident, the upselling under the guise of safety, the mismatch and confusion over the loaner, and the disrespectful comments about my daughter’s workplace, my trust is gone. I don’t understand how a store operates like this and still expects loyalty. We’ll be taking our business elsewhere, and I hope management or corporate steps in to uphold basic standards of integrity, accountability, and customer care. Buyer beware.

Disappointing Service and Unwelcoming Attitude

On my first visit, I asked the waitress a few simple questions about the menu and was met with impatience, as if I were an inconvenience. I ordered an iced tea that never arrived, yet it appeared on the bill. When I raised the issue, the staff response felt dismissive. The food was mediocre and did not redeem the experience. The atmosphere lacked hospitality, and I left feeling singled out and disrespected. Management should address staff training, customer care, and billing accuracy to prevent similar experiences for guests in the future and improve service.

California Burger impressed me today, but the star was the chocolate brownie delight sundae—rich, decadent, and easily among the best I’ve ever had. If you love chocolate, put this spot on your list. Friendly, helpful staff, quick service, and satisfying portions make it a must-try treat for dessert today.

This spot shines as a relaxed hangout for casual bites. The famed original-style pizza muffins were fine, more novelty than knockout. My calzone leaned dry, muting the flavors. Overall, the food is decent, serviceable rather than memorable—better for low-key meetups than culinary fireworks overall.

Wandering around Harrah's waiting for check in brought me to this burger spot.

I grabbed a basic burger and a Fat Tire, and the tab with tip hit nearly $30. Strip prices are expected, but this felt steep for a meh beer and a standard burger. Service was attentive and friendly, and the strictly enforced no-smoking policy was a relief given the haze outside the hostess stand. Convenient spot, but value is questionable; there are likely better bites for the price within walking distance.
Love it! This boutique brims with feathers, lace, and satin. Every visit tempts me to buy everything. Explore every corner—hidden treasures abound, and you might miss something delightful.

I haven't been to the property yet, but my initial impression of Bluegreen is positive. I spoke with a friendly OPC who explained their 90-minute presentation incentives: a $100 Visa gift card and a mini vacation, with bonuses like show tickets. Unlike other timeshare pitches I’ve endured, this approach felt relaxed and transparent, not pushy. The OPC answered questions clearly and referenced Yelp feedback, which adds confidence. I plan to schedule a tour when time allows to see whether the experience lives up to the promise. If the presentation stays courteous and the perks deliver as described, this could be a worthwhile introduction to Bluegreen’s offerings. Hoping experience matches the pitch.

Sandella’s shines with incredible flatbread—wheat is my favorite. The buffalo chicken wrap is absolutely outstanding. Healthy, tasty options abound, with clear calorie info on display. You can eat smart without sacrificing flavor. Don’t miss the rice bowls; they’re drool-worthy, too.

It's there not a zero star option? Watch your phone.

This location disastrously mixed up multiple customers’ iPhones on launch day, handing out protected devices tied to the wrong carriers. Several people received someone else’s phone, and activation triggered security flags as if the phones were stolen. The chain of custody was sloppy and unacceptable. If you shop here, verify IMEI and carrier before leaving, and demand proper documentation. Bottom line: poor management, poor controls—watch out.

NOTE: This review is only about the smoothies/juices

I really wanted to like this place. I’ve been hunting for a reliable local juice bar, and I thought this might finally be the one. I ordered two juices, hoping for a strong ginger kick, but none of the menu items leaned ginger-forward. The staffer helpfully said they could add ginger to any drink, so I went with Pucker Up! and Berry Me Alive, both with ginger. I initially wanted smalls to sample, yet at $4.50 plus an extra ginger charge, the value felt off, so I chose mediums.

Unfortunately, the flavors disappointed. Pucker Up! did make my lips pucker, but not in a good way; it was bland and sharply sour, and it left my stomach churning. Berry Me Alive tasted like a cup of frozen berries blended with ice—flat, dull, and surprisingly lifeless. I understand the practicality of frozen fruit, but these berries lacked depth and brightness. As for the ginger add-on, at fifty cents I expected a noticeable zing; I couldn’t taste it at all, which defeated the point of adding it.

The bill came to about $13 for the two medium drinks with ginger, and the experience simply didn’t justify the price. I don’t plan to return or spend more here experimenting. For now, I’ll drive to Thrive in Gilbert, where my money feels better spent and the flavors deliver.

One word comes to mind: Pretentious.

After a week of dining in and around Vieux Montréal, Le Local stands out for all the wrong reasons: it was the priciest stop and delivered the weakest meal. If you want to imagine the experience, picture slathering butter on a few $20 bills, chewing them, and chasing it with water while calling it a cocktail.

The evening started with a Mojito and a Martini, each priced north of ten dollars and both so diluted they were nearly indistinguishable from plain water. One round was more than enough.

Then came the poutine—an emblematic Montréal comfort food whose alchemy of crisp fries, squeaky curds, and rich gravy rarely disappoints. Somehow, Le Local managed to strip the dish of its soul, serving a version that failed on the basics and left us wondering how you botch something so simple.

Bread service did not redeem matters. At a restaurant charging premium prices, offering stale, flavorless bread with a gummy chew is unacceptable; fresh, warm, and aromatic should be the baseline, not a luxury.
