For mains, the veal burger was the lone bright spot: genuinely tasty and well-executed, yet still not compelling at the tariff demanded. By contrast, my wife’s fish arrived with an odd, off-putting flavor that made it difficult to eat; it went largely untouched.

What frustrates most is the disconnect between the restaurant’s aspirations and the plate. The polish and posturing promise one thing; the flavors and value deliver another. Given the abundance of excellent restaurants within walking distance, it’s baffling that Le Local enjoys more than three stars.

In a trip otherwise filled with memorable meals, this was the glaring misstep. Save your money and your appetite for virtually anywhere else. Montreal rewards curiosity; from neighborhood bistros to casual counters, you’ll find better cooking, stronger pours, and service that respects both palate and wallet.

Die Hagsfelder Stuben überzeugen mit prima Fleischqualität: Die Steaks kamen wie gewünscht medium und schmeckten ausgezeichnet. Dazu gab es schöne, cross gebratene und gut gesalzene Pommes, eine hervorragende Knoblauchrahm-Soße und einen reichlichen Beilagensalat mit leckerem Dressing. Bei großen Veranstaltungen ist die Speisekarte zwar eingeschränkt – das ist nachvollziehbar –, jedoch fehlten dabei attraktive Optionen für Vegetarier oder leichte Esser. Statt eines großen Salats wurde trotz vorhandener Zutaten lediglich Wurstsalat angeboten; die Bitte um einen gemischten Salat wurde abgelehnt. Daher insgesamt vier Sterne. Beim erneuten Besuch blieb die Küche schmackhaft, allerdings lag die Garstufe des Fleisches konsistent am unteren Ende von medium, was manche stören könnte. Ein Vorschlag: Hausgemachte Spätzle würden das Angebot zusätzlich aufwerten. Insgesamt bietet die Küche solide Qualität mit Fokus auf Fleisch und klassische Beilagen.

Meh. This store’s layout is confusing, with tacky displays that cheapen the experience. Prices feel predatory, especially on printer ink. Despite its massive footprint, there’s little of interest inside. It’s unfortunate such mediocrity exists really nearby.

Before you read on, you should probably know I don't like fudge...

The Fudge Kitchen’s reputation precedes the shop. When you tell people you live in Edinburgh, someone inevitably asks about it. Perched on the Royal Mile, it broadcasts an irresistible sugary scent that floats up the cobbles all day. I don’t like fudge, but I do love smelling it, and my brothers, who adore the stuff, never miss a chance to pop in for a free sample.

Yes, free samples. There’s usually a chunk of one of their specialties on the counter, tempting passerby. A word of caution, though: treat it as a taste, not a meal. My brother learned the hard way—mortified isn’t the word.

What really sets the place apart is the staff. They all but drag you inside, and I mean that in the nicest way possible. Friendly, funny, and relentlessly upbeat, they turn a quick visit into a little performance. During the festival they spill onto the street, bantering with performers and luring tourists into the shop, keeping the energy high.

Ultimately, it didn’t float my boat. Still, as a quick hit of Scottish tradition—and a calorie boost before tackling Edinburgh’s hills—it’s hard to fault. If you love fudge, the creamy slabs and rotating flavors will feel like paradise. If you don’t, go for the atmosphere, the theatrics, and that glorious smell. Prices can feel indulgent, but the experience is part of the package. A lively, iconic stop on the Royal Mile, even for skeptics.

A little disgusted. At the drive-thru on Wednesday, August 13 at 17:12, the employee by the window looked visibly unwell, leaning on the machine and repeatedly glancing over. She then stood up, wiped sweat from her face with an ungloved hand, and proceeded to handle our food. That’s a serious hygiene concern. If she was sick, she should have been sent home; if not, the manager needs to address training and food-handling standards. Disappointed.

If I had written this after my first experience here it probably would have been a 5 star review. However, after my last trip all it really warrants is now a 2.

My early visits to this Charlotte steakhouse, including during Restaurant Week, suggested a place worthy of its reputation. The kitchen delivered confident, well‑executed plates; even the prix fixe felt thoughtful. I still wish they’d bring back the original bacon‑laced macaroni and cheese; the lobster version adds cost without improving it.

Service on that first visit was impeccable—warm, attentive, and polished from greeting to farewell. A handwritten card arrived days later, underscoring a rare commitment to hospitality.

Unfortunately, my most recent experience told a different story. While we ordered from the Restaurant Week menu, every guest added paid sides, and we understand tipping norms. Still, our server barely acknowledged us, communication was perfunctory, and plates were delivered to the wrong table. When dessert arrived, we had to flag someone down for to‑go boxes—basic requests that should never become a hunt for attention.

Restaurant Week can strain dining rooms, but great places rise to the moment rather than telegraph disdain. If this is “one of the best steakhouses in Charlotte,” guests should feel respected regardless of menu choice. The contrast between visits was stark enough to tarnish the glow of the first impression.

For now, I won’t be planning a return. Consistency in service is as crucial as a properly cooked ribeye, and on my latest visit, hospitality missed the mark.

After two frustrating attempts, this auto service kept me on hold over 15 minutes each time. I even called from another phone to confirm anyone was helping—no one was. When I finally reached a person, I was parked another 25 minutes waiting for a manager. Utterly unacceptable. If I could, I'd give zero stars.

This is a really great exhibit.

From the moment you enter, the Titanic exhibit delivers an immersive experience. Guests receive a boarding pass linked to a real passenger, adding a poignant personal narrative that culminates at a board revealing each outcome. The collection of artifacts is extensive and evocative, highlighted by an impressive side panel from the ship. The staging is exceptional: a nighttime outdoor walkway simulates wind and ambience so convincingly you feel transported onto a cruise liner. The grand staircase replica is another standout, capturing the elegance of the era. The exhibit balances education, emotion, and spectacle, making it well worth the price of admission. It’s a memorable, engaging visit for history buffs, families, and anyone curious about the Titanic.

Too bad there is not an option for NO stars...

Meeting clients for lunch, my associate and I were seated in the back, left side, in one of the middle booths. The first red flag was the upholstery: a one-inch gap between the back and seat exposed the wooden frame underneath. Still, we tried to overlook it. The waitress and her trainee were friendly and promptly brought water.

About five minutes in, something moved in my peripheral vision. I looked down to find a cockroach in my lap. I flicked it to the floor and, by sheer will, didn’t scream. I informed my associate and the server quietly. Because we were awaiting clients, we couldn’t leave; we asked to move to a front table and white-knuckled our way through the meeting.

While the staff was kind, the state of the seating and the presence of a roach are absolute deal-breakers. Basic cleanliness and maintenance are non-negotiable. I will never return, and I cannot recommend this restaurant until serious repairs and pest control are addressed.

Great music and big-screen videos set high expectations at this club, but the experience quickly slid downhill. The go-go dancers were cute and enthusiastic, and the two-room layout sounded promising, yet both spaces felt identical and equally overcrowded. Seating was almost nonexistent unless you sprung for VIP, which offered little more than a spot barely better than the floor. When you’re tired, there’s nowhere to catch your breath, and when you’re ready to move, the dance floor is jammed with people who aren’t even dancing. Bodyguards seemed to hover at every turn, creating a tense, almost creepy vibe rather than a sense of safety. I’d heard it was poppin’—fun, full of cool people and nonstop dancing—but the crowd skewed bro-heavy and self-absorbed, with minimal interaction and a palpable dude-fest energy. If a dance club doesn’t give you space to actually dance, what’s the point? Despite the strong soundtrack and visuals, the lack of comfort, atmosphere, and room to move ruined the night for me. I won’t be rushing back unless they rethink capacity and seating.

Not bad Indian for West Island with reasonable prices. We mostly do takeout, so no comment on dine-in. Flavors can vary week to week, yet the food is usually good. Takeout discounts and birthday or anniversary coupons add value, making it a dependable neighborhood option overall.

Very impressed by the crystal design of this bar. The pictures don't do this place justice; it truly does need to be seen in person to be properly appreciated.

Step inside, and the promise dims. The interior delivers a familiar casino-bar experience: loud music, bustling crowds, and service that, while friendly, can be a touch slow. There’s nothing inherently wrong with that formula, but it clashes with the refined expectations set by the dazzling façade. To its credit, the bartender demonstrated notable skill, with well-balanced cocktails that hint at what this venue could achieve. Still, the space yearns for a more thoughtful program—quieter ambience, quicker service, and a menu that reflects the bar’s striking design. With stronger alignment between concept and execution, this could evolve from eye-catching attraction to genuinely exceptional destination. As it stands, beauty outpaces substance.

After a (somewhat) rough start, The Diamond is firing on all cylinders!

When The Diamond reopened, the early weeks were a lesson in growing pains: shoulder-to-shoulder crowds, long waits, and frequent “sorry, we’re out” apologies. Those days are largely behind it. It’s still lively, but the initial 45-minute lines have eased, and the kitchen now hums with confidence.

Signature fried pickles remain the best in town, shatter-crisp and well-seasoned. I’ve yet to tackle the fried chicken, but everything else has impressed. Burgers are massive, juicy, and cooked spot-on. My lone gripe is the menu’s “All the Way” and “Southern Style” presets, which imply you’re limited to two builds; in reality, you can choose any toppings, and clarifying that would make ordering friendlier. The pork chops are excellent—well-seared, tender, and properly seasoned—and the hamburger steak delivers exactly what comfort-food seekers want.

Service is fast and efficient, with servers who keep the pace without rushing you. The new late-night menu smartly streamlines favorites and leans into breakfast, perfect for post-show hunger or third-shift cravings. Thursday through Saturday, the doors stay open until 4 a.m., making The Diamond one of the city’s most reliable after-hours stops. With the gremlins gone and the kitchen in its groove, this neighborhood staple feels truly back.

Como se dice "meh"?

Aunt Chilada’s disappoints from the first sip: a watery, average $12 margarita and an $11 mojito mixed from a bottle. Chips come with a jarred-tasting salsa straight off the supermarket shelf. Entrees are overpriced and painfully mediocre; for once, I couldn’t even finish my plate. The tortillas were a low point—rubbery, flavorless, and inexplicably bad. How do you mess up a tortilla? Service didn’t help, wavering between inattentive and borderline rude. For these prices, you expect fresh flavors, competent technique, and basic courtesy. Instead, it’s a shrug in a sombrero. Never again—o, como dicen, nunca más. Save your money and your appetite elsewhere.

Unimpressed for a couple of reasons.

Service disappointed. Our waiter was pleasant but forgetful, and we repeated requests. Despite an empty dining room, our food took over 45 minutes, and staff seemed unsure who ordered what. The dishes varied from decent to good, depending on choice. My green beans had to be reordered and still arrived wrong. With better coordination and faster pacing, this place could improve, but now it feels disorganized and not worth the wait.

I stopped in on the fly to pick up a birthday treat for a dessert-averse friend and was immediately impressed by the service. The staff helped me choose a Coconut-Lemon Olive Oil Cake and even found a charming cat cookie to perch on top—perfect for a devoted cat person. The cafe was buzzing, with a parade of petite cakes tucked beneath gleaming stands, and I genuinely wished I had time to stay for a cup.

The cake itself was a quiet triumph: moist, gently lemony, with a whisper of coconut and none of the toothache sweetness that turns some people off. Eight of us enjoyed it, and the cat cookie, curiously berry-tinged, sparked smiles and conversation. Even the minimalist, off-size business card felt like a thoughtful touch—simple, distinctive, and to the point.

If this quick visit is any measure, this spot balances warm, intuitive service with well-tuned flavors. I can’t wait to return to sample more of those cute little cakes and finally linger over coffee. Recommended for both grab-and-go and leisurely hangs.

Had the sandwich for lunch yesterday. Was such a sad looking sandwich.

Tasty but tragically skimpy. My sandwich had so little filling that the top and bottom slices of bread touched. Bread alone doesn’t make a sandwich. Everything we ordered tasted good, but the lack of ingredients is frustrating, especially at these prices. Flavor is there; value and substance are not right now.

No Thanks!

A promotional stamp card promising free oil changes and bundled services set the stage for what should have been a straightforward maintenance visit. At Tire Works’ Pecos/Sunset location, the first attempt was derailed: staff said they were too slammed to handle an oil change that day. An appointment for the following day didn’t help. Arriving on time, the response was a shrug and a request to come back later or tomorrow, with a minimum two-hour wait. To their credit, they called around and found the Horizon Ridge location “wasn’t busy,” prompting a drive across town.

Upon arrival, Horizon Ridge quoted a 30–45 minute wait, possibly sooner. The actual wait stretched to an hour and 45 minutes—an especially trying delay with an antsy two-year-old in tow. In the waiting room, frustration felt universal, reinforcing the impression that over-scheduling and optimistic estimates are routine. When appointment systems don’t safeguard time slots and wait times are underestimated by such a margin, it signals a breakdown in communication, queue management, and respect for customers’ time.

This experience makes it hard to justify future visits. Terrible’s has offered more dependable timelines and service in the past, and reliability matters. Until Tire Works tightens its scheduling, honors appointments, and delivers transparent wait estimates, the perception will remain: customer service here feels like an afterthought.

If I could make it zero stars, I would.

My experience here was dreadful. Staff were incredibly rude, and after my insurer paid in full, they still sent me a bill with no justification. Reading reviews across multiple sites, I noticed a pattern of bad service and doctors who seemed incompetent. Based on my experience, I recommend going elsewhere for care. Save yourself the hassle—do your homework, read the reviews, and choose a different provider.

Convenient Midas Stop in Phoenix, but Promotions and Communication Disappoint Today

I pulled in after seeing a big sign: "free tire rotation with every oil change." Staff said they could finish within an hour, price $19.95. I dropped the keys and walked to Dunkin for an iced tea and bagel. After an hour, no call; I went back to find my car parked and the lifts down—clearly done. At the counter, I was told my car requires synthetic oil, adding $10. My last mechanic never mentioned it. Not thrilled by the surprise, but fine—I just wanted it finished.

I asked about the free tire rotation advertised. The answer: no rotation unless you explicitly ask or sign up for it. So the “with every oil change” part is more like “available upon request,” which defeats the point of the promise. Communication felt reactive instead of proactive—no status update and no heads‑up about the upsell.

For convenience, the location is great and the turnaround is solid. But value is about more than speed; it’s expectations set and met. Ken Bohl’s place on Thomas has longer hours, sharper pricing, and better service. They include a free 20-point inspection and tire rotation with every oil change—no prompting required. The transparency and follow‑through difference is noticeable.

I’ll likely take my business back to Ken Bohl next time. If this Midas wants to keep the banner up, they should make the free rotation truly automatic and communicate clearly about oil requirements and timing.

We left disappointed after a long-awaited visit to this BBQ spot. The burnt ends were just okay, and while the barbecue sauce was pretty good, the quesadilla was bland and the pulled pork sandwich was only passable. Across the board, the meat was super fatty—even for barbecue. The fries came dusted with so much powder they tasted like barbecue Lay’s chips rather than fresh fries. Service hovered at “just okay”: we noticed employees lounging near the food counter, absorbed in tablets or readers, and the “chef” made table visits twice, but only to the same table. I flagged that it was my husband’s birthday multiple times; not even a simple “happy birthday,” and apparently they don’t do anything for birthdays. More letdowns: no fresh-brewed tea (a staple at most BBQ joints) and no potato salad. To top it off, both of us felt ill for a couple days afterward, which sealed our decision not to return. It’s disappointing because my husband had been excited, having heard about the place from the DJ owner.

Target is not exactly my "go to" store.

As a shopper, I seldom find what I need at Target, and when I do, the prices feel steep. On a recent visit, I searched for a workout foam roller and was surprised to see basic foam priced over $40. I left and purchased a comparable roller on Amazon for $18 with free shipping. Beyond pricing, I’m uneasy about Target’s announced nationwide stance on firearms. While they say they’ll comply with local laws, I expect to see posted signage in my area, and if that appears, I’ll likely take my business elsewhere. Policies matter, and combined with limited selection and higher prices, Target continues to fall short of being my preferred store today.

Receptionist was rude to us as well, seemingly more interested in her word-search puzzle than greeting patrons. That said, the museum itself was fascinating, with plenty to engage young kids—our 3- and 6-year-old loved exploring the exhibits. A major downside was the heat; it felt nearly as hot inside as outside in mid-July, and it doesn’t seem like there’s air conditioning. The uncomfortable temperature dampened the experience, though the content of the museum made the visit worthwhile.

Warning: A Sunday funday could end up with you showing your ass to strangers. Not saying, just saying.

I go here a lot; it’s one of Charlotte’s Sunday spots. Lively vibe, nice view, and beer prices don’t sting. The food is hit-or-miss—some days solid, others just okay. As a bar, it excels; as a restaurant, I’m lukewarm. Come for drinks and atmosphere, keep expectations on the plates.

Items Selected: Carrot Cake Cupcake with Cream Cheese Frosting; Bourbon Pecan and Salted Caramel Danish; Strawberries and Cream Buttercake; Monkey Bread; Almond Croissant.

A sunny stroll from Lazy Janes leads straight to Batch Bakehouse on 1402 Williamson Street, where the display cases brim with a broader, more artisanal spread than its nearby neighbor. French techniques underpin American favorites, and the bakers themselves step to the front to answer questions and guide choices. After some spirited deliberation, I settled on five pastries, planning a daylong graze rather than a single sitting, and grabbed a perch at the small countertop to begin.

The opening act—Carrot Cake Cupcake with Cream Cheese Frosting—set a high bar. Moist crumb, warm spice, and a tangy, plush frosting created an immediate “eat-now” urgency; none of that one was making it home. The only misstep of the lineup was the Monkey Bread, which lacked the pull-apart decadence and caramelized depth found elsewhere. Redemption arrived swiftly with the Almond Croissant: laminated layers arching and shattering, feather-light yet deeply buttery, with frangipane that enriched rather than weighed down. I’d be surprised to find a better rendition in town.

Sugar fatigue threatened, but the Strawberries and Cream Buttercake coaxed a second wind. Some might quibble with its rounded, muffin-like format, yet the experience is undeniably luscious—dense, tender, and suffused with creamy berry richness that feels both nostalgic and polished. The finale, a Bourbon Pecan and Salted Caramel Danish, balanced indulgence with nuance: a buttery base, smoky whispers from baked bourbon, and candied pecans providing satisfying crunch, all lifted by a saline caramel thread that kept sweetness in check.

Batch Bakehouse excels at technique-driven comfort, marrying precision with generosity. Portions invite sharing or saving, the staff is engaged and knowledgeable, and the vibe suits both a quick bite and a slow, appreciative browse. Must-orders include the Almond Croissant and the Bourbon Pecan Danish; the Carrot Cupcake is irresistible; the Monkey Bread can be skipped. As a post–Lazy Janes follow-up or a destination all its own, Batch Bakehouse earns a spot on the repeat-visit list.

Pretty cool club, however, I don't have much to compare it to since it was my first trip to Vegas. We went on a Sunday night, and the music was okay, a mix of top 40, house, and hip-hop. At times it felt like the DJ wasn’t mixing, more like starting and stopping tracks. The club was packed, but wait times for the restroom and bar were surprisingly short. Drinks ran $10-$15, a bit pricey, though probably standard for Vegas. Overall, a solid night, if not particularly memorable overall.

Meadowbank Sports Centre stands out as one of Edinburgh’s premier sporting hubs, and every visit reinforces that impression. The complex offers a strong selection of floodlit Astroturf football pitches, ideal for evening fixtures and league play. Pitch hire represents good value when costs are shared among a team; for a casual kickabout, you may find cheaper alternatives elsewhere. Beyond football, Meadowbank boasts a bright swimming hall, expansive multi-sport halls, and a well-equipped gym, making it a versatile destination for training, recreation, and community events.

My most recent visit came on the night of the General Election, when the centre served as a vote-counting venue. Watching the operation unfold highlighted just how large, modern, and well-organized the facility is, with ample space and amenities to support large-scale gatherings. Whether you’re a regular athlete or an occasional visitor, Meadowbank’s breadth of facilities and polished environment make it a standout choice—a genuinely great sporting asset for Edinburgh.

Wow, authentic and delicious! The guacamole was the best I’ve ever had, and the Pablano Nogada impressed with richness. We shared three different tacos, each flavorful, with perfect, not oversized portions. Service shined: Ivette was upbeat, super friendly, and elevated the meal. A can’t-miss spot for vibrant flavors and warm hospitality.

Worst service I've ever gotten. McDonald's has better manners than the girl serving us. It took a minute to get our food which she couldn't get right. And who fills my sprite with water? I'll never go back. This place went to garbage quick.

Service was shockingly bad. The server was rude, disorganized, and our order took far too long only to arrive incorrect. One cup supposedly Sprite was water. For a basic meal, this was unacceptable. I won’t return; quality and professionalism have deteriorated dramatically and rapidly.

After cataract surgery with Dr. Aron Waite, I’m thrilled to have 20/20 vision again. Beyond the outstanding medical outcome, Dr. Waite and his team are completely patient-focused. The Henderson office runs with impressive efficiency and warmth; when my appointment was set for 2:30, I was seen at 2:30—refreshingly rare in Las Vegas and clearly a standard at New Eyes. The procedure itself was remarkably comfortable; I’ve had haircuts that were less pleasant. From clear communication to punctual, compassionate care, every step inspired confidence. I wholeheartedly recommend New Eyes to anyone considering cataract surgery. If I could, I’d give them six stars out of five. —Lonny Dolezal

Delicious food! Our server was attentive and genuinely friendly, making an already great spot even better. Johnny and I love this place for its standout Korean dishes with a fun local island twist—think spam musubi, chicken katsu, and loco moco—all executed with care. Flavors are bold without being overly spicy, perfect for sharing across the table. Not into Korean or Hawaii-style plates? No problem: there are solid cheeseburgers and fries, too. Warm service, versatile menu, and craveable flavors—I highly recommend you go try it!

Simply amazing value at this Palazzo spot. With a $100 food credit, we feasted and still only hit $85. Arriving around 4 p.m. on a Friday, the room was calm, and our server was both patient and lightning-fast. We shared three appetizers—sliders, a quesadilla, and decadent brie wontons—each one a hit. For mains, I paired a crisp small salad with their rustic cheese pizza—pure YUM. My dad devoured a Kobe beef entrée, while my husband tackled a huge, comforting chicken pot pie. Generous portions, great flavors, fair prices: we’ll happily return whenever we’re back at the Palazzo again soon.

Incredible service! We got a flat tire late Saturday, and they welcomed us with urgency. They immediately fixed the issue and had us back on the road in ten minutes. Fast, friendly, efficient—couldn’t ask for better. Thank you, team!

Locally Owned & Operated - the antidote to corporate chains!

Pleasantly surprised by friendly service and a reasonably priced lunch menu, I enjoyed a well-made Fish Sammy and Turkey Club—fresh buns, crisp lettuce, juicy tomato. The Chip Trio hit the mark: crunchy chips, salsa that woke my taste buds without overdoing it, and guacamole that tasted freshly mashed. The patio looks inviting, and the well-appointed bar adds polish. Locally owned and operated, this spot feels thoughtfully run and genuinely welcoming. I’m adding it to my patio list. A nice little thing going, and my pick of the day.

Love Macy’s for the great deals—especially around Christmas—and the steady everyday bargains. However, checkout needs better organization. I waited about 30 minutes in the home department because one cashier repeatedly needed assistance from another. Consider scheduling additional training on a slower weekday and adding staff during peak times to streamline checkout and improve the experience overall.

You get what you pay for...

This spot offers one of the cheaper massage options around, and that budget-friendly price sets the tone for the experience. My expectations may have been too high, but the core issue was a multilayered language barrier and a lack of attentiveness. I understand Mandarin reasonably well and caught bits of gossip between the therapists working on me and my wife. More troubling, despite our clear requests—my wife’s lower back, my nagging elbow—those areas received only a token three or four minutes of extra focus before the team reverted to their standard routine.

The session felt rigidly scripted: roughly 15 minutes on face and head, 15 on arms, 15 on feet, and the final 15 on back and neck. For customers seeking targeted relief, that format can make half the time feel wasted, simply because it doesn’t adapt to individual needs. If you’re fine with a predictable sequence and prioritizing price over personalization, it’s serviceable—and the low cost does soften the disappointment.

To their credit, Vivian followed up by text asking for feedback, which suggests they care and may improve. In the meantime, go in with calibrated expectations: value-driven, consistent, but not especially tailored. Hope future visits feel responsive.

I would give this place no stars if I could.

I booked a three-session LipoLaser package through a WeeklyPlus deal for $99, hoping for a modest improvement in stubborn cellulite after years of disciplined training, healthy eating, and daily exercise. As an engineer, I’m inherently skeptical of gadgets that promise spot fat reduction with LED paddles, but I was willing to see if there was any noticeable effect. There wasn’t. After the first session, I saw no change whatsoever, and the experience itself left me far more concerned about hygiene and professionalism than results.

From the moment I arrived, the facility appeared unclean. The bathroom had an unpleasant odor, hair on surfaces, a soiled toilet, and visible urine stains on the floor—none of which suggested routine or thorough cleaning. In the treatment room, the LipoLaser paddles did not appear to have been sanitized between clients, which immediately raised red flags. I almost walked out at that point.

Post-treatment, I was directed to stand on a vibration platform (similar to a Power Plate) and asked to remove my shoes. The platform itself looked filthy, and nearby I noticed what appeared to be dirty surgical instruments on a medical table—hardly reassuring. When I asked the staff member, referred to as a “nurse,” if there was anything available to clean my feet before putting my shoes back on, I was pointed to the bathroom and told to use paper towels. Nothing about this process felt safe, clean, or professional.

Beyond the lack of cleanliness, the treatment did not deliver on the advertised promise of spot fat reduction. Given the questionable sanitation and the absence of results, I will not be returning to use the remaining two sessions. I left feeling that the service was more about selling a “miracle” than providing credible, hygienic care.

If you’re considering LipoLaser for minor cosmetic improvements, do your research and vet the facility thoroughly. I’ll stick to evidence-backed routines like dry brushing, spin classes, and strength training—at least I can sanitize the equipment myself and trust the benefits.

Plaka is a good, but basic place to get breakfast, especially if you're on a budget. I don't have very many words to say about this place, but it does everything pretty well.

Plaka leans into a Greek theme without trying to recreate a full-on taverna vibe. Expect plenty of Greek-inspired touches on the walls and a general hint of the Mediterranean, more a nod than an immersive atmosphere. For many diners, that’s perfectly fine: it sets expectations and frames the menu without overpowering the experience. When the weather cooperates, the patio is a genuine perk. Sitting outside adds a breezy, relaxed feel and a bit of fresh air that’s hard to beat on a warm morning.

Service is one of Plaka’s quiet strengths. The staff works quickly and keeps things moving without sacrificing friendliness. It’s not the kind of over-the-top hospitality you’ll tell stories about, but you’ll be seated, served, and sent on your way with a smile. For breakfast, that’s exactly what most people want.

The menu itself is straightforward, but the kitchen executes it well. You’ll find the essentials—eggs, omelets, pancakes—alongside a few Greek twists that keep things interesting. Gyro omelets are a highlight, and swapping pita for toast is a simple touch that changes the rhythm of the plate. Breakfast potatoes deserve special mention: crisp, savory, and reliably satisfying for anyone who, like me, craves them.

Value is where Plaka really stands out. For what you pay, you get a solid, dependable breakfast. It’s one of those rare spots where a full meal tends to land around ten dollars, and it’s an excellent alternative when Mickie’s Dairy Bar is too far or too crowded.

Overall, Plaka earns a 4 out of 5. I’d recommend it to most people I know. It’s not wildly unique and it doesn’t take many risks, but it hits the basics and hits them well—a pleasant, affordable start to the day.

Disappointing from start to finish. When I asked for my Thai iced tea without ice, staff tried to tack on an extra dollar, which felt petty and absurd. The fresh spring roll sauce was so off-putting it nearly made me gag, and the overall food quality didn’t justify the high prices. I ordered three lunches, two marked Thai hot, yet both were barely mild—no heat, no depth. Service lacked warmth or personality, making the whole experience feel transactional and indifferent. To top it off, the eggplant dish contained only a couple tiny pieces of eggplant. Between the nickel-and-diming and bland dishes, I won’t be returning anytime soon, either.

This place is beautiful.
A refreshing escape from the smoky chaos of Strip hotels, this property impresses with swift check-in, beautifully appointed rooms, comfortable beds and pillows, and a huge bath. Peaceful, classy ambiance throughout. I loved every moment here and would gladly return.

Ugh! I should have read these reviews before!

I don’t usually complain, but my visit to this salon was a string of red flags. I booked a manicure and opted for gel nails with Ellen. During the service, my cuticles bled—small nicks, which I tried to shrug off, but in hindsight that should’ve been my warning. Then I decided to try eyelash extensions. Big mistake. I was told they’d look “very natural,” yet midway through the session I was pulled out so another client could use the same room for waxing—apparently they only have one multipurpose room for wax, lashes, and more. By the time I left, I had a thick, quarter-inch band of black glue on my lash line. When I pointed out how heavy and obvious it looked, the response was that otherwise they wouldn’t be noticeable. For gel with mood color, an eyebrow and upper-lip wax, and lashes, I was charged $70. The price can’t excuse poor technique, questionable hygiene, and chaotic scheduling. I won’t be back.

This particular location blows especially hard.

My recent visits to this store have been frustrating. Management presence is scarce, and when the manager is around, oversight feels more like fault-finding than leadership. I repeatedly observed friendly banter with some staff while others were reprimanded for similar behavior, which creates the impression of favoritism and inconsistent standards. It’s demoralizing for employees and uncomfortable for customers to witness.

Operational basics also need attention. Too often I saw product sitting on the sales floor, unrefrigerated, while an overworked employee tried to catch up alone. That’s a food safety red flag and a symptom of chronic understaffing. For a brand that promotes sustainability, there’s a lot of single-use plastic on everything, which clashes with the messaging.

If you prefer to support locally owned grocers, you may feel better shopping at community-based alternatives; this location feels corporate and impersonal without delivering reliability. I’d love to see clear leadership on the floor, fair and even-handed expectations for all staff, better staffing levels at peak times, and stricter adherence to food handling protocols. Until then, I can’t recommend this store, and I’ll be taking my business elsewhere.

My husband had been eager to eat here ever since we saw this spot featured on Man vs. Food years ago, our expectations were high. Unfortunately, the experience stumbled from the moment we walked in. Despite making eye contact with several employees, no one greeted us. We watched what appeared to be regulars breeze past and seat themselves, so we eventually did the same. It took about five minutes for a server to arrive, and when he did, his manner was standoffish and unhelpful.

We ordered and waited, hoping the food would redeem the rocky start. It was a mixed bag. My husband enjoyed his sandwich. My plate, however, was a disappointment: a so-called sirloin that tasted nothing like sirloin, soggy fries, and coleslaw I couldn’t finish.

Between indifferent service and uneven food, the visit didn’t live up to the hype. I wouldn’t choose to dine here again.

This beacon of light half way thru a five hour trip appeared as if a mirage in the distance...or, ya know, on the corner.

This spot felt like a mirage materializing at the corner when we needed it most. We tumbled in after hours on the road and made a beeline for the restrooms, which, to our relief, were spotless. Traveling nine strong, we couldn’t be seated at one table, but the staff placed us at two adjacent ones, a practical, comfortable solution.

Service, however, lacked warmth. Our waitress moved briskly but never mustered a grin, and the low energy colored the meal. The food itself landed squarely in the decent-to-good range. Pancakes arrived with a surprisingly tough exterior, yet the eggs were tender and flavorful, the biscuits and gravy bordered on divine, and my toast came mercifully light on butter, just the way I like it.

I requested two checks to simplify a nine-person tally, but a single bill appeared at the end. Fortunately, the tab was affordable, and our group split the cost without fuss.

In the end, this is a solid travel stop: clean, convenient, and reliably satisfying for the price. Not a destination restaurant, but exactly the kind of place you hope to find when the highway stretches on.

This was my first Vegas restaurant, and it rekindled my love of Toby Keith—America before it was cool. Beer in 32 oz mason jars set the tone. Service was slow, but the drunk food delivered: mac-and-cheese bites to die for, and some of the best fries I’ve ever had. Mainstream, sure, but I left satisfied and would return. The lively country vibe sealed the deal.

Ammaccapanes very bad customer will keep me from ever stepping foot inside again.

As a regular who works nearby, I’ve long appreciated Ammaccapanes for its location and welcoming service from Lindsay behind the bar and John at the door. Unfortunately, my visit on October 6, 2013, was so disappointing that it erased much of that goodwill.

A friend and I stopped in for beers and wings. I ordered a small pitcher of Kilt, my friend a Blue Moon, and we expected a relaxed experience. The room wasn’t busy, but as I finished my first beer and moved through a second, the wings still hadn’t arrived. When I asked to cancel the order—figuring wings are best enjoyed hot alongside a drink—the male bartender reacted with attitude and refused, saying he couldn’t void the ticket because he would have to pay for it himself. He checked the ticket time; it had been over 22 minutes for a simple wing order.

Whether that policy is accurate or not, it’s a troubling claim and a more troubling way to handle a guest. I made it clear I wouldn’t pay for food that never arrived in a reasonable time, settled the tab for our drinks, tipped generously—more than enough to cover the wings—and left feeling sad and frustrated.

What stings most is knowing Ammaccapanes can do better; Lindsay has always exemplified hospitality, and John has been unfailingly courteous. This experience underscored gaps in training, communication, and guest-first decision-making. Timely food, transparent policies, and respectful service are nonnegotiable. Until management addresses these basics and empowers staff to resolve issues without penalizing themselves or alienating customers, I won’t be returning—and I can’t recommend others do, unless Lindsay is behind the bar.

Bad, BAD experience!

I stopped in today expecting a quick, basic car wash/detail on a standard four-door Sonata, nothing fancy—the $23 package, not the $100 deluxe. The lot was practically empty when I pulled in: no line, three employees visible inside. What followed was an infuriating lesson in inefficiency and time frustration: I was trapped there for 55 minutes. An hour for the most basic service.

The process itself felt like a Parallel Universe where time stands still. You pull up on the right, the car disappears behind the building, then reappears on the left… and somehow it never progresses. Additional cars materialize, employees hover with spray bottles and towels, repeating the same motions over and over, yet my car sits, untouched, just one spot behind a looping scene. Most competent operations assign two or three workers per car, per lane. Here, five people floated across three lanes, sharing cars and attention, result: no focus, no flow, no finish.

The so-called system prioritized smaller tickets while longer waits piled up. I paid for the $23 package and watched as five $10 packages were processed ahead of me. Understaffed, overcomplicated, and mismanaged, the setup makes customers like me the collateral damage of a broken workflow. It’s not just the waiting; it’s the sense that no one is accountable for moving a vehicle from start to done.

And the outcome? Meh at best. After almost an hour, the car was barely improved—certainly not worth the time or the money. Bottom line: faced with a dirty car or another visit to Francis & Sons, I’ll choose the dirty car every time. Save your time, your sanity, and your cash, and take your business elsewhere.

Call me crazye, but I like Hot N Juicy more than Boiling Crab!

I went in hopeful and hungry, ordering clams, shrimp, and a whole lobster, and opted for The Whole Shebang. Unfortunately, the sauce was dominated by garlic—huge, coarse chunks that overwhelmed every bite and turned what should have been a craveable, buttery-spicy coating into a harsh, one-note experience. The lobster didn’t redeem it; it was noticeably overcooked, edging toward rubbery rather than sweet and tender.

The room itself is built for game day: big, lively, and ringed with flat-screen TVs, which makes it a convenient spot to catch a match with friends. But service sank the meal. With saucy, spicy seafood, water is essential, yet our table went roughly 15 minutes without a check-in. We literally paused eating because we were so thirsty. It wasn’t one server; it was a systemic inattentiveness.

Given the combination of uneven cooking and poor service, I’ll stick with Hot N Juicy.

The beer choices are unique and the food was pretty good. Definitely not worth the wait because the service was brutal. They were out of nitro so the stout was not available and they were out of lemons. They were also out of flight glasses. Overall it was very disappointing. It took forever to get our server to take our order and the food took almost an hour to get to our table.

This place offers a distinctive beer list and solid food, but the service undermined the experience. They were out of nitro, lemons, and flight glasses—disappointing for a beer-focused spot. The Refuge IPA, Oaked n Ordinary, and Santa Teresa were enjoyable, and the Arizona Trail burger was excellent. Overall, not worth the wait. I’m unsure I’d return, except to finally try that stout next time, if the nitro is working.

I've been a few times over the years but was just back recently for a company Christmas party or "holiday" party for the PC'ers out there.

At a recent company holiday gathering, the group setting made it easy to sample broadly: calamari, salad, chicken parm, meat lasagna, and two desserts. The kitchen’s strengths showed clearly. Calamari was tender and well-seasoned, a reliable starter. The meat lasagna was the undisputed standout—layers balanced with rich sauce, savory meat, and satisfying comfort—so good our table finished it in minutes. By contrast, the chicken parm skewed dry, lacking the juiciness and sauce synergy that make the classic sing. Desserts impressed across the board: a seven-layer chocolate–mint cake with a nostalgic Thin Mint vibe, and a lush, classic tiramisu, both polished off with smiles. Overall, this is a solid Italian-American option for group dining, with desserts and lasagna worth the trip. That said, considering value, it wouldn’t be my first-choice splurge when footing the bill myself. Great for sharing and for dessert lovers.

Not what I expected.
The owner greeted us right away and walked us through the menu, which was a nice touch. We didn’t realize it was counter service—I prefer places where you sit and order—but the staff was attentive. Service remained quick and helpful. I had the pumpkin waffle and Bobby chose a regular; both were thin yet airy. Mine lacked a strong pumpkin flavor, though. We wouldn’t make a special trip back, but if we’re nearby, we’d stop in again, for lunch someday.

Pushy, annoying sales tactics and prices that have more than doubled in the past year make this place a hard pass. Staff come off unprofessional: rude, arrogant, and disrespectful, with high turnover that speaks volumes. Even if they were the only option, I wouldn’t buy here. Too many better choices to waste time today.

Stumbled upon this spot when a pricier place around the corner scared me off, and I’m glad it did. The menu is reasonably priced and instantly evokes Chipotle—but with heftier burritos, generous fillings, and better melt. The team was friendly and impressively fast, assembling our orders before sliding them through an oven conveyor that crisps the tortilla and thoroughly melts the cheese. The result: a hot, satisfying, well-balanced burrito that feels like a great value. It’s new to the neighborhood, but it’s already a reliable go-to. I’d happily come back for another quick, delicious bite.

Yes, this venue is tiny—think tissue-box tiny—but that intimacy becomes part of its charm. The cozy space encourages a close, lively atmosphere, and the staff and performers are genuinely friendly. There’s impressive variety among the dancers and a broad, upbeat music selection that keeps energy high. The decor may surprise you, but you’re not here for the furniture. What matters is the consistently fun experience: every single visit has been memorable and enjoyable, and I’d recommend this spot over similar venues in the valley. It’s notably welcoming to women, with performers who make everyone feel comfortable while delivering standout lap dances. Special shout-out to Carissa—she’s a highlight worth seeking out here.

On another visit to see a friend, I found myself back at this reliable favorite—and for good reason. I can’t resist the 131 Maniac; one is never enough. The soup special—artichoke and mushroom in a cream base—was deeply flavorful, though a touch too thick, bordering on pudding. Still, it was tasty enough to take the rest home. Grilled artichokes remain a must-order and, once again, didn’t disappoint with their smoky, tender perfection. We skipped dessert at the table but snagged a banana cream pie to go. Consistently satisfying, welcoming, and craveable—a great spot for dinner every time.

I came into going here with high expectAtions because of all of the high reviews on yelp.

Roka Akor delivers in the glass: cocktails are excellent, and bartenders clearly know their craft. Happy hour is a draw with a wide mix of drinks and bites. The food shines, especially the cold plates—fresh, balanced, and worth ordering. Portions run small, though, and the tab climbs fast if you arrive hungry. This is a place to savor and splurge, not to stuff yourself. Want to ball out with top-tier drinks and refined bites? Come here; for feasting, look elsewhere.

Love the free weekend concerts—check the bands online first, quality varies. The mall offers an arcade, movie theater, and very solid shops and restaurants. Unfortunately, the free Wi‑Fi is terrible, disappointing when trying to stay connected during visits here.

I'm struggling here because I really really want to love this place.
Isabella’s boasts a beautiful location just down the street from my house, with an inviting atmosphere and sweeping views that set the stage for a great night. The trouble is, the food rarely rises to the occasion. I’ve tried the pizza and a salad; both were fine, but nothing to write home about. The cocktails, on the other hand, are solid—balanced and enjoyable—though the prices are what you’d expect for North Scottsdale (pun intended if you’ve been). The outdoor area is a genuine plus, especially for families, giving kids room to roam while adults relax. In the end, I’d recommend Isabella’s for lovely drinks on the patio during a comfortable Arizona evening, but I’d plan dinner elsewhere. Still, I keep going back, hoping it’ll click—like a mediocre relationship that should work, but just doesn’t. Maybe next time. A lovely spot, but not for meals.

The good: Delicious drinks, decent happy hour prices and an amazing view.

If you’re chasing skyline drama with your sundowner, this spot delivers. The panoramic view is genuinely stunning—one of those rare backdrops that can turn an ordinary happy hour into a memory. The bar program holds its own against the scenery: cocktails tasted fresh and balanced, and the happy hour pricing felt fair for the setting. It’s the kind of place you’d bring out-of-towners to impress them without annihilating your budget, at least on the beverages front.

Unfortunately, the glow faded fast once it was time to pay. Four of us arrived specifically for happy hour and, before ordering a single drink, told our server we needed separate checks. She assured us it would be easier to split everything at the end. When the bill came, it was a single check. We handed over payment methods and asked to be charged for our individual orders. She couldn’t recall who had what, so we wrote it all down—names, items, and how we’d each pay. She returned with four checks, but the splits were wrong. Because of “how their system works,” she said she couldn’t divide four identical cocktails into two and two on separate checks. When we asked her to move an item between checks to fix it, we were told she’d need a manager—who was downstairs, 107 floors below. After waiting, we gave up and paid the incorrect checks, losing about thirty minutes and a fair bit of patience.

Had we sprung the separate-check request at the end, this would be a different story. But we didn’t. Either the POS system is woefully rigid, or the process isn’t guest-centric. In any case, our server should have kept separate tabs from the start as requested.

Bottom line: come for the view and solid happy hour drinks, but insist on opening separate tabs up front—or be ready for a billing headache. Management would do well to fix the system and train staff to prioritize split checks when asked.
Boulders is great. I pass it daily—stop in! Lots of beer, and the pizza is excellent; the rest of the food is okay. It's hardly ever crowded, but the jukebox is awful. A solid neighborhood spot.

The food had no flavor.

This restaurant serves a generic, Americanized version of Italian cuisine that recalls chains like Macaroni Grill and Carrabba’s. The bread tasted flat and slightly stale unless drenched in olive oil to coax out any enjoyment. The tomato sauce had the unmistakable profile of a bottled grocery-store product—no depth, no slow-simmered character, nothing that felt authentic or homemade. Portions are undeniably generous and prices are friendly, but quantity and value can’t make up for the lack of flavor or craft.

Despite branding, it’s nowhere near a New York or Sicilian spot. The dining room was empty, and the front register was occupied by two older Italian staff focused on numbers, offering no greeting or eye contact. The atmosphere felt devoid of passion.

This seems tailored to diners who want the comfort of Olive Garden while believing they’re branching out. Expect stereotypical “Italian” dishes: heavy on cheese, light on nuance, big plates, and bargain pricing. If you prioritize volume over vibrancy, you’ll get your fill. If you’re chasing genuine Italian flavors, slow-cooked sauces, and a sense of hospitality, look elsewhere. The experience is bland, predictable, and forgettable.

I took my two boys, ages 9 and 12, to this spot on a Saturday afternoon (2/1/14) and picked the Mini Golf and Laser Tag package. The pricing is straightforward: Mini Golf runs $8.50 (students and seniors get $1 off with ID), with same‑day replay for $3 and family pricing at $30 for two adults and two children. Laser Tag is $7 with a $4 same‑day replay, and you can shave $2 off Laser Tag if you buy it with Mini Golf. There’s also an Unlimited Play option for $24.99. Glasses rental for the 3D course is $1.50.

The 3D Mini Golf ended up being the highlight. It’s an 18‑hole course with distinct themes, bright murals, and surprisingly polished set pieces. The artwork is playful—think familiar cartoon vibes, an alien cameo, even a nod to Super Mario. It feels imaginative without trying too hard, and the kids were immediately into it. A tip on the 3D glasses: they’re fun at first, but after about 10 minutes both the boys and I felt a bit woozy and ditched them after the third hole. If you’re sensitive to that kind of thing, you might skip the glasses and enjoy the art as-is. The holes themselves offer a nice mix of easy wins and mild challenges that keep kids engaged.

Laser Tag was a different kind of workout. With just the three of us, it became a fast-paced free-for-all. Before playing, you watch a short safety and how‑to video—quick, clear, and kid-friendly. The round lasted about seven minutes, which felt longer than it sounds when you’re sprinting around in the dark. Pro tip: avoid white clothing; under black lights it turns you into a glowing target. I finished with the lowest score, but the boys came out grinning, which is what counts.

Value-wise, the same‑day replay pricing is a smart way to extend the fun without emptying your wallet, and the family package for Mini Golf is solid. Keep an eye out for their weekly family specials—they’re genuinely good deals. Overall, it’s a clean, colorful, and well-organized place to burn off energy. The kids had a blast, and that’s a win in my book.

Las Vegas buffet culture has come a long way from the days of $4 all-you-can-eat spreads piled with dubious, cardiac-challenging fare. Some buffets still miss the mark—think Las Vegas Hilton, more Ken-L Ration than cuisine—but others deliver genuine value and flavor.

Enter the Paris buffet. For $17.99, you’re treated to a broad, fresh lineup that feels curated rather than chaotic. The carving station turns out rosy prime rib and moist roasted turkey, while surrounding islands offer an assortment of international dishes that are both well-seasoned and replenished frequently. The salad station is surprisingly thoughtful, complete with crisp greens, a range of dressings, and crunchy bits of fresh bacon for sprinkling. Desserts are legion; I didn’t sample many, but the array looked tempting. The showstopper, though, is the brie-and-bacon mac and cheese—indulgent, creamy, and worth the Lipitor joke.

Pro tip for any buffet, especially this one: do a full lap before committing. The saddest plate is the first plate filled too soon.

In a city where excess is routine and value can be elusive, Paris’s buffet strikes a satisfying balance of quality, variety, and price. It just might be the all-around best deal in Las Vagueness right now.

Found this spot through Groupon while sampling southwest breakfast joints. A little tricky to find - take Buffalo west, since Rainbow doesn’t go all the way through. Big plus: breakfast served until 3 p.m. on Sundays. Food was very solid, service on point, and the vibe relaxed. I’m definitely planning a return visit soon to tackle their chicken fried steak.

Visited about a year ago, right after dining at B&B, and the experience was disappointing. Service was sluggish and inattentive, continuing a pattern I’ve noticed at Mario Batali spots like Pizzeria Mozza, B&B, and San Marcos. My friend and I shared several dishes; a few were good, most were just okay. The low point was my main: pork chops so chewy I could barely get through two bites before giving up. The saving grace was dessert—easily the highlight and the reason this isn’t a two-star review. Also, double-check your reservation; mine was lost despite a confirmation call. Proceed for sweets, not mains—and skip entrées.

Was charged 50% more than what I paid in LA for alterations and the seat of my D&G suit pants will have to be redone. Had this done in October when I first moved to AZ and still can't get over how bad it is. Was ignored by a man sitting behind the counter reading when I first arrived, eventually I was helped by a woman from the back. When I returned a week later, as I was told, to pick up the items they hadn't been started. The hems were fine but pricey. The seat of my suit pants are not. Still haven't worn the suit - just looking at it upsets me. Opposite experience to the yelp postings I read.

In October, shortly after moving to Arizona, I brought in my D&G suit and a few items for alterations. From the start, the customer service disappointed: a man behind the counter ignored me while reading until a woman from the back finally helped. I was quoted a week turnaround, but when I returned, nothing had been started. Prices were 50% higher than what I’d paid in Los Angeles, and while the hems were passable, they were overpriced. The real issue was the seat of my suit pants, which now needs to be completely redone. I haven’t worn the suit because just looking at it upsets me. My experience was the complete opposite of the glowing Yelp reviews—poor communication, delays, and subpar workmanship.

The hubs and I stopped in here for dinner before seeing a show at The D, drawn by the renovation of the old Fitzgerald’s and its stylish, refreshed decor. Unfortunately, the shine was dulled by neglect: a visible layer of dust sat atop lighting fixtures and the ledge above our table—hard to ignore in the desert, where frequent dusting should be routine. It also raised uneasy questions about overall cleanliness.

Service was pleasant and attentive, but communication fell short. My husband’s shrimp pasta was fine—competent but unmemorable. I ordered a stuffed chicken breast with polenta cakes; the plate arrived with mashed potatoes instead. Our waiter checked and reported that the chef had changed the menu, though the printed menus hadn’t caught up and the staff hadn’t been briefed. To compound the disappointment, the chicken was dry.

There’s real promise here, thanks to the inviting atmosphere and generally friendly staff. Still, inconsistent execution and cleanliness lapses undermine the experience. For now, decor outpaces the kitchen, and diners seeking a reliably satisfying meal may be happier elsewhere. With tweaks, this cafe could fulfill its potential soon for most diners.

I'm surprised this place doesn't get better reviews. I spent a night out in Mill with friends and had a blast. The crowd is welcoming—lots of college kids and young professionals—and the vibe is energetic without being pretentious. You can dance anywhere, the music keeps the room moving, and the Niners-bar identity adds a fun team spirit. The venue is huge, with solid drinks and everything you'd want in a bar. Worth a visit.

I stayed at this hotel with my husband for a work conference, and that seems to be the primary draw here unless you’re coming for golf. Be aware: the JW Marriott sits a solid 30 minutes from the Las Vegas Strip, which makes dining, shows, and nightlife inconvenient. If you plan to spend most of your time on property, however, there’s plenty to appreciate.

The grounds are expansive and beautifully maintained, with a lovely, resort-style pool area. The hotel is massive, almost a self-contained village, with multiple restaurants and casual spots, including a convivial Irish pub. Our room was comfortable and quiet, with plush linens.

The highlight of my stay was the spa. After rotating through the hot and cold baths, I tried the signature waterfall-esque showers: turn one on and a torrent of water rushes from roughly nine feet overhead. The sensation is surprisingly powerful—stabilize yourself so you don’t get tossed against the tile—but it delivers a deep, water-driven massage that’s both invigorating and relaxing. The spa’s outdoor lounge area, dotted with several pools, is tranquil. Standard amenities like tea, fruit, steam room, sauna, and a large gym round out the experience.

Overall, this is a serene retreat best suited to conferences or low-key resort time. If your plans revolve around the Strip, the distance is a real drawback. But if you’re here to unwind on property, the spa and pool make it a satisfying stay.

I remember this place.
We frequented this spot when our family lived in Germany, visiting about once a month. We’d order whatever resembled American comfort food, and it always hit the mark. It became our easy night out so Mom didn’t have to cook, and it felt like a slice of home. Inside, the atmosphere was warm, the service charmingly friendly, and the food consistently excellent—reasons we kept returning. I miss it now and wish I’d taken photos to remember it better. If you’re nearby, give it a try; it’s the kind of place that becomes a tradition.

Bartenders are clueless and have no sense of customer service!

I ordered a Manhattan and got a bourbon martini—just whiskey with a splash of vermouth, harsh and unbalanced. When I asked about the missing bitters, the bartender shrugged, said they don’t have any, and walked away before I could respond. My friend’s drink was equally mishandled. Between poor technique and indifferent attitude, this bar fails at the basics. Save your money and your palate—avoid.

I’ve visited several TGI Fridays locations around Las Vegas, and this one felt noticeably quieter—surprisingly, the bar was nearly empty on a Friday night. Our group of 20 may have overwhelmed the service; the waitress struggled to check in consistently, though she remained courteous throughout. The food was fine but forgettable. My Chicken Cajun Pasta leaned too spicy for my taste, overshadowing its otherwise decent flavors. Overall, this branch is serviceable for a casual outing, but nothing stands out beyond the standard TGI experience.

This spot has earned my loyalty year after year. The carne asada tacos are consistently juicy and flavorful, but the chorizo tacos steal the show—two chorizo and one carne asada is my perfect trio. I’ll happily drive across town for it. The horchata is reliably creamy, never watery or bland. Beans taste fresh and homemade, and the salsas bring bright, balanced heat. Don’t skip the carne asada nachos; they’re hearty, crisp, and generously topped. I’ve never had a bad meal here, and prices remain refreshingly reasonable. If you want dependable, delicious tacos with thoughtful sides and drinks, this place delivers consistently.

Despite rarely finding the exact item I’m hunting for, I keep returning to this spot because the thrill of discovery is real. The buyer’s eye leans toward similar styles, which can be a plus if you share that taste—and it shows they know their customers. The name suits the place: it’s far tidier than many cluttered shops or abandoned-feeling spaces I’ve wandered into. Clean, fairly organized, and refreshingly unfussy, it’s not boutique-y, but no one comes here expecting that. What you will find: plenty of men’s clothing, a solid vinyl selection, and a friendly, lived-in vibe. The owner (and the folks who hang out there) are welcoming and helpful, adding to the sense of community. Come for the hunt, stay for the atmosphere; you never know what you’ll uncover on the next visit.

Well, so much for this guy. He seems to produce quality work, but we’ll never know. After a friendly phone chat, we scheduled an appointment for bathroom remodeling ideas: Monday, or Tuesday if Monday’s job ran long. Both days came and went with no visit and, worse, no call or text. A simple two-minute message to reschedule would have shown basic professionalism and respect for our time. Reliability matters as much as craftsmanship, and this experience undermined trust from the start. If he flakes on the initial appointment, what happens mid-project? Sadly, we’ll be looking elsewhere for a dependable pro.

An excellent value!

Dining at Mon Ami Gabbi on a bustling Sunday night proved to be a delightful surprise. Even with a full house, a last-minute reservation secured an indoor table within five minutes—much appreciated on a chilly evening—and the service remained attentive throughout. I visited with my mother, and we opted to share the beef Wellington special, a choice I don’t typically make but one I’m thrilled we did. The pastry-encased beef was tender and deeply flavorful, paired with a silky sauce and garlicky sautéed spinach. For two women, the portion was ideal; the richness makes a solo serving a bit much, but shared, it was melt-in-your-mouth perfect.

We began with a butter lettuce salad dotted with creamy goat cheese, crisp apples, and roasted beets, a fresh, balanced start. For sides, the butternut squash offered comforting sweetness while the green beans added a bright, snappy counterpoint. At our waiter’s suggestion, we finished with the bananas foster crepe, a warmly spiced, caramel-kissed dessert that capped the meal beautifully. Across courses, the kitchen demonstrated consistency and care.

A month prior, my husband treated me to the Eiffel Tower Restaurant at the Paris Hotel, and while the view there is undeniably spectacular, I preferred my dinner at Mon Ami Gabbi. It’s less formal and a bit noisier, but the overall experience—and especially the price-to-quality ratio—makes it the better pick. For excellent food, friendly service, and genuine value, Mon Ami Gabbi delivers. I would happily return and recommend it to friends soon.

Arthur’s has become the reliable highlight on our office “lunch train,” edging out nearby options when the craving is for a hot, honest sandwich. The signature triumph here is the Reuben, done the right way: crisply griddled, buttery rye that cracks as you bite, a bright tang of sauerkraut, generous layers of corned beef, and a cooling dollop of thousand island to tie it all together. Prefer poultry? The turkey version keeps the same balance and still satisfies. Beyond sandwiches, insiders swear by Arthur’s chicken gumbo. Multiple gumbo devotees in our building rank it the best within walking distance of the Atrium, and their mantra has become office lore: if it’s the soup of the day, your lunch plans are set. Get there early; by 1:30 it’s often gone, testament to its popularity. Not everything is a standout—skip the Caesar salad, which lacks punch and texture—but for fries that hit the spot and sandwiches that deliver warmth and comfort, Arthur’s is the jam. Friendly, fast, and consistently tasty, it’s an easy choice for a quick midday refuel that keeps us coming back week after week.

Previous reviewers couldn’t be more correct: Tokyo Stop is serious bang for your buck. The food comes out fast, the portions are generous, and the staff serve it up with a genuine smile. On my last visit, I simply said, “Give me whatever’s good,” and the owner-chef nodded, disappeared, and returned minutes later with a still-warm, wonderfully aromatic styrofoam box. Inside was a bed of steamed rice piled with spiced vegetables—cabbage, carrots, broccoli—and hefty chunks of crisp, white, breaded chicken katsu. On the side: plump gyoza with dipping sauce and a humongous mound of soybeans. No skimping here; it felt like a full, balanced meal that could easily stretch to two. Most impressive of all, the bill was around seven dollars. Delicious, fast, friendly, and priced like a steal, Tokyo Stop nails the quick-comfort niche. If you want big flavor, healthy portions, and a happy experience without denting your wallet, this spot is an easy recommendation. All grins from me today.

On every Las Vegas trip, I end up at this spot at least three times—and the 24-hour schedule makes it a savior for 3–5 a.m. munchies. The toasted, soft bread is craveable, and the sandwiches are impressively consistent. The Earl’s Club is my go-to, but honestly, I haven’t had a bad bite here. Service is quick, prices fair, and it’s ideal for a fast, satisfying meal at any hour. Pro tip: some pools won’t allow outside food, so finish your sandwich before heading in to avoid wasting leftovers and money.

Total disappointment, especially from The Mirage, which I value.

As a frequent Mirage guest and a fan of CPK in New York, I stopped in for a late-night takeout snack and hit a wall of indifference. The line was long, which I can forgive at that hour. What I can’t excuse is the service. The man with white sideburns who took my order was curt from the start—darting in and out, avoiding eye contact, and never cracking a smile. He pulled me aside to order, then walked off mid-sentence as I asked whether I could sit while waiting, leaving me stranded under a hundred stares. Not the Vegas hospitality The Mirage is known for. When my food was ready, he dropped the check and change without a thank-you and handed over a box. No bag. No basics. Dude, where’s my bag? For a brand I’ve trusted and a resort I respect, this was a letdown. Do better, Mirage CPK.

So far, I've been to this restaurant on three occasions: a brunch, a dinner and drinks with girlfriends.

Holder has become a reliable go-to for me, especially for daytime and dinner plans. My first visit was a brunch for a mini class reunion, and the team couldn’t have been kinder. They handled late arrivals and no-shows with patience, kept our table relaxed, and never rushed us. The standout sips and bites set the tone: a rich, clearly not-from-powder hot chocolate; thick, perfectly crispy bacon; eggs that stayed warm and well-cooked; and generous refills of coffee and tea. It all added up to a satisfying meal at a very reasonable price point.

Dinner confirmed the kitchen’s finesse and the front-of-house’s flexibility. We were a party of six with a reservation, including a lactose-intolerant diner, and staff took the time to consult the kitchen and navigate modifications without a fuss. My lobster ravioli with truffle and butter oil was beautifully executed—silky, aromatic, and indulgent—though the portion leaned small, as is often the case with richer pastas. I was still peckish and happily nibbled on some excellent fries from a friend’s plate. Dessert was a triumph: classic profiteroles with ice cream that hit all the right notes. I can’t speak to the final bill that night, but the experience felt polished.

For Valentine’s Day drinks with girlfriends, the vibe was lively if a bit chaotic on the reservation front. We were told they weren’t taking bookings, only to be asked about a reservation on arrival. Still, we snagged a bar table with a fun view of date-night energy. The drink list is broad and compelling, though pricing is firmly on the high side. Service was brisk; appetizers, less inspiring. Two drinks and a shared entrée topped $20 for me.

Bottom line: Holder shines for brunch and dinner—great service, well-executed classics, and a strong wine list. For drinks alone, consider your budget or look elsewhere.

I stayed at the hotel and tried both breakfast and lunch. Breakfast was a mixed bag: my french toast consisted of two battered slices—real maple syrup was a welcome touch—but the portion was small and the dish unremarkable. My partner’s egg white omelet fared better, accompanied by toast and potatoes, all well prepared. Lunch, unfortunately, was disappointing. The French onion soup was so salty it turned bitter, and the Caesar salad with a chicken breast tasted dominated by artificial lemon, with the chicken dried out and flavorless. The saving grace was the hot bread with fresh butter. Throughout, the atmosphere was pleasant and the service attentive, but based on the meals, dining here is worth skipping.

title: This should be called the porn hotel. Several of us were staying here for business. We came to the conclusion over lunch that this is less than desirable for a business traveller hotel, unless you are a porn producer.

We visited for a work trip and were struck by the hotel’s pervasive darkness: dim bulbs everywhere, shadowy corridors, and moody rooms. The studio-style layout centers the bed in the middle, which might suit those seeking a theatrical, 360-degree feel, but it’s impractical for business travelers who need clear zoning and easy navigation. Finding the bathroom in low light is a hassle, and the closet is tucked away so discreetly it feels like an afterthought. Music pumps through common spaces at high volume, with a pulsing, club-like soundtrack that makes conversation and calls difficult. Combined, these choices create a distinctly adult-film vibe rather than a professional environment.

If the aim is to court business guests, brighter lighting, quieter public areas, and more functional room plans would help tremendously. Alternatively, if the brand is intent on that retro, provocative theme, they could lean all the way in with playful touches—think 1970s-style mustaches on the bell staff and open-collar shirts with a relaxed, vintage flourish. As it stands, the hotel’s ambience is bold but misaligned with the needs of corporate travelers, who typically value clarity, comfort, and calm over theatrics. Consider practicality over mood lighting.

Probably one of the fewest Japanese restaurants that are decent in AZ.
This spot isn’t phenomenal, but it’s about as good as it gets. Prices are fair, and the sushi holds up. The dining room gets tight and crowded when busy, so don’t expect a really relaxing dinner—better for catching up with friends.

Uhhhh, not a mile long... not even close.

This mall isn’t the mile-long behemoth some hype suggests, but its funky U-shaped layout can be surprisingly disorienting. It took a map, three gals, and 15 minutes just to track down H&M. Beyond the quirky navigation, it’s your standard, dependable mall—nothing groundbreaking, yet perfectly fine for killing time after dinner with a leisurely stroll. Stores are familiar, selection adequate, and yes, I still managed to buy something. If you’re nearby and need an easy indoor wander, it does the trick.

Locals have a cheeky nickname for this Denny’s, but the experience is standard-issue. There’s little reason to seek it out unless you’re already in Downtown Phoenix—say, after an event—when its proximity and late hours make it convenient. It’s the classic Denny’s draw: open late, reliably cheap, good for friends on tight budgets. Beyond that, there’s nothing special to warrant a detour. If you’ve got a neighborhood Denny’s, go there; otherwise, consider other options.

We’re longtime PF Chang’s fans, but this Strip location disappointed. Our usual hot and sour soup arrived scant on broth and overloaded with vegetables, we felt like we were chewing our soup. When we asked for a fix, the server said it couldn’t be changed because it’s prepared in large batches and “all the same.” The other two dishes were acceptable, but the overall experience fell short, especially for such a prominent venue.

Mmmmm delicious pizza at a great price.

Stopped in while in town and was impressed from start to finish. Ordering is simple: choose your pie, pay, and swing back in 10–15 minutes for hot, bubbly goodness. I grabbed a medium 14-inch split half pepperoni, half mushroom for $9.10 ($7.50 plus $1.60 for toppings), and it was ready right after a quick walk. We snagged a seat outside—perfect spot to watch the world go by—and dug in. Ingredients were notably fresh, the cheese creamy and flavorful, and the crust nicely crisp without being too hard. They keep the menu focused on what they do best: pies, hoagies, and calzones. Excellent value, friendly efficiency, and consistently tasty slices. I’ll definitely be back for another.

Fresh yet forgettable sums up my recent visit to Baja Fresh. I ordered the mango chipotle chicken salad without the shell; it was fine, but the chicken portion felt tiny—maybe 2.5 ounces. The menu is surprisingly difficult to navigate if you’re watching calories: unless you choose a shell-less salad or a single taco, most items are 700+ calories. A veggie burrito clocks in at around 800. It’s been a long time since I last went, and this visit reminded me why. Decent ingredients, underwhelming value. I won’t be returning. Pricing and portions disappoint.

French food and I have a longstanding love affair. It’s my perfect way to dine: meat aplenty, but in demure, carefully considered portions—think a petite steak mignon, a silken duck leg confit, or a teasing sliver of foie gras. So when Blythe R of LunchQuest floated The Grain Store for lunch, I didn’t hesitate. The set lunch is a steal at £12.50 for two courses, especially when A La Carte mains hover around £23. On value alone, this kitchen signals confidence and generosity.

My salmon starter arrived like a whisper: small, pristine, and utterly divine—less a course than a promise. It did exactly what a starter should: sharpen anticipation without dulling hunger. The risotto that followed was its glorious counterpoint, a bowl as generous as it was aromatic. As the steam rose, so did the white wine perfume, paving the way for plump wild mushrooms to do their woodland dance. Cheese threaded through the rice invisibly, present on the palate but never cloying or gluey. Blythe, who knows a good risotto when one lands, declared it excellent; I could barely finish it, yet finish it I did.

Daytime ambiance is relaxed, with service that’s friendly, polite, and happily unobtrusive. The soundtrack leaned oddly toward Paolo Nutini—a quirk rather than a flaw—but the room itself feels date-ready, especially after dark. I’m already plotting a return by night to explore the full menu; I just need the right excuse. The Grain Store has that rare balance of value, craft, and restraint that keeps you thinking about the next visit even as you put down your fork. It all feels distinctly, delightfully French. The Grain Store, j’adore. Mais oui.

Title: I really only come here for work reasons. There was a conference being held here so I was forced to go, because I generally stay away from this hotel.

I’ll give credit where it’s due: the rooms I’ve seen are gorgeous—sleek, stylish, and the kind of “divine” that inspires Instagram envy. But luxury without hospitality is just a stage set, and that’s where this property loses me every time. I can’t enjoy sleeping under the same roof where some of the most consistent rudeness I’ve encountered in Vegas seems to happen.

Take a simple lost-and-found moment. I misplaced my keys; they were turned in—great. Yet the security manager proceeded to quiz me three separate times to describe them, each round more condescending than the last. Keys are keys; there’s only so much nuance to offer. Instead of feeling relieved, I felt talked down to, as if being a stressed guest needing help made me an inconvenience. The tone read less “we’ve got you” and more “prove you belong here.”

Then there was the bar encounter, which sealed it.
