Round two of drinks introduced our only real hiccup. Our server enthusiastically pushed a particular margarita, overriding my husband’s wish for a custom pour with his favorite tequila. When my husband asked for it on the rocks, it arrived up; the replacement was correct but just okay. The pushiness, while well-intentioned, detracted from the otherwise seamless service. Let customers order what they want—especially when they know their preferences.

Any lingering annoyance vanished with the entrée. We shared the seared scallops, and they were impeccable: deeply caramelized on the outside, buttery within, and seasoned to a tee. The accompanying grits were everything grits should be—creamy, rich, and comforting—elevated without losing their soul.

Dessert sealed the deal. The toasted coconut cake was transcendent: impossibly moist, layered with true coconut flavor, and the kind of slice that lingers in your memory long after the trip ends.

The ambiance leans a bit casual for the price point, but it’s pleasant and relaxed. Service was attentive overall, marred only by the drink detour. Still, Mesa Grill delivered the best food we had in Vegas, hands down. We left thrilled, full, and already plotting a return. Get the tiger prawn tamale, don’t skip the scallops, and save room for that coconut cake.
Love this place! Varied menu, tasty food, and quick, friendly service. I eat here at least once a month—always reliable and welcoming.

St. Patrick’s Day: Eight people at the bar and four bartenders, yet I waited 10 minutes for service. Put down phones, focus on guests, earn the tip. Efficiency and attentiveness matter on nights like this.

When the first location opened on Indian School, the food was impressive, largely thanks to the owner in the kitchen. Since expanding to multiple spots, quality has slipped. My biscuits and gravy were barely edible—so salty it was shocking. The menu leans heavily toward sugary breakfast items, which isn’t my preference. I’ve heard the chocolate chip pancakes are a standout, but overall the shift from chef-driven roots to a broader operation has dulled the experience.

Das Ettlinger Tor Karlsruhe hat sich zum pulsierenden Herz der Fächerstadt entwickelt und bietet Shopping mit echtem Weltstadtflair. Der architektonisch beeindruckende Boulevard lebt von Licht, Transparenz und eleganten Linien. Auf drei Ebenen eröffnen lichtdurchflutete, glasüberdachte Galerien rund 37.000 Quadratmeter Verkaufsfläche. Hier warten 130 Fachgeschäfte mit einer überwältigenden Vielfalt: Mode, Trends und Accessoires, Kosmetik, Beauty und Wellness, Literatur und Unterhaltungselektronik, bekannte Marken und gefragte Labels. Ergänzt wird das Angebot von einladenden Restaurants, Cafés und Bars, die zum Verweilen einladen.

Dank der zentralen Lage, direkter Anbindung über die Kriegstraße/B10 und 900 Parkplätzen ist das Center aus allen Richtungen komfortabel erreichbar. Service und Sauberkeit sind vorbildlich. Fazit: Ein „5‑Sterne“‑Kauftempel, der Karlsruhe ein gehobenes Einkaufsniveau und ein urbanes Erlebnis beschert.

I Only Rated It One Star Because I Had To—Otherwise, Zero

There’s one bright spot here: the owner. When a battery I’d purchased a week earlier failed, he swapped it out immediately—no hassle, no pushback. That kind of accountability matters.

Unfortunately, nearly every other aspect of my experience fell flat. Interactions with several staff members were consistently curt and unhelpful. Asking basic questions or requesting to sample more than one e-juice flavor seemed to be treated as an inconvenience rather than a normal part of choosing a product. For a shop built around taste-driven purchases, that tone sets the wrong expectation.

Worse, the house juices are wildly inconsistent. The flavor I sampled in-store did not resemble what I brought home—so different that it felt like a bait-and-switch, even if unintentional. This wasn’t an isolated incident for me, and a number of friends who vape report the same thing: a flavor can be enjoyable one week and markedly different the next. That level of variability undermines trust and makes repeat purchases feel like a gamble.

With tighter quality control on mixing and more attentive customer service—plus a clear policy for addressing mismatched flavors—this shop could be solid. As it stands, apart from the owner’s professionalism, I can’t recommend it. A disappointing, one-star experience.

Just like Morris' review....

The wonderful smell of barbecue greeted us at Tennessee Grill, raising hopes on a quick stop between Sedona and the Phoenix airport. Unfortunately, the experience didn’t match the aroma. Service was surprisingly slow despite a not-too-crowded dining room—maybe a big takeout order caused the delay. My tuna sandwich was just fair, and they were out of potato chips. My buddy’s chicken wrap was equally forgettable, nothing special. It’s a shame, because the owner and servers were genuinely friendly, which made leaving a critical note harder. For us, it was a first visit and likely the last.

I recently visited this nail salon with my mom and had mixed experiences. The gentleman who did my manicure and pedicure delivered fantastic French tips on both fingers and toes. He air-brushed my hands, resulting in clean, neat lines, and despite some difficulty understanding him, we communicated enough to achieve exactly what I wanted. Unfortunately, my mom’s simple solid color application fell short. There were small specks and smudges of polish left on the skin around her nails, which looked unprofessional, and she was placed under a UV lamp to dry—with the lamp switched off. The salon itself appeared fairly clean. Overall, skilled artistry for designs, but inconsistent basic polishing and attention to detail overall.

This was my first time going to a Ramen house, but I was lucky enough to have a Japanese friend with me.

Stepping into this ramen house as a first-timer felt easy, thanks to an English-friendly menu and helpful staff. The menu highlights three regional miso broths: Kome Miso from Hokkaido offers a full-bodied, hearty base; Shiro Miso from Kyoto leans fruity and natural; Mame Miso from Nagoya ends with a pleasing bitterness. Choose a pre-set bowl and then customize with as many toppings as you like.

I ordered the Kome Miso #4 Spicy Ramen. The pork was tender and flavorful, and the bowl felt balanced, though the heat was gentler than expected. Next time, I’d pick the extra-spicy add-on to turn up the kick. I also tried the fried chicken and fried shrimp, and both were standouts—crisp, juicy, and great for dipping into the broth. If you add just one topping, make it the fried chicken; it pairs beautifully with almost any bowl.

Don’t hesitate to visit solo: the staff speaks English, the menu is straightforward, and the flavors are worth exploring. Use these tips, trust your palate, and enjoy a satisfying ramen experience.

Went to Texaz on a whim wanting some steak and we were thoroughly disappointed.

Went to Texaz on a whim craving steak and left disappointed. My T-bone arrived small, grey, and unseared, with a filet portion barely the size of a JFK half dollar. My friend opted for the grilled shrimp instead of fried; one was raw and the rest were tiny—hardly worth the $16 price tag. On the plus side, the staff was friendly, and the potato wedges and biscuits were solid. Unfortunately, the kitchen missed the mark. Two stars, and I can’t recommend this spot.

They started out great, attentive, then somewhere along the way service spiraled down. Was steered in wrong direction and am now facing a high dollar repair. Towards the end keeping an appointment was becoming difficult, keeping up on service didn't even seem like a concern. Many opinions vary on pool maintenance so I took their opinion only to realize maybe their is a difference between adding chemicals and skimming a pool, and exactly knowing how to care for a pool and extending its lifespan.

They began strong—attentive, responsive, and seemingly knowledgeable. Over time, appointments slipped, follow-through lagged, and service quality spiraled. Worse, I was steered in the wrong direction, and now face a high-dollar repair that might have been avoided with proper guidance. I learned there’s a big difference between tossing in chemicals and truly understanding pool care that extends equipment lifespan. Opinions abound in pool maintenance, but expertise matters. If consistency and reliable advice are priorities for you, proceed cautiously and demand clear explanations and accountability.

After a few years away from Star Nails due to bad service, I gave them another chance. I used to get consistently great pedicures, but one rushed, 30-minute session made me stop going. This time, the pedicure itself was fine, yet the polish application was sloppy; one nail was so poorly done I had to completely redo it at home. For $35, I expect clean, careful polish and a finished look that lasts. I shouldn’t have to fix mistakes after leaving a salon. I’m not convinced they prioritize quality anymore, which is disappointing. With so many nail salons nearby, I may choose elsewhere.

Rooftop Gem with Great Drinks and Comfort Eats

I've been here several times, and the beer and wine are excellent. The rooftop seating is a highlight. I've tried the wings, tater tots, sausage platter, and hummus; each was fantastic. Pricing is reasonable, and happy hour deals are solid. Though they've only been open a month and are still ironing out a few kinks, the staff’s enthusiasm shines. I recommend stopping by once; I can’t wait to explore more of the menu.

Six-sample craft beer flights are the star here, making exploration both fun and low-risk. Instead of committing to a full pint that might miss your palate, you can sample three unfamiliar styles and then circle back to three trusted favorites to land the session on a high note. The menu mirrors that spirit of variety. Wings arrive with sauce on the side—an interesting twist that invites customization. A salad proved fresh and tasty, though a bit light for the price, especially when it matches the wings. The standout bite was the Sweet Potato Tacos, more akin to empanadas, crisp and comforting with a bright pesto dipping sauce.

As a longtime Southwestern eater, I wished for a bottle of house hot sauce or a signature table spice to add heat. The room runs loud at the moment, but the open floor plan and generous windows promise a lively, all-season spot once the acoustics are dialed in. Set squarely in the Evans Churchill district, it’s perfectly placed for a casual pint before or after a neighborhood pub crawl. For curious drinkers and grazers, this is a welcome addition. Expect to linger, compare notes, and discover a new go-to without buyer’s remorse here.

Been going to Juan's for over 10 years. It is family owned, they are great people but don't expect them to be gregarious, they seem somewhat shy.

This family-owned spot has been my go-to for a decade, serving comforting Mexican fare with a humble charm. The salsa is fresh, bright, and house-made—not the canned stuff some claim—though the chips can be hit-or-miss, occasionally not hot or crisp. Standouts include the chimichanga and carne asada tacos, generous, flavorful, and paired with simple yet satisfying beans and rice. The value is outstanding: it’s hard to find this quality and quantity for under eight dollars anywhere else. Cleanliness is impeccable, with consistently top marks from county health inspections. Expect lunchtime and Friday-night crowds, a clear sign of its popularity, and you’ll often spot local police eating here, too—a dependable indicator of a beloved neighborhood restaurant.

This is a good shop to visit that is not too far out from the city centre and well worth looking into if you are passing. The fish on offer here offers both good quality and reasonable pricing, which is as much as you can really ask for.

Conveniently located just beyond the city centre, this fishmonger delivers on freshness and value. The counters are tidy, the turnover seems brisk, and the staples—salmon, cod, haddock, and the like—look inviting and are priced sensibly. My main quibble is with the way prices are displayed solely in pounds. While it’s common in the trade, many shoppers think in kilos, and having to convert on the fly can be awkward. A dual display would be a small effort for the shop and a big help for customers, sparing us the mental arithmetic and making comparisons clearer. Even so, you do feel you’re getting a fair amount for your money, broadly in line with other reputable fishmongers.

Staff are welcoming and easy to chat with as they weigh your order and sort your change. The brief banter adds a pleasant human touch to the visit. I’ll admit I sometimes struggle with certain accents, so my contribution can trend toward nods and smiles, but the warmth comes through regardless.

The selection leans conservative—solid classics rather than adventurous variety. Most will be satisfied, but if you enjoy exploring lesser-seen species or specialty cuts, you may find the range a bit limited. That said, for dependable basics, fair pricing, and friendly service, this is a nice fishmonger to have nearby and a worthwhile stop when you’re passing through.

Some artisans seem blessed with a magic touch; Tracy’s happens to be dipped in chocolate. As warm and welcoming as her confections, she turns simple ingredients into fresh, melt-in-your-mouth bliss. I’ve chased her sweets across the Valley—from Citizen Public House and Arcadia Farms Market Place to Smeeks and the Downtown Phoenix Public Market—and they’re consistently excellent. Beyond those spots, she crafts made-to-order treats from her public kitchen, which means personalized boxes of joy are just an email away. Her silky caramels and snappy chocolates shine, and the desserts are downright irresistible. Feeling bold? Try the bacon pecan brittle: a cheeky mash-up of salty, smoky, and sweet that somehow lands perfectly. With fair prices and quality that never wavers, Tracy’s shop is my go-to for gifts and gatherings. I’m already earmarking a holiday haul—and maybe a little stash just for me.

I’ve been a loyal customer here for years, but today’s eyebrow wax was a nightmare. A new technician handled my brows, and I didn’t catch her name. My eyebrows came out completely uneven—one is super thin—and I’m genuinely embarrassed. Worse, she ripped skin below my brow; it bled, which has never happened to me here before. This was a shocking decline in quality and safety. I left upset and disappointed, and I can’t recommend getting waxed here anymore. I won’t be returning after this experience.

Good but not that great.

We opted for the tasting menu in the so-called Swan Court, paying an extra $10 for swans peering through the window—an upsell that felt silly in the dark. A request to split a wine pairing was curtly dismissed, a surprising hard no given many restaurants accommodate it.

The meal opened with a trio of amuses: a bacon-wrapped scallop that was fine, the others forgettable. Ironically, the standout of the night was the house-cured bacon served alongside the beef—astonishingly crisp without greasiness, with our server detailing their meticulous process of curing and slow-cooking between absorbent sheets. Unfortunately, the “duo of beef” was uneven: a flat-iron cut arrived dry and overdone, dulling what should have been a highlight.

Dessert brought a playful trio of sorbets with a guessing game; two were easy enough, while a pomegranate-cherry stumped us—pleasant, if hardly memorable. We left very full yet without the sense of wonder a great tasting menu should deliver. For context, L’Atelier de Joel Robuchon—pricier, yes—has left us dazzled on past visits; this experience simply didn’t approach that level.

Service oscillated between informative (on the bacon) and dismissive (on the pairing), lacking the warmth and polish we expect at this price point. My brother previously raved about the service here, but we didn’t see it. Between the awkward upsell, uneven execution, and uninspired hospitality, I wouldn’t return and would point friends toward stronger options in town. There were good moments, but not enough to justify the hype—or the check.

On the hunt for something new, inspired by a binge of travel shows, I set out to find blood sausage and pirozhki. The pirozhki mission fizzled—too many places closed—but I remembered a small shop up the street and took a chance. A quick call brought a rare flash of luck: they answered, and yes, they had blutwurst.

A short drive later, I stepped into a tiny, cool space with one or two customers and a lively hum of German floating through the room. It was charming and a bit disorienting—like stumbling into a corner of Berlin—but the cultural immersion added character. One gripe: three staffers were in the back smoking and chatting, while one person up front was helping another customer. I waited a good 10–15 minutes before someone emerged to assist. Also, bring cash or plan to spend at least $10; they won’t run a card for less.

Service, once it started, was warm and efficient. The woman who helped me quickly packed exactly what I wanted: blutwurst and kasseler, a smoked pork chop. I’d had kasseler before and figured it would be a reliable lunch if the blood sausage turned out to be an acquired taste.

Back home, I grilled both to a satisfying, toasty finish. The pork chop was solid—smoky and familiar, more comfort than revelation. The blutwurst, however, was a revelation. Deep and dark, it delivered a rich, layered flavor with an earthy backbone and a pronounced maltiness from barley that gave it structure and intrigue. There’s a subtle iron-tinged complexity, rounded and savory rather than metallic, with a pleasing snap to the casing and a lush, almost pâté-like interior. As Anthony Bourdain might have said, it’s a standout among tube-shaped foods—elevated, rustic, and utterly craveable.

Despite the wait and the card minimum, this shop proved worth the detour. If you’re adventurous or simply curious about German specialties, bring a little patience and some cash. You’ll be rewarded with honest, traditional flavors and a sense of place that’s hard to find elsewhere. I’ll be back—for more blutwurst, and maybe another run at pirozhki.

We ordered our "getting ready" food for our wedding day from Jason's Deli because of all the rave reviews from The Knot Las Vegas message board. Well, those reviews were all correct. Jason's Deli is really awesome.

For couples assembling a calm, well-fed start to their wedding morning, Jason’s Deli stands out. It was easy to place platters for 12. A quick phone call a couple days before secured the order and payment, and day-of service exceeded expectations.

Despite a shooting that shut down the Las Vegas Strip and snarled traffic across the freeways, our delivery driver was exceptional. He called every 15 minutes with location updates, turning what could have been a stressful delay into a reassuring countdown. When he arrived, he didn’t just drop at the door—he brought the trays straight to our suite with a friendly smile.

The food itself impressed: breakfast sandwiches arrived warm, the fruit was crisp and fresh, and even the coffee stayed hot in its jug. Everything tasted great, fueling our wedding party during hair, makeup, and final touches—and keeping this bride far from bridezilla territory.

Jason’s Deli delivered reliability, hospitality, and value when it mattered most. From ordering to delivery, the experience was smooth, thoughtful, and delicious. We’ll wholeheartedly recommend them to every bride planning a Las Vegas wedding. Viva Jason’s Deli indeed!

Early Dinner at Toby Keith’s

My husband and I stopped in for an early Saturday dinner and were pleasantly surprised. Despite seeing mixed reviews, our experience was smooth from start to finish. Our waitress was genuinely attentive; drinks were refilled without asking, and check-ins felt timely, not intrusive. The food was decent, classic pub fare prepared well, with satisfying portions. The atmosphere matched the meal: casual, comfortable, and upbeat without being loud. We’re curious to return in the evening for live music, which could elevate the vibe even more.

They’re closed on Mondays, so plan accordingly; our first attempt to dine here was thwarted. On a weekend dinner for two, service was welcoming and efficient, with attentive pacing and friendly staff.

The Baked Scallop Roll doesn’t win on looks—picture a creamy slop atop a California roll—but it absolutely delivers on flavor. While scallop is scarce and mushrooms dominate, the blend of mayo, scallop, mushrooms, and soy sauce creates a rich, savory bite I’d order again. At $12.95, it feels pricey for the amount of scallop, yet it remains a standout I’d still recommend.

The Salmon Salad Roll is a lighter counterpoint: no rice, just finely cut cucumber wrapping generous chunks of salmon. It’s delicately assembled and impressive, though I personally prefer the indulgent taste of the baked scallop roll.

Not everything hits. The Unagi-don arrived dry—the eel lacked its usual luscious glaze, and the rice didn’t help—making it a dish I wouldn’t order again.

The Chicken Udon Soup fares better. The broth is flavorful and comforting, with a healthy mix of onions, mushrooms, and broccoli. The chicken was a bit tough, but the overall bowl satisfied.

In sum, friendly service and memorable rolls make this spot worth a visit—just skip Monday and the unagi-don. Expect clean presentation, fair portions, and a menu with thoughtful variety. We’ll be back.

Visited this salon for the first time for both a pedicure and manicure, and unfortunately the experience was disappointing. The technician did a poor job; the next day my toenail polish peeled because it hadn’t dried properly. They did fix it, but four days later the gel and polish on my fingernail lifted, requiring another visit. When I returned, the technician was curt, and while attempting to repair the manicure, she nicked my skin. I paid $56 for both services, which felt like a waste given the quality and attitude. I won’t be back and can’t recommend this place based on my experience.

Ordering through the restaurant’s site via Eat24 was seamless, and delivery was impressively fast—definitely a strong start. Our House Lo Mein was decent, and the kitchen honored our request to omit celery and mushrooms, though they also skipped the baby corn, which was disappointing. The Wonton soup was the clear miss: rubbery, off-tasting dumplings that we couldn’t finish. Fried shrimp arrived soggy, suggesting they’d sat too long; steamed dumplings were doughy but passable. Ironically, the fortune cookies ended up being the highlight of a $30 order. If you can drive, consider a higher-rated spot; if you’re sticking with delivery, choose carefully. From this experience, rice and noodle dishes seem like the safest bets, while appetizers and soup may be hit-or-miss. Service was polite, but quality varied across the menu.

Come for the ambiance, NOT the food!

Capo’s nails the mobster vibe: a speakeasy-style entrance, dim lighting, and a vintage soundtrack that makes your first visit feel like stepping into a noir film. As an experience, it’s undeniably fun and perfect for a Vegas story. Unfortunately, the culinary side doesn’t live up to the show. The food is just okay—think bland pastas, overcooked entrées, and forgettable appetizers—and the prices seem geared more toward sustaining the theme than reflecting quality on the plate. Service was mixed on our last visit: our server was genuinely kind and attentive, but the bar staff was brusque and borderline rude, souring the mood with slow pours and snarky attitudes. If you’re hungry and hoping for a standout meal to savor, this isn’t the spot. If you’re hunting for atmosphere and a memorable tale, Capo’s will deliver—though what you might remember most is how mediocre the food was and how much you paid for it. After a couple visits, I’m not sure I’ll be back; I’ve had my fill of Vegas stories.

Hidden at the back of Stonecrest, in a storefront facing Regal Cinemas, Kabob Grill delivers the kind of quality Mediterranean fare that keeps cravings alive. On a recent Tuesday, my tahini-and-falafel fix brought Casey and me back, and—as usual—we left fat and happy.

The room is classy without pretense: tasteful décor, lighting, and a casual, relaxing vibe. Though the dining area is smaller than most, comfort isn’t compromised; conversation flows easily, there’s never a din, and I almost always spot families alongside couples enjoying a laid‑back meal.

Menu highlights abound. The grilled kafta kabobs—spiced ground beef, smoky and tender—are standouts, as is the succulent grilled lamb kabob. My latest favorite is the lamb kabob pita: a warm, overstuffed wrap packed with hommos, hearty lamb chunks, and tangy pickled vegetables. For sides, don’t miss the creamy baba ghannouj, crisp falafel, and the addictive potato harra.

Service is consistently excellent. The team here is unfailingly friendly and attentive without hovering, adding to the restaurant’s easy charm. For those 18 and older, there’s hookah available on the patio—a mellow finish to a satisfying meal.

In Ballantyne/South Charlotte, Kabob Grill is a must‑try.

Thanks to Groupon I Didn’t Have to Pay Full Price for This Mess!

I went to this salon hoping for a simple haircut and deep conditioning, and left wishing I’d chosen anywhere else—and anyone but Josh. The visit started promising: the receptionist was welcoming, offered me a drink, the music was upbeat, the space looked clean and well cared for, and I even appreciated the posted reminder asking people not to bring children unless they’re there for services.

Once I sat in Josh’s chair, the experience went downhill fast. His conversation was focused almost entirely on chatting with coworkers, not on me or my hair, and the overall tone felt unprofessional. Communication was minimal, yet the appointment dragged to nearly two hours for what should have been routine services.

I have naturally curly hair. Josh cut it while curly, then decided to straighten it—against my stated preference—because he said he needed to “make sure it was even.” In my many years of haircuts, no one has ever had to chop curly, then straighten, then cut again. When I questioned the approach, his response was a dismissive “ha ha, I know what I’m doing, I do this shit all day,” which did nothing to inspire confidence. Worse, he burned my scalp twice with the straightener, turning an already frustrating session into a painful one.

Thanks to Groupon, I didn’t pay full price for this mess, but a discount doesn’t excuse poor service and careless technique. I won’t be returning to Josh, and this experience makes me hesitant about the salon overall. That said, the environment and front-desk hospitality were solid, and other stylists here seem to have strong reviews. If you go, book with one of the well-reviewed women and steer clear of Josh. Choose wisely and protect your curls.

As an educated buyer, I appreciate the occasional gems at Lee’s. The selection can be impressive, with bottles that carry real age you won’t find at Total Wine, which focuses almost exclusively on recent releases. However, Lee’s size seems to compromise quality control. I’ve seen too many white wines and rosés lingering well past their prime—sometimes browned—still on the shelf, and returns can be inconsistent. Staff knowledge is hit-or-miss; less-informed shoppers risk being guided toward whatever inventory needs to move rather than what suits their palate. If you know your producers, vintages, and storage caveats, you can score excellent deals. If you don’t, shop carefully. Lee’s rewards the informed and can frustrate the casual buyer. Proceed with eyes open.

BEST. THAI. FOOD. IN. VEGAS. I’ve tried countless spots and remain a tough Thai critic, but this place wins. I crave the fried spinach salad, the curries are consistently great, and the drunken noodles are my favorite. If only it were closer—please open more locations!

The Bellagio impresses with room sizes that feel larger than remembered—genuinely spacious and comfortable. Despite the property’s age, the hotel has consistently invested in smart renovations, preserving its signature elegance while updating essentials. That commitment shows: the public spaces and guest rooms look fresh, refined, and far from a 15-year-old footprint. Perhaps most telling, the Bellagio continues to attract its longtime clientele, a testament to reliable service, quality finishes, and an enduring, upscale Vegas experience.

This has got to be the worst Wendy's I've ever been to.

Disappointing from start to finish. The value menu felt anything but: while many fast-food spots keep items in the $1–$2 range, this location’s lowest price was $1.50 and most hovered around $2.50, undermining the idea of “value.” Despite having one person ahead of me, the service dragged on painfully, suggesting staffing problems. When a quick meal costs more and takes longer than it should, there’s little incentive to return. I’ll look elsewhere.

The good: Our waiter provided excellent service and the food was very tasty. The lobster won tons were amazing.

There’s a tale of two venues here: the dining room that delivers and the door that derails. At the table, our server was exceptional—attentive, personable, and on top of every detail. Courses arrived at a good pace, drinks were spot-on, and the kitchen showed real finesse. The standout was the lobster won tons: delicate, richly flavored, and perfectly balanced, the kind of dish you remember and want to return for. If the review were about food and service alone, this would be a strong recommendation.

Unfortunately, the experience was bookended by a front-of-house gauntlet that took the shine off the night. Despite having a dinner reservation, we explained it to four different bouncers before being allowed to bypass the line, only to be met by a hostess who was brusque and inflexible about seating the party until every guest was present—even with one person en route from a delayed flight. We agreed to sit without her, yet our table wasn’t ready, and we waited at the bar for about 30 minutes with a pager. Meanwhile, a bouncer repeatedly flashed a flashlight at us, ordering “you can’t stand there,” which felt needless and unwelcoming.

After an expensive meal—over a hundred dollars per person on dinner and wine—we expected smoother access to the nightclub. Instead, we were told we needed to pay a cover and join the long corridor queue like anyone else, unless we had a “line pass” from our waiter. We hadn’t been advised of this, and the policy felt confusing and punitive to diners.

If you plan to transition to the club, proactively ask your server for a line pass before you finish dinner. Otherwise, consider taking your night elsewhere. Mix offered excellent food, stellar service, and thoughtful hospitality—our waiter there even escorted us into the lounge. Between the two, the kitchen here impresses, but the door policies may leave you wishing you’d gone with the smoother option.

This is such an awesome gym! Sitan Gym has become a beloved spot for our whole family. The scheduling is incredibly convenient, with kids’ classes running at the same time as adult sessions, so we can train together without juggling daycare. The facility is spotless and well maintained, and the atmosphere is welcoming from the moment you walk in. Every instructor is patient with beginners, deeply knowledgeable, and clearly passionate about their craft. They meet you where you are, push you safely, and celebrate your progress. I’ve never worked so hard, and I never expected to fall in love with Muay Thai—but I’m absolutely hooked. If you’ve been on the fence, stop waiting and head to Sitan Gym. You won’t regret it.

Really enjoyed this spot for both its food and quirky artwork and memorabilia. The banana and pumpkin breads were standout—moist, flavorful, and elevated by the butter. The omelette was solid, while the chicken-fried steak was just okay. Service was friendly and impressively fast. Would return.

I live nearby and decided to try this place—big mistake. This was the worst sushi I've had in ages. The rice was very dry, and the fish tasted like grade D. They seem to hide subpar cuts in their rolls. I’m kicking myself for going.

Weekend Stay in Vegas – Solid Value for $29

I stayed here last weekend and was surprised. After reading harsh reviews, I booked anyway because vegas.com had a $29 nightly deal, and it delivered value. The hotel isn’t fancy, but our room was clean on arrival and felt maintained. Parking was easy during the day; at night it can take a few minutes to find a spot, but you’ll get one. Check-in and check-out were straightforward and quick, with friendly staff. If you’re looking for budget lodging near the action and don’t need luxe amenities, this place works. I’d definitely return if they offer another great deal.

Cafe Diem’s menu reads like someone curated all my favorites from every kind of restaurant. Breakfast classics sit beside diner comfort, pub bites, and global staples like pad thai, bulgogi, loco moco, stir fry, bananas foster, crab cakes, and more. It’s the kind of variety that makes you excited to order.

Unfortunately, the cooking didn’t match the promise. The french toast arrived soggy, with no caramelized, crusty edges. The sausage gravy skewed oddly sweet, and the regular iced tea had an off flavor that was hard to enjoy. The shoestring sweet potatoes were shaved so thin that frying turned them into crispy, oily toothpicks rather than satisfying fries.

Service, though, was warm and welcoming; the owner and waiters were genuinely friendly and attentive. With such an ambitious, crowd-pleasing menu, a few tweaks in the kitchen could transform this spot into a must-visit. I’m rooting for improvements and hoping to make Cafe Diem a regular stop on future trips to Las Vegas.

I was referred to Gianni and ended up working with Jake, and both were fantastic. I’m not into tattoos and needed a small cover-up, so I was out of my comfort zone, but they made me feel at ease. Jake’s design exceeded my expectations. Professional, friendly, and talented—absolutely love this place. Truly recommend.

Wow. What a treat.

I haven’t even tasted the food yet; this review is strictly about delivery. I ordered through Grubhub around 11:30 p.m.—late, yes, but still three hours before the posted closing time. The order arrived about twenty minutes earlier than the app’s estimate. Unfortunately, everything else about the experience erased that goodwill.

The driver was curt on the phone upon arrival, and when he reached my door he literally shoved the bag into my hands. Part of the order slipped, hit the floor, and he simply said “ok” and walked away. No apology, no checking the spill, nothing. I had already tipped more than 20 percent on my card because I value service, especially at night, and I expected basic courtesy and care.

I’ll admit I was having a terrible evening—I had to say goodbye to my cat—and I was just hoping for a simple, fuss-free pizza delivery. Even without my emotions running high, this behavior felt rude and unprofessional. Food might be great, but service matters. After this, I won’t be ordering here again. Management should train drivers on respect and handling.

For the price, Spice Market Buffet is hard to beat. During two recent stays at Planet Hollywood, I was pleasantly surprised by the quality and selection. Without breaking the bank at high-end buffets like Bellagio, Spice Market delivers real bang-for-your-buck value. Standout dishes included chilled crab legs, Mediterranean kabobs, pork loin, and a decadent French silk pie. Affordable, tasty, and satisfying—I'd happily return.

As a longtime admirer of Mon Ami Gabi, I’ve come to expect polished service and confidently executed bistro fare. That’s why my latest visit was such a letdown. From the outset, our server’s standoffish demeanor set an awkward tone - aloof where hospitality should feel warm. Unfortunately, the evening’s low point was the kitchen’s handling of a special: bacon-wrapped sea bass. Halfway through, I discovered the center was noticeably undercooked - not a translucent edge, but a substantial raw portion. After a quick check from my dining companions, I flagged our waiter, who did return the plate to have the fish finished. While the correction was appreciated, the damage was done; it’s hard to relax into a meal once trust in basic execution wavers.

Mon Ami Gabi has, in my experience, delivered far better. That history makes this stumble more disappointing than infuriating. A refresher on service fundamentals - attentiveness, warmth, proactive problem-solving - along with tighter quality controls on specials would go a long way. Proper temp checks on thick cuts of fish and a more engaged recovery (a sincere apology, perhaps a comp or alternative dish) could have salvaged the evening. I hope this was an outlier. For now, my return is on hold, but not off the table entirely.

Once our go-to Thai spot, we ate here twice a month, but the past year has brought a slide in quality. It’s not just the entrees; even the once crazy-good spring roll dipping sauce has lost its punch. My heart is still with this place, yet I now stop by only occasionally. With new competition in S Chl, I sincerely hope they reclaim their former standards: fresh, balanced flavors and consistent execution, because when they’re on, this restaurant can be fantastic.

I have never been to Red Lobster up until this point in my life. I am 27. I never want to go back to Red Lobster ever again.

Whisked away to Red Lobster for my brother’s birthday dinner, I went in with an open mind and left wishing we had chosen literally anywhere else. From the first bite, the kitchen’s heavy hand with salt dominated the experience. It felt like the food was engineered to suit an aggressively iodized palate, and subtlety never stood a chance.

I ordered a shrimp duo featuring shrimp scampi and seafood-stuffed shrimp. Both missed the mark. The scampi arrived swimming in butter, more greasy than garlicky, and the stuffed shrimp lacked any memorable texture or flavor beyond salt and oil. My side salad came drowned in ranch—my mistake for not asking for it on the side—but the result was a limp, over-dressed afterthought. Even the famed Cheddar Bay Biscuits, a hallmark of the brand, were merely okay and oddly dry.

Others at our table opted for lobster tails. I tasted a few bites: decent, but far from exceptional. To be fair, I’ve rarely had life-changing lobster, but I’m confident Red Lobster isn’t where I’ll find it.

The bright spot was an appetizer plate from the build-your-own selection—clam strips and mozzarella sticks. Hard to mess up, and mostly fine. The clam strips satisfied that fried, briny craving; the mozzarella sticks could have used a bit more heat to achieve that ideal stretch.

Service, to its credit, was a highlight. Our waitress was friendly, efficient, quick with refills, and kept things moving. Yet when we mentioned it was my brother’s birthday, nothing happened—no small gesture, no complimentary dessert, just silence. In a chain known for standardized hospitality, that stung.

Bottom line: if I’m paying for seafood, I expect freshness, balance, and care. Here, everything felt blunt, salted into submission, and coated in butter. Red Lobster might suit those craving predictability, but for me, it’s a one-and-done. The atmosphere felt generic, the kind of nautical kitsch that aims for cozy but lands on dated, and the value proposition just didn’t align with the quality on the plate today.

I found this place on Yelp and decided to try it out

From the moment you walk in, the setup is simple and welcoming: cash register up front, a bright yellow menu to the right, around twenty seats across six tables, and a modest salad bar reminiscent of Roberto’s. The menu mirrors Roberto’s in many ways but adds its own twists, including a full breakfast lineup for early birds. I ordered the chimichanga—a deep-fried burrito—and it hit the spot. Crisp exterior, flavorful filling, and, refreshingly, none of that watery, greasy runoff that dampens plates elsewhere. Cutting it open revealed a clean, well-crafted bite every time. Service was straightforward, prices felt fair, and the space, while compact, works well for a casual meal. I’m already eyeing the churros and a couple of other items for my next visit. This is a solid neighborhood find I’d happily return to.

This casino sits just off the Strip and offers a quieter gaming floor with an old-school vibe. For Pai Gow fans, there’s one $5 table—a rare find and a draw if you want to stretch your bankroll while sipping a cold Corona and playing a few relaxed hands. The drawback is capacity: when that lone $5 table fills up, options are limited to waiting or switching games. Another miss for me is the lack of Pai Gow insurance, a side option I like to play when my hands run cold.

The property itself feels small and dated. It’s serviceable, but the décor leans old-fashioned, which isn’t my preference. I’ve visited several times and, aside from the usual wallet-lightening casinos are built for, the experiences were pleasant, if unremarkable. I haven’t stayed in the hotel, so I can’t speak to the rooms.

Overall, this is an acceptable spot for a low-stakes Pai Gow session, but not a destination I’d prioritize over more modern casinos with more tables.

The Cheesy Bread Was Awesome

Cheesy bread stole the show—gooey and perfect. Unfortunately, the pizza was a mess: cheese and sauce sliding everywhere, nowhere near Lou Malnati’s attention to detail. Friends praised the beer, and my root beer was solid. With execution this loose, I’m docking points despite highlights.

We had a BALL on this trip!

From start to finish, this Boulder City zipline experience was unforgettable. The weather was perfect, and the excitement amped up when a Telemundo crew arrived to film an “extreme adventure” segment—so who knows, we might even catch ourselves on TV. What really set the day apart, though, were the guides. They were knowledgeable, helpful, and genuinely UBER fun, the kind of team that clearly loves what they do. There were no “let’s just get this done” vibes—only enthusiasm, safety, and great energy. They offered bottled water regularly and never rushed anyone, patiently waiting for those who needed a moment on the hike between platforms.

Their dedication shone in one standout moment: a guest ignored instructions to secure personal items, and her hat took off on the very first line. Without hesitation, one guide climbed down steep, rocky terrain into the valley to retrieve it, while another later secured the hat properly to her pack. That level of care and effort is rare and speaks volumes about their commitment to guests.

As for the ziplines themselves—awesome. We all wished they were longer and had a “reverse” button so we could do it over instantly, but alas, gravity only goes one way. Even so, each run delivered pure adrenaline and sweeping canyon views, with smooth operations, clear instructions, and gear that inspired confidence. Hitting speeds approaching 65 mph while zipping and weaving through desert canyons is a rush you won’t forget.

If you’re visiting Vegas, living there, driving through, or even just daydreaming about it, do yourself a favor: book BC Flightlines online, head to Boulder City, sign in, suit up, and go. Bring a great crowd, a significant other, or fly solo—this adventure works for everyone. You will not regret it. It’s laughter, scenery, speed, and stellar service rolled into one.

What are you still waiting for? Get moving!

Seated promptly but never approached by a server, even after we asked staff to send someone—frustrating and disappointing. However, the manager later apologized and offered to comp some food, clearly monitoring Yelp and taking feedback seriously. Appreciated the accountability. Because of that, we’re willing to return and give them another chance to earn our business.

Stopped in for curry goat with rice and peas and cabbage—tender, flavorful, and satisfying. I sampled my friend's brown stewed red snapper, which was equally delicious. They were out of plantains, but Kola Champagne, a sweet cream-soda-like drink, hit the spot. Service was fair; despite the bustle, staff managed the crowd well. Overall, a tasty, comforting Caribbean meal worth revisiting soon.

Visiting for my husband's Christmas party, we had a delightful first-time experience. The calamari was the best I've ever had, crispy and tender. We both ordered steaks; mine was slightly undercooked and needed a touch more salt, but still tasty. I sampled three martinis, with Southern Peach as the standout. The S'mores dessert was good, capping the festive evening.

The ice cream is good.

This spot serves tasty ice cream. I haven’t tried the cupcakes at this location yet, but I loved them in LA and plan to sample them soon. I wish they served warm cookies—I hate them cold. Heard they offer a gluten-free cupcake, which is a big plus.

When my parents visited for the first time since our move from Chicago, fatigue turned dinner plans into a pizza night. My dad, late 60s, lifelong Chicagoan—South Side roots, nearly five decades on the North Side—knows his pizza. Chicago isn’t only deep dish; many of us swear by a proper, crispy, square-cut thin crust.

Having tried the regular crust before, we ordered the medium crust with sausage and onion, easy on the cheese—an owner-favorite combo. The verdict: fantastic. My dad took one bite, looked up, and said, “Kid, you found yourself a great pizza joint out here.” That’s high praise from someone raised among neighborhood institutions where quality is the baseline.

This place nails Chicago-style thin crust: balanced toppings, a restrained hand with cheese, well-seasoned sausage, and that essential crackly base that holds its own without flopping. The square cut isn’t a gimmick; it’s a way of eating. We start with the outer crust squares, working inward, saving the center pieces—those tender, crustless bites—for the next day. And yes, they’re best cold. We don’t reheat pizza.

If you’re from Chicagoland and longing for the family-style spots you grew up with, or simply curious about the Chicago thin tradition, this is your spot. Skip the floppy pie-cut slices and embrace a style built for sharing, for conversation, for that satisfying crunch.

Bravo to the team. The only thing my dad missed were the crinkle-cut fries and a side of garlic bread from his hometown haunts. No big deal—leaves more room for pizza. Consider us impressed, and consider this a new go-to when the craving hits. We’ll be back, and bringing fellow Chicago expats soon.

Awful!
My dish was literally dripping with oil—like a bowl of hot olive oil with a few pasta pieces. Absolutely gross. The service was terrible, staff unfriendly, and the whole experience disappointing. I expected much better. Won’t be back and do not recommend.

Lori made me feel completely at ease as I took the plunge from super-long hair to a chic short cut. As a short-hair newbie who struggled to describe what I wanted, she asked smart, targeted questions, translated my vague ideas, and delivered an exciting, flattering look that felt instantly “me.” I came in first thing in the morning and the place was quiet, but even on busy days—when the waiting area can feel cramped—they move efficiently and get you finished quickly. Best of all, I’ve never needed an appointment. Friendly, intuitive service and reliable pace make this my go-to spot for stress-free cuts.

I ordered the sampler plate to share with coworkers and was really let down. For a brand-new spot, this felt careless. The buffalo tenders arrived soggy and limp, while the mozzarella bites and fried pickles were soft instead of crisp—overall pretty unappetizing. It should be easy to nail at least one item on a basic sampler, but nothing impressed. I work next door and wanted to become a regular, yet this first experience was disappointing. Hoping they tighten up execution soon.

I’ve visited several Black Angus locations, and this one stands out. The atmosphere works equally well for lunch and dinner—comfortable, lively, and welcoming. Service is consistently friendly and generally efficient, and I’m impressed that the manager regularly circulates, checks on guests, and even clears plates—a rare, hands-on touch that sets the tone for the team. Pricing is my only hesitation: a $29 steak feels steep, and tacking on an extra charge for a simple side like asparagus doesn’t sit quite right. Still, the quality keeps me coming back. The steaks are cooked perfectly, well-seasoned, and reliably delicious. Despite the price, I’ll definitely return with friends and family alike.

After a major storm destroyed my roof, garage door, HVAC, and trim, I faced the largest insurance claim of my life. Jared and his crew took charge, managed every detail, and delivered upgrades I truly loved. Four years later, while selling the house, I misplaced the contract buyers needed to verify the materials’ strong warranty. Jared stepped in again, tracked down the documentation, and saved the deal. Exceptional service, real professionalism, and genuine respect—this is the team you want on your side today.

Happy hour is awesome with great prices and generous pours. The hummus and quinoa balls are must-tries. Cozy, inviting ambiance, and staff are wonderfully friendly and polite. We especially love Haley—she’s beautiful, courteous, and always remembers our drinks. Highly recommend this spot.

Don't get alterations done once you purchase the suit!

We ordered 12 suits for our bridal party, and the in-house alterations turned a simple hem into a fiasco. My fiancé’s pants came back with nearly six inches of fabric folded up inside the leg, making them bulky, heavy, and visibly misshapen. Staff admitted the job was botched and “fixed” it while we waited, but the result was worse: obvious holes in the fabric you could spot from across the room. We had to replace the pants entirely and took the new pair to a competent tailor elsewhere.

To top it off, the suit wasn’t pressed when we picked it up; it looked like it had been lying on the floor. Between poor workmanship, dismissive attitude, and lack of quality control, this experience was unacceptable. Inspect thoroughly, skip their alterations, and be wary of the “big sale” pitch. Our trust is gone.
